title: How Much Does Corpus Choice Change Dependency-Distance Estimates?
summary: Dependency-distance estimates derived from a single corpus are routinely treated as properties of a language, yet this assumption has not been tested across independently compiled corpora. We compared mean dependency-distance estimates across 38 same-language treebank pairs from Universal Dependencies v2.18, using concordance correlation, Bland-Altman analysis, and a twelve-specification multiverse design. Cross-treebank agreement was moderate at best: substituting one treebank for another reversed nearly 40 percent of pairwise language orderings, and treebank choice accounted for roughly 29 percent of between-group variance. This disagreement substantially exceeded within-treebank sampling error and persisted across all twelve preprocessing specifications. Nevertheless, every treebank confirmed dependency-length minimization (normalized ratio below 1). The data are more consistent with MDD as a corpus-conditioned composite of grammatical, register, and annotation factors than as a stable language-level parameter: the qualitative DLM universal survives corpus substitution, but the ordinal cross-linguistic ranking does not.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether mean dependency distance (MDD) is really a stable property of a language or mostly an artifact of particular treebanks, and finds that while all treebanks support dependency-length minimization, cross-linguistic rankings of languages by MDD are highly unstable across corpora.
AI.motivation: Researchers often treat mean dependency distance estimates taken from one treebank as language-level parameters and use them to compare languages. However, it has not been systematically tested whether MDD values are robust across independently compiled treebanks of the same language. If they are not, many cross-linguistic claims based on such comparisons may be unreliable.
AI.method: Using Universal Dependencies v2.18, the authors identified 38 pairs of treebanks that represent the same language. For each pair, they computed mean dependency distance under twelve different preprocessing and analysis specifications (a multiverse analysis). They then assessed agreement between treebanks by (i) concordance correlation, (ii) Bland–Altman analysis of differences vs. means, and (iii) examining how often substituting one treebank for another would change pairwise language orderings and how much variance in MDD is attributable to treebank choice.
AI.result: Cross-treebank agreement on MDD for the same language was only moderate. Switching from one treebank to another reversed nearly 40% of pairwise language orderings and treebank identity explained about 29% of the between-group variance in MDD. These discrepancies were larger than expected from sampling error within a treebank and remained robust across all twelve preprocessing choices. Nonetheless, every treebank exhibited dependency-length minimization, with normalized dependency distances below 1.
AI.conclusion: Mean dependency distance behaves less like a stable language-internal parameter and more like a corpus-conditioned measure shaped jointly by grammar, register, and annotation practices. While the qualitative universal of dependency-length minimization is robust to corpus choice, the quantitative cross-linguistic ranking of languages by MDD is not. Consequently, researchers should be cautious about treating single-treebank MDD estimates as language-level properties and about drawing fine-grained typological conclusions from them.

title: Memory as transformation: LETHE, a self-referential gan-inspired architecture
comment: Accepted at XXV CIM - Colloquio di Informatica Musicale, L'Aquila, 2026
summary: LETHE (Latent-parameter Evolution with Temporal Hierarchical quasi-Equilibrium) is a self-referential sonic-oblivion system implemented in SuperCollider. It adopts the formal vocabulary of Generative Adversarial Networks in a closed configuration without external datasets or supervision after initialization. Audio is processed by a 3 x 3 mixing matrix built around two delay lines; its nine coefficients and two delay times evolve through the interaction of a five-feature linear discriminator and a random-perturbation optimizer analogous to single-sample REINFORCE. The discriminator compares current energy behavior with an archive of the initial state and guides parameter updates. Circular, fixed, and live sources can be mixed independently. Across fixed and circular sessions with an ablation control, the active generator is necessary for parametric evolution ($Δc_{22}=0.000$ in all 15 ablation sessions). Situated in the tradition of self-referential electroacoustic music, LETHE delegates the sonic outcome to an adaptive closed loop whose parametric space is defined by the composer.

AI.tldr: LETHE is a self-evolving audio system that uses a GAN-inspired feedback loop on its own initial sound state, without external data, to adapt delay-matrix parameters and generate self-referential electroacoustic music.
AI.motivation: To create an autonomous, self-referential electroacoustic music system that can evolve its sonic behavior over time without relying on external datasets or continuous human supervision, while still allowing the composer to define the boundaries of the parametric space.
AI.method: Implement a closed-loop audio system in SuperCollider where sound is processed by a 3×3 mixing matrix around two delay lines. The system has nine mix coefficients and two delay times that are adapted via an interaction between: (1) a five-feature linear discriminator that measures current energy behavior against an archive of the initial state, and (2) a random-perturbation optimizer akin to single-sample REINFORCE. The formal structure borrows terminology from Generative Adversarial Networks but operates without external data, using only the system’s own initial state as reference. The system supports circular (feedback), fixed (pre-recorded), and live sources that can be mixed independently. An ablation study is carried out by disabling the generator to test its necessity for parameter evolution.
AI.result: Experimental sessions with both fixed and circular configurations, including ablation controls, show that when the active generator is disabled, the system’s parameters do not evolve (reported as Δc_{22}=0.000 in all 15 ablation sessions). This supports the claim that the generator component is essential for the observed parametric evolution in the full system.
AI.conclusion: LETHE successfully realizes a self-referential, adaptive, GAN-inspired audio system in which sonic output is governed by an internal feedback loop instead of external training data. The composer defines the parametric space, but the detailed sonic behavior is delegated to the evolving dynamics of the closed loop. The study’s ablation results validate the functional role of the active generator in driving parameter evolution, situating LETHE within the lineage of self-referential electroacoustic music systems.

title: Evidence Integration in Large Language Models
summary: Despite increasing reliance on LLMs that reason with external evidence supplied by tools, retrieval-augmented generation, other agents, and users, how LLMs integrate such evidence into decisions they have already begun to form remains largely unclear. We present a distributional theory in which evidence shifts the receiver's distribution of initial answers, driven by a receiver prior weight and a candidate evidence tilt, leading to three predictions. First, candidates more probable to the receiver are more persuasive. Second, receivers more readily integrate characteristic errors of their own than foreign errors from different sources. Third, identical evidence can improve weaker models and harm stronger ones. We confirm these over ten million trials, twelve LLMs from four families, and eight domains, four of them scientific discovery tasks in the physical and life sciences: quantum mechanics, physics, genetics, and molecular biology. The law also yields a receiver-relative reliability frontier: receiver-congruent errors depress performance more steeply than random errors of the same rate. LLMs also integrate candidates even after internally verifying their invalidity (93-100% with propositional constraints; up to 99.4% on held-out physical and life-sciences reasoning), demonstrating evidence integration is a receiver-specific control policy over existing distributions, determined by receiver properties rather than scalar trust in the evidence source. Causal interventions show candidate integration is implemented late in the network, as a structured sequence of steps admitting external candidate answers, promoting them, and transporting them into the answer state. Representations of verification are decodable but have little causal impact on answers. A J-lens decomposition shows the state underlying verbalized verification is fully dissociable from that underlying candidate integration.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a distributional theory for how LLMs integrate external evidence into partially formed answers, and empirically validates it across many models and tasks.
AI.motivation: Although LLMs are increasingly used with tools and external evidence (retrievers, other agents, user hints), we lack a clear understanding of how these models actually incorporate such incoming evidence into decisions that are already in progress. This gap makes it hard to predict when external evidence will help or hurt model performance and why models sometimes follow wrong suggestions even after checking them.
AI.method: The authors develop a formal distributional model where external evidence shifts the model’s internal distribution over candidate answers according to two key quantities: a receiver prior weight (how strongly the model relies on its own initial beliefs) and an evidence tilt (how much the external candidate nudges that belief distribution). From this, they derive theoretical predictions about persuasion and error integration. They then test these predictions in over ten million trials using twelve LLMs from four model families on eight domains, including four scientific reasoning benchmarks in quantum mechanics, physics, genetics, and molecular biology. They perform causal interventions in the activation space to locate when and how candidate evidence is integrated, decode internal representations of verification, and apply a J-lens decomposition to separate components of the network state related to verification versus candidate integration.
AI.result: The experiments support three main predictions: (1) external candidates that are already more probable under the model’s internal beliefs are more persuasive; (2) models more easily absorb their own characteristic error patterns than unfamiliar error patterns from other sources; and (3) the same piece of evidence can help weaker models while harming stronger ones. The authors also identify a receiver-relative reliability frontier, showing that errors aligned with the model’s prior (“receiver-congruent errors”) hurt performance more than random errors at the same rate. Surprisingly, models often still integrate candidate answers after internally verifying that they are invalid (93–100% of such cases on propositional tasks and up to 99.4% on physical and life-science reasoning tasks). Causal analyses reveal that candidate integration happens late in the network as a structured sequence: admitting external candidates, amplifying them, and then moving them into the final answer state. Verification representations are decodable but exert little causal influence on the actual output. J-lens decomposition shows that the state used for verbalized verification is dissociable from the state driving candidate integration.
AI.conclusion: Evidence integration in LLMs behaves like a receiver-specific control policy over an internal answer distribution rather than a simple scalar trust in the evidence source. Persuasion depends strongly on the model’s own priors and characteristic error modes, which explains why identical evidence can have opposite effects on weak versus strong models and why models often follow suggestions they have internally checked as wrong. Mechanistically, external candidate integration is implemented late in the forward pass and largely insulated from the internal verification circuitry, as confirmed by causal and representational analyses. This framework clarifies when and how external tools and agents will successfully steer LLMs and highlights the risk posed by receiver-congruent errors that align with the model’s existing beliefs.

title: MedProb: Probing Internal Representations of Vision-Language Models for Medical Question Answering
summary: Medical visual question answering (Med-VQA) is often assumed to require medical fine-tuning, large models, or complex multi-agent pipelines. We revisit this assumption with \textbf{MedProb}, a lightweight probing framework that predicts multiple-choice Med-VQA answers from frozen VLM representations without free-text generation. Across PATH-VQA, SLAKE, and VQA-RAD, MedProb recovers substantially more answer-relevant signal than prompting and performs stronger than medical VLMs and agentic systems. Probing also reduces the apparent gap between small and large models compared to prompting, suggesting that smaller VLMs contain more recoverable Med-VQA signal than generation-based evaluation reveals. Across 14 matched general-purpose and medical VLM pairs, medical adaptation does not consistently improve this linear decodability. Finally, free-text generation exhibits an answer-position bias of up to 10 percentage points, whereas MedProb also has positional bias, however, it is impacted differently than prompting. Our main results target the multiple-choice/multiclass Med-VQA setting; we additionally show the probe can be extended to open-ended generation via a rejection-sampling scoring procedure.

AI.tldr: MedProb is a lightweight probing framework that predicts multiple-choice medical VQA answers from frozen VLM features, outperforming prompting, medical VLMs, and multi-agent systems while revealing that smaller and non-medically-adapted models contain more usable Med-VQA information than generation-based methods suggest.
AI.motivation: Existing Med-VQA approaches often assume that strong performance requires medically fine-tuned models, large vision–language models, or complex multi-agent pipelines, and they typically rely on free-text generation. The authors question whether these components are truly necessary and whether current evaluation via prompting underestimates the information already present in frozen VLM representations, especially for smaller or non-medically-adapted models.
AI.method: They introduce MedProb, a lightweight probing framework that trains a simple probe (e.g., linear or similarly low-capacity classifier) on top of frozen representations from vision–language models to directly predict multiple-choice answers without generating free text. They systematically compare MedProb to prompting-based approaches, medical VLMs, and agentic systems on multiple Med-VQA benchmarks (PATH-VQA, SLAKE, VQA-RAD). They also evaluate 14 pairs of general-purpose vs. medically adapted VLMs to assess how medical adaptation influences linear decodability, analyze answer-position biases in free-text generation vs. probing, and extend the probe to open-ended generation via a rejection-sampling scoring procedure.
AI.result: MedProb extracts substantially more answer-relevant signal from frozen VLMs than standard prompting, achieving better performance than specialized medical VLMs and multi-agent systems on PATH-VQA, SLAKE, and VQA-RAD. It reduces the performance gap typically observed between small and large models under prompting, indicating that smaller VLMs actually encode more Med-VQA-relevant information than generation-based evaluation reveals. Across 14 general-purpose/medical VLM pairs, medical fine-tuning does not consistently increase the linear decodability of correct answers. Free-text generation shows strong answer-position bias (up to 10 percentage points), while MedProb also exhibits positional bias but in a different pattern. The framework can also be adapted to open-ended Med-VQA via a rejection-sampling-based scoring extension.
AI.conclusion: Linear probing on frozen VLM representations using MedProb is a strong and often superior approach for multiple-choice Med-VQA compared to prompting, medical VLMs, and agentic pipelines. The findings challenge the assumption that high Med-VQA performance demands large, medically fine-tuned, or complex models, revealing that smaller and general-purpose models already encode substantial recoverable medical question-answering signal. Medical adaptation does not reliably improve linear decodability, and free-text generation introduces notable answer-position biases that MedProb is affected by differently. Probing thus offers a simpler, more robust, and more informative way to evaluate and leverage VLMs for Med-VQA, with extensions possible to open-ended tasks.

title: EXAONE Forecast for Finance
summary: This technical report presents EXAONE Forecast for Finance (EXAONE Finance), a financial time series (TS) foundation model (TSFM) tailored to financial forecasting. Recent TSFMs achieve strong zero-shot performance through large-scale pretraining. However, they are primarily developed for general-domain TS and largely rely on self-attention backbones whose computational cost grows quadratically with sequence length and variate count. Moreover, they assume fully observed inputs and are pretrained on corpora that fail to capture the unique dynamics of financial markets. These limitations hinder their applicability to finance, where long, many-channel, intermittently observed panels are common. To address these challenges, EXAONE Finance adopts an attention-free architecture, replacing self-attention with two simple yet effective linear-time operators: 1) a causal 1D convolution for temporal mixing and 2) a group-aware pooling multi-layer perceptron (MLP) for variate mixing. Furthermore, a masked context augmentation exposes the model to contiguous missing spans during training, improving robustness to the missingness pervasive in financial markets. EXAONE Finance is pretrained on a large-scale financial corpus covering not only equities but also foreign exchange, commodities, crypto-assets, fixed income, and macroeconomic indicators. On FinVerse, a financial forecasting benchmark covering diverse asset classes, EXAONE Finance attains state-of-the-art performance, ranking first across all three evaluation tiers---point-forecast accuracy, cross-sectional asset ranking, and portfolio profitability.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces EXAONE Finance, a specialized financial time series foundation model that replaces self-attention with linear-time temporal and variate mixing, is trained with masked context augmentation on a broad multi-asset financial corpus, and achieves state-of-the-art results on the FinVerse benchmark in accuracy, ranking, and portfolio profitability.
AI.motivation: General time series foundation models, though strong in zero-shot settings, are inefficient for long and high-dimensional financial series due to quadratic-cost self-attention, assume fully observed data, and are pretrained on non-financial or generic time series that miss the specific dynamics of financial markets. This creates a gap between existing TSFMs and the practical requirements of financial forecasting, where sequences are long, multivariate, and often contain substantial missing data across many asset classes. The authors aim to close this gap by designing a TSFM that is computationally scalable, robust to missingness, and trained specifically on rich financial data.
AI.method: The authors propose EXAONE Finance, built on an attention-free architecture using two linear-time operators instead of self-attention: (1) a causal 1D convolution for temporal mixing to capture dependencies over time, and (2) a group-aware pooling MLP for variate mixing to model interactions across multiple time series (e.g., different assets or indicators). To handle intermittent observations common in finance, they introduce a masked context augmentation scheme that deliberately creates contiguous missing spans during pretraining, making the model robust to real-world missingness patterns. The model is pretrained as a foundation model on a large, diverse financial corpus including equities, FX, commodities, crypto, fixed income, and macroeconomic indicators, enabling broad coverage of financial dynamics.
AI.result: On FinVerse, a comprehensive financial forecasting benchmark spanning multiple asset classes, EXAONE Finance achieves state-of-the-art performance. It ranks first across three distinct evaluation tiers: (1) point-forecast accuracy (predictive precision on future values), (2) cross-sectional asset ranking (ordering assets by expected performance), and (3) portfolio profitability (realized returns when constructing portfolios from its forecasts). These results demonstrate both predictive strength and practical economic value, surpassing prior TSFMs and other baselines.
AI.conclusion: EXAONE Finance shows that an attention-free, linear-time architecture tailored for financial time series, combined with masked context augmentation and pretraining on a broad multi-asset financial corpus, can overcome key limitations of existing general-domain TSFMs. The model scales better to long, high-dimensional, and intermittently observed financial data and delivers superior performance on a rigorous financial forecasting benchmark. This validates the value of domain-specialized TS foundation models and suggests that efficient non-attention architectures can be competitive or superior to attention-based models in finance-oriented time series tasks.

title: Adapting from Downturns: Prediction of Long-Term Conversational-Skill Development in Mental-Health Crisis Counselors
comment: To be presented at EMNLP 2026. Code available at convokit.cornell.edu
summary:
How do people learn to become better conversationalists? This question is especially important in the context of mental-health counseling, where conversational skills are essential, yet volunteer counselors often have limited access to supervision and structured feedback. Understanding how counselors develop their ability to steer conversations toward positive outcomes -- and identifying early which counselors are (not) on track to improve -- can help prioritize support for the counselors who need it most.
  In this work, we introduce the task of predicting, early in a conversationalist's career, whether they will eventually improve at steering conversations toward positive outcomes, and demonstrate the feasibility of this task in the case of volunteer mental-health crisis counselors. Our central insight is that people may struggle with particular kinds of moments in a conversation, and that what is especially revealing of their likelihood of future improvement is how they learn to handle those moments over time. We operationalize this insight by designing a method that identifies the types of moments a counselor initially struggles with, captures how they adapt their response when they re-encounter similar moments in subsequent conversations, and learns which early adaptations predict improvement months or even years later. While this future-prediction task is challenging, our counselor-adaptation approach yields better results than baselines that learn directly from the conversation transcript.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a way to predict, early in a counselor’s career, whether they will later improve at steering conversations toward positive outcomes, by modeling how they adapt to specific challenging conversational moments over time.
AI.motivation: Volunteer mental-health crisis counselors play a crucial role, but many have limited access to supervision and structured feedback. Not all counselors improve at the same rate, and support resources are scarce. Being able to understand and forecast which counselors are likely (or unlikely) to improve their conversational effectiveness would allow programs to target training, mentoring, and oversight to those who need it most. The authors want to move beyond static evaluation of conversations and instead understand the learning and adaptation process counselors go through as they encounter difficult conversational situations repeatedly.
AI.method: The authors formulate a prediction task: given only data from the early phase of a counselor’s activity, predict whether the counselor will eventually become better at steering conversations toward positive outcomes. They propose a counselor-adaptation model centered on “challenging moments” within conversations. First, they identify types of moments in conversations that counselors initially struggle with. Then, they track how each counselor responds to similar types of moments when they reappear in later conversations, modeling changes in their responses as evidence of learning or adaptation. This temporal pattern of adaptation is encoded as features and fed into a predictive model that links early adaptation behaviors to long-term improvement. Performance is compared to baseline models that rely mainly on static features from raw conversation transcripts.
AI.result: The proposed counselor-adaptation approach can predict, better than baseline transcript-based models, which counselors will later improve at leading conversations to positive outcomes. Even though forecasting long-term improvement is inherently difficult, incorporating information about how counselors change their responses to recurring challenging moments yields higher predictive accuracy and more informative signals about future growth.
AI.conclusion: Modeling how counselors adapt to specific challenging conversational moments over time provides a useful signal for predicting long-term improvement in their conversational effectiveness. This adaptation-based approach outperforms baselines that treat conversations as static text, suggesting that learning dynamics, not just conversational content, matter for forecasting counselor development. Such models could be used in practice to identify early which volunteer counselors need extra support, enabling more efficient allocation of supervision and training resources in mental-health counseling services.

title: From Matching Models to Recruiting Agents: A Systematized Narrative Review of AI Recruitment Systems, Evaluation, and Governance
comment: 53 pages, 4 figures, 10 tables; companion literature-coding and search-log CSVs included in the source package
summary: Artificial intelligence in recruitment has shifted the object being automated from profile pairs and ranked lists to multi-stage workflows that retrieve evidence, compare candidates, and support or execute actions. This systematized narrative review traces that development from bilateral retrieval and behavioral ranking through neural person--job matching, large language model (LLM) components, and tool-using recruiting agents. Using a purposive search and coding protocol updated through 23 July 2026, plus targeted updates through 2 September 2026, we organize 40 representative works with supporting industrial and legal sources. This synthesis is not a prevalence estimate. We analyze three coupled transitions: from similarity to reciprocal suitability, from a model to a compound workflow, and from offline prediction to evidence- and productivity-aligned evaluation. Across document understanding, retrieval, ranking, assessment, interviewing, sourcing, and human handoff, we distinguish field-, pair-, list-, case-, trajectory-, and outcome-level evidence. Persistent gaps arise because behavioral labels confound exposure, preference, and qualification; private and synthetic data limit external validity; final-output scores conceal pipeline failures; and, within the coded set, privacy is not directly evaluated and no row jointly evaluates utility, fairness, privacy, and security. These observations describe the coded set rather than the field as a whole. We therefore introduce a staged mapping from evaluation evidence to the strongest defensible claim, together with an agenda for reciprocal, evidence-grounded, temporally controlled, selective, and auditable systems. Progress should be judged by whether workflows retrieve the right evidence, preserve uncertainty, support contestable decisions, and improve outcomes under explicit cost and risk constraints.

AI.tldr: The paper is a systematized narrative review of AI in recruitment, showing how systems have evolved from simple similarity-based matching toward complex, multi-stage, evidence-driven workflows, and proposing an evaluation framework focused on evidence quality, uncertainty, contestability, and real-world outcomes under cost and risk constraints.
AI.motivation: AI hiring tools have moved beyond simple profile matching and ranked candidate lists to complex, multi-step workflows that search for evidence, compare candidates, and even automate actions. Despite rapid adoption and regulatory attention, there is no clear, structured overview of how these systems are changing, what kinds of evidence they rely on, and how well they are evaluated for utility, fairness, privacy, and security. The paper is motivated by the need to understand these developments, identify systematic gaps in current research and practice, and provide guidance for making stronger, defensible claims about what recruitment AI can actually do safely and effectively.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematized narrative review using a purposive search and coding protocol, initially covering work up to 23 July 2026 and then updated selectively to 2 September 2026. They curate 40 representative research and industry papers, supplemented with industrial and legal sources, and code them along dimensions such as task type (e.g., retrieval, ranking, assessment, interviewing, sourcing, handoff), type of evidence (field, pair, list, case, trajectory, outcome), and evaluation focus (e.g., utility, fairness, privacy, security). They then analyze transitions in the field: from similarity-based to reciprocal suitability matching, from single models to compound workflows, and from static offline prediction to evidence- and productivity-aligned evaluation.
AI.result: The review finds that AI recruitment has evolved toward multi-stage, tool-using workflows that incorporate components like neural person–job matching and large language models, spanning tasks from document understanding and retrieval to interviewing and human decision support. The authors identify systematic gaps: behavioral labels often mix exposure, preference, and qualification, undermining validity; dependence on private and synthetic datasets weakens external validity; aggregate final scores obscure failures and biases in earlier pipeline stages; and in the coded set, privacy is not directly evaluated and no work jointly evaluates utility, fairness, privacy, and security. They also categorize the evidence used in evaluations into field-, pair-, list-, case-, trajectory-, and outcome-level evidence, highlighting uneven coverage and weak links to real-world outcomes.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that many existing claims about recruitment AI are not well supported by the available evaluation evidence, at least in the coded sample. To address this, the authors propose a staged mapping from the strength and type of evaluation evidence to the strongest defensible claims that can be made about a system. They argue that progress should be measured not by algorithmic accuracy alone but by whether workflows: (1) retrieve the right evidence, (2) preserve and communicate uncertainty, (3) enable contestable and auditable decisions, and (4) actually improve hiring and organizational outcomes under explicit cost and risk constraints. They propose an agenda for designing reciprocal, evidence-grounded, temporally controlled, selective, and auditable recruitment AI systems, and they stress that their findings describe the coded corpus, not the entire field, while still indicating important directions and gaps for future research and regulation.

title: VERGE: Verification-Enhanced Refinement for Grounded Extraction of Early-Onset Colorectal Cancer Symptoms in Clinical Notes
summary: Early-onset colorectal cancer is increasing among younger adults, yet red-flag symptoms in this age group have no evidence-based guidelines for follow-up testing, and structured encounter data do not capture the detail needed to support early detection and inform follow-up, including symptom duration, context, and fam- ily history, an established colorectal-cancer risk factor. This study aimed to develop and evaluate an automated method for extracting six red-flag symptoms and family-history risk status from free-text clinical notes. We developed VERGE, an agentic workflow in which an initial label and evidence are proposed using retrieval-augmented generation, then passed through a bounded verification- refinement cycle that checks textual grounding and clinical validity, corrects and rechecks a claim until resolved or a limit is reached, and escalates unresolved claims for human review. VERGE was evaluated on 4,033 clinician-labeled note-finding pairs against a single-agent baseline, a rule-based clinical language-processing baseline, and an alternative underlying language model. Compared with the single-agent baseline, VERGE reduced false positive find- ings, improving precision from 0.764 to 0.849 and MCC from 0.681 to 0.730, a balanced gain across the precision-recall trade-off, and resolved most flagged errors autonomously, with human review required for only 1.5 percent of claims. These results indicate that a bounded, verification-based workflow can reduce unnecessary positive findings without sacrificing the ability to detect true ones. This approach offers a path toward more reliable and trustworthy clinical language-processing tools to support colorectal cancer risk assessment in younger patients.

AI.tldr: The paper develops VERGE, an automated, verification-based workflow using large language models to reliably extract early-onset colorectal cancer red-flag symptoms and family-history risk from free-text clinical notes, reducing false positives while maintaining sensitivity.
AI.motivation: Early-onset colorectal cancer is rising in younger adults, but there are no evidence-based guidelines for follow-up on red-flag symptoms in this age group. Existing structured encounter data lack key details such as symptom duration, context, and family history, which are crucial for early detection and risk assessment. There is a need for robust clinical language-processing methods that can accurately extract these nuanced signals from free-text notes without generating excessive false positives that would burden clinicians and patients.
AI.method: The authors designed VERGE, an agentic workflow built on retrieval-augmented generation and iterative verification. First, a language model proposes an initial label (presence/absence of each red-flag symptom and family-history risk) and cites text evidence from the clinical note. This claim then enters a bounded verification–refinement loop: the system checks whether the claim is textually grounded in the note and clinically valid, corrects it if needed, and rechecks until either the claim is resolved or a preset iteration limit is reached. Unresolved or uncertain claims are escalated for human review. VERGE’s performance was evaluated on 4,033 clinician-labeled note–finding pairs and compared against a single-agent LLM baseline, a rule-based clinical NLP baseline, and a variant using an alternative language model.
AI.result: Compared with the single-agent LLM baseline, VERGE substantially reduced false positives, increasing precision from 0.764 to 0.849 and improving Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) from 0.681 to 0.730, indicating a better-balanced performance over the precision–recall spectrum. The verification loop resolved the majority of initially flagged errors autonomously, requiring human review for only 1.5% of claims. VERGE maintained the ability to detect true positive findings while limiting over-calling symptoms or risk factors. Results against the rule-based and alternative-LLM baselines further supported that the verification-based workflow, rather than any specific model alone, drives these gains.
AI.conclusion: A bounded, verification-based agentic workflow such as VERGE can make clinical language-processing systems more reliable by lowering unnecessary positive findings without sacrificing detection of true ones. For early-onset colorectal cancer, this enables higher-fidelity extraction of red-flag symptoms and family-history risk from free-text notes, potentially supporting earlier and more accurate risk assessment in younger patients. More broadly, the approach illustrates how structured verification and selective human escalation can improve trustworthiness and clinical applicability of LLM-driven tools in healthcare documentation analysis.

title: Harbor Adapters and Harbor-Index: Infrastructure and a Curated Meta-Dataset for Large-Scale Agentic Evaluation
summary: Evaluating agents on the growing number of agentic benchmarks is challenging because they often require complex environments and agent integrations. We introduce Harbor Adapters, a unified evaluation infrastructure for agentic benchmarks. Our work makes three contributions. First, we develop benchmark adapters that port more than 80 benchmarks to evaluate arbitrary agents, and validate them through rigorous code review and parity experiments. Second, we conduct a large-scale evaluation of 8 models spanning capability tiers across 54 benchmarks; every model is run with Terminus-2 and with one of 3 native harnesses. This enables a broader analysis of agent capabilities and failure modes than was previously possible. Third, we introduce Harbor-Index, a curated set of 82 difficult, diverse, and high-quality tasks spanning 29 benchmarks, refined from the adapted suite through difficulty filtering, AI and human audit, and an audit-and-fix loop. Harbor-Index preserves the challenge and breadth of large-scale agentic evaluations while being affordable to run; no evaluated model-harness configuration exceeds 30% pass rate, and the strongest (GPT-5.5 with Codex) reaches 28.0%. We release the adapters, evaluation results, in-depth analysis, and Harbor-Index as open-source artifacts to support more reliable and comprehensive evaluation of language-model agents.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Harbor Adapters, a unified infrastructure that makes it easy to evaluate diverse language-model agents across many existing agentic benchmarks, and distills a challenging, curated subset called Harbor-Index.
AI.motivation: Agentic benchmarks for language models are rapidly proliferating, but they are hard to use consistently because each typically has its own complex environment, integrations, and evaluation harness. This fragmentation makes it difficult to compare agents, understand their failure modes at scale, or run broad, reproducible evaluations. The authors aim to standardize and simplify evaluation so that arbitrary agents can be tested reliably across a wide set of tasks.
AI.method: 1) They build benchmark adapters that ‘port’ over 80 existing agentic benchmarks into a common infrastructure that can evaluate arbitrary agents, then validate these adapters via code review and parity experiments against the original benchmarks. 2) They run a large-scale empirical study: 8 different models (covering a range of capabilities) are evaluated on 54 benchmarks, each using both a unified harness (Terminus-2) and, where available, the benchmark’s own native harness. 3) From the adapted benchmark suite, they construct Harbor-Index by filtering for difficulty and quality using automatic difficulty measures, AI audits, human audits, and an iterative audit-and-fix loop, resulting in a smaller but still diverse set of tasks.
AI.result: They successfully adapt more than 80 benchmarks to a unified agent evaluation framework, demonstrating parity with original benchmark behavior. Their large-scale study across 8 models and 54 benchmarks exposes detailed patterns of agent capabilities and failure modes. Harbor-Index is created as a curated collection of 82 challenging tasks from 29 benchmarks, chosen for difficulty, diversity, and quality. Empirically, all tested model–harness combinations achieve under 30% pass rate on Harbor-Index, with the best-performing configuration (GPT-5.5 with Codex) scoring 28.0%, indicating that the index remains far from saturated.
AI.conclusion: Harbor Adapters provide a practical, validated way to run unified, large-scale evaluations of language-model agents across many previously fragmented agentic benchmarks. Harbor-Index offers a compact yet challenging and representative subset of tasks that is economical to run while still discriminating between strong agents. By releasing the adapters, benchmark results, analyses, and Harbor-Index as open source, the authors aim to enable more reliable, comprehensive, and comparable evaluation of agentic LLM systems going forward.

title: You Really Didn't Get That? Benchmarking Social Pragmatic Inference for Indirect and Playful Chinese Online Comments
comment: Accepted to the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026), Main Conference
summary: Chinese online comments often convey social meaning through indirect and playful language that is hard to interpret without context. Existing evaluations largely organize items around predefined phenomena or controlled pragmatic categories, leaving open whether models can distinguish plausible readings of what a naturally occurring comment is doing in a particular exchange. We introduce a benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs can recover such situated pragmatic meanings. From more than 200,000 public Chinese social media interaction records, we construct 4,735 human-validated diagnostic items, each pairing a target comment with reconstructed preceding context and plausible misreadings. We evaluate eight LLMs as both question writers and solvers in a cross-writer setting. The task is challenging: the strongest model achieves 81.42% leave-writer-out accuracy. Across all eight models, the mean leave-writer-out accuracy is 68.70% while human accuracy was 90.8%. Case analysis shows that models often recognize broad irony or playfulness while misidentifying the mechanism or interactional move.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a benchmark to test whether LLMs can correctly interpret the pragmatic meaning of naturally occurring Chinese online comments in context, and finds a large gap between human and model performance.
AI.motivation: Indirect, playful, and context-dependent language is pervasive in Chinese online comments, but existing evaluations mostly rely on predefined categories or controlled setups that do not reflect the real difficulty of interpreting such comments in natural interactions. The authors want to know whether LLMs can actually recover what a real comment is pragmatically doing in its original conversational context and to quantify the performance gap with humans.
AI.method: The authors collect over 200,000 public Chinese social media interaction records and from them construct 4,735 human-validated diagnostic items. Each item consists of a target comment, its reconstructed preceding conversational context, and several plausible but incorrect pragmatic interpretations (misreadings). They then evaluate eight different LLMs both as question writers (creating items) and as solvers (choosing the correct interpretation) in a cross-writer evaluation setting where a model does not solve questions it wrote itself. They compare model accuracies to human performance and conduct case analyses of typical model errors.
AI.result: The best-performing LLM reaches 81.42% accuracy in a leave-writer-out setup, while average performance across all eight LLMs is 68.70%, substantially below human accuracy of 90.8%. Error analyses show that models are often able to detect general irony or playfulness but fail to identify the specific pragmatic mechanism or the fine-grained interactional move being made by the comment.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs, even strong ones, struggle to fully recover situated pragmatic meanings of Chinese online comments in realistic conversational contexts. While they often capture coarse-grained attitudes like irony, they frequently misinterpret the specific function of a comment in an interaction. The benchmark the authors introduce exposes this gap and provides a more realistic and challenging testbed for improving LLMs’ pragmatic understanding of context-rich, indirect online discourse.

title: Data-Optimized Contingency Screening: A Machine Learning Approach to Power System Security
comment: Accepted for presentation at the 3rd EIE International Conference on Computing, Networking, Robotics and Telecommunication (EIECon), 2025. To appear in IEEE Xplore
summary: Ensuring the security of the power system is essential for stability and reliability, especially in the event of disruption. Effective classification of contingency in power systems enables proactive decision-making and mitigates large-scale breakdowns and failures. This study explores the use of machine learning algorithms to classify security levels of contingencies in power systems into safe, moderate or severe classes. For this approach, Newton-Raphson load flow method extracts system data from contingency scenarios, using Overall Performance Index (OPI) as safety measure. For data pre-processing, Synthetic Minority Over-Sampling Technique (SMOTE) and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is used to address class imbalance and reduce dimensionality, respectively. K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN), Random Forest (RF) and Support Vector Machines (SVM) is trained and evaluated on datasets generated through N-k contingency scenarios for k equal 1, 2, and 3 on IEEE-14 and IEEE-30 bus systems using four hybrid pre-processing configurations: normalized, SMOTE-balanced, PCA-transformed, and a combined SMOTE PCA-transformed. Performance is assessed by precision, recall and F1 score, with priority given to the severe contingency classes. The RF achieved the highest F1 scores of 0.97 in IEEE-30 and 0.86 in IEEE-14, SVM benefits significantly from PCA and improves the accuracy of the classification, while KNN is best suited for SMOTE and PCA conversion. The findings show that PCA contributes more than SMOTE to the overall performance of the model. However, SMOTE improves recall but can introduce false positives and is therefore a compromise of accuracy. This study highlights machine learning as a scalable and powerful alternative to traditional contingency analysis, which improves the assessment of security in real time.

AI.tldr: The paper uses machine learning with various preprocessing pipelines to classify power system contingencies (safe / moderate / severe) and finds Random Forest with PCA-based preprocessing performs best, showing ML as an effective alternative for real‑time security assessment.
AI.motivation: Traditional contingency analysis in power systems is computationally heavy and may be too slow or inflexible for real‑time security assessment under multiple line or component outages (N‑k contingencies). There is a need for fast, accurate classification of contingency severity (safe, moderate, severe) to support proactive decision‑making and prevent cascading failures, especially as systems grow more complex. The study aims to see whether modern machine learning methods, with proper handling of class imbalance and high dimensionality, can provide better or at least comparable, scalable security assessment.
AI.method:
1) Generate contingency scenarios for N‑k outages (k = 1, 2, 3) on standard IEEE‑14 and IEEE‑30 bus test systems.
2) Run Newton–Raphson load flow for each scenario to obtain operating point and compute an Overall Performance Index (OPI), which quantifies security level.
3) Label each scenario into three classes (safe, moderate, severe) based on OPI thresholds.
4) Apply four data preprocessing configurations: (a) normalization only, (b) SMOTE to balance minority classes, (c) PCA for dimensionality reduction, and (d) SMOTE + PCA.
5) Train three classifiers—K‑Nearest Neighbours (KNN), Random Forest (RF), and Support Vector Machines (SVM)—on each dataset configuration.
6) Evaluate performance using precision, recall, and F1 score, with special emphasis on the severe contingency class.
AI.result: Random Forest achieves the best overall performance, with F1 scores of 0.97 on the IEEE‑30 bus and 0.86 on the IEEE‑14 bus. SVM performance improves markedly when PCA is applied, indicating that SVM benefits from reduced and decorrelated feature spaces. KNN works best when both SMOTE and PCA are used. PCA contributes more to model performance than SMOTE across models and datasets. SMOTE increases recall, particularly for the severe class, but at the cost of more false positives, thus lowering precision and overall accuracy. Overall, the experiments show that the models can reliably distinguish safe, moderate, and severe contingencies in the tested systems.
AI.conclusion: Machine learning classifiers, especially Random Forest enhanced with PCA-based preprocessing, can effectively classify the security level of power system contingencies in near real time, potentially substituting or complementing traditional contingency analysis techniques. While PCA is strongly beneficial for performance, SMOTE must be used carefully due to its tendency to inflate false positives despite improving recall. The work supports the view that data‑driven methods are scalable and practical tools for online security assessment in modern power systems, particularly when attention is focused on identifying severe contingencies.

title: Evaluation of Phonetic Encoding Algorithms on Transcription Datasets
summary: In this work, a novel evaluation scheme built on a generalized variant of the Rand Index measure, namely, the Hüllermeier-Rifqi Index, is proposed in order to assess how well phonetic encoding algorithms conform to word-based transcriptions in IPA (International Phonetic Alphabet) notation. For this objective, the discordance score is obtained by calculating the absolute difference between the pairwise similarity values of ground-truth transcriptions and those of corresponding phonetic encodings, which are computed using normalized edit distance as a permutation dependent string metric. The resulting score is subsequently adjusted with respect to that of a random string generator incorporating the same alphabet as the encoder under consideration. A wide range of phonetic encoders were evaluated as such on multi-lingual transcription datasets along with their recall capabilities based on the collision rate. The validity of the proposed scheme is further supported by its applicability in measuring the orthographic transparency of a language when the writing system is viewed as an inherent phonetic representation.

AI.tldr: They propose a new, principled way to evaluate phonetic encoding algorithms by comparing how closely their outputs mimic true IPA transcriptions, using a generalized Rand Index variant and normalized edit distance, and they show it works across languages and can even quantify how phonetic a writing system is.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of phonetic encoding algorithms are often task-specific, language-specific, or heuristic, making it hard to compare encoders objectively and across languages. There is a need for a general, quantitative scheme that measures how faithfully an encoder approximates true phonetic transcriptions (IPA) and that can also characterize properties like orthographic transparency of writing systems.
AI.method: They build an evaluation scheme on the Hüllermeier-Rifqi Index, a generalized Rand Index for comparing similarity structures. For each pair of words, they compute similarity of: (1) the ground-truth IPA transcriptions and (2) the corresponding phonetic encodings, using normalized edit distance as a permutation-dependent string metric. The discordance score is the absolute difference between these pairwise similarities. This discordance is then adjusted by comparing it to the score of a random string generator using the same alphabet as the encoder. They apply this scheme to multiple phonetic encoders on multilingual transcription datasets and also analyze recall via collision rate (how often different words get the same encoding). Finally, they interpret the scheme as a way to measure orthographic transparency when treating a script as an implicit phonetic encoding of speech.
AI.result: The scheme produces quantitative discordance scores that distinguish performance of various phonetic encoders across multiple languages, and it yields meaningful recall/collision-based insights about their behavior. When applied to orthographies, it provides a measure that reflects how transparently a writing system encodes pronunciation. The random-baseline adjustment shows that the scores are not trivial or explained by chance-like encodings.
AI.conclusion: The Hüllermeier-Rifqi-Index-based evaluation framework is an effective, language-agnostic way to assess how closely phonetic encoders approximate IPA transcriptions and to compare different encoders. Its random-baseline normalization makes the scores interpretable and robust. Beyond encoder evaluation, the same framework can be used to quantify orthographic transparency by treating the writing system as a phonetic encoder of speech sounds.

title: Iris: Climbing to the Search Frontier
summary: We present Iris-mini and Iris-pro, two search agents trained at the 35B-A3B and 397B-A17B scales, together with the data pipeline and training recipe behind them. Tasks are reverse-constructed from the hyperlink structure of a web corpus: we author multi-hop chains over an entity graph distilled from a seed page and its out-links, rewrite every non-answer entity into a descriptive reference so that no clue can be resolved by string matching, and admit only questions that a reference model fails closed-book yet solves once the supporting evidence is supplied. These questions are then turned into trajectories, which are filtered at both the trajectory and the turn level before SFT. The policy is then optimized by RL against live search, with the reward judge and the observation summarizer served inside the training cluster, and with over-long rollouts interrupted at the request level and resumed from their committed prefix at the next step. We alternate the two stages in a procedure we call SFT-RL climbing, returning the hardest solved and most efficient rollouts of each RL round to the next supervised pass. Because inference-time context management is worth more on these benchmarks than most reported differences between systems, we evaluate every benchmark both with and without it, holding the tool set, the context limit, and the judge fixed. All results come from a single ReAct agent, with no sub-agents and no test-time verification. With management enabled, on BrowseComp, BrowseComp-ZH, DeepSearchQA, and HLE the two models reach $82.2/84.8/86.9/52.3$ and $88.6/85.1/92.9/56.4$, the strongest overall results among open-source search agents in their respective parameter ranges. We plan to release the model weights together with the complete recipe for data construction, training, and evaluation.

AI.tldr: Introduces Iris-mini and Iris-pro search agents trained with a novel data construction pipeline and an alternating supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (SFT-RL climbing) scheme, achieving state-of-the-art results among open-source search agents of similar size.
AI.motivation: Existing search agents underperform on complex multi-hop web reasoning tasks, and reported gains are often confounded by differences in tooling and context management rather than genuine agent capability. The authors aim to build stronger, scalable search agents and a rigorous training and evaluation recipe that better isolates true agent quality.
AI.method: 1) Construct synthetic but realistic multi-hop web questions from a hyperlink-derived entity graph around seed pages, rewriting entities descriptively to prevent string-matching shortcuts and filtering for questions that require external evidence. 2) Convert questions into trajectories and apply strict filtering at both trajectory and turn levels before supervised fine-tuning (SFT). 3) Optimize the policy via reinforcement learning against live search, with in-cluster reward judging and summarization, and a mechanism to cut off and later resume long rollouts. 4) Alternate SFT and RL in an SFT-RL climbing loop, reusing the best, most efficient RL rollouts as supervised data for the next round. 5) Evaluate with and without explicit context management while holding tools, context limit, and judge fixed, using a single ReAct-style agent without sub-agents or test-time self-verification.
AI.result: Two models, Iris-mini (35B-A3B scale) and Iris-pro (397B-A17B scale), achieve strong performance on several search benchmarks. With context management enabled, they obtain scores of 82.2/84.8/86.9/52.3 and 88.6/85.1/92.9/56.4 on BrowseComp, BrowseComp-ZH, DeepSearchQA, and HLE respectively, outperforming other open-source search agents in their parameter ranges under a controlled evaluation setup.
AI.conclusion: The proposed data pipeline and SFT-RL climbing training procedure yield highly capable search agents that set new performance levels among open-source systems of similar size. Careful handling of context management and a controlled evaluation framework are crucial for meaningfully comparing search agents. The authors intend to release models and the full recipe, enabling reproducible research and further progress in web search agents.

title: The Anatomy of an ASR Hallucination
summary: ASR systems sometimes produce fluent text that is unrelated to the speech they receive. We view these hallucinations as one possible consequence of a broader grounding failure, in which the transcript is no longer adequately guided by the audio. To understand where this failure becomes possible, we study two independently trained Conformer-Large recognizers - one CTC and one RNN-T - under environmental degradation and speaker-background shift. In both models, the final encoder stage emerges as a critical boundary: bypassing the final block causes divergence on nearly every utterance, whereas bypassing middle blocks has little effect. At this same stage, the representations become more compact, text becomes readable by the trained decoder, and grapheme information becomes explicit. Importantly, the intervention produces garbled or repetitive output rather than fluent fabrication. Our result therefore identifies a mechanistic precondition for hallucination - the failure to produce adequately grounded output - not the complete origin of naturally occurring hallucinations. Together, the results reveal a consistent terminal-stage dependency for grounded recognition across two decoder families and multiple distribution shifts.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates where and how grounding failures that enable hallucinations arise in end-to-end ASR models, finding a critical role for the final encoder stage.
AI.motivation: ASR systems can output fluent but semantically unrelated text (hallucinations), indicating failures of grounding between audio and transcript. To reduce such failures, we need a mechanistic understanding of where in the model this decoupling from the audio becomes possible, especially under distribution shifts like noisy environments or speaker/background changes.
AI.method: The authors analyze two independently trained Conformer-Large ASR models (one CTC-based and one RNN-T-based) under environmental degradation and speaker-background shift. They perform intervention experiments by bypassing different encoder blocks (intermediate vs final) and observe the impact on recognition behavior, representation properties, and decoder-readability (grapheme information, compactness).
AI.result: They find that the final encoder stage is a critical boundary for grounded recognition in both models. Bypassing the final block causes transcript divergence on nearly every utterance, while bypassing middle blocks has minimal effect. At this stage, representations become more compact, more directly expose grapheme information, and become readable by the decoder. The induced failures lead to garbled or repetitive output rather than coherent hallucinations, showing that this layer is a precondition site for grounding failure rather than the sole source of natural hallucinations.
AI.conclusion: Grounded ASR recognition depends critically on the terminal encoder stage across different decoder architectures and distribution shifts. This stage marks where audio representations are transformed into compact, grapheme-explicit forms that the decoder can easily interpret, and disruption here enables the type of grounding failure that can precede hallucinations. The work identifies a mechanistic precondition for hallucinations rather than a full explanation of their natural occurrence, clarifying where to focus efforts for improving robustness and grounding in ASR models.

title: A Removal Based Approach to Improve LLM Faithfulness at Test-Time
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for consequential decisions, making their explanations an important tool for auditing model behavior. Unfortunately, these explanations can be unfaithful, failing to reflect the actual reasoning underlying the model's decisions. We consider a setting in which an LLM provides both an answer and an explanation in response to a question. We identify two distinct dimensions of unfaithful explanations: incompleteness, meaning that the explanation omits factors that influence the answer, and unsoundness, meaning that the explanation cites factors that did not influence the model's answer. Existing approaches to improving LLM faithfulness include training-time methods, which require access to model weights and extensive computational resources, and test-time methods that largely focus on addressing unsoundness. We introduce a test-time approach that directly targets incompleteness. We remove from the input the concepts not credited in the model's explanation and re-query the model on the reduced input. This eliminates unmentioned influences while preserving the influence of mentioned concepts. Across two datasets, multiple model families, and two independent faithfulness metrics, our approach improves explanation faithfulness compared to both standard prompting and prompting to encourage faithfulness. Our method is model-agnostic and can be applied at inference time without modifying model parameters, providing a flexible mechanism for reducing hidden influences and improving the reliability and safety of LLM-assisted decision making.

AI.tldr: They propose a test-time, model-agnostic method to make LLM explanations more faithful by removing unmentioned concepts from the input and re-querying, thereby targeting incomplete explanations and improving faithfulness across models and datasets.
AI.motivation: LLMs are used in high-stakes settings, so their explanations are needed to audit and trust their decisions. However, explanations are often unfaithful: they may omit real decision factors (incompleteness) or mention irrelevant ones (unsoundness). Existing methods either need retraining/access to weights or mainly handle unsoundness, leaving a gap for a simple, inference-time way to directly address incompleteness.
AI.method: In a setting where an LLM outputs both an answer and an explanation, the authors parse the explanation into a set of credited concepts. They then construct a reduced version of the original input by removing concepts that are not mentioned in the explanation, and re-query the same LLM on this reduced input. This procedure is intended to remove hidden, uncredited influences while preserving the influence of concepts the model explicitly cites. They evaluate this process across datasets, model families, and faithfulness metrics, comparing against standard prompting and prompts that encourage faithfulness.
AI.result: The proposed test-time intervention increases the faithfulness of LLM explanations, as measured by two independent metrics, on two datasets and across several model families. Compared with baseline prompting and with prompts that explicitly ask for faithful explanations, their method yields higher alignment between explanations and the actual features driving model decisions.
AI.conclusion: A simple, model-agnostic, inference-time procedure—removing unmentioned concepts from the input and re-querying—can systematically reduce hidden influences and improve explanation faithfulness, specifically addressing incompleteness. This enhances the reliability and safety of LLM-assisted decision-making without requiring access to model internals or retraining.

title: A Systematic Evaluation of Cross-Lingual Consistency Enhancement Methods in Multilingual Language Models
comment: Preprint. All code and datasets will be released upon publication
summary: Multilingual language models often produce inconsistent answers to semantically equivalent questions across languages, motivating methods to improve cross-lingual consistency (CLC). However, existing methods are typically evaluated using different models, tasks, and protocols, leaving their relative strengths unclear. In this work, we present a unified evaluation of representative CLC-enhancement methods for question answering, spanning inference-time interventions and post-training approaches across three model families and three closed-form benchmarks. The results show that post-training methods are generally more reliable, with direct distribution alignment consistently improving CLC across all model-dataset combinations, while other methods are more sensitive to answer format and the breadth of language coverage. Notably, cross-domain transfer is limited unless source and target tasks share similar output formats. We further investigate whether CLC enhancement hurts models' ability to respond differently *when needed*, that is, when asked culture-dependent questions. Across two benchmarks of culturally diverse question answering, we find no systematic degradation in controlled closed-form evaluation, whereas open-ended generation reveals occasional accuracy reductions, particularly for non-English responses. Our work highlights the need to evaluate CLC enhancement for both cross-domain robustness and culturally appropriate variation, informing future work in post-training and benchmark development.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates and compares methods to improve cross-lingual consistency (CLC) in multilingual language models for QA, finding post-training distribution alignment most reliably improves consistency without clearly harming culturally appropriate variation, though some non-English open-ended performance can drop.
AI.motivation: Multilingual LMs often answer semantically equivalent questions differently across languages, which is undesirable for many applications. Existing techniques to enhance cross-lingual consistency are hard to compare because they are tested on different models, tasks, and setups. The authors aim to systematically benchmark and understand these methods, their reliability, robustness across domains, and their impact on culturally sensitive questions where differing answers may actually be correct.
AI.method: They conduct a unified evaluation of representative CLC-enhancement methods for question answering, covering both inference-time interventions and post-training approaches. Experiments span three model families and three closed-form QA benchmarks to assess consistency gains. They particularly test post-training methods that directly align output distributions across languages, and analyze cross-domain transfer when source and target tasks differ in format. They also use two culturally diverse QA benchmarks and evaluate both controlled closed-form and open-ended generation to test whether enforcing CLC harms the model’s ability to vary answers appropriately for culture-dependent questions.
AI.result: Post-training methods, especially direct distribution alignment, consistently and reliably improve cross-lingual consistency across all model-dataset combinations. Other methods show more variable performance, being sensitive to answer formats and the range of languages covered. Cross-domain transfer of CLC improvements is limited if the source and target tasks differ in output format. On culturally dependent questions, closed-form evaluations show no systematic degradation in the model’s ability to provide culturally appropriate variation, but open-ended generation reveals occasional accuracy drops, particularly for non-English outputs.
AI.conclusion: Direct distribution alignment as a post-training strategy is a generally effective way to improve cross-lingual consistency in multilingual QA, outperforming more fragile inference-time methods. However, CLC gains do not automatically transfer across tasks with different output formats, and enforcing CLC can sometimes harm open-ended performance, especially in non-English responses. The authors argue that future work on CLC should jointly consider cross-domain robustness and preservation of culturally appropriate variation, and that benchmarks and post-training methods must be designed with these trade-offs in mind.

title: Why Better Models Can Create Riskier Systems: Evidence from LLM Agents in Financial Markets
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are being deployed at scale in consequential real-world systems, from financial markets to content moderation to hiring. We show that improving individual model capability can degrade rather than improve system-level outcomes. We hypothesize that shared training and architectures can lead more capable LLMs to behave more similarly, creating correlated actions that do not diversify away. We develop a general framework showing how this correlation creates a non-diversifiable risk floor and test its predictions in financial markets using an agent-based simulation with LLM traders of varying general-purpose capability. We find that: (1) frontier LLMs exhibit significantly correlated behavior that increases with capability; (2) when their shared reasoning is accurate, increasing agent participation reduces market-level risk; and (3) when agents share a common misinformation environment, the same correlated behavior becomes a liability. Together, these results identify a capability paradox: improving individual models does not necessarily produce better system-level outcomes. Whether the same dynamics arise in other domains is an open empirical question.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that making individual large language models (LLMs) more capable can worsen overall system outcomes because similar models act in correlated ways, creating non‑diversifiable risk, illustrated via financial-market simulations.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly embedded in high‑stakes systems such as financial trading, content moderation, and hiring. Designers often assume that improving individual model capability improves system performance. However, when many systems use similarly trained, similarly architected frontier LLMs, their decisions may become correlated. This raises the concern that system-level risk may actually increase as capability rises, especially in environments where many agents rely on the same potentially flawed information or reasoning patterns. The paper is motivated by the need to understand and quantify this potential “capability paradox.”
AI.method: The authors build a general theoretical framework describing how correlated behavior among LLM-based agents leads to a non‑diversifiable “risk floor” at the system level. They then instantiate this in an agent-based simulation of financial markets where agents use LLMs of different general-purpose capabilities as trading decision-makers. They measure behavioral correlations among different LLMs, examine how these correlations vary with capability, and run market simulations under different informational environments, including accurate shared reasoning and shared misinformation scenarios.
AI.result: First, they find that “frontier” (more advanced) LLMs behave more similarly to each other than weaker models, and this behavioral correlation increases with model capability. Second, when the LLM agents share accurate reasoning, increasing the number of participating LLM agents lowers market-level risk, as diversification of accurate strategies is beneficial. Third, when the same correlated reasoning is exposed to a shared misinformation environment, the correlation becomes harmful: market-level risk increases because many agents simultaneously make similar erroneous decisions that cannot be diversified away.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that improving individual LLM capabilities does not guarantee better system-level performance; indeed, it can create a “capability paradox” in which higher capability leads to more correlated and thus riskier collective behavior. Correlation induced by shared training and architectures yields a non-diversifiable risk floor that persists even as more agents participate. This has implications for deploying LLMs in real-world, high-stakes domains, emphasizing the need to account for correlated failures and systemic risk rather than focusing solely on individual-model accuracy. Whether similar dynamics occur in domains beyond financial markets remains an open question the authors highlight for future empirical work.

title: What Attention Recalls and Recurrence Controls in Hybrid Language Models
comment: Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026. 13 pages, 3 figures, 8 tables. Code: https://github.com/kirillTerra/split-prefill
summary: Hybrid language models combine attention with a fixed-size recurrent state, but the role of each channel remains unclear. We introduce two cache-level interventions. Split-prefill keeps only the KV cache or only the recurrent state from a prefilled context, then generates an answer. State-swap pairs the KV cache from one context with the recurrent state from another in a single forward pass. On Qwen3.5 and Falcon-H1, the two channels split sharply by function. Exact retrieval survives only through attention (64-98% of full accuracy) and collapses to zero through recurrence. Output language and persona reverse the pattern: both survive recurrence (70-80% and 3-5x) while KV-only drops to ~1% language accuracy. State-swap confirms this causally: the answer takes its value from the KV side and its language from the recurrent side. Recurrent-only generation also accepts words that were never in the context but share meaning or parts with seen items. Attention provides a lookup over what was said; the recurrent state shapes how the model says it next.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how hybrid language models split functionality between attention (KV cache) and a recurrent state, showing attention retrieves factual content while recurrence controls style, language, and persona.
AI.motivation: Hybrid models that mix attention with a recurrent state are promising for efficiency and long-context handling, but it is unclear what each channel actually does. Understanding this division of labor can guide architecture design, interpretability, and safe deployment.
AI.method: The authors design two interventions on hybrid models (Qwen3.5 and Falcon-H1). In Split-prefill, they prefill with context, then during generation keep only the KV cache or only the recurrent state, measuring performance on retrieval, language, and persona tasks. In State-swap, they combine the KV cache from one context with the recurrent state from another in a single forward pass to causally test which channel controls what aspects of the output.
AI.result: They find a sharp functional split. Exact retrieval performance is preserved only via attention (64–98% of full accuracy) and collapses to zero when relying solely on recurrence. Conversely, output language and persona are largely preserved through the recurrent state (70–80% language accuracy, large persona effects), while KV-only generation nearly loses these (around 1% language accuracy). State-swap runs show answers adopt factual content from the KV side but stylistic and linguistic properties from the recurrent side. Recurrent-only generation can also produce semantically or morphologically related words not present in the context.
AI.conclusion: In these hybrid models, the attention KV cache primarily serves as a content lookup for what was said, while the recurrent state primarily governs how the model expresses it (language, style, persona, generalization). This functional separation suggests a principled division of roles between attention and recurrence in hybrid architectures and offers a handle for targeted control and analysis of model behavior.

title: Corporate Language Model (CLM): Transforming Tacit and Fragmented Enterprise Knowledge into a Sovereign, Auditable, and Executable Corporate Intelligence Layer
summary: Enterprise AI deployments fail not from model inadequacy, but because organizations lack a structured substrate encoding how they decide, negotiate, and execute. Generic LLMs carry no firm-specific ontological priors; RAG remains brittle, with no path to executable action; static playbooks encode logic but cannot reason or adapt. This demands an architecture treating tacit-knowledge capture, ontological grounding, sovereign deployment, and auditable actuation as co-designed from the start. This paper introduces the Corporate Language Model (CLM), a framework transforming a firm's structured, unstructured, multimodal, and tacit knowledge into an ontology-grounded enterprise foundation upon which reasoning and governed execution are composed. CLM has five capability planes and four architectural pillars: a Neurosymbolic Mesh coupling generative models with a knowledge graph; a Skill Graph where reusable tactics, personas, objections, and goals are typed and composed; Living Digital Twins modeling functional areas as reasoning surrogates; and a Deep Security Layer enforcing sovereignty, traceability, and human oversight. A Spec-as-Code paradigm bridges grounded intent and executable artifact. CLM is one instantiation of this foundation-centric class. Four contributions follow: CLM is defined as a distinct object of study; the Skill Graph is introduced for compositional explainability by construction; the Wisdom Listener effect is proposed, whereby tacit-capable foundations compound in value with use, connecting to dynamic capabilities and organizational learning; and evidence from a JCI-accredited tertiary hospital in Brazil instantiates three of the six maturity stages under LGPD.
