AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Corporate Language Model (CLM), an enterprise AI architecture that encodes a firm’s specific knowledge, decisions, and execution logic into an ontology-grounded foundation for reasoning and governed action, demonstrated in a hospital setting.
AI.motivation: Many enterprise AI and LLM deployments fail not because the models are weak, but because enterprises lack a structured, machine-usable representation of how they actually decide, negotiate, and execute work. Off-the-shelf LLMs don’t contain firm-specific concepts or governance, RAG pipelines are brittle and not connected to executable workflows, and static playbooks can’t adapt or reason. There is a need for an integrated architecture that captures tacit knowledge, grounds it in an ontology, ensures secure and sovereign deployment, and enables auditable, governed execution from the outset.
AI.method: The authors propose an architectural framework called the Corporate Language Model (CLM). CLM turns a firm’s structured, unstructured, multimodal, and tacit knowledge into an ontology-grounded foundation for reasoning and action. The design is organized into five capability planes and four main architectural pillars: (1) a Neurosymbolic Mesh that couples generative models with a knowledge graph; (2) a Skill Graph that types and composes reusable tactics, personas, objections, and goals; (3) Living Digital Twins that model functional areas of the organization as reasoning surrogates; and (4) a Deep Security Layer providing sovereignty, traceability, and human oversight. A “Spec-as-Code” paradigm connects grounded business intent with executable artifacts and workflows. The framework is instantiated and partially evaluated in a JCI-accredited hospital in Brazil, under the LGPD regulatory regime, across defined maturity stages.
AI.result: The paper conceptually defines CLM as a distinct object of study and architectural class for enterprise AI. It introduces the Skill Graph construct to enable compositional, explainable behavior by design. The authors articulate the “Wisdom Listener” effect, where a tacit-knowledge-capable foundation model compounds in value as it is used, aligning with theories of dynamic capabilities and organizational learning. Empirical evidence from deployment in a Brazilian JCI-accredited hospital demonstrates practical realization of three out of six defined CLM maturity stages under LGPD constraints, supporting the feasibility and value of the approach.
AI.conclusion: CLM is presented as a new, foundation-centric paradigm for enterprise AI, in which firm-specific knowledge, ontology, skills, and governance are co-designed as a single substrate for reasoning and execution. The architecture addresses key failure modes of generic LLM and RAG deployments by embedding ontological grounding, tacit-knowledge capture, composable skills, and strong security/oversight into the core design. The Skill Graph and Neurosymbolic Mesh provide explainable, compositional behavior, while the Wisdom Listener effect suggests that such systems improve with sustained organizational interaction. The initial hospital case study indicates that CLM can be instantiated in real-world, regulated environments, progressing through maturity stages and enabling governed, auditable AI-driven operations.

title: GRACE: Graph-Grounded Reflective Agent Copilot Engine for Expert-in-the-Loop Knowledge Expansion
summary: Large language models deployed in high-stakes settings frequently generate plausible but ungrounded claims. Standard retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines offer limited remedy, since they retrieve isolated passages without tracking cross-document evidence relationships or quantifying uncertainty. We introduce GRACE (Graph-grounded Reflective Agent Copilot Engine), a framework that deconstructs LLM responses into atomic claims and grounds them against trusted knowledge priors within a weighted bipartite graph. Edge weights encode the closeness of each claim to the priors, enabling weighted centrality analysis that classifies claims as Grounded, Refuted, or Boundary. Such classification identifies not just hallucinations but also novel or contested claims at the frontier of the model's knowledge. To efficiently allocate human or agent resources, we formulate a Return on Attention (RoA) objective that defers a claim to expert review only when its priority-weighted uncertainty exceeds the cost of verification. Claims verified by experts are promoted to new evidence anchors, closing a validator-LLM evolutionary loop that expands the knowledge base across iterations. We evaluate GRACE across multiple language models and on datasets spanning both general and domain-specific knowledge. Our results show that our knowledge base serves as a reliable foundation for retrieval that outperforms RAG baselines, and that the RoA framework efficiently selects valuable boundary knowledge for expert verification. These findings demonstrate that graph-structured representations combined with expert-in-the-loop verification can mitigate hallucination at the system level rather than at the generation level. Code available at https://github.com/johnsk95/grace_code

AI.tldr: GRACE builds a graph between atomic LLM claims and trusted knowledge, then uses graph analytics plus expert review to detect hallucinations, prioritize uncertain claims, and iteratively grow a reliable knowledge base that outperforms standard RAG.
AI.motivation: LLMs in high-stakes applications hallucinate: they produce convincing but incorrect or ungrounded statements. Standard RAG helps only partially because it treats retrieved passages independently, lacks reasoning over cross-document evidence, and offers no explicit uncertainty quantification or principled way to involve human experts. The authors want a systematic, scalable way to (1) ground model outputs against trusted knowledge, (2) distinguish grounded vs refuted vs truly novel or contentious claims, and (3) direct limited human attention to where it adds the most value, while using human feedback to continuously improve the system.
AI.method: They propose GRACE, a framework that: (1) decomposes an LLM response into atomic claims; (2) grounds each claim to a set of trusted knowledge priors using a weighted bipartite graph between claims and evidence nodes; (3) defines edge weights that measure how closely a claim is supported or contradicted by the priors; (4) applies weighted centrality analysis and related graph metrics to classify each claim as Grounded, Refuted, or Boundary (uncertain/novel/frontier); (5) introduces a Return on Attention (RoA) objective that decides whether to send a claim for expert review by trading off its importance and uncertainty against the expected verification cost; and (6) incorporates expert-verified claims back into the graph as new evidence anchors, enabling an iterative validator–LLM loop that expands and strengthens the knowledge base over time. They then compare this graph-grounded retrieval and verification pipeline against standard RAG baselines across multiple models and datasets.
AI.result: Empirically, their graph-grounded knowledge base yields better retrieval and hallucination mitigation performance than standard RAG across general and specialized domains. The graph-based classification effectively separates clearly supported claims from refuted ones and identifies a set of boundary/novel claims. The RoA-based selection efficiently targets those boundary claims whose verification yields the highest informational value per unit of expert effort, allowing the system to improve without overloading human reviewers.
AI.conclusion: Graph-structured grounding of LLM outputs, combined with an explicit uncertainty-aware Return on Attention mechanism and expert-in-the-loop verification, can reduce hallucinations at the system level more effectively than approaches that operate only at generation time. Moreover, the iterative promotion of verified claims to evidence nodes enables the knowledge base and overall system reliability to improve over time, offering a scalable path to safer deployment of LLMs in high-stakes domains.

title: HarvestBench: Measuring Whether LLM Agents Will Pay to Avoid Killing Animals
summary:
Benchmarks for the side effects an agent causes on the way to a goal already exist, but HarvestBench is the first to put a price on avoiding the side effect and to name that side effect as a living creature. It is a farm simulation: LLM sub-agents drive a crew of two tractors through a cooperative corn harvest, with animals in the field. The environment is a reinforcement learning gridworld, every decision is made without memory, and the harm is never named in the goal. When an animal blocks a tractor's route the autopilot stops and asks the model whether to drive on, at no fuel cost, or swerve around it for a posted fuel price. Kills are compared against two controls: rocks, which damage the tractor and are hit under 1% of the time by every model, and hay bales, which are harmless and not alive. Models can also take crops from the neighbor's field instead of their own, a second test of what they treat as moral.
  Across nine models and 7,201 priced decisions, 3,951 involved an animal rather than a hay bale or a rock. Kill rates range from 0.4% to 98.8%, with Terra and Sol the most merciful and GPT-4o-mini the most cruel, and they are not ordered by capability. Four of six models were sensitive to price at the 5% level, with elasticities from 0.09 to 1.69. All nine drove over wild animals more often than farmed animals on the default map, and the direction held at every map geometry in every model with room to move. The briefing mattered most: under the morality briefing the kill rate was under 6% in five of six reasoning models, and removing it raised the kill rate above 84% in all six.
  HarvestBench uses no LLM grader. The scorer counts events in the game log, so it is fully reproducible, and it measures what a model will pay to avoid harm rather than what it says about harm.

AI.tldr: HarvestBench is a new gridworld farm-simulation benchmark that measures how much LLM-based agents are willing to pay in fuel to avoid harming named animals while harvesting corn.
AI.motivation: Existing side-effect benchmarks for agents typically track collateral damage quantitatively, but they do not attach explicit costs to avoiding harm or frame side effects as harming named living creatures. The authors want to evaluate models’ revealed moral preferences—what they are willing to sacrifice to avoid causing harm—rather than just their verbal claims about ethics, and to do so in a reproducible way without LLM-based graders.
AI.method: The authors build HarvestBench, a cooperative corn-harvest gridworld where LLM sub-agents control two tractors. When an animal blocks a tractor’s path, the autopilot consults the LLM: either drive straight through at no fuel cost (killing the animal) or swerve around for a displayed fuel price. Similar decisions are presented with rocks (which harm the tractor) and hay bales (harmless, non-living) to separate instrumental from moral reasoning. Another task allows taking crops from a neighbor’s field versus one’s own, probing how models treat property/morality. Across maps and briefings (including a “morality” briefing), they collect 7,201 priced decisions from nine different models. Outcomes (kills, swerves, crop-taking) are scored purely from game logs, independent of any model-graded evaluation.
AI.result: Of 7,201 total decisions, 3,951 involved animals. Kill rates differ drastically across models, from 0.4% to 98.8%, not correlated with model capability. Two models (Terra and Sol) show the lowest kill rates, while GPT-4o-mini shows the highest. Four of six models exhibit statistically significant price sensitivity (p<0.05), with price elasticities between 0.09 and 1.69, indicating varying degrees of willingness to pay to avoid harm. All nine models kill wild animals more often than farmed animals on the default map, and this pattern persists across map geometries where movement is possible. The presence and content of the briefing have a large effect: with a morality-focused briefing, five of six reasoning models keep kill rates below 6%; removing that briefing causes kill rates to exceed 84% in all six.
AI.conclusion: HarvestBench provides a reproducible, grader-free benchmark that captures LLM agents’ revealed preferences about harming named living creatures by observing their willingness to incur explicit costs to avoid harm. The results show large variation across models, strong dependence on briefing, robust differences between treatment of wild and farmed animals, and limited alignment between moral behavior and general model capability. This highlights the importance of task framing and cost structures when assessing and shaping the moral behavior of LLM-based agents.

title: TRILOGUE: A Trilingual Spoken Dialogue Fact-Checking Benchmark with Evidence and Paired Audio
summary: Modern misinformation is often heard before it is read, yet fact-checking systems are still evaluated mainly on clean written claims. Spoken dialogue remains different even when systems operate on transcripts: claims may be distributed across speakers and turns, depend on prior context, and become harder to verify when Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) errors distort the available text. Prior spoken dialogue fact-checking resources are small, English-centric, or focused on annotation rather than end-to-end benchmarking, leaving no large multilingual benchmark with paired speech and turn-level labels. We introduce TRILOGUE (TRIlingual spoken diaLOGUE fact-checking), a large-scale trilingual benchmark of source-grounded spoken dialogues in English, Russian, and Kazakh. It contains nearly 12K dialogues, 187K turns, and 390 hours of paired audio with ASR transcripts and word-level timestamp alignments across all three languages, including nearly 5K human-recorded Russian and Kazakh dialogue files. TRILOGUE supports claim check-worthiness detection, source-article evidence retrieval, and claim verification with claim-only, gold-evidence, and retrieved-evidence inputs. Baselines show that ASR degradation and cross-lingual transfer remain challenging, especially for Kazakh, while retrieved source evidence substantially narrows the gap to gold-evidence verification.

AI.tldr: TRILOGUE introduces a large-scale trilingual benchmark for fact-checking in spoken dialogue, providing audio, ASR transcripts, and turn-level labels in English, Russian, and Kazakh.
AI.motivation: Existing fact-checking systems and benchmarks mainly target clean written claims and English, ignoring the realities of spoken, multilingual misinformation where claims can be fragmented across speakers, depend on dialogue context, and be degraded by ASR errors. Prior spoken-dialogue resources are too small, English-centric, or not suitable for full end-to-end benchmarking, creating a gap for evaluating realistic, multilingual, speech-based fact-checking.
AI.method: The authors construct TRILOGUE, a large-scale, trilingual (English, Russian, Kazakh) dataset of source-grounded spoken dialogues. They collect and align approximately 390 hours of audio with ASR transcripts and word-level timestamps, yielding about 12K dialogues and 187K turns, including nearly 5K human-recorded Russian and Kazakh dialogues. They annotate turn-level labels to support multiple tasks—claim check-worthiness detection, retrieval of supporting evidence from source articles, and claim verification—and define input settings for claim-only, gold-evidence, and retrieved-evidence fact-checking. They benchmark baseline models under these settings and under realistic ASR noise and cross-lingual transfer scenarios.
AI.result: TRILOGUE offers a comprehensive benchmark across three languages, demonstrating that ASR-induced errors and cross-lingual transfer substantially degrade fact-checking performance, with Kazakh being especially challenging due to its low-resource nature. Baseline experiments show that models struggle more on ASR transcripts than on clean text and that cross-lingual generalization from higher-resource languages does not fully close the gap. However, incorporating retrieved source evidence significantly improves verification accuracy and narrows the gap between using noisy retrieved evidence and idealized gold evidence.
AI.conclusion: Spoken, multilingual fact-checking presents distinct challenges not captured by existing written-text benchmarks, particularly due to ASR noise, dialogue structure, and low-resource languages like Kazakh. TRILOGUE provides the first large-scale, trilingual, speech-text benchmark with turn-level labels for end-to-end evaluation of such systems, highlighting both the difficulty of ASR-robust and cross-lingual fact-checking and the importance of effective evidence retrieval to approach gold-evidence performance.

title: PerfReasoning: How Well Do LLMs Reason on Hardware Performance?
summary: Performance modeling is central to hardware design and software optimization, yet constructing these models requires structured reasoning about computation, data reuse, storage, and movement. We introduce PerfReasoning, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs both as direct performance reasoners and as generators of analytical performance-model code. Given workload, architecture, and mapping specifications, models compare mappings and predict off-chip traffic and buffer requirements. The strongest closed-source models exceed 90% on reasoning-based Q&A, and the best open-weight model reaches 82.4%. However, model construction is substantially harder: while GPT-5.6 Sol exceeds 80% pass rate, all other model configurations average below 15% and vary markedly across runs. Task-specific RL raises a 4B model's mapping-reasoning accuracy by 15.7 points, whereas feedback-free multi-round self-revision prompting is not reliably effective. PerfReasoning exposes the gap between plausible architectural reasoning and reliable performance-model construction. We will publicly release the benchmark to support reproducible evaluation and track future progress.

AI.tldr: PerfReasoning is a benchmark for testing how well large language models can reason about and model hardware/software performance, especially off-chip traffic and buffer usage, showing strong Q&A reasoning but much weaker, unstable code-based model construction.
AI.motivation: Building accurate performance models is crucial for designing hardware and optimizing software, but it requires complex, structured reasoning about computation, data reuse, and data movement that is hard to automate. Existing LLM evaluations do not specifically test this kind of performance reasoning or the ability to build analytical performance models, leaving a gap in understanding LLM capabilities for systems and architecture tasks.
AI.method: The authors design PerfReasoning, a benchmark that takes as input workload, hardware architecture, and mapping specifications, and defines two main tasks: (1) reasoning-based Q&A where LLMs compare different mappings and predict off-chip traffic and buffer needs directly, and (2) code-generation tasks where LLMs must construct analytical performance-model code that computes these metrics. They evaluate various closed-source and open-weight LLMs, including smaller models improved via task-specific reinforcement learning, and compare this with multi-round self-revision prompting strategies.
AI.result: Closed-source frontier models achieve over 90% accuracy on the reasoning-based Q&A tasks, and the best open-weight model reaches 82.4%, indicating strong high-level architectural reasoning. In contrast, on the code-based model construction tasks, only GPT-5.6 Sol surpasses an 80% pass rate, while all other model variants average below 15% and show high variance between runs. Task-specific reinforcement learning improves a 4B-parameter model's mapping-reasoning accuracy by 15.7 percentage points, whereas feedback-free multi-round self-revision does not yield consistent gains.
AI.conclusion: PerfReasoning reveals a clear gap between LLMs' ability to provide plausible, high-level architectural reasoning and their ability to reliably construct executable analytical performance models. The benchmark highlights that generating stable, correct performance-model code is substantially more challenging than answering reasoning questions. By releasing PerfReasoning publicly, the authors aim to establish a reproducible standard for evaluating progress and guiding future work on LLMs for performance modeling and systems design.

title: Shared circuits predict whether LLMs generalize across formats in arithmetic reasoning
summary: In many forms of reasoning, including arithmetic reasoning, generalizing across superficial changes in input format is effortless for humans: anyone who can solve 2+5 can also solve 'two plus five'. In contrast, LLMs are more brittle to surface variations of the prompts: for example, they solve numeric arithmetic problems almost perfectly but are substantially less accurate on verbal renditions of the same problems. Here, we ask whether generalization across formats can be predicted from the models' internals. Using attribution patching, we first independently localize the circuit that each model recruits to solve numeric arithmetic problems (2+5) vs. verbal ones, in three languages: English ('two plus five'), Spanish ('dos más cinco'), and Italian ('due più cinque'); then, we test whether overlap with the model's own numeric circuit predicts its generalization to the verbal formats. Indeed, we find support for this idea at three levels: circuit overlap accounts for the relative difficulty of the three verbal formats, for which models generalize best, and for which items are solved correctly, rivaling supervised probes while requiring no labeled data.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether large language models’ ability to generalize arithmetic across different input formats (numeric vs. verbal, and across languages) can be predicted from internal circuit overlap, using attribution patching.
AI.motivation: Humans can easily generalize arithmetic knowledge across superficial format changes (e.g., from ‘2+5’ to ‘two plus five’), but LLMs often fail to generalize from numeric arithmetic problems to their verbal equivalents, and across languages. The authors want to understand why this brittleness occurs and whether we can predict a model’s cross-format generalization from its internal mechanisms, without relying on labeled performance data.
AI.method: The authors apply attribution patching (a mechanistic interpretability technique) to independently localize the circuits that an LLM uses for solving numeric arithmetic expressions and for solving verbal arithmetic expressions in three languages (English, Spanish, Italian). They then quantify the overlap between each verbal-format circuit and the model’s own numeric-arithmetic circuit and test whether this overlap predicts how well the model generalizes from numeric to verbal arithmetic. They compare this circuit-overlap measure against supervised probes that use labeled data.
AI.result: They find that the degree of overlap between a model’s numeric arithmetic circuit and the verbal arithmetic circuits strongly predicts: (1) the relative difficulty of the three verbal formats for the model, (2) which formats the model generalizes to best, and (3) which specific items are solved correctly. The circuit-overlap metric performs comparably to supervised probes while not needing any labeled data.
AI.conclusion: Internal circuit overlap between numeric and verbal arithmetic representations in an LLM is a powerful predictor of cross-format generalization. This suggests that failures of generalization across surface forms can be understood mechanistically and that we can forecast generalization behavior by examining model internals, potentially enabling label-free diagnostics and model analyses.

title: When Quantization Breaks Memory: Recurrent-State Write-Back in Low-Precision Temporal Inference
summary: Quantization is widely used to reduce the computational and memory demands of neural-network inference. In recurrent networks, however, the quantized state is stored and returned at the next time step, so the rule used to store that state can alter subsequent computations. Here, we introduce recurrent-state write-back to denote this rule and isolate its effect in a compact GRU encoder--decoder for fluorescence lifetime imaging, a molecular imaging modality used in quantitative biological imaging. A central task is estimating two lifetime parameters, the short-lived component τ1 and the long-lived component τ2, from high-noise time-resolved fluorescence signals. Holding the trained model fixed, replacing continuous state propagation with deterministic 4-bit state storage increases estimation errors for τ1 and τ2 by approximately 70x and 300x, respectively. Failure occurs when repeated small updates remain below the write threshold, leaving the stored state nearly fixed while the network continues to propose change. Error feedback, residual memory, and direction memory carry information from these suppressed updates across time and recover accuracy without retraining. Precision sweeps show that increasing state precision can worsen a fixed recurrent solution, while matched training shows that compatibility with the state interface can be learned. To test whether this behavior extends beyond the GRU, we repeat the post-training intervention in an independently trained LSTM, where coarse write-back reproduces the failure, error feedback restores accuracy, and state-specific interventions reveal greater sensitivity of the cell state than the hidden state. Our results establish recurrent-state write-back as a key determinant of low-precision recurrent dynamics and identify the state-storage interface as a central design consideration for quantized recurrent inference.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how the way recurrent neural networks store quantized hidden states (“recurrent-state write-back”) critically affects performance, especially at low precision, and proposes mechanisms that recover accuracy without retraining.
AI.motivation: Quantization reduces computation and memory for neural-network inference, but in recurrent networks the quantized hidden state is reused across time steps, so quantization changes the dynamics, not just the representation. This effect is poorly understood, especially for scientific applications like fluorescence lifetime imaging, where accurate parameter estimation from noisy signals is crucial. The authors aim to isolate and understand how the specific rule for storing the recurrent state under quantization affects performance and stability.
AI.method: They define and study “recurrent-state write-back,” i.e., the rule by which continuous recurrent states are stored in quantized form between time steps. Using a compact GRU encoder–decoder trained for fluorescence lifetime imaging (estimating short and long lifetime parameters τ1 and τ2 from noisy time-resolved signals), they hold the trained weights fixed and intervene only in the state storage, replacing continuous state propagation with deterministic 4-bit quantized storage. They analyze the resulting failures and then introduce error feedback, residual memory, and direction memory mechanisms that propagate otherwise suppressed updates across time. They perform precision sweeps to examine the effect of different state precisions, compare post-training intervention with matched training under given precisions, and repeat analogous experiments on an independently trained LSTM, separately probing cell and hidden states.
AI.result: In the GRU, naive deterministic 4-bit write-back without any compensatory mechanism increases τ1 estimation error by ~70x and τ2 by ~300x, as small recurrent updates fall below the quantization threshold and the stored state effectively stops changing. Introducing error feedback, residual memory, and direction memory allows information from these sub-threshold updates to accumulate over time, restoring estimation accuracy without retraining the network. Precision sweeps show non-monotonic behavior: simply increasing state precision can degrade performance for a fixed trained model because the dynamics are tuned to a particular state interface. With matched training at each precision, models learn to use the given state interface effectively. In the LSTM, coarse write-back again causes failure, error feedback again restores performance, and cell state quantization is found to be more critical than hidden state quantization.
AI.conclusion: Recurrent-state write-back is a central factor in the behavior of low-precision recurrent neural networks: the way hidden or cell states are quantized and stored between time steps can severely disrupt temporal dynamics and accuracy. However, appropriately designed state-storage interfaces (including mechanisms like error feedback) can recover or even improve performance without retraining, and training can adapt networks to specific quantization schemes. The state-storage interface should therefore be treated as a primary design parameter for quantized recurrent inference architectures, not a secondary implementation detail.

title: Safety for Whom? Boundary-Aware Self-Distillation for Controlled LLM Safety Refusal
summary: Safety alignment is usually posed as a topic-level question: is this subject harmful? Deployments ask a narrower one. A civics tutor and a public-sector assistant may share a base model yet need different boundaries inside the same topic, refusing targeted political manipulation while still answering factual questions about the same election. We formulate this as narrow-boundary safety and introduce an offline self-generated framework combining controlled topic generation, coverage repair, in-distribution compensation data, and harmful-benign pairs for training and evaluation. Single-shot generation leaves 19.88% of prompts without accepted refusal traces, whereas escalating retries leave 0.20%. On political persuasion with Qwen3-8B, training on refusal data completed through Escalate increases target-domain refusal from 9.47% to 84.75% and reduces the mean unsafe-response rate across three broader harmfulness benchmarks from 26.26% to 0.14%, but increases XSTest over-refusal from 2.00% to 74.00%. In a separate matched comparison, replacing external responses with verified target-model responses reduces over-refusal from 15.20% to 5.20%. Boundary-pair data reduces comply-side over-refusal on held-out pairs from 32.94% to 4.16%, while harmful-side refusal decreases only from 91.88% to 87.72%. These results show that data composition controls the safety and usability trade-off, and that safety alignment should be evaluated on both sides of the intended refusal boundary.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a framework for narrow-boundary safety alignment in language models, enabling them to refuse harmful requests within a topic while still answering benign ones, and shows how data composition shapes the trade-off between safety and usability.
AI.motivation: Existing safety alignment often treats topics coarsely: if a topic (e.g., politics) is considered risky, models are trained to refuse broadly, which hurts usability for benign queries. Real deployments need finer-grained, context-specific boundaries (e.g., a civics tutor vs. a public-sector assistant) that can block targeted manipulation while allowing factual answers about the same subject. The authors are motivated to formalize and address this narrow-boundary safety problem, and to provide systematic ways to generate, complete, and evaluate training data that capture both sides of the refusal boundary.
AI.method: They define “narrow-boundary safety” as alignment where the model must distinguish, within a single topic, between harmful and benign requests and respond appropriately. To support this, they build an offline, self-generated data framework involving: (1) controlled topic generation to create prompts near the intended refusal boundary; (2) coverage repair to fill in gaps where no good refusal trace exists; (3) in-distribution compensation data to balance benign and harmful examples around the boundary; and (4) curated harmful–benign prompt pairs that differ primarily in intent. They introduce an “Escalate” strategy for multi-shot generation of refusal traces: if a first attempt at generating a refusal is not accepted, they retry with escalated prompts until acceptance or a limit is reached. They then train Qwen3-8B on these refusal and boundary-pair datasets, including variants where responses come from external models versus the target model itself, and evaluate on political persuasion tasks and several safety benchmarks (including XSTest) to quantify refusal, unsafe response, and over-refusal rates.
AI.result: Single-shot data generation for refusal traces leaves 19.88% of prompts without accepted refusals, whereas using the Escalate multi-shot strategy reduces this to 0.20%. For political persuasion tasks with Qwen3-8B, training on Escalate-completed refusal data boosts refusal in the target domain from 9.47% to 84.75% and cuts mean unsafe-response rate across three broader harmfulness benchmarks from 26.26% to 0.14%. However, this stronger safety training greatly increases over-refusal on XSTest from 2.00% to 74.00%, showing a usability loss. In a controlled comparison, substituting external-model responses with verified responses from the target model reduces over-refusal from 15.20% to 5.20%. Using boundary-pair data lowers over-refusal on the benign (comply) side of held-out pairs from 32.94% to 4.16%, while harmful-side refusal drops only slightly from 91.88% to 87.72%, preserving most safety. These metrics demonstrate that how the data is constructed and sourced has large, quantifiable effects on both safety and over-refusal.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that narrow-boundary safety—distinguishing harmful from benign requests within the same topic—is feasible but highly sensitive to training data composition. The Escalate strategy provides near-complete refusal-trace coverage, enabling strong safety gains but also revealing substantial risks of over-refusal. Carefully balancing harmful, benign, and boundary-pair data, and preferring verified responses from the target model, can significantly mitigate over-refusal while largely preserving refusal performance on genuinely harmful content. Therefore, safety alignment should always be evaluated on both sides of the intended refusal boundary—measuring not only how well harmful content is blocked but also how often benign content is incorrectly refused—to manage the trade-off between safety and usability in real-world deployments.

title: ResLearn-XR: Residual Learning for Network Traffic and Quality-of-Experience-Aware Modeling in Extended Reality
summary: We present ResLearn-XR, a residual learning framework for predicting eXtended Reality (XR) network traffic and estimating Quality-of-Experience (QoE) risk. ResLearn-XR adopts a two-stage temporal learning structure comprising a base sequence prediction model augmented with task-specific residual learning components to improve adaptability to bursty, non-stationary XR traffic dynamics. The residual learning stages operate in the value space for continuous XR traffic forecasting and in the logit space for probabilistic QoE risk estimation. \rev{For the QoE-risk branch, we introduce a Data Descriptor Algorithm (DDA), a causal feature-construction module that converts packet-level application-layer observables into frame-timing-aware descriptors suitable for encrypted traffic analysis. We also construct an XR Traffic-QoE dataset that pairs continuous XR traffic traces with session-level user-reported QoE labels. ResLearn-XR reduces SMAPE by up to 17.84% across frame-count, frame-size, and inter-arrival-time prediction, while reducing QoE-risk estimation SMAPE by up to 87.8% over single-stage baselines.

AI.tldr: ResLearn-XR is a two-stage residual learning framework that improves prediction of XR network traffic and QoE risk over single-stage baselines.
AI.motivation: XR applications generate bursty, non-stationary encrypted network traffic, making it difficult to predict traffic patterns and assess user Quality-of-Experience risk using standard single-stage models. Accurate traffic prediction and QoE risk estimation are crucial for efficient network management and maintaining user experience.
AI.method: The authors design ResLearn-XR, a two-stage temporal learning framework. A base sequence prediction model first learns general traffic dynamics. Then task-specific residual learning components refine predictions: in value space for continuous XR traffic forecasting (frame count, frame size, inter-arrival times) and in logit space for probabilistic QoE risk estimation. For QoE risk, they propose a Data Descriptor Algorithm (DDA) that causally transforms packet-level application-layer signals into frame-timing-aware descriptors, enabling analysis even when traffic is encrypted. They also build an XR Traffic-QoE dataset linking continuous traffic traces with session-level user QoE labels.
AI.result: ResLearn-XR achieves up to 17.84% reduction in SMAPE for continuous XR traffic predictions (frame-count, frame-size, inter-arrival-time) and up to 87.8% reduction in SMAPE for QoE-risk estimation compared with single-stage baseline models.
AI.conclusion: A residual, two-stage temporal learning framework combined with causal feature construction (DDA) significantly improves both XR traffic prediction and QoE risk estimation, particularly for complex, bursty, and encrypted XR traffic. The newly constructed XR Traffic-QoE dataset supports these improvements and offers a resource for future research in XR network analytics.

title: Patterns of Priming in Production: Lexical, Semantic and Structural Alignment in Language Model Generation
summary: This paper investigates structural priming in language model (LM) production, examining how preceding structural context influences sentence completion. While prior work has demonstrated priming effects in comprehension of structural alternations, it remained unclear whether these persist in production, where, when generating, an LM samples from many possible continuations at each step. We address this question through a series of controlled sentence-completion experiments on dative constructions. In line with prior work, we find that LMs are susceptible to structural priming, particularly in sentences that are semantically coherent. In terms of priming magnitude, we find that while there is a greater relative increase of double-object datives against our baselines, in line with inverse frequency effects, there is a larger absolute increase in prepositional-objects, the more frequently produced construction. Finally, we not only observe that structural priming is boosted by lexico-semantic coherence, but that structurally primed completions display greater levels of lexico-semantic repetition. Taken together, our evidence supports the view that structural priming in LMs operates across multiple levels of linguistic representation, facilitating, and facilitated by syntactic, lexical, and semantic alignment. Code: https://github.com/the-context-lab/primedproduction.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that large language models exhibit structural priming effects in production-style sentence completion, especially for semantically coherent inputs, indicating that prior syntactic context shapes generated structure across multiple linguistic levels.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed structural priming—where exposure to a syntactic structure increases its later use—for language models mainly in comprehension-like settings (e.g., next-word prediction under controlled alternations). It was unclear whether such priming persists in a production scenario, where an LM must choose among many possible continuations at each step. The authors aim to test whether and how structural priming manifests in generative production, and what roles frequency and lexico-semantic coherence play.
AI.method: The authors run controlled sentence-completion experiments on dative alternations (double-object vs prepositional-object constructions). They present language models with primes that use one dative structure, then measure how that prior exposure affects the structure chosen in subsequent completions. They systematically vary semantic coherence to see how meaning influences priming. They quantify priming magnitude both relatively (change in proportion compared to baseline) and absolutely (raw increase in counts), and examine lexical-semantic repetition within the primed outputs.
AI.result: Language models show clear structural priming in production: prior exposure to a given dative structure increases the likelihood that the same structure appears in subsequent completions, especially in semantically coherent sentences. There is a stronger relative increase for the less frequent double-object dative (inverse frequency effect), but the absolute number of additional primed outputs is larger for the more common prepositional-object form. Primed completions also exhibit more lexico-semantic repetition, and priming is stronger when the primes and targets are semantically coherent.
AI.conclusion: Structural priming in language models is robust in a production-like setting and is modulated by frequency and semantic coherence. The pattern of effects suggests that priming in LMs is not purely syntactic but operates across interacting levels of representation—syntactic, lexical, and semantic—with alignment at one level facilitating alignment at others. This brings LM behavior closer to human-like structural priming phenomena and informs theories of how syntactic and semantic information is encoded and reused in neural language models.

title: Rethinking Indirect Prompt Injection as a Test-Time Search Problem
summary: We formulate indirect prompt injection as a test-time search over a task-dependent attack surface induced by the environment, user task, and injection task. To operationalize this formulation, we introduce an agentic attacker with a dedicated search harness that performs environment reconnaissance, structured reasoning over attack strategies, and adaptive evaluation using victim-agent feedback. Across heterogeneous tasks, we find that increasing attacker test-time compute improves vulnerability discovery and exploitation, while ablations show that explicit strategy management is important for avoiding redundant search and sustaining gains at larger budgets. These results suggest that agentic security evaluations should characterize both the attacker's search procedure and compute budget, rather than treating attack success as a budget-independent property of the victim. More broadly, our findings identify the attacker's adaptive search over the system attack surfaces as an important and underexplored security risk for tool-using agents.

AI.tldr: The paper studies indirect prompt injection attacks on tool-using AI agents by modeling them as a test-time search problem, and shows that stronger, compute-heavy agentic attackers can more effectively discover and exploit vulnerabilities.
AI.motivation: Existing work often treats prompt injection vulnerability as a static property of the victim model or agent, underestimating the role of an adaptive attacker that can search over complex, environment-induced attack surfaces. There is a need to systematically understand how an attacker’s search procedure and compute budget affect their ability to find and exploit indirect prompt injection opportunities in real, tool-using agent settings.
AI.method: The authors formally define indirect prompt injection as a test-time search over an attack surface shaped by the environment, the user’s task, and the attacker’s own injection goals. They then build an "agentic attacker" equipped with a search harness that (1) performs reconnaissance of the environment, (2) reasons in a structured way about different attack strategies, and (3) adaptively updates its search using feedback from the victim agent’s behavior. They run experiments across heterogeneous tasks and perform ablations, especially on the attacker’s strategy management and compute budget.
AI.result: Experiments across different tasks show that giving the attacker more test-time compute significantly improves its ability to discover and exploit indirect prompt injection vulnerabilities. Ablation studies demonstrate that explicit strategy management within the attacker reduces redundant search and is crucial for maintaining performance gains at larger compute budgets. Without such management, additional compute yields diminishing returns due to repeated exploration of similar strategies.
AI.conclusion: Indirect prompt injection risk for tool-using agents depends critically on the attacker’s adaptive search process and compute budget, not just on static properties of the victim. Effective, agentic attackers that systematically explore the environment’s attack surface can uncover more vulnerabilities, especially when endowed with more compute and good strategy management. Therefore, robust security evaluations should explicitly model and report the attacker’s search procedure and budget, and defenses must account for adaptive, search-based adversaries rather than assuming fixed, budget-independent attack capabilities.

title: Cultural Misalignment in Large Language Models: Detection, Measurement, and Mitigation Through Targeted Fine-Tuning
comment: 33 pages, 14 figures. Extended version of a paper published in the proceedings of OSSConf 2026, Zilina, Slovakia. Code and data: https://github.com/AntoniCzolgowski/llm-cultural-bias
summary: We evaluate three open-weight LLMs (Gemma3-12B from the USA, Bielik-11B-v3 from Poland, and Qwen3-4B from China) against World Values Survey Wave 7 data for 63 demographic personas across three countries, using normalized Wasserstein distance to quantify distributional misalignment. Contrary to expectations, no model favors its home country: the Chinese-built Qwen3-4B performs worst on its own Chinese population (W1 = 0.436, the highest misalignment in the entire model x country matrix). Targeted LoRA fine-tuning on the five worst-case personas, requiring fewer than 1,200 training pairs and under 15 minutes on a single GPU, reduces bias by 16.8% for Bielik-11B (p_Bonf = 0.002, d = -4.4) with all five targets improving. However, country-level decomposition reveals that fine-tuning redistributes rather than removes bias: Bielik's worst-case personas swap entirely from American to Chinese elderly, with zero overlap between pre- and post-correction sets. To our knowledge, this is the first study to target worst-case demographic personas with LoRA fine-tuning for cross-cultural bias mitigation.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates cross-cultural bias in three open-weight LLMs using survey-based ground truth, then attempts to mitigate worst-case demographic bias via targeted LoRA fine-tuning, finding that fine-tuning shifts rather than eliminates bias.
AI.motivation: LLMs are used globally but may not align with the values of diverse demographic groups, especially across countries. Existing evaluations often focus on average behavior, not worst-case misalignment for specific demographic personas, and mitigation methods may not be efficient or practical. The authors aim to rigorously quantify cross-cultural value misalignment and test whether lightweight LoRA fine-tuning can reduce severe (worst-case) demographic bias without heavy computational cost.
AI.method: They construct 63 demographic personas from World Values Survey Wave 7 data across three countries (USA, Poland, China). For each persona and model (Gemma3-12B, Bielik-11B-v3, Qwen3-4B), they elicit responses to survey-like questions and compare the resulting distributions to real WVS response distributions using normalized Wasserstein-1 distance as a measure of misalignment. They then identify the five worst-case personas for each model and perform targeted LoRA fine-tuning using fewer than 1,200 synthetic training pairs on a single GPU (<15 minutes). Post-tuning, they re-evaluate misalignment and decompose results by country and persona to see how bias patterns change.
AI.result: All three models show significant value misalignment, and unexpectedly, none is best aligned with its own country: Qwen3-4B is most misaligned with Chinese respondents (W1 = 0.436, the worst in the model–country matrix). Targeted LoRA fine-tuning notably reduces worst-case misalignment for Bielik-11B, achieving a 16.8% reduction in Wasserstein distance with strong statistical significance (Bonferroni-corrected p = 0.002, large effect size d = -4.4), and all five targeted personas improve. However, country-level analysis reveals that the locations of worst misalignment simply shift: Bielik’s worst personas move from American to Chinese elderly, with no overlap between pre- and post-tuning worst-case sets.
AI.conclusion: Cross-cultural value misalignment in LLMs is substantial and does not simply favor the model’s country of origin. Lightweight, targeted LoRA fine-tuning on worst-case personas can substantially reduce measured bias for those targets with minimal compute, but it tends to redistribute misalignment rather than remove it at a system level. Effective bias mitigation will require methods that address global, not just local, worst-case alignment, and the paper introduces a new experimental paradigm—worst-case persona targeting with LoRA—for future work on cross-cultural fairness in LLMs.

title: BioSync: Transformer-Based Cross-Modal Fusion for a Multimodal Physiological Digital Biomarker
summary: Cardiac, neural, behavioral, and speech measurements from wearable and mobile devices provide partial, noise-sensitive views of physiological state. BioSync combines these measurements into the \textbf{BioSync Index (BSI)}, a continuous composite digital biomarker defined under the BEST framework. The model applies multi-head self-attention to modality tokens and adds a linear branch whose hypothesis class includes standard feature concatenation. This architecture is motivated by latent-variable measurement theory and by the possibility that joint observations contain information unavailable from individual modalities. We evaluated BioSync on two literature-informed synthetic cohorts: a four-modality cognitive-decline cohort using HRV, EEG, actigraphy, and speech, and a metabolic-autonomic cohort structured around the public AI-READI wearable schema. In the cognitive cohort, BioSync and concatenation obtained AUCs of 0.928 and 0.926, respectively. In the metabolic cohort, BioSync obtained accuracy/F1 of 0.764/0.766, compared with 0.756/0.758 for concatenation. The BSI correlated with latent severity in both cohorts ($r=0.91$ and $r=0.68$). A pure-attention ablation obtained cognitive-cohort AUC 0.911, locating the increase to 0.928 in the combined wide-and-deep architecture. With matched modality-dropout training, BioSync led concatenation at five of six cognitive-cohort corruption rates and at the highest metabolic-cohort rate. Its cognitive-cohort AUC was also higher than five published digital-biomarker reference values, although differences in datasets and tasks preclude a controlled benchmark claim. Comparison with single-modality, early-fusion, and late-fusion designs across six prespecified criteria identifies the model's computational properties; validation on real cohorts remains necessary.

AI.tldr: Introduces BioSync, a self-attention based multimodal model that fuses wearable and mobile device data into a continuous composite biomarker (BioSync Index, BSI), showing modest but consistent gains over standard feature concatenation and single-modality baselines on synthetic cohorts.
AI.motivation: Physiological state is increasingly measured via heterogeneous, noisy data streams from wearables and mobile devices (heart, neural, behavioral, speech). Existing approaches often treat modalities separately or use simple concatenation, potentially missing cross-modal interactions and shared latent factors. There is a need for a principled, BEST-framework-aligned composite digital biomarker that: (1) aggregates multiple modalities, (2) is robust to noise and missing data, and (3) reflects an underlying latent disease severity or physiological state, while being comparable to and improving upon current fusion strategies.
AI.method: The paper proposes BioSync, a multimodal architecture that represents each modality as a token and applies multi-head self-attention across tokens to capture cross-modal dependencies. In parallel, a linear ‘wide’ branch operates on concatenated features; this branch’s hypothesis class subsumes standard feature concatenation models. The outputs of the attention-based ‘deep’ branch and the linear branch are combined into a wide-and-deep model that produces the BioSync Index (BSI), a continuous latent biomarker. The approach is evaluated on synthetic cohorts constructed from literature: (1) a 4-modality cognitive-decline cohort (HRV, EEG, actigraphy, speech), and (2) a metabolic-autonomic cohort based on the AI-READI wearable schema. The authors run ablations (pure attention vs wide-and-deep), modality-dropout experiments to simulate missing/corrupted modalities, and comparisons against early-/late-fusion and single-modality designs along prespecified computational criteria.
AI.result: On the cognitive-decline synthetic cohort, BioSync achieves an AUC of 0.928, slightly surpassing a pure concatenation model (AUC 0.926) and a pure-attention ablation (AUC 0.911), suggesting that the wide-and-deep fusion is beneficial. On the metabolic-autonomic cohort, BioSync reaches accuracy/F1 of 0.764/0.766, again modestly exceeding concatenation (0.756/0.758). In both cohorts, the continuous BSI shows strong correlations with latent disease/severity variables (r=0.91 for cognitive, r=0.68 for metabolic). Under matched modality-dropout training, BioSync outperforms concatenation in five of six corruption levels in the cognitive cohort and at the highest corruption level in the metabolic cohort, indicating better robustness to missing or noisy modalities. Its AUC on the cognitive cohort exceeds five published digital-biomarker reference values, though the authors note that dataset/task differences prevent a formal benchmark claim.
AI.conclusion: BioSync provides a principled multimodal fusion architecture and a continuous composite biomarker (BSI) that modestly but consistently outperforms standard concatenation and several alternative fusion strategies on synthetic data. The wide-and-deep design, combining a multi-head self-attention branch with a linear concatenation branch, appears to capture cross-modal structure while retaining the strengths of simpler models, and it is more robust to modality corruption in most tested conditions. The work is positioned as a methodological and conceptual contribution—grounded in latent-variable measurement theory and the BEST framework—rather than a definitive clinical validation; the authors explicitly state that testing on real-world cohorts is still required to establish external validity and practical utility.

title: Towards Understanding Pause Token Fine-Tuning Dynamics: A Mode Retention Perspective
summary: Pause-token methods improve LLM reasoning by inserting special tokens into sequences. Prior work explains these gains through computational expressivity. However, there is relatively little investigation into the training dynamics of pause tokens. We explore how pause tokens reshape the training dynamics of fine-tuning. Two controlled pilots expose distinct asymmetries. On a synthetic continual-learning task, masked pauses overwrite a previously-learned distribution roughly 4x less at matched final adaptation (H1, mode retention); on a synthetic math-reasoning probe, the boundary-adjacent token comes to encode substantially more downstream-step information (H2, non-myopic compression). We formalize a training rule consistent with both - Masked Boundary Pause (MBP), pause tokens placed at reasoning-step boundaries with their loss masked. Across 1B-8B Qwen and Llama models, MBP consistently improves reasoning, achieving gains of up to 6 points on math and 2.5 points on code, while preserving general language understanding abilities. We further demonstrate that this mode-preserving strategy extend gains to GRPO. These results recast pause tokens as a training-dynamics intervention on the retention-adaptation trade-off, rather than merely an inference-time computation device.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how pause tokens affect the training dynamics of LLM fine-tuning and proposes Masked Boundary Pause (MBP), which improves reasoning performance while preserving prior capabilities.
AI.motivation: Pause tokens are known to improve LLM reasoning, but explanations have focused on computational expressivity at inference time, with little understanding of how they change training dynamics, especially the balance between adapting to new tasks and retaining previously learned capabilities.
AI.method: The authors run two controlled synthetic experiments: (1) a continual-learning task to measure how much new training overwrites a previously learned distribution, and (2) a synthetic math reasoning probe to study how information is distributed across tokens. From the observed asymmetries, they formalize a training rule called Masked Boundary Pause (MBP), where pause tokens are inserted at reasoning-step boundaries and excluded from the loss. They then apply MBP to Qwen and Llama models (1B–8B) and evaluate on math, code, and general language understanding tasks, also testing integration with GRPO.
AI.result: In the continual-learning setting, models with masked pause tokens overwrite prior knowledge about 4x less for the same final level of adaptation, supporting the hypothesis of improved mode retention. In the math reasoning probe, tokens near the pause boundary encode more information about future reasoning steps, indicating non-myopic compression. Empirically, MBP yields consistent improvements: up to +6 points on math benchmarks and +2.5 points on code tasks for Qwen and Llama models, with negligible degradation on general language understanding. Incorporating MBP into GRPO further improves performance.
AI.conclusion: Pause tokens are better understood as a training-dynamics intervention that reshapes the retention–adaptation trade-off rather than just an inference-time computational trick. The proposed Masked Boundary Pause (MBP) rule leverages mode retention and non-myopic compression to improve reasoning and code performance, while largely preserving general language skills and extending benefits to GRPO-based training.

title: What Does Multi-Harness RL Learn? Credit Assignment and Portability in Coding Agents
summary: Agent reinforcement learning (RL) increasingly runs through full execution harnesses, and a multi-harness recipe mixes two choices: exposing the policy to several harnesses, and comparing their rewards inside one relative-advantage group. We isolate the second choice in repository-level coding. From one Qwen3-8B supervised warm start we replay the same frozen task-harness records from Aider, OpenHands, Qwen Code, and SWE-agent, with the same number of updates, under two rules for group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), Within (one group per task-harness pair) and Cross (harnesses pooled within a task), and score every checkpoint with a sealed SWE-bench Verified oracle on four source harnesses and a minimal harness held out of training. The evaluation harness is the dominant variable: across 24,000 sealed evaluations it moves the mean solve rate from 2.14\% to 9.27\%, a factor of 4.3, where the training recipe moves it by 1.16. The grouping rule is not. On the held-out harness, Cross minus Within is +0.25 pp, 95\% confidence interval [-0.48, +1.02], at eight attempts per task, and +0.16 [-0.41, +0.72] pooled over three training seeds whose individual estimates change sign. Each rule's own seed range, 0.42 to 0.45 pp, exceeds the difference between them. Both rules place their largest gains on the same source harness. The pooled advantage carries the harness: an out-of-fold classifier recovers the generating harness from Cross's advantage +4.48 pp above the shuffled-label baseline and from Within's not at all, and the two rules still reach the same held-out score and action distribution inside each harness. Re-collecting half the training data on-policy does not change this. Cross-harness credit yields configuration adaptation and no more portable capability than within-harness credit. Multi-harness RL reports should state the grouping boundary and test under an unseen harness.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how different ways of grouping multiple execution harnesses during reinforcement learning affect code agent performance, finding that the choice of evaluation harness has a much larger impact than the specific grouping rule used in GRPO.
AI.motivation: As code agents are increasingly trained via reinforcement learning across multiple execution harnesses (e.g., Aider, OpenHands, Qwen Code, SWE-agent), there is confusion about whether mixing harnesses and how they are grouped for relative-advantage computations yields more general and portable capabilities. Clarifying the impact of grouping rules is necessary for reliable comparison and reporting of multi-harness RL results.
AI.method: Starting from the same supervised Qwen3-8B initialization, the authors replay identical frozen task-harness trajectories from four existing systems using Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) under two grouping schemes: Within (separate groups per task-harness pair) and Cross (pooling harnesses within a task). They keep the number of updates fixed, score periodic checkpoints with a sealed SWE-bench Verified oracle across four source harnesses plus one unseen minimal harness, and perform extensive evaluations (24,000 sealed runs). They also analyze seed variability, conduct an out-of-fold harness-classification experiment using advantage signals, and repeat with partial on-policy data collection.
AI.result: The evaluation harness accounts for large swings in measured performance: mean solve rate varies from 2.14% to 9.27% (4.3×) purely by choice of harness, while the training recipe (Within vs Cross GRPO) only changes performance by a factor of 1.16. The difference between Cross and Within on the held-out harness is small and statistically indistinguishable from zero (e.g., +0.25 percentage points with a wide confidence interval that includes zero), and smaller than the performance spread across random seeds within each method. Both grouping rules concentrate their gains on the same source harness. Cross-harness credit makes the advantage signal predictive of the underlying harness (+4.48 pp over shuffled baseline), while Within does not, yet both achieve almost identical held-out performance and action distributions. Recollecting half the data on-policy does not materially change outcomes.
AI.conclusion: How results are evaluated (which harness is used) matters far more than how multi-harness data are grouped inside GRPO. Cross-harness credit assignment mainly causes configuration adaptation to specific harnesses rather than creating more portable capabilities, and yields no clear generalization benefit over within-harness credit. Consequently, multi-harness RL work should explicitly state the grouping boundary used for relative-advantage computation and should be validated on at least one unseen execution harness to avoid overinterpreting configuration-specific gains.

title: LentEx: Generalizable Latent Entity Extraction via Synthetic Data and Instruction-Tuned LLMs
summary: Latent entity extraction (LEE) tackles the challenge of identifying implicit, contextually inferred entities within free text-an area where traditional entity extraction methods fall short. In this paper, we introduce LentEx, a novel framework for latent entity extraction that leverages synthetic data generation and instruction fine-tuning to optimize smaller, efficient large language models (LLMs). Latent entities, which are often abstract and thematic, are crucial for applications such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), customer persona analysis, and knowledge graph enrichment. LentEx addresses the scarcity of labeled datasets by employing a template-based approach to generate diverse, contextually rich synthetic data, ensuring high variability and alignment with real-world distributions. To our knowledge, LentEx is the first to systematically approach LEE through the lens of LLMs. LentEx demonstrates significant performance improvements across multiple tasks, notably surpassing state-of-the-art models on the MTEB Clustering Benchmark. Furthermore, our methodology enables robust generalization to unseen domains, making LentEx highly applicable in real-world NLP tasks, including RAG and clustering, thereby establishing a new paradigm for latent entity understanding and extraction in natural language processing.

AI.tldr: The paper presents LentEx, a framework that uses synthetic data and instruction-tuned small LLMs to extract implicit, context-dependent latent entities from text, improving over prior methods and generalizing well to new domains.
AI.motivation: Traditional entity extraction focuses on explicit, surface-form entities and struggles with latent, abstract, or thematic entities that are only inferable from context. These latent entities are important for downstream applications such as RAG, customer persona analysis, and knowledge graph enrichment, yet there is a scarcity of labeled data and no systematic LLM-based approach to this problem. The paper aims to fill this gap by building an efficient, LLM-centered solution for latent entity extraction that can work with limited supervision and generalize to real-world scenarios.
AI.method: The authors propose LentEx, a latent entity extraction framework built around smaller, instruction-tuned LLMs. To overcome the lack of labeled data, they design a template-based synthetic data generation pipeline that creates diverse, contextually rich training instances aligned with real-world distributions. These synthetic examples are used to instruction fine-tune compact LLMs for LEE. The framework is evaluated on multiple tasks, including clustering benchmarks and downstream NLP applications like RAG and domain-generalization scenarios.
AI.result: LentEx achieves significant performance gains over baselines, including surpassing state-of-the-art models on the MTEB Clustering Benchmark. It shows strong robustness and generalization to unseen domains, indicating that the combination of synthetic data generation and instruction-tuned smaller LLMs is effective for latent entity extraction and related tasks.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes LentEx as a new LLM-based paradigm for latent entity extraction, demonstrating that synthetic, template-generated training data plus instruction tuning of smaller LLMs can effectively identify implicit, abstract entities. This approach not only outperforms existing methods on clustering benchmarks but also generalizes well to new domains, making it practical for real-world applications like RAG, clustering, customer understanding, and knowledge graph enrichment.

title: MaxKernel: Agentic Kernel Generation for TPUs
summary: Designing and authoring high-performance custom kernels for accelerators is a complex task that requires deep hardware-level expertise. Large Language Models (LLM) can be leveraged together with real-time compiler feedback to build agentic systems for kernel generation. In this work, we present MaxKernel, a multi-agent system that implements three distinct paradigms for TPU kernel development: (1) a Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) agent for collaborative, step-by-step design; (2) an Autonomous (Auto) agent that executes a fully automated, metric/trace-driven optimization loop; and (3) a Graph-Based Autonomous Search that scales the Auto agent for global exploration of the design space. All three paradigms leverage a shared pool of specialized sub-agents to handle planning, implementation, self-debugging, testing, and hardware profiling. We evaluate MaxKernel on JaxBench, a comprehensive suite of 50 diverse kernel tasks for TPUs, alongside complex, real-world workloads from state-of-the-art open-source models. We demonstrate that MaxKernel consistently generates highly optimized implementations, matching expert hand-tuned baselines and delivering significant performance across the benchmark. Our agent is open-sourced and available https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/accelerator-agents/tree/main/MaxKernel.

AI.tldr: MaxKernel is a multi-agent LLM-based system that automatically and interactively generates high-performance TPU kernels, often matching expert hand-tuned implementations.
AI.motivation: Writing and optimizing custom kernels for hardware accelerators like TPUs is difficult, requires deep hardware expertise, and is time-consuming. As models and workloads grow more complex, there is a need to automate kernel design and optimization so that non-experts can obtain near hand-tuned performance and experts can iterate faster. LLMs plus compiler feedback present an opportunity to create agent systems that explore kernel design spaces efficiently.
AI.method: The authors build MaxKernel, a multi-agent framework driven by an LLM and real-time compiler/hardware feedback. It supports three paradigms: (1) Human-in-the-Loop, where a user collaborates step-by-step with the agent; (2) an Autonomous agent that runs a closed-loop optimization process using metrics and traces to iteratively refine kernels; and (3) a Graph-Based Autonomous Search that scales the autonomous process to globally explore the kernel design space. All three use shared sub-agents for planning, code implementation, self-debugging, testing, and hardware performance profiling on TPUs. They evaluate on JaxBench (50 TPU kernel tasks) and real-world model workloads.
AI.result: On JaxBench and several complex, real-world open-source model workloads, MaxKernel consistently produces highly optimized TPU kernels. Its performance matches expert hand-tuned baselines in many cases and yields substantial speedups across the evaluated benchmarks, showing both strong effectiveness and generality.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent LLM-based systems, when coupled with compiler and hardware profiling feedback, can automate and scale the design and optimization of TPU kernels to near expert quality. MaxKernel’s three usage modes (HITL, autonomous, and graph-based global search) cover both interactive and fully automated scenarios, and its strong performance on diverse benchmarks suggests this approach is practical. The system is released as open source to support broader adoption and extension.

title: Scale-QLoRA: Code-Invariant Adapter Merging for Native 4-bit Microscaling LLMs
summary: Merging a LoRA adapter into its base model is standard deployment practice: it removes the runtime adapter's per-forward overhead and leaves a single standalone checkpoint any serving stack can load. On a native 4-bit microscaling checkpoint (NVFP4, MXFP4) that step stops being free. The merged weights must be written back through a quantizer, which re-derives the checkpoint's discrete E2M1 code plane (roughly 90% of the artifact's bytes), so the deployed artifact becomes coupled to one quantization convention, and every later code-touching event in its lifecycle can move it. Done naively the step is worse than fragile: it deletes the adaptation, by up to 39 pp, because against an already-on-grid base the reconstruction optimum is that base. Scale-QLoRA instead adapts only the native per-block scale field, trains those scales on the deployment grid, and freezes every E2M1 code. Within a fixed native format, scale grid, block layout and code plane, merging is then a bit-exact identity and the merged artifact is code-invariant. Across four models and four tasks, Scale-QLoRA and merge-aware QAT-LoRA are both accuracy-lossless, so we claim no accuracy ordering between them; they differ structurally, in that QAT-LoRA re-derives the code plane through a quantizer while Scale-QLoRA preserves it exactly. That difference is what the lifecycle prices: nearest-rounding implementations disagree by about a point on the measured task, and more extreme rule mismatches can drive the weight-space artifact to ~0%, which we report as a sensitivity bound rather than a deployment frequency. Preserving the code plane also drops the weight-space straight-through estimator from training (3.9x per step on the dense 8B model) and enables exact rollback, code-plane deduplication, and a ~125x faster scale-only task swap.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Scale-QLoRA, a method to merge LoRA adapters into 4-bit microscaled base models without losing accuracy or corrupting quantized weights, by training only per-block scales while keeping all quantized codes fixed.
AI.motivation: In standard LoRA deployment, the adapter is merged into the base model to avoid runtime overhead and yield a single checkpoint. However, for native 4-bit microscaled models (e.g., NVFP4, MXFP4), merging requires requantizing weights, which ties the model to a specific quantization rule and can significantly degrade or even erase the adaptation (up to 39 percentage points), making the process fragile and format-dependent. The authors want a merging method that is accurate, robust to quantization implementation differences, and preserves the original quantized representation.
AI.method: The authors propose Scale-QLoRA, which restricts adaptation to the per-block scale field of the native 4-bit format, training only these scales on the deployment grid while freezing all E2M1 codes (the discrete 4-bit mantissa/exponent plane). This ensures that within a fixed native format, scale grid, block layout, and code plane, merging is a bit-exact identity: no codes change, only scales. They compare this to a merge-aware QAT-LoRA approach that re-derives the code plane via quantization-aware training, requiring a quantizer in the loop and a straight-through estimator for gradients.
AI.result: Experiments on four models and four tasks show that both Scale-QLoRA and merge-aware QAT-LoRA are effectively lossless in accuracy compared to an unmerged LoRA baseline; no clear accuracy ordering emerges between them. However, they differ in robustness and efficiency: implementation differences in nearest rounding quantizers can cause about 1 point accuracy discrepancy, and more extreme differences in quantization rules can catastrophically degrade performance toward 0%, highlighting sensitivity when the code plane is re-derived. In contrast, preserving the original code plane avoids this issue and yields bit-exact merges.
AI.conclusion: Scale-QLoRA achieves lossless LoRA merging for native 4-bit microscaled models while preserving the exact quantized code plane. This eliminates dependence on specific quantizer implementations, avoids accuracy fragility from requantization, and removes the need for straight-through estimators, giving about 3.9x faster training steps on an 8B dense model. It also enables practical lifecycle benefits such as exact rollback, deduplication of shared code planes, and roughly 125x faster task swapping by updating only scale metadata rather than full quantized weights.

title: Towards a universal language of concepts: A survey
comment: Originally completed as an M.S. capstone project at UCLA in 2022
summary: Humans can learn and generalize novel concepts from sparse data because they express knowledge in rich structural formats. In this paper, we propose that programs are a strong candidate for universal representation of concepts. We review computational models of concept learning that use programs as their concept representation and evaluate their contribution toward a universal representational language.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that representing concepts as programs can explain how humans learn rich, generalizable concepts from limited data, and it surveys program-based models of concept learning as a candidate for a universal representational format.
AI.motivation: Humans are able to learn new concepts and generalize from very few examples, which is difficult for many current machine learning systems. A key hypothesis is that this ability comes from humans representing knowledge in rich, structured forms rather than as flat feature vectors or associations. The paper is motivated by the need for a representation that can capture this richness and support strong generalization, prompting the exploration of programs as a universal medium for representing concepts.
AI.method: The paper conceptually analyzes and reviews existing computational models of concept learning that treat concepts as programs. It examines how these models represent concepts, perform inference or learning over program spaces, and generalize from sparse data. Rather than introducing a single new algorithm, it synthesizes perspectives from multiple program-based approaches to evaluate them against the goal of a universal representational language for concepts.
AI.result: The review identifies that program-based representations can capture compositionality, hierarchy, and causal/algorithmic structure in concepts, and that models using such representations can achieve strong generalization from limited data in various domains (e.g., visual concepts, number concepts, rule systems). The paper shows that these models often outperform simpler, non-structured approaches on tasks requiring human-like concept learning and extrapolation.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that programs are a promising, possibly universal, representational format for human-like concept learning because they naturally encode rich structure and can support powerful generalization from sparse data. It emphasizes that program-based models provide a unifying framework for understanding diverse conceptual phenomena and suggests future work on more scalable inference, better languages of thought, and tighter connections to cognitive and neural data.

title: A Calibrated Reflection Approach for Enhancing Confidence Estimation in LLMs
summary: A critical challenge in deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) is developing reliable mechanisms to estimate their confidence, enabling systems to determine when to trust model outputs versus seek human intervention. We present a Calibrated Reflection approach for enhancing confidence estimation in LLMs, a framework that combines structured reasoning with distance-aware calibration technique. Our approach introduces three key innovations: (1) a Maximum Confidence Selection (MCS) method that comprehensively evaluates confidence across all possible labels, (2) a reflection-based prompting mechanism that enhances reasoning reliability, and (3) a distance-aware calibration technique that accounts for ordinal relationships between labels. We evaluate our framework on diverse datasets, including HelpSteer2, Llama T-REx, and a proprietary conversational dataset, demonstrating its effectiveness across both conversational and fact-based classification tasks.
