This work contributes to the broader goal of developing reliable and well-calibrated confidence estimation methods for LLMs, enabling informed decisions about model trust and human judgement.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Calibrated Reflection framework to improve confidence estimation in LLM outputs so systems can better decide when to trust the model or escalate to humans.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used in real applications, but they often provide overconfident or poorly calibrated probabilities for their answers. This makes it hard to know when their outputs are trustworthy and when human oversight is needed, especially in safety- or cost-critical scenarios. The paper aims to address this by developing more reliable and better-calibrated confidence estimation methods tailored to LLMs and to tasks where labels may have ordinal relationships.
AI.method: The method, called Calibrated Reflection, combines structured reasoning with a distance-aware calibration scheme. It has three main components: (1) Maximum Confidence Selection (MCS), which evaluates and compares confidence over all possible labels instead of focusing only on the chosen one; (2) a reflection-based prompting mechanism that asks the LLM to reason about and reflect on its own answers, improving the reliability of the internal signals used for confidence; and (3) a distance-aware calibration technique that explicitly models how far apart labels are in an ordinal space, so errors between nearby labels are treated differently from errors between distant labels. The framework is tested on multiple datasets, including HelpSteer2, Llama T-REx, and a proprietary conversational dataset, covering both conversational and factual classification tasks.
AI.result: Experiments on HelpSteer2, Llama T-REx, and an internal conversational dataset show that the proposed framework provides more effective and better-calibrated confidence estimates than baselines across both conversational and fact-based classification tasks. This leads to improved decisions on when to trust the LLM vs. defer to humans.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that combining reflection-based prompting with maximum confidence selection and distance-aware calibration yields more reliable confidence estimation for LLMs. This supports safer and more informed deployment of LLM systems by enabling better decisions about model trust and human intervention, and contributes generally to research on calibration and uncertainty estimation in large language models.

title: Data-Driven Discovery of Composition-Dependent Constitutive Models for Hyperelasticity and Viscoelasticity of Digital Materials
comment: 40 pages including references, 9 figures in the main manuscript. Supplementary material is available upon request from the corresponding author
summary: Digital materials fabricated by multi-material 3D printing are designed as controlled mixtures of stiff and compliant constituents, yielding effective responses that span more than an order of magnitude in apparent stiffness and exhibit strongly nonlinear, composition-dependent, and rate-dependent dissipative behavior. Classical finite-strain viscoelastic models represent such behavior with closed-form strain energy functions for equilibrium and non-equilibrium stresses as well as evolution of internal variables, which may limit flexibility when a single constitutive model is expected to generalize across materials and loading rates. Here, we present a data-driven multi-material constitutive modeling framework that generalizes a formulation by Bergström and Boyce. The proposed framework retains the structure of the classical model, namely multiplicative kinematics, invariant-based strain-energy functions, and a scalar dissipative evolution law directed along the normalized nonequilibrium deviatoric stress. For the equilibrium branch, the data-driven discovery framework either directly predicts closed-form model parameters as functions of composition or automatically constructs a polyconvex strain-energy function using neural ordinary differential equations (NODEs). The nonequilibrium branch kinetics are learned similarly, either by directly identifying closed-form parameters across compositions or by using appropriately constrained artificial neural networks. Using multi-rate uniaxial compression data across multiple material compositions, we show that the proposed formulation captures rate-dependent stiffness and hysteresis across compositions while preserving thermodynamic consistency.

AI.tldr: They develop a data-driven constitutive model for multi-material 3D-printed polymers that generalizes a classical viscoelastic model to accurately capture composition- and rate-dependent stiffness and dissipation.
AI.motivation: Multi-material 3D-printed structures are made from mixtures of stiff and compliant phases. Their overall mechanical behavior (stiffness, nonlinearity, dissipation, rate effects) changes strongly with composition and loading rate. Classical viscoelastic models use fixed closed-form equations that are often too rigid to generalize well across different compositions and strain rates, limiting predictive accuracy and design flexibility. A more flexible, data-driven yet thermodynamically consistent framework is needed to capture the full range of behaviors in a unified way.
AI.method: They start from the Bergström–Boyce finite-strain viscoelastic framework (multiplicative decomposition of deformation, invariant-based strain-energy functions, scalar evolution law along normalized nonequilibrium deviatoric stress). Within this structure, they introduce a data-driven layer. For the equilibrium response, they either (i) learn how closed-form material parameters depend on composition, or (ii) construct a polyconvex strain-energy density using neural ODEs. For the nonequilibrium (viscoelastic) branch, they similarly either fit composition-dependent closed-form kinetic parameters or employ constrained neural networks to learn the evolution laws. The model is trained and validated using multi-rate uniaxial compression tests over a range of material compositions.
AI.result: The proposed model reproduces the observed rate-dependent stiffness and hysteresis for multiple compositions of 3D-printed digital materials. It accurately captures how apparent stiffness spans more than an order of magnitude and how dissipation varies with composition and loading rate, while maintaining the structural features of the Bergström–Boyce formulation and satisfying thermodynamic requirements such as polyconvexity and positive dissipation.
AI.conclusion: A data-driven constitutive framework embedded in a classical finite-strain viscoelastic structure can successfully model complex, composition- and rate-dependent behavior of multi-material 3D-printed polymers. By learning either closed-form parameter maps or directly the strain energy and kinetic laws with constrained neural networks / NODEs, the approach provides a unified, thermodynamically consistent tool for predicting mechanical responses across a family of digital materials, facilitating design and optimization of multi-material printed structures.

title: Rhythms of Work: Multi-Scale Interpretation of Human Behavioral Traces for Workplace Agents
summary: Runtime traces are becoming a central substrate for understanding agentic systems, yet interpretation has focused largely on what the agent did. Workplace agents face the complementary problem: interpreting the human activity that surrounds them. Hours of low-level events carry rich evidence about a user's state but are too granular to reason over directly, and flattening them into one stream or compressing them into a single embedding both treat "summarize the user's behavior" as if it had one correct answer. We argue instead that behavioral interpretation is resolution-dependent: the same trace should admit multiple addressable interpretations at different temporal resolutions. We construct a multi-resolution vocabulary of semantically normalized operators, recurring motifs, coherent episodes, and day-level rhythms, each preserving the structure salient at its own horizon. Applied to 667 million human-attributed events from a large commercial productivity suite (50,000 users, 100 organizations), it yields 120 operator types, thousands of motifs, 25 episode types, and five day-rhythm archetypes. We validate it on real telemetry: re-running the entire pipeline on a disjoint 2,000-user sample recovers the same taxonomy (structural stability), and on held-out users the full representation forecasts a user's next episode more accurately than a flat-operator baseline, a 17% relative macro-F1 gain (predictive validity), so the abstractions preserve future-relevant information rather than merely describe it. A controlled resolution ablation then shows that no single level is optimal across questions: different agent-facing questions about the same trace are best answered at different resolutions. Behavioral trace interpretation for agents should therefore be multi-resolution and query-conditioned: an agent should access the temporal grain a question needs, not one universal summary.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multi-resolution framework for interpreting human behavioral traces from digital workplace telemetry, showing that different temporal resolutions yield complementary, query-dependent insights and improve prediction over flat representations.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches to interpreting runtime traces and activity logs often treat human or agent behavior as something that can be summarized with a single, flat representation (e.g., one event stream or one embedding). This ignores that behavior unfolds over multiple time scales and that different tasks or questions require different temporal granularity. Workplace agents, which must understand surrounding human activity to be helpful, need structured, interpretable, and reusable abstractions from massive amounts of low-level telemetry. The authors aim to build such a structured, multi-resolution representation and test whether it is stable, predictive, and useful across questions.
AI.method: The authors design a hierarchical, multi-resolution vocabulary for human behavioral traces derived from low-level events in a large commercial productivity suite. They define and learn: (1) semantically normalized operator types from raw low-level events; (2) recurring motifs as common local patterns of operators; (3) coherent episodes as longer, semantically meaningful activity segments; and (4) day-level rhythms as archetypal temporal structures in a workday. They apply this pipeline to 667 million human-attributed events from about 50,000 users across 100 organizations, extracting 120 operator types, thousands of motifs, 25 episode types, and five day-rhythm archetypes. They then evaluate the learned taxonomy on new data for stability and predictive power, and run a resolution ablation to compare performance of different levels of the hierarchy on various predictive tasks.
AI.result: From the large telemetry dataset, the framework discovers a rich multi-level taxonomy: 120 operator types, thousands of motifs, 25 episode types, and five distinct day-rhythm archetypes. When re-run on a disjoint 2,000-user sample, the pipeline recovers essentially the same taxonomy, demonstrating structural stability. Using held-out users, the full multi-resolution representation outperforms a flat-operator baseline in forecasting a user's next episode, achieving a 17% relative macro-F1 improvement, showing predictive validity. The resolution ablation study reveals that no single temporal resolution is best for all questions; different prediction or interpretation tasks perform best when using different levels of the hierarchy.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral interpretation from runtime traces is inherently resolution-dependent: there is no single canonical summary of a user's behavior. A multi-resolution, query-conditioned representation—spanning operators, motifs, episodes, and day-level rhythms—captures stable, future-relevant structure in human activity traces. For agentic systems operating in workplaces, agents should dynamically choose the temporal granularity that matches the question they are answering, rather than rely on one fixed, flattened summary or embedding of behavior.

title: From Answers to Interpretations: Rethinking Ambiguity-Induced Aleatoric Uncertainty Estimation in LLMs
summary: A key challenge in reliable LLM deployment is recognizing when uncertainty reflects irreducible variability in the task rather than limitations in the model's knowledge. In language tasks, a central source of such aleatoric uncertainty is input ambiguity or underspecification, where multiple interpretations remain plausible. Existing decomposition methods estimate aleatoric uncertainty by generating multiple clarifications of the input, querying the model for an answer under each clarification, and comparing the resulting answers. We argue that answers are not necessary for identifying ambiguity: they are often redundant, add avoidable cost, and can mislead through epistemic leakage. We support this claim theoretically, and propose a clarification-only approach that estimates this ambiguity-induced component directly from the space of plausible interpretations, without answers to the clarified inputs. Using ambiguity detection as an operational evaluation across three benchmarks, this direct approach improves AUROC (63.34 vs. 60.85), reduces computational cost by 4-26x in output tokens and 2.2-3.5x in API calls, and yields estimates with substantially lower correlation with epistemic uncertainty. Overall, our results suggest that ambiguity-induced aleatoric uncertainty is better estimated from the interpretation space than from the response space.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a cheaper, more reliable way to detect ambiguity-induced (aleatoric) uncertainty in LLM tasks by analyzing possible input interpretations instead of generating and comparing answers.
AI.motivation: In deploying LLMs reliably, it is crucial to distinguish between uncertainty due to inherent task ambiguity (aleatoric) and uncertainty from lack of knowledge or model limitations (epistemic). Existing aleatoric decomposition methods require generating explicit answers to multiple clarified versions of the input, which is costly and can contaminate aleatoric estimates with epistemic effects (epistemic leakage). The authors want a method that isolates ambiguity-driven uncertainty more cleanly and efficiently.
AI.method: They theoretically analyze why using answers to clarified inputs is unnecessary and potentially harmful for estimating ambiguity. Based on this, they introduce a clarification-only method that samples or explores the space of plausible interpretations/clarifications of the original input and directly measures ambiguity from this interpretation space, without querying the model for final task answers. They then operationalize this as an ambiguity detection task and evaluate it on three benchmarks, comparing performance and cost to answer-based decomposition methods.
AI.result: Across three benchmarks, the clarification-only approach improves ambiguity detection performance (AUROC 63.34 vs. 60.85), substantially cuts computational cost (4–26× fewer output tokens and 2.2–3.5× fewer API calls), and produces aleatoric uncertainty estimates that are much less correlated with epistemic uncertainty, indicating cleaner separation of the two uncertainty types.
AI.conclusion: Ambiguity-induced aleatoric uncertainty in language tasks is more accurately and efficiently captured by modeling the space of plausible interpretations of the input rather than by generating and comparing answers to clarified inputs. Answers are often redundant, introduce extra cost, and risk epistemic leakage, so clarification-only methods should be preferred for decomposing uncertainty in LLM deployments.

title: When Do Internal Probes Beat Reading the Answer? Miscalibrated Readouts and Behavior-Concealed Knowledge in Language Models
summary: A 0.6B language model, asked to verify 1,200 logical conclusions (half valid, half corrupted by a single semantic edit), answers YES every time. Judged by behavior it discriminates nothing; linear probes on its hidden states read the correct verdict at 0.96 AUC, transferring to unseen logical structures and separating foils built from exactly the words of the true conclusion (0.90). We ask where the verdict is lost, and find the dominant failure is a single scalar. The verdict survives to the model's own output logits (margin AUC 0.89) along a well-aligned readout direction; a saturated decision threshold, offset by +4.6 sigma, erases it. The diagnosis generalizes: across 90 semantic-label configurations of a five-model, three-family factorial, behavioral accuracy collapses onto a single function of threshold offset (Spearman -0.93) while margin ranking moves far less. Across a 13x scale range, internal knowledge saturates while free-form behavior is non-monotone: an 8B model underperforms its 4B sibling through an answer-channel failure rather than the threshold; forced-choice accuracy is monotone. The diagnosis is actionable: a one-parameter correction, never fit on evaluated structures, repairs behavior from 50% to 81% (0.6B); calibrated margin decoding recovers 94% at 8B; few-shot prompting works the same way, recentering the threshold (+4.6 sigma to 0.0 sigma) while preserving ranking. Comparing probe to margin separates three regimes: concealed, miscalibrated, and undetected. On a maze task built so foils carry no surface cues, the audit correctly reports the third. In the standard generation setting, answer-surface features and heuristic labels reproduce published probing results without any internal access.

AI.tldr: The paper finds that small language models internally compute correct logical validity judgments, but their final YES/NO behavior hides this knowledge due to a mis-set decision threshold, which can be fixed with simple post-hoc calibration.
AI.motivation: Large language models often appear to fail at logical reasoning when judged by their answers, but interpretability tools like linear probes sometimes show that models internally represent the right information. This paper aims to pinpoint where and how this internal knowledge is lost between hidden states and final outputs, and whether the gap can be systematically diagnosed and repaired.
AI.method: The authors use a 0.6B-parameter language model on a controlled logical validity task with 1,200 conclusions (half valid, half corrupted by a minimal semantic edit). They train linear probes on hidden states to detect the correct YES/NO verdict and analyze the model’s output logits and decision threshold. They then extend this analysis across multiple model families and sizes, varying label semantics, and use metrics like AUC and threshold offset to characterize behavior. Finally, they test corrective decoding schemes (one-parameter threshold shifts, calibrated margin decoding, few-shot prompting) and apply the diagnostic to a maze task and standard generation settings.
AI.result: The base 0.6B model outputs YES for all 1,200 items (50% accuracy), but linear probes achieve ~0.96 AUC on hidden states and ~0.89 AUC on the output-logit margin, showing that the model internally distinguishes valid from invalid conclusions. The main failure is a single scalar: the effective decision threshold is shifted by about +4.6 standard deviations, saturating the YES decision and erasing discrimination. Across five models and three families with 90 label configurations, behavioral accuracy largely collapses onto a function of this threshold offset (Spearman correlation -0.93), while ranking quality (margins) varies less. Scaling shows internal knowledge improving monotonically, but free-form behavioral accuracy can be non-monotone; an 8B model performs worse than a 4B sibling on free-form answers due to an answer-channel failure, not worse reasoning. Applying a one-parameter correction boosts the 0.6B model’s accuracy from 50% to 81%; at 8B, calibrated margin decoding recovers 94% accuracy. Few-shot prompting also primarily recenters the threshold without changing the underlying ranking. The probe-vs-margin comparison reveals three regimes—concealed, miscalibrated, and undetected knowledge—and on a maze task designed to avoid surface cues, the method correctly reports the undetected regime. In standard generation benchmarks, surface-level features can replicate some probing-style findings even without internal access.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that, at least for the studied logical tasks, many apparent reasoning failures in language models are not due to an absence of internal knowledge but to how that knowledge is read out through a poorly calibrated decision channel. A single scalar threshold can largely explain dramatic gaps between internal representations and overt behavior, and simple post-hoc or prompting-based recalibrations can substantially repair performance without changing the underlying model. This suggests that evaluations focused only on final outputs can underestimate models’ latent reasoning abilities, and that distinguishing concealed, miscalibrated, and truly absent knowledge is crucial for both interpretability and capability assessment.

title: IPGeoAI: Transformer-Based Geolocation with LLM Semantic Fusion
summary: Accurate city-level IP Geolocation is an important enabler for the modern digital ecosystem, underpinning services ranging from local content delivery and targeting to digital rights enforcement. However, traditional heuristic and database-driven methods often struggle to resolve the complex, non-linear allocation patterns of modern network infrastructures, particularly within the exploding IPv6 address space and transient mobile networks. In this paper, we introduce IPGeoAI, a novel deep learning model architecture that reframes geolocation from a static lookup problem to a sequential modeling task. Our approach utilizes the Transformer Encoder to capture hierarchical dependencies inherent in IP subnet structures. We propose a method to resolve geographic ambiguity by integrating unstructured semantic context via a Zero-Shot LLM Feature Extraction pipeline. We utilize Large Language Models to transform raw, noisy Autonomous Systems (AS) descriptions into structured, domain-specific metadata (such as 'University' vs. 'ISP' or 'Global' vs. 'Local') via an offline pre-computation process. By fusing these semantic signals into the network via a Multi-Head Cross-Attention module, we bridge the gap between numerical network topology and real-world semantic identity. Extensive offline evaluation on a proprietary dataset spanning 200,000 cities demonstrates that IPGeoAI significantly outperforms a leading external vendor in city-level granularity. By adopting a hierarchical inference strategy that refines coarse-grained country signals, our model achieves a 6% improvement in city-level accuracy while extending coverage to 100% of the traffic. Furthermore, in large-scale online production tests, the model drove a statistically significant +0.35% improvement in our 1st-tier downstream use cases metric.

AI.tldr: IPGeoAI is a Transformer-based IP geolocation system that treats IPs as sequences, enriches them with LLM-derived AS semantics, and achieves better city-level accuracy and full coverage compared to a leading vendor, with measurable online gains.
AI.motivation: Existing IP geolocation methods (heuristics, databases) cannot reliably resolve complex, non-linear address allocation patterns, especially for IPv6 and mobile networks. There is a need for more accurate, scalable city-level geolocation that can handle modern network dynamics and support critical downstream services (local content, targeting, rights enforcement).
AI.method: Reframe IP geolocation as a sequential prediction problem over IP/subnet structures using a Transformer Encoder to model hierarchical dependencies. Extract semantic metadata from noisy Autonomous System descriptions using an offline Zero-Shot LLM pipeline (classifying ASes as University vs ISP, Global vs Local, etc.). Fuse these structured semantic features with numerical network features via a Multi-Head Cross-Attention module. Use a hierarchical inference strategy that first predicts coarse country-level signals and then refines them to city-level predictions.
AI.result: On a proprietary dataset covering 200,000 cities, IPGeoAI outperforms a leading commercial vendor at city-level resolution, achieving a 6% increase in city-level accuracy while providing 100% coverage of observed traffic. In online production A/B tests, deploying IPGeoAI yields a statistically significant +0.35% improvement in a primary downstream business metric for first-tier use cases.
AI.conclusion: Modeling IP addresses with Transformers and enriching them with LLM-derived AS semantics enables materially better city-level IP geolocation than traditional database-driven approaches. The method scales to modern IPv6 and mobile environments, improves coverage, and delivers measurable business impact, suggesting that combining numerical network topology with semantic identity is a powerful paradigm for geolocation and related network intelligence tasks.

title: PetQA: Benchmarking Veterinary Knowledge and Clinical Reasoning
summary: We introduce PetQA, a Korean long-form question-answering (QA) benchmark for evaluating veterinary knowledge and clinical reasoning in large language models (LLMs) and large vision-language models (LVLMs). PetQA contains 10,076 text-only and 8,751 multimodal QA pairs derived from real-world questions about dogs and cats, paired with answers from expert veterinarians. Its test split, PetQA-Bench, further includes annotations for question types and clinical conditions. We evaluate eighteen models using ROUGE, BERTScore, and LLM-as-a-judge metrics for factuality and helpfulness under three settings: zero-shot inference, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). The benchmarking results provide an overview of the strengths and limitations of current models in addressing veterinary clinical queries and highlight the need for more effective adaptation methods to develop clinically reliable AI systems for veterinary care. To facilitate broader use, we additionally provide translated versions of PetQA-Bench in five languages.

AI.tldr: PetQA is a Korean long-form QA benchmark focused on veterinary clinical questions about dogs and cats, with text and multimodal data, used to evaluate and stress-test LLMs and LVLMs under different settings.
AI.motivation: Existing QA benchmarks rarely target veterinary medicine, especially in Korean and multimodal settings. As LLMs and LVLMs begin to be used for pet healthcare advice, there is a need for a realistic, domain-specific benchmark built from real clinical questions and expert answers to assess their knowledge, reasoning, and reliability.
AI.method: The authors construct PetQA with over 10k text-only and nearly 9k multimodal QA pairs from real-world dog and cat questions, each answered by veterinarians. They create a dedicated test split, PetQA-Bench, annotated with question types and clinical conditions. They then benchmark 18 language and vision-language models using automatic metrics (ROUGE, BERTScore) and LLM-as-a-judge ratings of factuality and helpfulness, across three usage paradigms: zero-shot, retrieval-augmented generation, and supervised fine-tuning.
AI.result: The 18 evaluated models show varied but overall limited performance in accurately and helpfully addressing veterinary clinical queries. The results reveal clear strengths and weaknesses of current LLMs/LVLMs across configurations (zero-shot, RAG, SFT) and highlight that none yet achieve consistently reliable, clinician-level guidance in this domain.
AI.conclusion: PetQA serves as a challenging, realistic benchmark for assessing veterinary clinical reasoning in both LLMs and LVLMs, demonstrating that current systems are not yet sufficiently reliable for unsupervised veterinary use. The released multilingual versions of the test set enable broader research into methods such as better adaptation, training, and alignment techniques to build safer, clinically trustworthy AI tools for veterinary care.

title: Reducing Hallucinated Transcripts in Whisper via Hallucination Space Projection
summary:
Whisper is a widely used foundation model for automatic speech recognition (ASR), but its generative decoder can produce fluent hallucinated transcripts for inputs containing little or no speech. We propose a training-free, inference-time method to reduce these hallucinations using low-rank projection of decoder activations. A compact hallucination-associated subspace is estimated from non-speech calibration data, and decoder hidden states are projected away from this subspace during inference.
  We evaluate two variants: always-on, which applies projection to all inputs, and gated, which applies it only when Whisper predicts that an input is likely non-speech. Across non-speech benchmarks, always-on projection reduces average hallucination rate (HR) from 31.31% to 2.44%, a 92.21% relative reduction, while gated projection reduces HR to 3.74%, an 88.05% relative reduction, with lower false rejection of genuine speech. On LibriSpeech, gated projection increases absolute word error rate (WER) by 0.33-4.39 percentage points and yields false-rejection rates (FRR) of 0.41--9.97% across model and split settings.
  These results show that low-rank activation projection can substantially suppress Whisper hallucinations without retraining, while providing a controllable trade-off between hallucination suppression and speech recognition performance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a training-free, inference-time method that projects Whisper’s decoder activations away from a hallucination-associated low-rank subspace, dramatically reducing non-speech hallucinations while modestly impacting ASR performance.
AI.motivation: Whisper, a widely used ASR foundation model, often produces fluent but hallucinated transcripts when given inputs with little or no speech (e.g., silence, noise). This is problematic for reliability and safety in real-world deployments. There is a need for a simple method that can mitigate such hallucinations without retraining or modifying the original model.
AI.method: The authors estimate a compact, low-rank subspace in the decoder’s activation space that is associated with hallucinations, using only non-speech calibration data. During inference, they project the decoder’s hidden states away from this hallucination subspace. They test two variants: (1) always-on projection applied to all inputs; and (2) gated projection, which is only applied when Whisper itself predicts that the input is likely non-speech, providing a controllable trade-off between hallucination suppression and preserving normal ASR performance.
AI.result: On non-speech benchmarks, the always-on variant reduces average hallucination rate from 31.31% to 2.44% (92.21% relative reduction). The gated variant reduces hallucination rate to 3.74% (88.05% relative reduction) with fewer false rejections of genuine speech. On LibriSpeech, the gated approach increases word error rate by 0.33–4.39 absolute percentage points and yields false rejection rates between 0.41% and 9.97%, depending on model size and dataset split.
AI.conclusion: Low-rank projection of decoder activations at inference time can substantially suppress hallucinations in Whisper without any retraining. The approach offers a tunable trade-off between hallucination suppression and ASR accuracy, demonstrating that hallucination behavior is concentrated in a compact subspace that can be mitigated via simple linear operations.

title: Tracing Audio Grounding and Answer Selection in Audio LLMs
summary: Audio Large Language Models (Audio LLMs) have advanced in audio understanding, yet they can still predict the answer by reasoning from textual cues or linguistic priors rather than the provided audio. A common remedy is to train models on data whose answers cannot be inferred from text alone. This approach can improve performance, but what changes within the model remains unclear. In this paper, we ask what must happen inside the model for the audio to actually determine the answer. Our findings are threefold. (1) Replacing the audio with silence or unrelated audio causes substantially larger performance degradation in the trained model than in the pretrained model. (2) Acoustic information most strongly shapes the model's representations of the answer choices in early-to-middle layers, while training mainly increases the influence of audio information on the final prediction in middle-to-late layers. (3) The weights learned during training have their largest impact in specific layer bands. Together, these results provide a mechanistic account of how training strengthens the use of acoustic evidence in Audio LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper studies what changes inside Audio Large Language Models when they are trained to truly rely on audio, rather than just textual priors, and provides a mechanistic explanation of how training makes acoustic evidence more influential in predictions.
AI.motivation: Although Audio LLMs are designed to use audio input, they can often answer correctly by exploiting textual biases or linguistic priors without really depending on the audio. Prior work tries to fix this by training on data where the answer cannot be inferred from text alone, but it is unclear how this training actually changes the internal computations of the model. The authors aim to understand, at a mechanistic level, what must happen inside the network for audio to genuinely determine the answer.
AI.method: The authors compare a pretrained Audio LLM with a version further trained on audio-dependent data. They perform intervention experiments (replacing the input audio with silence or unrelated audio) and measure performance degradation. They analyze internal representations layer by layer, focusing on how acoustic information affects representations of answer choices and the final prediction. They also conduct weight-level analyses to locate which layer ranges (bands) contribute most to the increased reliance on audio after training.
AI.result: (1) When the audio input is replaced by silence or unrelated audio, the performance of the trained model drops much more than that of the pretrained model, indicating the trained model depends more on audio. (2) Acoustic information most strongly shapes the internal representations of answer choices in early-to-middle layers; training primarily boosts the influence of audio on the final decision in middle-to-late layers. (3) The new weights learned during training have their largest functional impact within specific contiguous groups of layers, rather than being uniformly important across the network.
AI.conclusion: Training on audio-dependent data makes Audio LLMs genuinely rely more on acoustic evidence, and this reliance is implemented in a structured way across layers: early-to-middle layers encode audio-influenced representations of candidate answers, middle-to-late layers convert this information into audio-dependent final predictions, and particular layer bands contain the most critical learned weights. This provides a mechanistic account of how training strengthens the use of audio in Audio LLMs.

title: La Agente Óptima: Towards Agentic Self-Driving Laboratories
summary: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) combine automated experimentation with adaptive decision-making to accelerate scientific discovery. Their operation nevertheless often depends on human specialists who translate scientific objectives into executable closed-loop campaigns. Specialists adjust them as data and operating conditions change. Here, we present La Agente Óptima, an agentic framework that constructs and supervises Bayesian optimization campaigns across computational and experimental systems while maintaining a persistent optimization state. By separating large language model (LLM) reasoning from executed campaigns, Óptima runs repetitive optimization loops consistently, returns control to the agent only when progress requires interpretation or campaign revision, and keeps every decision auditable. We evaluate Óptima across ablation studies, five digital discovery tasks, and two physical platforms. Throughout, Óptima maintained executable campaigns as both the scientific problem and execution environment evolved. In a closed-loop contact angle optimization campaign, Óptima identified and corrected a mid-run measurement failure, bringing the contact angle from 71.4 to 67.8 degrees, just above the 64-66 degree range. From this result, Óptima correctly inferred that the target was likely unattainable with the available reagents and recommended changing the formulation. In a five-day multi-objective flow-chemistry campaign, Óptima increased the yield from 30% to 59% over 23 experiments. Despite substantial inference costs, it cost less and used substantially less starting material than a human-directed campaign, while selecting a more mass-efficient operating point. These results show that LLM-based agents can make rigorous, long-running optimization campaigns accessible to domain scientists without specialist setup, expanding the scope of SDLs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces La Agente Óptima, an LLM-based agent that autonomously designs, runs, and supervises Bayesian optimization campaigns for self-driving laboratories (SDLs), keeping them robust, auditable, and adaptable over long-running digital and physical experiments.
AI.motivation: Self-driving laboratories can accelerate discovery but still require human specialists to encode scientific objectives into closed-loop optimization campaigns and to adjust them as conditions and data evolve. This human dependency limits scalability, accessibility to non-expert domain scientists, and the robustness of long-running campaigns. The authors aim to reduce reliance on such specialists by creating an agentic framework that can autonomously manage and adapt optimization workflows while maintaining rigor and traceability.
AI.method: The authors design La Agente Óptima, an agentic framework that decouples LLM-based reasoning from the execution of Bayesian optimization loops. Óptima maintains a persistent optimization state, constructs executable campaigns, and delegates repetitive optimization steps to an execution layer. Control is returned to the LLM agent only when higher-level interpretation, troubleshooting, or campaign revision is needed. The framework is tested through ablation studies, five digital discovery tasks, and two physical experimental platforms, including contact-angle optimization and multi-objective flow chemistry.
AI.result: Óptima successfully maintained and updated executable optimization campaigns as both the scientific tasks and experimental environments changed. In a contact-angle optimization experiment, it detected and corrected a mid-run measurement failure and improved the contact angle from 71.4° to 67.8°, recognizing that the specified target range (64–66°) was likely unattainable with the current reagents and recommending a formulation change. In a five-day multi-objective flow-chemistry campaign, Óptima improved yield from 30% to 59% in 23 experiments, using less starting material and costing less overall than a human-directed campaign, while identifying a more mass-efficient operating point.
AI.conclusion: La Agente Óptima demonstrates that LLM-based agents can autonomously design, manage, and adapt rigorous, long-running Bayesian optimization campaigns across digital and physical self-driving labs. By preserving a persistent optimization state, separating reasoning from execution, and intervening only when necessary, the framework makes advanced optimization workflows more accessible to domain scientists without specialist support, thereby broadening the practical impact and scalability of SDLs.

title: CAGE: Coherence-Aware Graph Encoding for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Traditional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems score each passage independently against the query, assembling context sets that may be individually relevant yet collectively incoherent. We introduce Coherence-Aware Graph Encoding (CAGE), a reranking framework that models "between-chunk coherence" across four dimensions: Intra-Domain Relevance, Noise Resistance, Informational Bonding, and Factual Consistency. Our pipeline transforms retrieved passages into directed heterogeneous entity graphs, amplifies factual anchors via min-out-degree reweighting, encodes structural patterns through a Relational Graph Convolutional Network, and fuses inter-chunk coherence with query relevance for final ranking. Evaluated across four multi-hop benchmarks, CAGE matches or outperforms strong baselines including monoT5 in Recall@5 on bridge-dominated datasets and consistently improves downstream Exact Match, demonstrating that structurally coherent context yields more precise answers even when retrieval recall is comparable or lower.

AI.tldr: They propose CAGE, a graph-based reranker for RAG that selects sets of passages that are not only relevant individually but also structurally coherent with each other, leading to better multi-hop QA answers.
AI.motivation: Standard RAG ranks passages one by one vs. the query, which can yield context sets that don’t fit together: passages may be on-topic but mutually inconsistent, redundant, or lacking the multi-hop connections needed to answer complex questions. The authors want a retrieval reranker that explicitly prefers collections of passages that form a coherent information structure across chunks, especially for multi-hop reasoning tasks.
AI.method: They build a reranking framework called Coherence-Aware Graph Encoding (CAGE). First, the initially retrieved passages are converted to a directed heterogeneous entity graph where nodes and relations capture entities and their cross-passage links. They then reweight the graph via a min-out-degree scheme to highlight strong factual anchor nodes. Next, they apply a Relational Graph Convolutional Network (R-GCN) over this graph to encode structural patterns that reflect four coherence dimensions: intra-domain relevance, noise resistance, informational bonding, and factual consistency. Finally, they combine this learned inter-chunk coherence signal with standard query–passage relevance scores to rerank the passages for RAG.
AI.result: On four multi-hop QA benchmarks, CAGE performs as well as or better than strong reranking baselines like monoT5 in terms of Recall@5, particularly on datasets with many bridge questions that require linking multiple pieces of evidence. Even when its retrieval recall is similar to or slightly lower than baselines, using CAGE-selected contexts yields consistently higher downstream Exact Match scores, indicating more accurate answers from the QA model.
AI.conclusion: Modeling coherence across retrieved chunks via graph structure and R-GCN encoding leads to better context sets for RAG. Rather than maximizing independent relevance per passage, CAGE explicitly prefers structurally coherent groups of passages, which improves multi-hop QA answer quality even without large gains in traditional retrieval recall metrics.

title: Extremely Sparse Supervision Incentivizes Reasoning Ability
summary: Large language models demonstrate increasingly strong reasoning capabilities through effective post-training. Yet, prevailing post-training methods optimize over massive numbers of tokens, implicitly assuming that effective learning must be token-intensive. We revisit this assumption in the on-policy distillation (OPD) setting, which naturally admits dense teacher supervision at every generated token. Using the Qwen3 family, we discover a counter-intuitive phenomenon: reasoning can be effectively incentivized by an extremely small fraction of generated tokens--as few as one or two tokens per reasoning trajectory, corresponding to only 0.05% of all tokens. Surprisingly, this sparse supervision in most cases matches or surpasses full-token training in improving reasoning ability, despite excluding the vast majority of generated tokens from the training objective. This phenomenon is consistently observed across nine teacher--student configurations spanning different model scales on mathematical reasoning tasks, and is further validated on coding reasoning, Llama models and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)-based reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR). Interestingly, such extremely sparse supervision may be closer to the natural learning process: rather than correcting every step word by word, one reflects on a few critical reasoning steps, updates prior understanding, and continues the trial-and-error, avoiding micro-level corrections while remaining remarkably effective. Overall, our results challenge the assumption that effective post-training must be token-intensive and point to a new direction for understanding and designing more efficient post-training algorithms.

AI.tldr: The paper finds that in on-policy distillation, supervising only 1–2 carefully chosen tokens per reasoning trajectory (≈0.05% of tokens) can match or outperform full-token training for improving reasoning, drastically reducing post-training compute.
AI.motivation: Current post-training methods for large language models typically optimize over very large numbers of tokens, assuming that effective learning requires dense, token-level supervision. This is computationally expensive and may not reflect how humans learn from sparse, high-value feedback. The authors want to test whether dense supervision is actually necessary in on-policy distillation, where the teacher can in principle supervise every generated token, and to understand if much sparser supervision can still drive strong reasoning improvements.
AI.method: The authors work in the on-policy distillation (OPD) setting using Qwen3 models as the main testbed. They generate reasoning trajectories and apply teacher supervision not to all tokens, but to an extremely small subset—sometimes as few as one or two tokens per trajectory. They compare this "sparse token" objective to standard full-token distillation across nine teacher–student model scale combinations on mathematical reasoning benchmarks. They further replicate and validate the phenomenon on coding reasoning tasks, with Llama models, and in a PPO-based reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR) setup, to test robustness beyond the initial OPD/Qwen3 configuration.
AI.result: They observe a counter-intuitive result: supervising only 1–2 tokens per reasoning trajectory (around 0.05% of total generated tokens) is often as good as, or even better than, supervising every token for improving reasoning abilities. This pattern holds across multiple teacher–student scale pairings, tasks (math and coding reasoning), model families (Qwen3 and Llama), and even in a separate RLVR PPO regime, indicating that the effect is robust and not an artifact of a particular setup.
AI.conclusion: The work challenges the widespread assumption that effective post-training of large language models must be token-intensive. It shows that extremely sparse, strategically placed supervision in OPD can suffice to elicit strong reasoning improvements, aligning more closely with human-like learning where feedback focuses on key steps rather than every word. This suggests a new direction for designing more compute-efficient and conceptually grounded post-training algorithms based on sparse but high-impact supervision.

title: ConsensusBench: Benchmark of Consensus Nodes for LLM Reasoning via Outcome Reward Densifying
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become one of the primary paradigms for reasoning enhancement of large language models (LLMs). In particular, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and related algorithms have demonstrated strong performance with outcome-level rewards. However, these methods depend solely on the final answer, without feedback regarding which intermediate steps contribute to success or failure. As task complexity and reasoning trajectory length increase, such sparse final-answer rewards become increasingly insufficient. To address this limitation, we introduce ConsensusBench, a novel dataset designed to provide rule-based process-level signals. We posit that a correct final answer relies on a small set of intermediate conclusions throughout the reasoning process, which can be seen as a verifiable sub-outcome. We identify these sub-outcomes by filtering correct trajectories from N rollouts and clustering semantically equivalent intermediate statements. We call these clustered statements as Consensus Nodes. By integrating a rule-based process reward derived from these nodes into GRPO-style algorithms, we develop a new reinforcement learning signal named ConsensusPR. It directly reduces the reward sparsity of outcome reward across long reasoning trajectories. To facilitate systematic process-level evaluation, we introduce three metrics to our benchmark: Final Answer Accuracy (Acc), Node Coverage Rate (NCR), and Tokens per Node (TPN). Experiments across AIME 2024, AIME 2025, GSM8K, MATH-500, and our ConsensusBench demonstrate that the proposed method consistently surpasses GRPO-style approaches, highlighting the practical value of consensus nodes in guiding reasoning.

AI.tldr: Paper mitigates sparse final-answer rewards in RL for LLM reasoning by introducing process-level supervision via consensus intermediate nodes and a new benchmark and reward scheme that improves performance over GRPO-style methods.
AI.motivation: Existing RL methods for LLM reasoning, like GRPO, rely on sparse outcome-level rewards that only evaluate the final answer. As reasoning tasks grow more complex and trajectories longer, such sparse supervision becomes inadequate because it fails to indicate which intermediate steps are helpful or harmful. The paper aims to provide structured, process-level feedback that can guide LLMs through long reasoning chains more effectively.
AI.method: The authors construct a dataset called ConsensusBench that provides rule-based process-level signals. They assume that a correct final answer depends on a small number of key intermediate conclusions, treated as verifiable sub-outcomes. From N sampled reasoning rollouts, they filter those that yield correct final answers and then cluster semantically equivalent intermediate statements to form "Consensus Nodes." Using these nodes, they define a rule-based process reward and integrate it with GRPO-style reinforcement learning, resulting in a new signal named ConsensusPR that augments outcome-level rewards with node-level feedback along the trajectory.
AI.result: Using the proposed ConsensusPR signal and the ConsensusBench dataset, the authors train LLMs and evaluate them on multiple reasoning benchmarks: AIME 2024, AIME 2025, GSM8K, MATH-500, and ConsensusBench itself. Across all these tasks, models trained with ConsensusPR consistently outperform those trained with standard GRPO-style methods that only use final-answer rewards, demonstrating improved reasoning performance under process-level supervision.
AI.conclusion: Process-level feedback via consensus-based intermediate nodes effectively reduces reward sparsity in RL for LLM reasoning and yields better performance than purely outcome-level approaches. ConsensusBench and the ConsensusPR signal show that identifying and rewarding a small set of key, verifiable sub-outcomes can more effectively guide long reasoning trajectories, suggesting a promising direction for future RL algorithms for LLM reasoning and for designing benchmarks that measure intermediate reasoning quality, not just final answers.

title: Does the Selected Object Reach the Reader? Auditing Identity Handoffs in Grounded Language-Model Pipelines
comment: 15 pages, 1 figure, 23 tables. Accepted to the GroundLM Workshop (Grounding Language Models: Learning Faithfully and Efficiently) at EMNLP 2026
summary: Grounded language-model pipelines can be divided into three stages: selecting an object, retrieving passages for it, and using that evidence to answer. If the selected object must reach the reader, losing it breaks the handoff. Benchmark recall checks the dataset-linked object, which can differ. We audit 600 HybridQA questions across three selector families. On 1,463 resolvable records where the selected object matches the dataset-traced passage, exact key lookup and exact title matching return the object every time. With every ranked rule given the same decoded selected title, body-only BM25 omits it on 389 records (26.6%) at cutoff five, while hybrid retrieval with reranking omits it on 14 (1.0%). The two identities differ on 329 of 1,792 resolvable records. With original-question rankings, their top-five checks disagree on 106 records (5.9%). Frozen reader comparisons associate the aligned object's presence with 28.6 to 31.0 points higher exact match. In a deliberately selected 64-item cohort, removing that passage sharply lowers exact match, while removing a similar-length comparison passage does not reproduce the drop. We release the Returned-Object Profile (ROP), an executable record of the target, returned-ID field, cutoff, membership rule, and complete expected population, with data and an offline replay.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how well grounded language-model pipelines keep track of the specific object they’re supposed to answer about, showing that retrieval often drops the right object and proposing a profiling resource (ROP) to measure and replay this behavior.
AI.motivation: Modern grounded LLM systems work in stages: choose an entity/object from the question, retrieve supporting passages, then answer. Existing evaluations usually check recall against dataset-annotated passages, which may not match the object actually selected by the model. If retrieval fails to return the model-selected object, the pipeline’s handoff breaks, harming answer accuracy. The authors want to expose and quantify this object-level recall problem and its impact on downstream QA performance.
AI.method: They audit 600 HybridQA questions, examining three different families of object selectors. For each question, they compare two notions of the ‘target object’: (1) the dataset-traced passage/object and (2) the object actually selected by the pipeline. They then test several retrieval configurations—exact key lookup, exact title matching, body-only BM25 at fixed cutoff, and a hybrid retrieval with reranking—measuring whether the selected object’s passage appears in the top-k results. They analyze disagreements between dataset-linked and selector-chosen objects, and run controlled experiments with a frozen reader model, including ablations where they remove either the true target passage or a length-matched decoy, to isolate the effect of returning the aligned object. Finally, they package the experimental setup into the Returned-Object Profile (ROP), which records all parameters and expected results for offline replay.
AI.result: On 1,463 resolvable records where the selected object matches the dataset-traced passage, exact key lookup and exact title matching always return the correct object. In contrast, body-only BM25 at cutoff 5 fails to retrieve the selected object in 389 cases (26.6%), whereas a hybrid retrieval with reranking fails in only 14 cases (1.0%). Across 1,792 resolvable records, the dataset-linked object and selector-chosen object differ in 329 cases. Using original-question rankings, top-5 recall checks based on these two object definitions disagree on 106 cases (5.9%). Experiments with a frozen reader show that having the aligned object in the retrieved set is associated with a 28.6–31.0 point gain in exact match. In a hand-picked 64-item cohort, removing the target passage leads to a sharp drop in exact match, but removing a similar-length comparison passage does not cause a comparable decrease.
AI.conclusion: Object-level recall is critical for grounded LLM pipelines: the system must successfully pass the selected object through retrieval to the reader to maintain high QA accuracy. Standard benchmark recall metrics that only look at dataset-linked passages can misrepresent this, because they may focus on a different object than the one chosen by the selector. The authors show that naïve BM25 retrieval often drops the selected object, while hybrid retrieval with reranking greatly improves object recall, and that this recall strongly predicts answer accuracy. They release the Returned-Object Profile (ROP) to standardize how object recall is recorded, analyzed, and replayed, enabling more precise evaluation and debugging of retrieval in grounded QA systems.

title: Choosing the Right Language Mode at Inference Time for Multilingual Reliability
summary:
Multilingual large language models often struggle to reason in low- to mid-resource languages. Prior work has shown that translation can improve multilingual reasoning by helping models access stronger English-centric representations. This raises a central question: How much translation is needed for multilingual large language models to reason reliably, and when does more translation instead trigger interference and overconfidence?
  Using LLaMA and Qwen models, we run extensive experiments varying text scope and language mode (target-only, English-only, bilingual) to evaluate both accuracy and reliability.
  Our results reveal a clear trade-off: English context often improve understanding and recover errors caused by non-English comprehension, yet adding redundant bilingual context intensifies interference. We address this trade-off with Reliability-Aware Adaptive Inference (RAAI), a training-free test-time framework that (i) performs Expected Calibration Error (ECE)-aware routing and prompt fusion, and (ii) uses a mid-layer Risk Index (RI) to gate sequential reasoning, allocating compute only when it is likely to help and suppressing harmful bilingual redundancy. Across two model families, RAAI enhances accuracy by 25-37.7% on low-resource languages and lowers calibration error by approximately 3-6%, with the most pronounced benefits in the lowest-resource language tiers.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how much and what type of translation context helps multilingual LLMs reason reliably, and proposes a test-time framework (RAAI) that adaptively uses bilingual prompts and model confidence signals to boost accuracy and calibration in low-resource languages.
AI.motivation: Multilingual LLMs underperform in low- and mid-resource languages, especially on reasoning tasks. Prior work shows that translating to English can help by leveraging stronger English-centric representations, but it is unclear how much translation is beneficial and when additional bilingual context starts to hurt by causing interference and overconfidence. There is a need to characterize this trade-off and to design methods that can use translation selectively and reliably at test time, without retraining models.
AI.method: Using LLaMA and Qwen model families, the authors systematically vary (1) text scope and (2) language mode (target-only, English-only, bilingual) to test accuracy and reliability across languages. They identify a trade-off where English context helps comprehension but redundant bilingual context leads to interference. To mitigate this, they propose Reliability-Aware Adaptive Inference (RAAI), a training-free, test-time framework. RAAI performs Expected Calibration Error (ECE)-aware routing and prompt fusion, and computes a mid-layer Risk Index (RI) to gate sequential reasoning. This allows the system to allocate extra compute only when it is likely to help and to suppress harmful bilingual redundancy.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple languages and two major model families show that RAAI substantially improves performance in low-resource settings: it increases accuracy by 25–37.7% on low-resource languages and reduces calibration error by about 3–6%. The gains are largest for the lowest-resource language tiers, demonstrating that adaptive use of bilingual context and risk-aware gating can mitigate interference and improve reliability.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that while adding English translation context can significantly aid multilingual reasoning, naïvely using redundant bilingual prompts can trigger interference and overconfidence. By explicitly modeling reliability and adaptively controlling when and how bilingual information is used via RAAI, multilingual LLMs can achieve substantially better accuracy and calibration, especially in low-resource languages, without requiring additional training.

title: $τ^τ$-Bench: An Environment for End-To-End, Realistic Agent Construction
summary: LLM agents are rapidly becoming production software, deployed to handle customer service, adjudicate disputes, and operate internal systems. Notably, the work of building them is increasingly handed to coding agents, yet existing benchmarks say little about whether an AI system can deliver one under the conditions of a real client engagement. We introduce $τ^τ$-bench (pronounced hyper-tau-bench), a benchmark that makes agent construction the task. A developer agent is given the records a business actually keeps, a client who holds requirements, a production API that operations must run through, a codebase to inherit, and limits on serving cost and models: the same starting point a real engagement provides. From these it must deliver a complete customer-service agent, scored by deploying that agent against held-out simulated users. Across 53 tasks spanning four domains, the strongest configuration, Claude Opus 5 under Claude Code, passes just 23.9% of evaluation simulations. Meanwhile, an expert-authored reference ceiling scores 82.2%. The failures mirror ones human agent developers see: models issue shallow queries in place of deep comprehension of the records, communicate almost nothing to the client, and experiment too little with agent architecture and serving spend, shipping the first design that runs. We aim for $τ^τ$-bench to turn the work of cooperative agent building into a measurable target for coding agents.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces τ^τ-bench, a benchmark for evaluating whether coding LLM agents can build production-ready customer-service agents under realistic constraints, finding that current top systems perform far below an expert-designed ceiling.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM and coding-agent benchmarks do not reflect the real-world process of building production LLM agents for businesses. As LLM agents are increasingly tasked with customer service, dispute resolution, and system operation, there is a need to measure whether an AI developer can actually construct a robust, cost-constrained agent from real business artifacts and interactions with a client, not just solve isolated coding problems.
AI.method: The authors design τ^τ-bench, where the task itself is to build a customer-service agent. A developer agent is provided with realistic inputs: business records, a client holding requirements, access to a production API through which all operations must go, an inherited codebase, and constraints on serving cost and model choices. The agent must iteratively develop and ship a complete customer-service agent. Performance is evaluated by deploying the produced agent against held-out simulated users across 53 tasks in four domains. Different LLM-based coding configurations (e.g., Claude Opus 5 under Claude Code) are benchmarked and compared to an expert-authored reference solution.
AI.result: The strongest evaluated configuration, Claude Opus 5 running within Claude Code, successfully handles only 23.9% of evaluation simulations, while a human expert-authored reference solution reaches 82.2%. Observed failures resemble those seen in human-led agent engineering: the models use shallow instead of deep understanding of business records, barely interact with the client to clarify requirements, and do limited exploration of design choices regarding agent architecture and serving costs, often shipping the first workable design.
AI.conclusion: τ^τ-bench provides a realistic, challenging benchmark that reframes evaluation from solving micro-tasks to constructing end-to-end cooperative agents under real-world constraints. Current leading coding agents significantly underperform expert baselines, exposing key weaknesses in requirement elicitation, deep data understanding, and design exploration. The benchmark is intended to guide and measure progress on building AI systems that can reliably collaborate in developing production-grade agents.

title: Controlling and Assessing Appropriate Persona Use in LLM-based Dialogue Generation
summary: In persona-based dialogue generation (PDG), LLMs often overuse persona attributes by incorporating them regardless of dialogue context, resulting in unnatural responses. Despite its practical significance, the underlying causes remain unexplored, with no method to mitigate this problem or metric to assess the appropriateness of persona use. To address these issues, we first conduct a comprehensive analysis of LLM-based PDG, revealing that LLMs exhibit a systematic bias to incorporate all given persona attributes, and that existing metrics fail to capture contextual appropriateness. Building on these findings, we propose Self-CONtrastive Persona Overuse Suppression (SCONPOS) to mitigate overuse by directly intervening in LLMs' internal representations at the prompt encoding stage, without requiring any response generation. We further propose the Persona Appropriateness Score (PAS), a novel metric that penalizes both overuse and underuse. Experimental results demonstrate that SCONPOS systematically reduces overuse, and PAS captures the contextual appropriateness of persona use.

AI.tldr: The paper studies why large language models overuse persona attributes in dialogue generation and proposes methods to both reduce this overuse and measure appropriate persona usage.
AI.motivation: Persona-based dialogue generation aims to make responses more consistent and personalized by conditioning on a set of persona attributes. However, current LLMs tend to inject these attributes into responses even when contextually inappropriate, leading to unnatural and forced dialogues. There is little understanding of why this happens, no targeted mitigation method, and no good metric for evaluating whether persona information is used appropriately (neither too much nor too little).
AI.method: The authors first perform a systematic analysis of LLM behaviour in persona-based dialogue tasks, examining how often and under what conditions models incorporate persona attributes. They find a bias toward using all provided attributes and show that existing evaluation metrics do not capture whether this usage is contextually appropriate. Based on these insights, they introduce SCONPOS (Self-CONtrastive Persona Overuse Suppression), which intervenes on the model’s internal representations during prompt encoding, before generation, to suppress inappropriate persona overuse. They also design PAS (Persona Appropriateness Score), a new metric that explicitly penalizes both excessive and insufficient use of persona information relative to the dialogue context.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations show that SCONPOS consistently reduces persona overuse in LLM-generated dialogue responses without requiring modifications at generation time. The proposed PAS metric better reflects the contextual appropriateness of persona usage than existing metrics, distinguishing between overuse, underuse, and suitable use of persona attributes.
AI.conclusion: LLMs used for persona-based dialogue generation have an inherent bias to incorporate all available persona attributes, which existing metrics fail to assess properly. By intervening at the representation level during prompt encoding (SCONPOS) and introducing a dedicated evaluation metric (PAS), the paper provides both a practical mitigation strategy and a more faithful way to quantify appropriate persona use, leading to more natural and contextually fitting persona-based dialogues.

title: Leveraging Imperfect Restoration for Data Availability Attack
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2024. Equal contribution by Yi Huang, Jeremy Styborski, Mingzhi Lyu - cite in any order
summary: The abundance of online data is at risk of unauthorized usage in training deep learning models. To counter this, various Data Availability Attacks (DAAs) have been devised to make data unlearnable for such models by subtly perturbing the training data. However, existing attacks often excel against either Supervised Learning (SL) or Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) scenarios. Among these, a model-free approach that generates a Convolution-based Unlearnable Dataset (CUDA) stands out as the most robust DAA across both SSL and SL. Nonetheless, CUDA's effectiveness against SSL is underwhelming and it faces a severe trade-off between image quality and its poisoning effect. In this paper, we conduct a theoretical analysis of CUDA, uncovering the sub-optimal gradients it introduces and elucidating the strategy it employs to induce class-wise bias for data poisoning. Building on this, we propose a novel poisoning method named Imperfect Restoration Poisoning (IRP), aiming to preserve high image quality while achieving strong poisoning effects. Through extensive comparisons of IRP with eight baselines across SL and SSL, coupled with evaluations alongside five representative defense methods, we showcase the superiority of IRP. Code: https://github.com/lyumingzhi/IRP

AI.tldr: They propose a new data poisoning method, Imperfect Restoration Poisoning (IRP), that keeps image quality high while making data unusable for both supervised and self-supervised deep learning models, outperforming prior attacks and resisting defenses.
AI.motivation: Online images are widely scraped to train deep learning models, often without consent. Data Availability Attacks (DAAs) aim to protect data owners by making their shared data unlearnable via small perturbations. Existing DAAs usually work well for either supervised or self-supervised learning, not both, and the current best model-free method (CUDA) has weak effects on SSL and suffers a strong trade-off between visual quality and poisoning strength. There is a need for a principled attack that is robust across learning settings without degrading image quality.
AI.method: The authors theoretically analyze how the current state-of-the-art model-free attack, the Convolution-based Unlearnable Dataset (CUDA), operates. They show that CUDA induces sub-optimal gradients and uses a strategy of creating class-wise bias to poison data. Based on these insights, they design Imperfect Restoration Poisoning (IRP), a new perturbation mechanism that modifies images in a way that resembles imperfect restoration—preserving visual quality for humans but leading learning algorithms to exploit misleading cues. They then systematically compare IRP against eight existing poisoning baselines under both supervised and self-supervised training setups, and test it under five representative defense strategies.
AI.result: IRP consistently outperforms eight baseline DAAs in both supervised and self-supervised learning settings, achieving stronger degradation of model performance while maintaining higher image quality than CUDA and other methods. Moreover, when evaluated alongside five prominent defense techniques, IRP remains more effective than competing attacks, demonstrating strong robustness to current defenses.
AI.conclusion: A careful theoretical dissection of CUDA reveals its gradient-related limitations and its reliance on class-wise bias, explaining its shortcomings, especially in SSL and in preserving image quality. Leveraging these insights, the proposed IRP attack successfully reconciles strong poisoning power with high image fidelity and exhibits superior robustness across learning paradigms and defenses. This positions IRP as a new state-of-the-art approach for data availability attacks that protect online images from unauthorized model training.

title: How Do Language Models Represent and Use Phonological Information for Allomorph Selection?
summary: Language models are trained on tokenized text that obscures the sound structure of words, yet they reliably produce morphemes whose form is phonologically conditioned. It remains unclear whether they rely on item-specific memorization or rule-like generalization and, if the latter, how that generalization is implemented. We therefore ask whether this phonological condition is represented within language models and how it is causally used for allomorph selection. For the English indefinite article a/an, we show that the phonological condition is encoded along a single linear direction in trigger-token embeddings, that this direction causally drives article selection in token-level wug tests, and that, at the article-prediction position, the model forecasts the upcoming trigger token and uses the forecasted trigger's phonological feature to choose the article. We then ask whether this rule-like generalization extends beyond English article selection, both to allomorph selection in other languages and to explicit phonological judgment. Together, these results provide a mechanistic account of phonologically conditioned allomorph selection in language models, and dissociate this generation-time ability from explicit metalinguistic judgments.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how language models implement phonologically conditioned allomorph selection (e.g., a vs. an) and finds a clear, causal, low-dimensional representation that drives their choices.
AI.motivation: Although language models are trained on text-only, they still consistently use phonologically conditioned morphemes (like a/an before vowel sounds). It is unknown whether this is due to memorizing specific word combinations or learning abstract rules, and, if rules exist, how exactly they are represented and used internally. The paper aims to uncover the internal representation and causal mechanisms underlying such phonological conditioning.
AI.method: The authors focus first on the English indefinite article alternation a/an. They analyze internal representations (trigger-token embeddings) in language models to see whether the relevant phonological condition (vowel vs. consonant onset) corresponds to a particular linear direction. They perform causal interventions and token-level wug tests (using novel or nonce items) to test whether manipulating that direction affects article choice. They also examine the prediction-time behavior of the model, asking whether it internally forecasts the upcoming word and uses its inferred phonological feature to select the correct article. Finally, they extend the analysis to other phonologically conditioned allomorphy patterns in other languages and to tasks involving explicit phonological judgments.
AI.result: They find that the phonological feature relevant to a/an choice is encoded in a single linear direction within trigger-token embeddings. Manipulating this direction causally changes the model’s article selection in controlled wug-style experiments, showing the representation is not merely correlational. At the point of predicting the article, the model internally forecasts the likely upcoming trigger token and then uses the predicted trigger’s phonological property to decide between a and an. They also obtain evidence that similar mechanisms support phonologically conditioned allomorph selection in other languages, whereas explicit phonological judgment tasks dissociate from this generation-time mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Language models implement phonologically conditioned allomorph selection through a compact, linear representation of the relevant phonological feature, which is causally involved in generation. The models appear to forecast upcoming tokens and use the inferred phonological property of these tokens to choose the correct allomorph (e.g., a vs. an). This demonstrates a mechanistic, rule-like generalization rather than mere memorization, and it shows that the internal processes used during generation differ from those engaged when models are asked to make explicit metalinguistic or phonological judgments.

title: SiLR: Structure-Preserving Admission and Process Reward for LLM Tool Agents
comment: 13 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables. Appendix includes full proofs, attack-family constructions, and the extended process-reward study
summary: A runtime gate for an LLM tool agent is usually cast as a filter. In a ReAct loop a rejected proposal is followed by another at the same state, so the gate is a search operator over the proposal stream whose admission criterion shapes which trajectories are reachable. We study post-violation recovery admission, where progress must be admitted while the system is still in violation, and identify the scalar projection trap: an aggregate-score gate accepts a locally improving proposal and commits the trajectory to a plateau. SiLR instead shadow-executes each proposal and admits it under a product order over the branch-level violation state (overloaded-branch support and per-branch severity). We prove that no scalar surrogate is sound for this order, so the failure is representational, not a matter of threshold tuning. On mined Gym-ANM scenarios, SiLR recovers 21/21 multi-action episodes against 0/21 for terminal and 9/21 for the best scalar gate, significant across the full 24-scenario benchmark. The terminal-versus-structured dichotomy holds across three model families and in CityLearn. Because admission rests on deterministic simulation, the LLM lies outside the trust boundary: a magnitude-redistribution attack that defeats both scalar and support-only baselines is contained only by the full per-branch predicate. With two constraint families active, every tested scalar projection admits physically unsafe actions; support-only admits the largest fraction (63.2% of 42,410; product order 0). In the hardest dual-family traces, scalar gates recover only through that unsafe class. Reused as a GRPO process reward, it outperforms its count projection in every mined scenario and is the only tested reward whose ungated policy exceeds the untrained base (0.844 vs. 0.778). Scalar projection loses the violation geometry at both design points; only the full product order is structurally sufficient.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a core failure mode of scalar gating for LLM tool agents under safety constraints and proposes a product-order based runtime gate (SiLR) that preserves violation geometry, enabling reliable recovery and safer, more capable plans.
AI.motivation: Runtime safety filters for LLM tool agents are typically scalar gates over proposals (e.g., single risk score with a threshold). In a ReAct loop, these gates are not just filters, but search operators that determine which trajectories are reachable. When constraints are violated and must be recovered from, naive scalar aggregation can trap the agent on plateaus: locally improving but globally unrecoverable states. Existing work often assumes that better scalarization or threshold tuning can fix this.
