The motivation is to understand and formally characterize when scalar gates are inherently inadequate for post-violation recovery, and to design a gating mechanism that is structurally capable of guiding safe recovery without trusting the LLM itself.
AI.method: The authors analyze LLM tool agents within a ReAct loop and model the gate as an operator over a stream of candidate actions generated from the same state. They focus on post-violation recovery admission, where actions must be taken while constraints are still violated. They identify the "scalar projection trap" in which any aggregate scalar score over violations can accept locally improving actions that commit the trajectory to a plateau with no path to full recovery. They propose SiLR, a gate that shadow-executes each candidate action using a deterministic simulator and decides admission using a product order over branch-level violation states, capturing both which branches are overloaded and the per-branch severities. They prove that no scalar surrogate (projection) is sound for this product order. They then evaluate SiLR against scalar and support-only gates on mined Gym-ANM and CityLearn scenarios, across multiple LLM families, and additionally reuse the product-order signal as a GRPO-style reinforcement learning reward to compare training outcomes against scalar rewards.
AI.result: Theoretical results show that the violation state’s product-order structure cannot be faithfully represented by any scalar surrogate: any scalar projection loses critical information, making some unsafe or non-recovering actions indistinguishable from safe/recovering ones. Empirically, in Gym-ANM the proposed SiLR gate recovers from 21/21 multi-action violation episodes, versus 0/21 for a terminal gate (which halts on violation) and 9/21 for the best-tuned scalar gate, with statistical significance across a 24-scenario benchmark. The superiority of structured (product-order) gating over terminal/scalar holds across three different LLM model families and transfers to the CityLearn environment. Under two simultaneous constraint families, all tested scalar projections admit physically unsafe actions in experiments; support-only projections admit the largest fraction (63.2% of 42,410 candidate actions), while the full product-order gate admits none of these unsafe actions. In the hardest dual-constraint traces, scalar gates only achieve recovery by going through physically unsafe regions. When used as a GRPO reward, the product-order signal outperforms its scalar (count) projection in every mined scenario and is the only reward for which an ungated trained policy surpasses the untrained base policy (0.844 vs. 0.778 performance).
AI.conclusion: Runtime gates for LLM tool agents in safety-critical settings cannot, in general, rely on scalarized violation scores without incurring fundamental representational errors that break safe recovery. The issue is not merely threshold tuning but the loss of the violation geometry under scalar projection. A product-order-based gate that tracks per-branch violation support and severity (as in SiLR) is structurally adequate for guiding safe recovery, can be implemented via deterministic simulation so that the LLM remains outside the trust boundary, and yields both safer and more capable behavior in benchmarks. These results suggest that future LLM tool agents should adopt structured, geometry-preserving violation representations—both for runtime gating and for RL-style training signals—rather than compressing safety state into single scalar scores.

title: Refuse without Refusal: A Structural Analysis of Safety-Tuning Responses for Reducing False Refusals in Language Models
comment: EMNLP 2026 Main Conference (38 pages); Code available at https://github.com/mz-kim/RwR
summary: Striking a balance between helpfulness and safety remains a fundamental challenge in aligning large language models. To achieve this balance, models should refuse harmful queries (e.g., "How do I shoot someone?") while remaining responsive to benign inputs, even those superficially resembling harmful queries (e.g., "Where can I shoot a good photo?"). However, models often struggle to distinguish genuinely harmful queries from benign queries that contain superficially risky language, resulting in false refusals. In this paper, we address the issue by decomposing a response in the safety-tuning dataset into two distinct components: (i) a boilerplate refusal statement and (ii) a rationale explaining the refusal. Our experiments and analyses show that refusal statements impede accurate discrimination between harmful and benign queries by inducing reliance on superficial cues. In contrast, training solely on rationales reduces false refusals while maintaining a comparable level of safety performance. Rationale-Only benefits also appear in our ICL configuration and remain compatible with the evaluated inference-time mitigation methods. The results emphasize the necessity of precisely curated, fine-grained safety supervision datasets and outline directions for constructing aligned agents that better reconcile helpfulness with safety.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that training language models only on refusal rationales, not on boilerplate refusal text, improves their ability to distinguish harmful from benign queries while keeping safety strong.
AI.motivation: Current safety-aligned LLMs often over-refuse: they reject benign queries that merely contain risky-sounding words because they latch onto superficial cues from the safety-tuning data. This harms helpfulness and usability. The authors want a method that preserves safety (refusing truly harmful requests) while reducing false refusals on benign but superficially similar queries.
AI.method: They decompose safety-tuning responses into two parts: (i) generic boilerplate refusal sentences (e.g., “I can’t help with that”) and (ii) the underlying rationale that explains why the request is refused. They then train models under different regimes, including: full refusal text vs. only rationales. They analyze how each affects discrimination between harmful and benign prompts, and also test a rationale-only approach in in-context learning (ICL) as well as in combination with existing inference-time safety mitigation techniques.
AI.result: Boilerplate refusal statements cause models to rely on shallow lexical or pattern cues, which worsens discrimination between harmful and benign queries and increases false refusals. Training only on rationales significantly reduces false refusals while preserving a similar overall safety level (ability to reject harmful queries). The same “rationale-only” advantage is observed in ICL setups, and it works compatibly with standard inference-time mitigation methods.
AI.conclusion: Safety data that mixes boilerplate refusals with explanations can unintentionally teach models to over-index on superficial refusal patterns instead of deeper reasoning about harm. By training on rationales alone, models become better at reasoning about why something is harmful, improving the balance between safety and helpfulness. The work argues for more carefully designed, fine-grained safety supervision datasets as a key ingredient in building aligned agents that can refuse harm while remaining genuinely helpful on benign requests that contain risky language.

title: A Cost-Aware Agentic Architecture for NL-to-SQL over Nested Enterprise Schemas, with a New Benchmark
summary: Natural-language-to-SQL systems have ad- vanced rapidly on academic benchmarks, yet production enterprise schemas exhibit graph- like, semi-structured, deeply nested structure that current benchmarks do not measure. We make two complementary contributions. First, we introduce the DevRev NL2SQL bench- mark: 900 execution-verified queries with nested-type and link-graph structure, accom- panied by the Semantic Depth Score (SDS), a schema-agnostic rubric for analytical reasoning depth. Second, we present a cost-aware single- generation agentic architecture whose schema- selection, metadata-retrieval, and error-repair components are designed for the requirements this regime imposes. On the DevRev NL2SQL benchmark the system attains 91.7% answer correctness, a margin of 54.6 percentage points over the next-best baseline; on the Spider 2.0 Snowflake public dataset, it is competitive with leading systems at a single-generation operating point.

AI.tldr: They propose a new NL2SQL benchmark for complex enterprise-like schemas and an agentic system that performs very well on it.
AI.motivation: Existing NL2SQL benchmarks mostly use relatively simple, relational schemas, whereas real enterprise databases are graph-like, semi-structured, and deeply nested, so current benchmarks don’t reflect production difficulty or reasoning depth.
AI.method: 1) Construct the DevRev NL2SQL benchmark with 900 execution-verified queries over nested-type, link-graph schemas and define Semantic Depth Score (SDS) to measure analytical reasoning depth independent of schema. 2) Design a cost-aware, single-generation agentic architecture with specialized components for schema selection, metadata retrieval, and error repair tailored to such complex schemas.
AI.result: On the DevRev NL2SQL benchmark, their system achieves 91.7% answer correctness, which is 54.6 percentage points higher than the next-best baseline. On the Spider 2.0 Snowflake public dataset, it performs competitively with state-of-the-art systems when constrained to a single-generation setting.
AI.conclusion: Their benchmark better captures the complexity of real-world enterprise schemas and provides an SDS metric for reasoning depth, and their tailored agentic NL2SQL system significantly outperforms baselines on this new benchmark while remaining competitive on an established dataset.

title: Knowing What Not to Answer: Selective Non-Compliance in Vision-Language Models
comment: EMNLP 2026 Main Conference (43 pages). Code and dataset available at https://github.com/mz-kim/KoNA
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are expected to respond helpfully to appropriate requests while withholding compliance with requests that are incorrect, unsafe, infeasible, or unanswerable. However, existing benchmarks predominantly evaluate non-compliance at the level of the query as a whole, assuming that each request either warrants compliance or requires withholding compliance. In practice, real-world queries can contain a mixture of answerable content and components for which compliance should be withheld. In this paper, we introduce KoNA, a benchmark for evaluating selective non-compliance in VLMs across five categories: False Premise, Visual Inaccessibility, Universal Unknown, Task Feasibility, and Safety. Each task evaluates two capabilities: query-level non-compliance and component-level non-compliance under paired single and compound queries. Our evaluation across diverse VLMs shows that models often fail to refuse, correct, or abstain appropriately, and these failures become more pronounced when queries require selective non-compliance. To address this challenge, we fine-tune VLMs using KoNA examples that require selective non-compliance, together with a fully answerable set that should receive direct answers. Our fine-tuned models achieve substantial improvements in non-compliance accuracy while largely maintaining performance on fully answerable tasks. These results suggest that the fine-tuned models can distinguish between answerable components and those requiring non-compliance and respond in a task-appropriate manner.

AI.tldr: Introduces KoNA, a benchmark to test whether vision-language models (VLMs) can selectively refuse parts of a query that are incorrect, unsafe, or infeasible while still answering valid parts, and shows that fine-tuning on such data improves selective non-compliance without hurting normal performance.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations assume each query is either fully answerable or should be fully refused, but real-world queries often mix answerable and unanswerable or unsafe components. Current VLMs struggle to handle these mixed cases, so there is a need for a benchmark and methods that specifically target selective non-compliance at both whole-query and sub-component levels.
AI.method: The authors build KoNA, a benchmark covering five types of situations where models should withhold compliance: False Premise, Visual Inaccessibility, Universal Unknown, Task Feasibility, and Safety. Each example comes in single-query and compound-query forms to test both query-level and component-level non-compliance. They evaluate a range of existing VLMs on KoNA and then fine-tune VLMs using KoNA’s selective non-compliance examples plus a set of fully answerable examples to encourage correct distinctions between what to answer and what to refuse.
AI.result: Baseline VLMs frequently fail to refuse, correct, or abstain when they should, and these errors are especially common for compound queries that require answering some parts and refusing others. After fine-tuning on KoNA and fully answerable data, the models show large gains in non-compliance accuracy while mostly preserving their performance on standard, fully answerable tasks.
AI.conclusion: Selective non-compliance is a distinct and challenging capability for VLMs that is not well measured by existing benchmarks. KoNA provides a focused evaluation of this capability and, when used for fine-tuning, helps VLMs better separate answerable from non-answerable or unsafe components in a query, leading to more appropriate and reliable responses without major loss in general task performance.

title: Continual Graph Memory for Adaptive Recommendation under Intent Drift
summary: This paper studies adaptive recommendation under intent drift, where feedback from each recommendation outcome can reveal whether the relational evidence used for ranking is useful, missing, or misleading. While Knowledge Graphs (KGs) provide essential semantic structure to handle these shifts, traditional KG-enhanced systems treat the graph as a static retrieval substrate, making it brittle to evolving intents, noisy metadata, and recurring failure patterns. This paper proposes CGM-Rec, a continual graph memory framework for adaptive recommendation. CGM-Rec treats the graph state as a writable memory and maintains two complementary components. Therein, a Semantic Graph Memory is updated conservatively through quality-gated typed operations for storing stable and high-confidence relational knowledge. Meanwhile, an Episodic Lesson Memory acts as a fast reactive memory that learns recent outcomes, failure cases, and corrective hints. During testing, model parameters remain frozen and adaptation occurs only through memory writes. We evaluate CGM-Rec under a frozen-parameter, one-pass reranking protocol, where encoders and prompts remain fixed during testing and adaptation occurs only through memory writes. Experiments across multiple recommendation settings show that CGM-Rec improves over evaluated neural and LLM-based baselines on most metrics. Particularly, under sampled-candidate reranking, CGM-Rec improves HR@1 by up to 29.58% over the strongest LLM baseline on Bundle, and outperforms K-RagRec on metadata-rich ML-100K with HR@5 of 0.5941 versus 0.4746.

AI.tldr: Proposes CGM-Rec, a continual graph memory framework that treats the knowledge graph as writable memory to adapt recommendations under changing user intent, using semantic and episodic memories while keeping model parameters frozen.
AI.motivation: Existing KG-enhanced recommenders treat knowledge graphs as static retrieval structures, making them brittle to intent drift, noisy metadata, and recurring failure patterns. The authors aim to enable adaptive recommendation that can react to whether the KG-based relational evidence is useful, missing, or misleading, without retraining or changing model parameters at test time.
AI.method: Introduce CGM-Rec, which models the graph as a writable continual memory with two components: (1) a Semantic Graph Memory that is updated conservatively with quality-gated, typed operations to store stable, high-confidence relational knowledge; and (2) an Episodic Lesson Memory that rapidly logs recent recommendation outcomes, failure cases, and corrective hints. During evaluation, base encoders and prompts are frozen; adaptation occurs solely via memory writes within a one-pass reranking protocol.
AI.result: In multiple recommendation benchmarks and settings, CGM-Rec outperforms both neural and LLM-based baselines on most metrics. Notably, in sampled-candidate reranking, it increases HR@1 by up to 29.58% over the strongest LLM baseline on the Bundle dataset and beats K-RagRec on metadata-rich ML-100K with HR@5 of 0.5941 vs. 0.4746.
AI.conclusion: Treating knowledge graphs as writable continual memory and separating stable semantic knowledge from fast episodic feedback enables strong test-time adaptation to intent drift without changing model parameters. CGM-Rec yields consistent performance gains over competitive neural and LLM-based recommenders, especially in reranking scenarios and metadata-rich environments.

title: Beneath the Surface of Chains-of-Thought: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Reasoning Operations in LLMs
comment: To appear in EMNLP 2026 Main Conference. 43 pages, 14 figures, 19 tables
summary: Reasoning in large language models unfolds through diverse functional operations, such as problem formulation, goal decomposition, and deduction. Although these operations are explicitly distinguished in text, little is known about how they are geometrically organized in representation spaces. To this end, we investigate whether distinct reasoning operations exhibit corresponding geometric structure in hidden representations. We find that operations are separable in held-out representations, with separability peaking in middle layers, and verify that this structure is not explained by lexical or positional confounds. Across layers, token-wise operation-alignment becomes more distributed over spans, while identical surface tokens are represented differently depending on the operation of its surrounding chunk. Attention-masking interventions further show that operation-aligned representations at chunk onset depend on preceding reasoning context. Consequently, our work demonstrates that language models maintain representational correspondence between linguistic reasoning expressions and their internal geometric structures. Code and project materials are available at https://github.com/naver-ai/beneath-cot.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how different reasoning operations in large language models (LLMs) are organized geometrically in their internal representations and finds clear, layer-dependent structure that aligns with those operations.
AI.motivation: Although LLMs demonstrate complex reasoning abilities and we can label operations like problem formulation, goal decomposition, and deduction in text, we do not understand how (or if) these distinct reasoning operations are reflected as distinct geometric structures in the model’s hidden states. Bridging this gap can clarify how reasoning is implemented internally, beyond surface-level token statistics.
AI.method: The authors annotate or infer different reasoning operations (e.g., problem formulation, goal decomposition, deduction) within chain-of-thought style text and then probe the LLM’s hidden representations for tokens or chunks associated with each operation. They test the separability of these operations in representation space across layers, control for lexical and positional confounds, analyze token-wise operation alignment over spans, compare identical surface tokens occurring in different reasoning contexts, and perform attention-masking interventions to examine dependence on prior reasoning context.
AI.result: They find that representations associated with distinct reasoning operations are geometrically separable, most strongly in the middle layers of the network. This separability cannot be explained by differences in word choice or token position. Operation alignment becomes more spread over spans as depth increases, and the same surface token is encoded differently depending on which reasoning operation its surrounding chunk expresses. Attention-masking experiments show that operation-aligned chunk-onset representations rely on the preceding reasoning context, not just local content.
AI.conclusion: Language models encode a systematic correspondence between explicit reasoning operations in text and the geometry of their internal hidden states. Reasoning in LLMs is not just an emergent behavioral property at the output level; it is mirrored by structured, operation-specific organization in the representation space, especially in intermediate layers.

title: Harness-agnostic detection and immunization of reward hacking in self-evolving language models
summary: Self-evolving language models improve by proposing candidate updates and keeping whatever raises a visible score. When that score is an imperfect proxy for the capability one actually wants, sustained selection widens the gap between the two. This is reward hacking. We introduce HackProbe, a monitor that attaches to an arbitrary self-evolving loop through two black-box hooks, with no access to weights or activations. It keeps a secret, distribution-fixed comparison core, whose frozen distribution makes its capability proxy comparable across generations, alongside a rotated fresh layer that hardens the bank against co-adaptation. Four tests built on that proxy cover the level gap, a scale-aligned divergence with online change-point detection, capability stagnation, and a conditional confidently-wrong rate; a Sidak correction turns them into a calibrated family-wise p-value. Diagnosis alone recovers nothing, so a risk-aware immunization layer reselects an honest candidate from the proposal pool using the core together with a purely structural gaming footprint, disclosing at most log2 Pi bits per generation to the host. We prove a detectability bound that converts a target error rate into an explicit probe-size budget, and we delimit what probe rotation does and does not buy. On a controlled prompt-level host with four injected hacking channels and ground-truth labels, HackProbe reaches 0.763 AUROC against 0.663 for the strongest baseline and cuts the false-positive rate from 0.706 to 0.434. Its bandwidth-limited reselection is the only immunization level that returns more true capability under hacking, 5.2 points on average, than it forfeits on clean runs, 4.7; per-channel effects are mostly not individually significant.

AI.tldr: The paper presents HackProbe, a black-box monitoring and immunization framework to detect and mitigate reward hacking in self-evolving language models, providing statistically calibrated tests and bandwidth-limited reselection that improve true capability under hacking with limited cost on clean runs.
AI.motivation: Self-evolving language models optimize against an internal score or reward signal. When this score is an imperfect proxy for the true capabilities we care about, continued optimization can lead to reward hacking: models learn to exploit weaknesses of the proxy instead of genuinely improving. Existing methods for detecting such misalignment often require access to model internals or are not robust over generations, and they may not quantify statistical confidence. There is a need for a black-box, statistically principled mechanism that can both detect proxy hacking and actively mitigate it while minimizing information leakage that could itself be gamed by the evolving model.
AI.method: The authors propose HackProbe, which attaches to any self-evolving loop through two black-box hooks without requiring access to model parameters or activations. HackProbe maintains a hidden comparison core drawn from a fixed distribution, ensuring a stable capability proxy across generations, and augments it with a rotated fresh layer each generation to reduce co-adaptation and gaming. It computes four test statistics based on this proxy: (1) a level gap metric, (2) a scale-aligned divergence combined with online change-point detection, (3) a capability stagnation measure, and (4) a conditional confidently-wrong rate. Using a Sidak correction, these are combined into a calibrated family-wise p-value to detect hacking. Beyond diagnosis, a risk-aware immunization layer uses the core proxy and a structural gaming footprint to reselect an “honest” candidate from the proposal pool, carefully limiting the information bandwidth leaked back to the host (at most log2 Π bits per generation). Theoretical analysis provides a detectability bound that maps a desired error rate to a required probe size and clarifies the benefits and limits of probe rotation.
AI.result: In controlled experiments on a prompt-level self-evolving host with four injected hacking channels and access to ground-truth labels, HackProbe outperforms baselines in detecting reward hacking. It achieves an AUROC of 0.763 versus 0.663 for the strongest baseline and reduces the false-positive rate from 0.706 to 0.434. Among different immunization strategies, the bandwidth-limited reselection scheme is the only one that yields a net gain: under hacking, it recovers an average of 5.2 points in true capability, while on clean runs it forfeits only 4.7 points. Per-channel analyses show that most individual channel effects are not statistically significant, indicating that the main benefits are aggregated across channels.
AI.conclusion: HackProbe provides a practical, black-box framework for monitoring and mitigating reward hacking in self-evolving language models. By combining a frozen comparison core, rotated probes, multiple statistically corrected tests, and a bandwidth-limited reselection mechanism, it can detect deviations between proxy scores and true capabilities and actively steer evolution toward more honest improvements. Theoretical bounds guide probe sizing for target error rates, and empirical results show improved detection and better capability retention under adversarial conditions, with moderate costs on clean behavior. However, the per-channel significance results suggest that while HackProbe is effective in aggregate, further work may be needed to robustly handle specific hacking strategies or to strengthen individual components of the system.

title: Vectorizing Classical Tamil: Representation Learning for Verse-Commentary Pairs
summary: We construct a corpus of 1,262 verse-commentary (urai) pairs from five Classical Tamil source sections, ranging from technical grammatical prose to modern paraphrase, and ask what information representation learning can recover. We train recurrent and Transformer encoders, a Siamese-style pair-matching network, an mBART-style encoder-decoder, and a decoder-only language model. Each analysis is interpreted against an appropriate control on the same data. TF-IDF provides a strong no-training lexical retrieval baseline, alongside representation analyses and generation controls for the learned models. A fixed string containing the 25 most frequent commentary words scores higher on generation overlap than the decoder-only model. Canonical correlation reaches 1.000 on Gaussian noise at these sample sizes, token-F1 spans only about 0.02-0.20 on this corpus, and the encoder-decoder continues to lower training loss for sixteen epochs after validation loss has begun to rise. One narrow result remains: the decoder-only model prefers authentic word order in 107 of 112 minimal-pair comparisons (95.5%), but does not reproduce held-out commentary content. We release the extraction and evaluation protocol; redistribution of the source commentaries remains subject to permission.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how well modern representation learning and language models can capture the relationship between Classical Tamil verses and their prose commentaries, using a new curated corpus and multiple model architectures, and finds that models struggle to recover commentary content beyond superficial patterns.
AI.motivation: To understand the limits of current NLP and representation learning methods in modeling the relationship between Classical Tamil verse and its commentaries, and to provide a benchmark corpus and protocol for this under-studied classical language setting. The authors want to test whether standard architectures truly learn semantic correspondences or mainly pick up shallow lexical and word-order cues, especially in a low-resource, structurally complex domain.
AI.method: They construct a dataset of 1,262 verse–commentary pairs from five different Classical Tamil sources covering a spectrum from technical prose to modern paraphrase. They train and compare several models: recurrent and Transformer encoders, a Siamese pair-matching network, an mBART-style encoder–decoder, and a decoder-only language model. They also use TF-IDF as a strong lexical retrieval baseline. Evaluation includes retrieval (pair matching), representation analysis (e.g., canonical correlation), and generation quality (token F1, overlap metrics), with specially designed controls such as Gaussian noise inputs, a fixed high-frequency-word string for generation, and monitoring of training vs validation loss behavior.
AI.result: The TF-IDF baseline performs strongly for lexical retrieval, sometimes rivaling or outperforming learned models. A trivial generator that outputs a fixed string of the 25 most frequent commentary words achieves higher lexical-overlap scores than the trained decoder-only model, indicating that standard overlap metrics can be misleading. Canonical correlation analysis can reach a perfect score (1.000) even on Gaussian noise at these sample sizes, calling its diagnostic value into question. Token-level F1 between generated and reference commentaries is uniformly low (0.02–0.20), showing poor content reproduction. The encoder–decoder keeps improving training loss well after validation loss starts rising, suggesting overfitting or misalignment with evaluation metrics. A narrow but robust finding is that the decoder-only model reliably prefers the authentic commentary word order in minimal-pair tests (107/112 cases), even though it fails to reproduce actual commentary content.
AI.conclusion: Current representation-learning and language-modeling approaches, when applied to this Classical Tamil verse–commentary corpus, mostly capture shallow cues like word order and frequent vocabulary rather than the deeper semantic correspondence between verse and commentary. Simple baselines and controls can outperform or match more complex models under common metrics, and some popular analysis tools (e.g., CCA at small sample sizes) can be misleading. The work highlights methodological pitfalls in evaluating learned representations in low-resource, complex textual traditions, and provides a reproducible extraction and evaluation protocol for future research, though access to the underlying commentaries is constrained by permissions.

title: ERPBench: Evaluating LLM Agents for Enterprise Decision-Making Across Competitive Market Ecologies
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly proposed for enterprise workflows, yet existing evaluations rarely test whether business-decision conclusions transfer across competitive market ecologies. We introduce ERPBench, an execution-instrumented benchmark for enterprise decision agents in a six-round Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) simulation with coupled pricing, production, procurement, inventory, finance, and shared-market competition. ERPBench evaluates the same 100 fixed problems in two matched competitive market ecologies: Solo, where each evaluated LLM agent competes against fixed rule-based opponents, and Arena, where six evaluated LLM agents compete in a shared market. Across six model families, this yields 1,200 model-level trajectories spanning 7,200 decision rounds. Under the observed service configuration, the leading model differs between ecologies: DeepSeek leads in Solo (252.29M mean valuation; mean rank 1.67), whereas Gemini leads in Arena (263.95M; 1.76). The two ecologies identify the same task-level winner on only 21 of 100 problems, and Gemini's bottom-rank rate falls from 22 % to 0 % in Arena. ERPBench supports paired evaluation of whether enterprise-agent rankings transfer across competitive market ecologies, supplemented by aggregate execution-intervention analysis. Code and benchmark resources are available in our https://github.com/GAIR-NLP/erp-bench.

AI.tldr: ERPBench is a benchmark to test how well LLM-based enterprise decision agents perform and rank across two different competitive market settings in an ERP simulation.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of LLM agents for enterprise workflows usually look at single-agent or fixed-opponent setups and do not test whether performance rankings remain stable when agents interact and compete in realistic, shared markets. This gap matters because enterprises care about agent behavior and robustness under competition and changing market ecologies, not only in isolated scenarios.
AI.method: The authors build ERPBench, a six-round ERP simulation environment that couples pricing, production, procurement, inventory, finance, and shared-market competition. They define 100 fixed decision problems and evaluate LLM agents in two matched ecologies: (1) Solo, where each LLM agent plays against fixed rule-based opponents, and (2) Arena, where six LLM agents play simultaneously in a shared market. They test six model families, generating 1,200 model trajectories over 7,200 decision rounds, and instrument execution for detailed intervention and analysis.
AI.result: Under their evaluation configuration, different models come out on top in different ecologies: DeepSeek has the best performance in Solo, while Gemini leads in Arena. The two ecologies agree on the best model for only 21 of the 100 tasks. Gemini’s worst-place (bottom-rank) frequency drops dramatically—from 22% in Solo to 0% in Arena—showing that relative model rankings can change substantially between market settings.
AI.conclusion: ERPBench reveals that enterprise-agent rankings do not reliably transfer between isolated and shared competitive market ecologies. It provides a paired evaluation framework, with execution-level instrumentation, for studying how LLM-based enterprise decision agents behave and rank under different competitive conditions, enabling more realistic assessment of their suitability for enterprise deployment.

title: Can Activation Steering Capture Multidimensional Authorship Style?
summary: Activation steering has shown promise for controlling LLM generation along well-defined attributes, but it remains unclear whether it can handle the multidimensional and hard-to-define nature of authorship style. We ask whether structured contrastive prompting along rhetorically-motivated dimensions can construct rich style representations directly in activation space, bypassing the need for natural language style descriptors or dedicated training. We find that the resulting directions share a common authorship backbone while conflicting on aspect-specific residuals that carry genuine stylistic signal, explaining why naive aggregation fails. We operationalize this in Aspect-Aware Activation Steering (A3S), a training-free framework that merges per-aspect contrastive directions with interference-aware aggregation and tunes steering strength per instance. A3S improves authorship style transfer where it is genuinely multi-aspect, outperforms a trained baseline in preference evaluations on out-of-domain benchmarks, and keeps target-exemplar overlap consistently low.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a training-free method (A3S) that builds multi-aspect authorship style controls directly in a model’s activation space using structured contrastive prompts, achieving better and more faithful style transfer than baselines while avoiding content copying.
AI.motivation: Existing activation steering methods work well for simple, single attributes (e.g., sentiment) but struggle with the complex, multidimensional nature of authorship style. It is unclear how to construct rich style representations in activation space without hand-crafted style descriptors or additional training, and naive aggregation of multiple style directions tends to fail. The authors aim to understand and improve how to model and control authorship style as a combination of multiple rhetorical aspects directly in a model’s internal activations.
AI.method: They use structured contrastive prompting along carefully chosen rhetorical aspects (e.g., perspective, register, structure) to induce activation differences representing each aspect of style. Analyzing these directions, they find a shared “authorship backbone” plus aspect-specific residuals. They propose Aspect-Aware Activation Steering (A3S), which: (1) derives per-aspect contrastive directions in activation space; (2) aggregates them with an interference-aware procedure that accounts for conflicts between aspects; and (3) adaptively tunes the steering strength for each instance at generation time. The entire approach is training-free and operates purely via activation manipulation and prompting.
AI.result: Empirically, A3S improves authorship style transfer performance specifically in settings where style is genuinely multi-aspect, outperforming both naive aggregation of directions and a trained baseline system. Human or preference-based evaluations on out-of-domain benchmarks favor A3S generations, and quantitative analysis shows that overlap with target exemplars remains consistently low, indicating that the method captures style rather than copying content. The analysis of activation directions also confirms the presence of a shared authorship backbone with aspect-specific residual components.
AI.conclusion: Authorship style can be effectively represented and controlled as a structured combination of aspect-specific directions in activation space, without additional training or natural-language style labels. By recognizing and managing interference between aspects, A3S achieves more faithful, multi-dimensional style transfer and avoids content memorization. This suggests activation steering, when made aspect-aware, is a powerful tool for fine-grained stylistic control in large language models.

title: Train What You Deploy:Token-Faithful Post-Training of a Production Coding
summary: Existing post-training pipelines for coding and terminal agents suffer severe token and control fidelity errors: simplified training environments mismatch production deployments, and offline token reconstruction from agent logs distorts original prompts and conflates policy calls with background model operations. We present a fidelity-aware training coupling framework that retains trainer-side sampling over original prompts, eliminates spurious model calls via a negotiated training protocol, and restricts loss computation to verifiable token spans with closed-failure guarantees. We further propose Certified Divergence Proximal Policy Optimization (C-DPPO), which establishes tight two-sided TV certification bounds, adaptive-K rules, budget-aware sequence guarantees, and error-robust policy masking atop standard DPPO. Evaluated on matched Baize5B and Baize10B models with identical training and test protocols on TMax-100, C-DPPO yields a consistent +3.0-point performance gain over standard DPPO across model scales. Certificate audits validate the reliability and full operational coverage of our certified training pipeline.

AI.tldr: They propose a new, higher-fidelity post-training framework and a certified variant of PPO (C-DPPO) for coding/terminal agents, reducing training–deployment mismatch and improving reliability and performance.
AI.motivation: Post-training pipelines for coding and terminal agents are currently low-fidelity: training environments differ from real deployment, and reconstructing tokens from logs corrupts prompts and mixes agent policy outputs with background model operations. This leads to inaccurate gradients and unreliable policies. The authors want a training pipeline that more faithfully reflects actual agent behavior and provides certifiable guarantees on training accuracy and coverage.
AI.method: They design a fidelity-aware training coupling framework that (1) keeps trainer-side sampling over the original, uncorrupted prompts, (2) uses a negotiated protocol to exclude spurious or non-policy model calls from training, and (3) computes loss only over token spans that can be verified, with formal guarantees that any failures are closed and known. On top of this, they introduce Certified Divergence Proximal Policy Optimization (C-DPPO), which modifies DPPO with: tight two-sided total-variation (TV) divergence certification bounds between old and new policies, adaptive-K update rules, budget-aware per-sequence guarantees, and robustness to errors through policy masking.
AI.result: On Baize5B and Baize10B models, evaluated under a matched training and testing setup on the TMax-100 benchmark, C-DPPO achieves a consistent +3.0 point gain in performance compared to standard DPPO, regardless of model scale. They also run certificate audits showing that the theoretical certification properties hold in practice and that their training pipeline covers the full range of operational behaviors.
AI.conclusion: Their fidelity-aware coupling framework and C-DPPO algorithm significantly improve the reliability and performance of coding/terminal agents by aligning training more closely with deployment and adding formal certification guarantees. The consistent performance gains and successful certificate audits suggest this approach is a robust upgrade over standard DPPO-based post-training for such agents.

title: Recurrence Is Not Enough: Causally Validating Multilingual SAE Translation Features in Gemma 2 and 3
summary:
Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features are increasingly used to explain and steer language-model behavior, but it remains unclear whether a feature found in one language context plays the same causal role when processing prompts in another language. We study this question using translation-initiation features (Wu et al., 2026). We reproduce the SAE feature discovery method from Wu et al. in Gemma 2 and extend it to multilingual settings that vary prompt language, source language, and target language. We then test whether features that recur across settings affect translation behavior by amplifying or ablating their activations during inference. We also examine whether the method can be applied to Gemma 3.
  In both models, we observe an identical finding: although we can find more than 20 features that activate frequently across all discovery settings, causal validation shows that nearly all have small or inconsistent effects. In contrast, one feature -- Gemma 2's (L10, 5717) and Gemma 3's (L20, 2456) -- consistently improves COMET scores when amplified and degrades them when ablated across 23 language settings. These results show that feature recurrence can overstate cross-lingual transfer, while identifying a language-agnostic translation-initiation direction in Gemma 2 and Gemma 3.

AI.tldr: They test whether sparse autoencoder features that signal translation initiation in one language context play the same causal role across many languages in Gemma 2 and Gemma 3, and find that most recurrent features don’t, except for a single robust, language-agnostic translation-initiation direction in each model.
AI.motivation: Sparse autoencoder features are widely used to interpret and steer language models, but it’s unclear whether a feature discovered in one language setup truly generalizes and has the same causal effect in other languages. Prior work (Wu et al., 2026) focused on monolingual or limited settings. This paper wants to rigorously test cross-lingual transfer of such features, specifically those tied to starting a translation, because this matters for building reliable, interpretable, and controllable multilingual models.
AI.method: They reproduce Wu et al.’s SAE-based feature discovery pipeline on Gemma 2, then extend it to many multilingual configurations that systematically vary prompt, source, and target languages. They identify SAE features associated with translation initiation that recur across these different discovery settings, then perform causal interventions at inference time by amplifying or ablating these features to see how translation quality changes. They repeat the process on Gemma 3 to check whether the findings hold across model generations.
AI.result: Across both Gemma 2 and Gemma 3, they discover 20+ SAE features that frequently recur across all multilingual discovery settings, but causal tests show that almost all of these have weak, small, or inconsistent influence on translation behavior. Only one feature per model—Gemma 2’s (layer 10, feature 5717) and Gemma 3’s (layer 20, feature 2456)—behaves robustly: amplifying it systematically improves COMET translation scores, while ablating it degrades them, and this pattern holds across 23 language-pair settings.
AI.conclusion: Simply observing that an SAE feature recurs across multiple language discovery contexts is not enough to infer that it has a stable, shared causal role; recurrence overstates true cross-lingual transfer. However, there does appear to be a single, approximately language-agnostic translation-initiation direction in both Gemma 2 and Gemma 3, which can be used to reliably steer translation behavior. The work highlights the need for causal validation, not just feature overlap, when claiming cross-lingual interpretability or control.

title: Predicting Spatiotemporal Mobile Sensing-Based PM2.5 Concentrations Using Low-Rank Adapted Spatially Attentive Graph Neural Network
comment: 24 Pages, 14 Figures, World Conference of Transport Research2026 Transport Research
summary: Urban air quality can vary significantly along transit corridors, necessitating high-resolution monitoring. This work introduces a novel mobile-sensing dataset from Surat, Gujarat, India, comprising PM$*{2.5}$ concentrations, meteorological variables (temperature, humidity, wind speed, wind direction), and land-use features. To represent the spatiotemporal data as a graph, two node-definition strategies were used: (i) uniform segmentation (200--400~m intervals) and (ii) DBSCAN clustering to adaptively group dense observations. For each node, rolling mean and standard deviation of meteorological variables were computed. To model this high-dimensional data, we propose a SA-GNN for fine-grained, short-term PM$*{2.5}$ forecasting and hotspot identification. We compared SA-GNN with LSTM, RNN, GRU, and ANN models. These models performed well on low-resolution data but had difficulty capturing rapidly changing patterns in urban air quality. SA-GNN employs cluster-specific GRUs to capture localized temporal dependencies and a Graph Attention Network to learn spatial heterogeneity. This hybrid architecture effectively models rapid fluctuations and complex spatial interactions. On our dataset, SA-GNN achieved $R^2 = 0.95$, RMSE $= 6.8$, and MAE $= 4.2~\si{\micro\gram\per\meter\cubed}$, outperforming all baseline models. Combining spatial clustering with adaptive attention significantly improves forecasting, enabling real-time, fine-grained monitoring and supporting personalized exposure tracking and timely alerts for healthier cities.

AI.tldr: They build a graph-based deep learning model (SA-GNN) using mobile air-pollution measurements along roads in Surat to predict short-term, fine-scale PM2.5 and identify hotspots, outperforming standard time-series models.
AI.motivation: Urban air pollution can change drastically over small distances and short times along transit routes, affecting human exposure. Conventional fixed-station monitoring and coarse-resolution models miss these fine-scale variations, limiting their usefulness for real-time exposure management and localized alerts. There is a need for models that can exploit dense mobile-sensing data and capture both rapid temporal fluctuations and complex spatial heterogeneity at street scale.
AI.method: They collect a mobile-sensing dataset along transit corridors in Surat, India, including PM2.5, meteorology, and land-use features. They convert these spatiotemporal observations into graphs using two node-definition strategies: uniform segmentation of routes into 200–400 m segments and adaptive DBSCAN clustering of dense measurement locations. Each node is enriched with rolling mean and standard deviation of meteorological variables. They then propose SA-GNN, a hybrid Spatial-Attention Graph Neural Network that uses cluster-specific GRUs to learn localized temporal dynamics at each node/cluster and a Graph Attention Network layer to model spatial heterogeneity and interactions between nodes. They compare SA-GNN against LSTM, vanilla RNN, GRU, and ANN baselines on fine-grained, short-term PM2.5 forecasting and hotspot identification tasks.
AI.result: SA-GNN achieves strong predictive performance with R^2=0.95, RMSE=6.8, and MAE=4.2 µg/m³ on their Surat mobile-sensing dataset, and it consistently outperforms LSTM, RNN, GRU, and ANN models. Baseline models perform adequately on coarser data but struggle with rapidly varying urban air quality, whereas SA-GNN better captures short-term fluctuations and localized patterns due to its spatial attention and cluster-specific temporal modeling.
AI.conclusion: Graph-based modeling that combines spatial clustering, cluster-specific temporal modules, and adaptive attention substantially improves fine-scale PM2.5 forecasting from mobile-sensing data. The proposed SA-GNN can deliver real-time, high-resolution air-quality estimates along transit corridors, enabling hotspot detection, personalized exposure tracking, and timely alerts that support healthier urban environments.

title: A Systematic Comparison of Multilingual Interpretability Methods Reveals Anisotropy-Driven Failures
summary: Multilingual language models develop shared cross-lingual representations, and various interpretability methods claim to quantify this sharing. These methods have been developed largely in isolation, and when they disagree, it is unclear whether the disagreement reflects a property of the model or an artifact of the measurement. We compare four sharing metrics (CKA, ANC, GMM dominance per token, and ILO) across 21 base models from five families (125M-14B parameters) and correlate each with cross-lingual transfer on five downstream tasks. We find that the metrics differ in their quantification of cross-lingual sharing in these models and suggest that the disagreement traces to anisotropy, the tendency of representations to cluster in a narrow cone of the embedding space. Only ILO's correlation with cross-lingual transfer (Spearman's $ρ= 0.90$) survives controls for model size, family, and per-task variation. We therefore recommend ILO as the primary sharing metric, to be reported alongside anisotropy diagnostics.

AI.tldr: The paper systematically compares four metrics for measuring cross-lingual representation sharing in multilingual language models and finds that only ILO reliably predicts cross-lingual transfer performance, especially after controlling for confounds like model size and family.
AI.motivation: Multilingual language models are known to develop shared cross-lingual representations, but the field lacks consensus on how to measure the degree of this sharing. Multiple interpretability metrics (e.g., CKA, ANC, GMM dominance, ILO) have been proposed independently, and they often disagree. When these metrics conflict, it is unclear whether the discrepancy reflects genuine model behavior or limitations of the metrics themselves. This ambiguity hampers our ability to understand and improve cross-lingual transfer, motivating a systematic comparison of sharing metrics and their relationship to actual downstream performance.
AI.method: The authors evaluate four metrics of cross-lingual representation sharing—CKA, ANC, GMM dominance per token, and ILO—across 21 base multilingual models from five different model families, ranging from 125M to 14B parameters. They quantify the degree of cross-lingual sharing each metric reports and analyze how these measurements relate to structural properties of the representation space, with a particular focus on anisotropy (the clustering of representations in a narrow region of embedding space). They then correlate each sharing metric with empirical cross-lingual transfer performance across five downstream tasks, using statistical controls to factor out confounding variables like model size, model family, and per-task variability. Spearman correlation is used to measure the strength of association between sharing metrics and transfer performance.
AI.result: The four sharing metrics provide discrepant estimates of cross-lingual representation sharing in the tested models. The authors trace much of this disagreement to anisotropy in the embedding spaces: metrics are differently sensitive to the tendency of representations to concentrate in a narrow cone. When correlated with cross-lingual transfer performance, most metrics show weaker or non-robust associations once controls for model size, family, and task-specific effects are applied. In contrast, ILO maintains a strong and robust correlation with cross-lingual transfer, achieving a Spearman correlation of 0.90 even after these controls. This suggests that ILO is less confounded by anisotropy and model-scale factors than the other metrics examined.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that commonly used cross-lingual sharing metrics (CKA, ANC, GMM dominance per token) can be misleading or inconsistently aligned with actual cross-lingual transfer performance, in part because of their sensitivity to anisotropy in representation spaces. ILO stands out as the only metric whose correlation with transfer performance remains strong and robust under statistical controls, indicating it is a more reliable indicator of meaningful cross-lingual sharing. The authors therefore recommend that future work use ILO as the primary metric for quantifying cross-lingual representation sharing and report it together with anisotropy diagnostics to better interpret metric values and disentangle genuine sharing from representational artifacts.

title: SQL-Zero: Self-Evolving Text-to-SQL
summary: Training a competitive Text-to-SQL agent usually depends on human-annotated natural-language/SQL pairs, which are expensive, domain-specific, and a bottleneck for scaling to new databases. We show it is possible to train a competitive solver with zero annotated pairs. We introduce SQL-Zero, a proposer-solver self-play in which a challenger and a solver start from the same base LLM and the only ground truth is execution against the database itself. The challenger generates SQL pairs calibrated to the solver's current difficulty (targeting "hard but solvable"), and both roles are updated with GRPO in alternating turns, with a template-level repetition penalty on the challenger to prevent diversity collapse. Training on BIRD databases with no labels, self-play improves over the zero-shot base on BIRD dev by 6.6 points at 3B and 7.3 points at 7B. It also scores higher than a matched control trained under the same recipe on human BIRD gold over the same databases, although an exact paired test does not resolve that margin. Transfer depends on scale: at 3B every iteration outperforms the base on unseen Spider databases and under lexical perturbation (Spider-Syn), where it also degrades less than the matched BIRD-gold control, whereas at 7B only the first iteration preserves transfer.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SQL-Zero, a self-play framework that trains a Text-to-SQL agent without any human-annotated NL/SQL pairs, using only database execution as supervision, and achieves competitive performance and some transfer to new datasets.
AI.motivation: Human-annotated natural-language/SQL pairs are expensive, domain-specific, and limit the scalability of Text-to-SQL systems to new databases. The authors want to remove this dependence and show that a competitive Text-to-SQL model can be trained without any labeled examples, relying instead on automatic supervision from database execution.
AI.method: They introduce SQL-Zero, a proposer-solver (challenger-solver) self-play setup where both agents start from the same base LLM. The challenger generates natural language/SQL pairs that are aimed to be challenging but solvable for the current solver. The only ground truth signal is whether the SQL executes correctly against the database. Both challenger and solver are updated with GRPO (a reinforcement learning-style optimization) in alternating turns. A template-level repetition penalty is applied to the challenger to avoid mode collapse and encourage diverse query templates. Training is done on BIRD databases without labels.
AI.result: On the BIRD dev set, self-play training without labels improves performance over the zero-shot base model by 6.6 points for a 3B model and 7.3 points for a 7B model. The SQL-Zero model even outperforms a control model trained on human BIRD gold annotations under the same training recipe, though the performance margin is not statistically confirmed by a paired test. Regarding transfer, at 3B scale all self-play iterations outperform the base model on unseen Spider databases and under lexical perturbations (Spider-Syn), with less degradation than the BIRD-gold control. At 7B scale, only the first self-play iteration maintains such transfer benefits.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that competitive Text-to-SQL systems can be trained without any human-annotated NL/SQL pairs using a self-play scheme that relies solely on database execution as supervision. The SQL-Zero approach can match or even surpass models trained on human-labeled data in-domain, and at smaller scales it also improves robustness and transfer to new databases and perturbed inputs, though transfer benefits become less consistent at larger scales.

title: Reinforcement Learning for improving Large Language Models' Catalan text simplification capabilities
comment: Accepted at CLEAR-TEXT 2026: Readability and text simplification workshop at the International Conference Computational Linguistics in Bulgaria (CLIB 2026)
summary: Although automatic text simplification (ATS) is critical for accessibility, its progress has not matched the rapid evolution of broader natural language processing techniques. This paper investigates the application of reinforcement learning (RL) to improve the quality of ATS for low-resource languages using Large Language Models (LLMs). The paper introduces a novel reward function, designed to guide LLMs toward a targeted simplification style with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), that combines the SARI metric with specific penalty components. The effectiveness of GRPO with this reward function is motivated and demonstrated by post-training IberianLLM-7B-Instruct on the ASSET dataset. After post-training on the English ASSET, the model's ATS performance improves on two curated Catalan benchmarks while also successfully suppressing previously observed negative behaviors. Cross-lingual transfer learning is explored by translating ASSET into Catalan and Spanish and post-training the model on each version, but these fail to show a significant improvement on the out-of-domain benchmark.

AI.tldr: They use reinforcement learning with a new reward to improve text simplification by LLMs, showing gains for Catalan using English training, but limited benefits from simple cross-lingual transfer.
AI.motivation: Automatic text simplification helps accessibility, especially for readers with lower literacy or cognitive impairments, but current systems—particularly for low-resource languages—lag behind general NLP advances. Existing ATS often relies on supervised fine-tuning with limited parallel data and does not adequately control simplification style or avoid undesirable model behaviors. There is a need to exploit modern LLMs and reinforcement learning to better steer simplification quality and style, and to explore whether improvements learned in a high‑resource language can transfer to related, low‑resource languages.
AI.method: They take IberianLLM-7B-Instruct and apply reinforcement learning using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). They design a custom reward function that blends the SARI simplification metric with penalty terms targeting undesired behaviors and to enforce a particular simplification style. They post-train the model on the English ASSET dataset under this RL setup. They also create translated versions of ASSET in Catalan and Spanish to study cross-lingual transfer by post-training on each language version and then evaluating on curated Catalan benchmarks, including out-of-domain data.
AI.result: Post-training the model with GRPO and the new reward on English ASSET yields improved automatic text simplification performance on two curated Catalan benchmarks, even though the training data is in English. The RL procedure also reduces or suppresses previously observed negative behaviors of the model. However, when they translate ASSET into Catalan and Spanish and post-train on these translated datasets, the resulting models do not achieve significant additional gains on an out-of-domain Catalan benchmark, indicating limited benefits from this straightforward cross-lingual data augmentation approach.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement learning with a carefully crafted reward (combining SARI and penalties) can effectively steer an LLM toward higher-quality, better-behaved text simplification and that improvements learned from English can transfer to a related low-resource language like Catalan. Nevertheless, naive cross-lingual transfer via simple dataset translation and post-training does not substantially improve performance on out-of-domain data, suggesting that more sophisticated multilingual or domain-robust approaches are needed for stronger cross-lingual gains in ATS.

title: Model Retirement Creates Reproducibility Risk in Biomedical AI Publications
summary:
Background. Large language models (LLMs) are being adopted in biomedical research at a rapid and accelerating pace, yet commercial services that host many widely used models operate under deprecation schedules that can complicate scientific reproducibility.
  Methods. We searched PubMed for original research articles from 2022 through March 2026 that applied a specific LLM to a biomedical task. An extraction agent identified model names from 61,077 article abstracts with human reviewers validating a subset for extraction accuracy. Extracted model names were normalized to canonical model identifiers. Lifecycle data (release date, retirement date, status) were compiled for the 50 most frequently used models.
  Results. We identified 8,931 paper-model mentions spanning 5,242 unique publications after restricting the analysis to the 50 most frequently used models. Among these mentions, 77.7% cited a commercial closed-weight model. Overall, 42% involved a model that was already retired by the time of official publication or is scheduled to retire within two years of publication. The median interval from publication to model retirement was 538 days.
  Conclusion. Many biomedical publications using LLMs are on a trajectory toward computational non-reproducibility after publication. Model deprecation should be treated as a core reporting and preservation issue for biomedical research.

AI.tldr: The paper finds that many biomedical studies using large language models rely on commercial models that are or will soon be deprecated, threatening computational reproducibility.
AI.motivation: As large language models become widely used in biomedical research, many studies depend on commercial, closed-weight services that follow deprecation schedules. When these models are retired or updated, it becomes difficult or impossible to reproduce published computational results. The paper aims to quantify how common this problem is and how quickly it arises after publication.
AI.method: The authors searched PubMed for original research articles between 2022 and March 2026 that used a specific LLM for a biomedical task. They applied an extraction agent to 61,077 abstracts to detect cited LLM names, with human reviewers validating a subset. Model names were normalized to canonical identifiers. For the 50 most frequently used models, they compiled lifecycle data including release dates, retirement dates, and current status, then analyzed temporal relationships between publication dates and model deprecation.
AI.result: From 61,077 abstracts, the study found 8,931 paper–model mentions across 5,242 unique publications, focusing on the 50 most frequently used models. Of these mentions, 77.7% involved commercial closed-weight models. Overall, 42% of mentions referred to a model that was already retired by the time of official publication or was scheduled to retire within two years after publication. The median time from publication to model retirement was 538 days.
AI.conclusion: A substantial fraction of biomedical LLM research depends on models that become deprecated or retired relatively soon after publication, putting studies on a path toward computational non-reproducibility. The authors argue that model deprecation must be treated as a fundamental reporting and preservation issue in biomedical research, implying a need for better documentation, model archiving strategies, and possibly a preference for stable or open models in some contexts.

title: Generating Constructive Feedback on Stories via Reinforcement Learning
summary: Constructive feedback is crucial for creative writers to refine their storytelling abilities. Since receiving feedback from human experts is often costly and time-intensive, large language models (LLMs) offer a scalable and efficient alternative as automatic writing assistants. Despite their potential, research indicates that LLM-generated feedback is often generic, lacks actionability, and fails to identify which writing issue is most critical. To address these limitations, we present a reinforcement learning approach that steers LLMs to generate constructive feedback without the need for ground-truth feedback. We train our model using group relative policy optimization (GRPO) with a novel multi-component reward function aiming at constructiveness: it prioritizes feedback that is uniquely tailored to the story, helps to improve story quality, and addresses the most critical writing issue. In automatic and human evaluation across three story corpora, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art LLMs (including Gemini) and competitive baselines. We find that providing actionable suggestions is the main driver of feedback constructiveness.

AI.tldr: They train an LLM with reinforcement learning (GRPO) and a custom reward to give more constructive, specific, and prioritized feedback on creative writing, outperforming strong baselines.
AI.motivation: Constructive, expert feedback helps creative writers improve, but expert time is scarce and expensive. LLMs could scale feedback, yet current LLM feedback is often generic, non-actionable, and poor at prioritizing the most important issues in a story. There is a need for a training method that specifically optimizes feedback quality without requiring ground-truth feedback annotations.
AI.method: The authors propose a reinforcement learning framework using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to fine‑tune an LLM to generate better writing feedback. They design a multi-component reward function targeting different aspects of constructiveness: story-specificity (avoiding generic comments), contribution to improving story quality, and correct identification of the most critical writing issue. The model is trained without relying on gold-standard human feedback, instead using this reward signal to iteratively steer the policy toward more constructive feedback behaviors.
AI.result: On three different story corpora and using both automatic metrics and human judgments, the RL-trained model produces feedback that is more constructive than that of strong baseline systems, including state-of-the-art LLMs such as Gemini. Analyses indicate that the component of the reward encouraging actionable suggestions contributes most strongly to the gains in constructiveness.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing LLMs with GRPO and a carefully designed, multi-faceted reward can significantly improve the constructiveness of automated feedback for creative writing, even without ground-truth feedback labels. Actionability—offering concrete revision suggestions—emerges as the key factor for impactful feedback, suggesting future systems should explicitly target this property when training writing assistants.

title: FinalityBench: An Effect-Level Benchmark for Agent Decisions Under Delayed and Conflicting Financial Finality
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. Code, corpus generator and all result files: https://github.com/abhisheksharma2411/finalitybench Archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.22262591
summary: A merchant's payment processor, ledger, ERP and bank feed are updated by messages that get delayed, duplicated, dropped and reordered, so for minutes at a time the four hold contradictory beliefs about the same order. An agent resolving the exception must decide whether to ship goods, re-submit a capture, refund or wait, knowing some of those cannot be undone. We present FinalityBench, an executable benchmark for that decision. It keeps a hidden canonical event log and derives each system's view from a separately faulted delivery stream, so disagreement follows from specified fault semantics rather than being authored. Grading is on executed monetary effects: an episode is scored by the merchant's terminal economic position, relative to a privileged reference told when the pending capture resolves. The corpus of 321 tasks includes 45 twin pairs (90 tasks): tasks whose four system views are identical at the decision instant, whose authoritative probes both return unknown, and whose eventual correct dispositions differ. That snapshot indistinguishability is checked under every evaluation seed rather than assumed; equivalence over all interaction traces is not claimed. Over 14,445 graded episodes from nine programmatic policies, ranking by single-task accuracy and by paired loss disagree in 7 places: a ship-on-first-sign policy is second-best by accuracy at 65.7% and worst in the suite by paired loss, because it cannot tell the two members apart. A runtime gating irreversible actions on an authoritative finality probe reaches 85.4% and, unlike every polling policy, loses nothing to pass^5; its residual loss is almost entirely one archetype, which prices finality information directly. Language models reach the same exact rate as the hand-written gate on a stratified subset, lose about twice as much money, and discover the finality-gating strategy without being told it.

AI.tldr: FinalityBench is a benchmark for decision-making under inconsistent financial system states caused by unreliable message delivery, scoring policies by their realized economic outcomes rather than simple accuracy.
AI.motivation: In real-world payment processing, different systems (payment processor, ledger, ERP, bank feed) see inconsistent, delayed, or faulty information about the same transaction due to message delays, duplication, drops and reordering. Human or automated agents must make irreversible decisions (ship, refund, re-capture, wait) under this uncertainty, but existing evaluations tend to assume clean, authored states or focus on classification accuracy, not economic consequences under realistic message faults. There is a need for an executable benchmark that reflects these operational realities and evaluates policies by their economic impact.
AI.method: The authors build FinalityBench, which maintains a hidden canonical event log for each order and derives each system’s visible state via separate, fault-injected delivery streams that simulate realistic messaging anomalies. They define tasks where an agent must choose actions given four inconsistent system views and partial authoritative probes. The benchmark includes 321 tasks, including 45 "twin pairs" whose observable states and probe results are identical at decision time but whose eventual correct actions differ. Episodes are scored by the merchant’s final monetary position relative to an oracle that knows when pending captures resolve. The authors run nine programmatic decision policies across 14,445 graded episodes, compare metrics (single-task accuracy vs paired loss), and also evaluate language models on a stratified subset.
AI.result: They show that naïve metrics can be misleading: a simple ship-on-first-sign policy achieves 65.7% accuracy yet performs worst by paired loss, because it mishandles indistinguishable twin tasks. A policy that gates irreversible actions (like shipping) on an authoritative finality probe achieves 85.4% accuracy and, unlike polling-based policies, suffers no extra loss from pathological adversarial cases (pass^5). Its remaining losses are concentrated in a single archetype that explicitly prices finality information. Language models, when evaluated on a stratified subset, match the hand-written gate’s accuracy but incur roughly twice the monetary loss, though they independently discover the finality-gating strategy without explicit instruction.
AI.conclusion: FinalityBench provides a realistic, executable environment to study decision-making under inconsistent financial records caused by messaging faults, scoring policies by actual economic outcomes rather than surface accuracy. The experiments demonstrate that higher classification accuracy does not guarantee better financial performance, especially in indistinguishable twin scenarios. Policies that gate irreversible actions on robust finality signals perform best and are robust to adversarial conditions. Language models can learn such strategies but currently lag in economic efficiency, highlighting both their promise and the need for more loss-aware training and evaluation in transactional domains.

title: On Epistemic Diversity in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used not only to retrieve information, but to answer questions, explain, teach, and support inquiry. In such settings, evaluation cannot be exhausted by accuracy or alignment alone. A system may give a correct answer while still narrowing users' access %to knowledge. to alternative valid answers, explanations, or reasoning routes. Drawing on the broader notion of epistemic diversity in philosophy and social epistemology, we formalize it in the context of LLMs as the range of valid answers, explanations, and reasoning routes that an LLM exposes to users. We argue that epistemic diversity is a useful evaluation dimension for settings where LLMs are used to support knowledge-intensive tasks. We propose a preliminary framework for conceptualizing and measuring epistemic diversity in LLMs, and operationalize it in two domains. We find that frontier LLMs often exhibit epistemic narrowness, repeatedly collapsing large valid answer spaces onto small canonical subsets. These findings suggest that LLM evaluation should move beyond accuracy-oriented paradigms and treat epistemic diversity as an important dimension of model capability.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that evaluating large language models (LLMs) only by accuracy and alignment is insufficient and introduces epistemic diversity—the breadth of valid answers, explanations, and reasoning paths—as a critical, measurable dimension of model performance.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used for explanation, teaching, and inquiry support, a purely accuracy-focused evaluation misses an important risk: models can systematically narrow the space of ideas users see, even when they answer correctly. This can constrain users’ understanding, creativity, and critical thinking. The authors are motivated by concerns from philosophy and social epistemology about pluralism and diversity of viewpoints, and they want to translate these concerns into a concrete evaluation criterion for LLMs.
AI.method: The authors (1) import and adapt the philosophical notion of epistemic diversity to the context of LLM interactions; (2) define it as the range of valid answers, explanations, and reasoning routes an LLM reveals; (3) design a preliminary conceptual and quantitative framework to measure this property; and (4) apply this framework in two specific domains to analyze model outputs, comparing how often models converge on a narrow set of canonical responses versus reflecting a broader valid answer space.
AI.result: Applying their framework to frontier LLMs in two domains, they find that models frequently display epistemic narrowness: instead of exploring the broad space of valid answers or explanations, they tend to default to a small, repeated subset of canonical responses. This happens even when many alternative, equally valid answers exist, revealing a systematic pattern of collapsed diversity in model outputs.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that current LLM evaluation practices are incomplete if they center solely on accuracy or alignment. Epistemic diversity should be treated as a distinct and crucial dimension of model capability, especially for knowledge-intensive applications. The authors advocate incorporating measures of epistemic diversity into evaluation protocols and further developing methods to quantify and improve this aspect of LLM behavior.

title: PLUME: Parameter-Efficient Personalization of Large Language Models via Low-Rank User Modulation in Shared Subspaces
summary: Personalizing large language models (LLMs) is essential for delivering AI assistance that aligns with individual users' styles, intents, and preferences. While per-user fine-tuning can substantially enhance personalization quality, it introduces significant parameter and storage overhead, limiting scalability to large user populations. We propose PLUME (Personalized Low-Rank Adaptation through User Modulation and Shared Subspace), a lightweight framework that achieves efficient and expressive per-user adaptation by leveraging a shared task-specific subspace. Specifically, PLUME first learns a global task subspace from aggregated user data. Personalization is then achieved by training only a lightweight small square matrix within this subspace, enabling each user to obtain a tailored model while keeping shared components fixed. Cross-layer shared parameters and rank-1 residual terms are further introduced to significantly reduce redundancy while maintaining expressiveness. Experiments on multiple personalized text generation benchmarks demonstrate that PLUME achieves comparable or superior performance to strong baselines, while reducing per-user parameters by over 95%. These results establish shared-subspace modulation with minimal residuals as a scalable and semantically grounded approach to LLM personalization.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes PLUME, a highly parameter-efficient method for personalizing large language models by learning a shared task-specific subspace and only training tiny per-user adapters within it.
