AI.motivation: Personalizing LLMs via per-user fine-tuning greatly improves alignment with individual user preferences but is not scalable because each user requires many additional parameters and storage. The authors want a method that preserves personalization quality while drastically cutting per-user overhead.
AI.method: They introduce PLUME, which first learns a global, task-specific low-rank subspace from aggregated user data. Personalization is then done by training, for each user, only a small square matrix that operates inside this fixed subspace, with all large shared components kept frozen. To further cut redundancy while retaining expressiveness, they share parameters across layers and add lightweight rank-1 residual terms. This yields per-user modules that are much smaller than typical fine-tuning or LoRA adapters.
AI.result: Across several personalized text generation benchmarks, PLUME matches or outperforms strong personalization baselines while reducing per-user trainable parameters by more than 95%, showing that the approach is both effective and highly parameter-efficient.
AI.conclusion: Shared-subspace modulation with very small residual adapters provides a scalable, semantically meaningful solution to LLM personalization, enabling high-quality per-user models with minimal parameter and storage cost.

title: MABPD: Multi-Agent Bias Probing & Detection via Structured Argument Debate
comment: 20 pages, 6 figures. Accepted to the EMNLP 2026 Main Conference. Code: https://github.com/Subaru-5999/MABPD
summary: Media bias in news articles operates through subtle linguistic cues---loaded language, selective framing, and strategic omission---that resist single-model detection and have traditionally required large annotated corpora for supervised training. We ask whether structured multi-agent deliberation can serve as a principled, training-free alternative to supervised classification for this task. We introduce MABPD (Multi-Agent Bias Probing & Detection), a pipeline in which three specialized LLM agents analyze an article from complementary perspectives and resolve disagreements through a Structured Argument Debate (SAD) protocol. SAD implements a domain-motivated asymmetric burden of proof---biased claims without grounded textual evidence carry zero weight---combined with role-weighted voting and post-consensus verification, replacing task-specific supervised decision boundaries with explicit deliberative structure. Ablation confirms that this structured deliberation, not mere agent parallelism, drives performance: removing the debate module reduces F1 by up to 10.6 points. On the BABE benchmark (4,121 expert-annotated sentences), MABPD achieves 83.4% macro F1 on the held-out test split---within 0.7 percentage points (pp) of the supervised SOTA (MAGPIE, 84.1% macro F1; Horych et al., 2024)---without any task-specific training or threshold tuning on annotated data. Cross-dataset evaluation on the SemEval 2019 HyperPartisan corpus (644 articles) yields 75.0% zero-shot accuracy, within 7.2 pp of the supervised SOTA accuracy (82.2%; Kiesel et al. 2019), confirming transfer across annotation regimes. We release the full pipeline and evaluation code.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multi-agent, debate-based LLM framework (MABPD) that detects media bias in news text nearly as well as supervised state-of-the-art models, but without any task-specific training data.
AI.motivation: Media bias manifests through nuanced linguistic and contextual cues that are hard to capture with a single model and typically require large annotated datasets for supervised learning. Acquiring such labeled data is expensive and often domain-specific, limiting generalization. The authors aim to explore whether structured interaction among multiple large language model agents can provide a principled, training-free alternative to traditional supervised classifiers for bias detection, achieving competitive performance while improving transfer across datasets and annotation schemes.
AI.method: They introduce MABPD (Multi-Agent Bias Probing & Detection), a pipeline built from three specialized LLM agents that each analyze a news article from distinct, complementary perspectives. These agents engage in a Structured Argument Debate (SAD) protocol that enforces an asymmetric burden of proof: any claim of bias must be backed by explicit textual evidence; otherwise, it is discarded. The protocol combines role-weighted voting among agents with a post-consensus verification step. This replaces learned decision thresholds with an explicit deliberation and argumentation structure. Ablation studies remove elements such as the debate module to quantify their impact on performance.
AI.result: On the BABE benchmark of 4,121 expert-annotated sentences, MABPD attains 83.4% macro F1 on the held-out test set, coming within 0.7 percentage points of the supervised state-of-the-art model (MAGPIE at 84.1% macro F1). In ablation experiments, eliminating the debate component of the pipeline decreases F1 by up to 10.6 points, showing that structured deliberation is critical rather than simple parallel agent usage. In cross-dataset evaluation on the SemEval 2019 HyperPartisan corpus (644 articles), MABPD reaches 75.0% zero-shot accuracy, within 7.2 percentage points of the supervised SOTA (82.2%), indicating good transfer across different annotation regimes.
AI.conclusion: Structured multi-agent deliberation via MABPD provides an effective, training-free approach to media bias detection that performs close to supervised state-of-the-art systems on benchmark datasets. The asymmetric burden-of-proof design and explicit debate protocol are key to its success, enabling robust detection based on grounded textual evidence rather than learned task-specific thresholds. The promising cross-dataset performance suggests that such deliberative structures may generalize well across differing definitions and annotations of bias. The authors make their full pipeline and evaluation code publicly available to support further research and application.

title: Aplaud: Adaptive Personalized Low-Rank Decomposition for User-Specific LLM
summary: In this paper, we study the problem of personalized survey response prediction using fine-tuned large language models (LLMs). This task poses unique challenges: limited per-user training data, scalability of model storage, and the need to exploit shared structure across survey questions. To address these issues, we propose Aplaud (Adaptive Personalized Low-rank and User-specific Nested Decomposition), a lightweight and scalable framework for LLM personalization. Aplaud extends the LoRA paradigm by separating adaptation into a frozen, shared low-rank basis and a compact user-specific correction, augmented with a rank-one residual for finer personalization. To further reduce per-user parameter cost and mitigate overfitting, the correction matrix can be factorized into an even lower-rank form. Empirical results demonstrate that Aplaud achieves efficient, scalable personalization across users while outperforming state-of-the-art LoRA-based personalized LLM approaches in both generalization and inference efficiency.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Aplaud, a lightweight, scalable framework to personalize large language models for predicting individual survey responses, improving both accuracy and efficiency over existing LoRA-based methods.
AI.motivation: Personalizing LLMs for individual users in tasks like survey response prediction is challenging because each user has very few training examples, storing a separate large model per user is infeasible, and different survey questions share structure that should be leveraged. Existing approaches based on LoRA personalization either use too many parameters per user, do not scale to many users, or overfit to scarce user data. The authors aim to design a method that uses minimal additional parameters per user while still capturing user-specific behavior and generalizing well.
AI.method: The authors introduce Aplaud (Adaptive Personalized Low-rank and User-specific Nested Decomposition), which refines the LoRA adaptation strategy. Instead of a single low-rank adaptation per user, Aplaud decomposes adaptation into (1) a frozen, shared low-rank basis used across all users and (2) a compact user-specific correction that adjusts this basis for each individual. Additionally, a rank-one residual term is added to enable finer-grained personalization when needed. To further reduce per-user parameter count and prevent overfitting in low-data regimes, the user-specific correction matrix itself can be factorized into an even lower-rank representation. This yields a nested low-rank structure that balances expressiveness and parameter efficiency.
AI.result: Experiments on personalized survey response prediction tasks show that Aplaud provides more accurate predictions (better generalization) than state-of-the-art LoRA-based personalization baselines, while also requiring fewer additional parameters per user and enabling more efficient inference. The nested low-rank and rank-one residual design leads to improved scalability when supporting many users, with lower storage and computation costs than competing methods.
AI.conclusion: Aplaud offers an effective way to personalize LLMs for many users in data-scarce settings such as survey response prediction. By decoupling shared and user-specific adaptation through a nested low-rank structure plus a rank-one residual, it achieves a favorable trade-off between personalization quality, parameter efficiency, and scalability. The framework demonstrates that fine-grained yet lightweight user adaptations are feasible on top of a shared backbone LLM, suggesting broader applicability to other personalization scenarios beyond surveys.

title: MMTClinic: Multimodal, Multilingual Time Series Question Answering and Reasoning Benchmark for Clinical Domain
summary: Time-series data in clinical settings is crucial for capturing dynamic changes in a patient's health over time, enabling timely diagnosis, personalized treatment, and early detection of critical events. However, the development of clinically reliable and linguistically inclusive medical AI systems remains a significant challenge, primarily due to the lack of multimodal, multilingual, and time-series-grounded benchmarks that reflect the complexity of real-world clinical scenarios. To fill this gap, we present MMTClinic, a benchmark designed to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on complex reasoning and question-answering tasks involving clinical time-series. MMTClinic combines text, medical images, and multivariate physiological signals and includes 30,000 QA pairs (15,000 multiple choice questions (MCQs) and 15,000 open-ended questions) across five languages: English, Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, and Tamil. These questions cover three important clinical tasks---mortality prediction, heart rate forecasting, and SOFA score estimation. We evaluate 13 state-of-the-art LLMs in zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought settings. Our evaluation reveals notable differences in model performance across tasks, languages, and modalities, highlighting current limitations in clinical reasoning capabilities. MMTClinic provides a valuable resource for advancing multilingual, multimodal, and time-series-aware medical AI research. The dataset will be made publicly available on successful acceptance of the work.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MMTClinic, a multilingual, multimodal, time-series-focused benchmark for evaluating LLMs on complex clinical reasoning and QA tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing medical AI benchmarks rarely combine clinical time-series with multimodal (text + images + physiological signals) data and multilingual coverage, limiting the development and fair evaluation of clinically reliable and linguistically inclusive systems.
AI.method: The authors construct MMTClinic, a benchmark of 30,000 QA pairs (15k MCQs, 15k open-ended) in five languages (English, Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Tamil), grounded in text, medical images, and multivariate physiological signals, covering three clinical tasks: mortality prediction, heart rate forecasting, and SOFA score estimation. They then evaluate 13 state-of-the-art LLMs under zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought prompting regimes.
AI.result: The evaluation shows substantial variation in LLM performance across different tasks, languages, and modalities, exposing weaknesses in current models’ clinical reasoning, especially in multilingual and multimodal, time-series-grounded settings.
AI.conclusion: MMTClinic fills a critical gap by providing a comprehensive, publicly available benchmark for assessing and driving progress in multilingual, multimodal, time-series-aware medical AI and clinical reasoning with LLMs.

title: DCFA: Dual-view Causal-inspired Attribution for Failure Reasoning in LLM-based Multi-agent Systems
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems have experienced rapid growth in recent years. Despite their promise, such systems remain fragile, frequently exhibiting reasoning and coordination errors that can lead to system-level failures. Failure attribution in such systems relies on tracing natural language interactions among agents to identify the decisive error, which refers to the earliest action whose correction can reverse system failure. There are two key challenges: 1) Shallow attribution: Existing methods often capture only minor deviations, such as incomplete retrievals or formatting errors, which verification mechanisms can correct, while missing the decisive cause of system failure. 2) Contextual degradation: As the length of the system traces increases, the model's reasoning ability rapidly deteriorates. To address these challenges, we propose DCFA, a training-free framework for failure attribution. DCFA integrates a global module that constructs structured causal-inspired dependency graphs from system traces to identify the initial decisive error, and a local module that applies local counterfactual-inspired reasoning to refine causal-inspired attribution. Experiments on the Who&When benchmark across six LLMs show that DCFA improves step-level accuracy by up to 8.27% over state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DCFA, a training-free framework that performs more accurate failure attribution in LLM-based multi-agent systems by combining global causal-inspired graphs with local counterfactual-style reasoning, significantly improving step-level attribution accuracy.
AI.motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems are increasingly used but remain brittle, often failing due to complex reasoning and coordination errors among agents. Current failure attribution methods either focus on superficial issues (like formatting or partial retrieval) or struggle with long interaction traces where model reasoning degrades, making it difficult to pinpoint the earliest decisive error whose correction would avert system failure. There is a need for a robust, scalable way to trace and explain failures in such systems.
AI.method: The authors propose DCFA, a training-free framework for failure attribution in multi-agent LLM systems. DCFA has two main components: (1) a global module that converts the full natural-language interaction trace into a structured, causal-inspired dependency graph over actions and their relations, and then uses this graph to locate the earliest action that could have caused the final failure (the initial decisive error); and (2) a local module that performs local counterfactual-inspired reasoning over candidate error steps, refining the attribution by testing whether altering these steps would change the final outcome. The approach does not require additional training of models and operates directly on existing LLM traces.
AI.result: On the Who&When benchmark evaluated across six different LLMs, DCFA substantially outperforms existing state-of-the-art failure attribution baselines. Specifically, it improves step-level attribution accuracy by as much as 8.27%, indicating that it more reliably identifies the true decisive error in complex multi-agent traces.
AI.conclusion: DCFA provides a more reliable, training-free solution for failure attribution in LLM-based multi-agent systems by combining global causal structure analysis with local counterfactual-style checks. This dual approach mitigates shallow attribution and performance degradation on long traces, leading to significantly better identification of decisive errors and offering a path toward more diagnosable and robust multi-agent LLM systems.

title: CC-Mediation: Evaluating Large Language Models for Cross-Cultural Conflict Mediation
summary: Cross-cultural mediation by large language models (LLMs) requires deciding both when to intervene and how to respond in culturally grounded conflicts. Progress on this problem has been limited by the lack of (1) mediation datasets with measurable downstream effects and (2) principled metrics for evaluating intercultural stance change. To address these gaps, we introduce CC-Mediation, a cross-cultural mediation benchmark of $1{,}661$ ten-turn dialogues grounded in the Developmental Model of Intercultural Sensitivity (DMIS), containing culturally grounded conflicts, mediation interventions, and post-intervention trajectories. We further propose two DMIS-based evaluation metrics: Trajectory AUC, which measures the persistence of intercultural improvement over time, and a signed Wasserstein-1 distance, which measures the magnitude and direction of shifts in intercultural stance. Both metrics show strong agreement with human judgment of DMIS-grounded stance shift. Using CC-Mediation, we find that current LLMs have limitations on both axes: intervention timing (when) failure stems from a positional prior that ignores dialogue content, while mediation strategy (how) failure arises from a late-layer elicitation collapse rather than a knowledge deficit.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CC-Mediation, a benchmark and metrics to evaluate how well LLMs mediate culturally grounded conflicts and change intercultural stances over time, showing current models struggle with both when to intervene and how to mediate.
AI.motivation: Cross-cultural mediation with LLMs requires not just good responses but also good timing and measurable improvements in intercultural understanding. Existing work lacks (1) datasets with realistic mediation dialogues and observable downstream stance changes and (2) principled, quantitative metrics rooted in intercultural theory to evaluate how people’s stances shift. This gap prevents rigorous analysis and improvement of LLMs as mediators in intercultural conflicts.
AI.method: The authors construct CC-Mediation, a benchmark of 1,661 ten-turn dialogues based on the Developmental Model of Intercultural Sensitivity (DMIS). Each dialogue includes a culturally grounded conflict, one or more mediation interventions, and the post-intervention evolution of intercultural stance. They then design two DMIS-grounded evaluation metrics: (a) Trajectory AUC, capturing how much and how persistently intercultural stance improves over the dialogue; and (b) a signed Wasserstein-1 distance over DMIS levels, quantifying both magnitude and direction of stance change. They validate these metrics against human judgments and use the benchmark to probe LLM behavior, including when models choose to intervene and what mediation strategies they employ, analyzing internal activations (early vs late layers) to diagnose failure modes.
AI.result: The new metrics (Trajectory AUC and signed Wasserstein-1 distance) correlate strongly with human judgments of intercultural stance shifts, suggesting they are valid and interpretable evaluation tools. When evaluated on CC-Mediation, current LLMs exhibit two main limitations: (1) they often fail at intervention timing, seemingly relying on a positional prior about where to intervene in the dialogue instead of reacting to the actual conversational content; and (2) their mediation strategies underperform not because they lack conceptual knowledge about mediation or intercultural sensitivity, but because desired behaviors collapse at later network layers during elicitation, indicating a representational or decoding issue rather than a pure knowledge gap.
AI.conclusion: CC-Mediation provides a theoretically grounded benchmark and two DMIS-based metrics to quantitatively evaluate LLM-mediated cross-cultural dialogue and stance change. The study shows that current LLMs are not reliable intercultural mediators: they mis-time interventions and their strategy use degrades due to late-layer elicitation collapse, despite having relevant underlying knowledge. This framework enables more precise diagnosis of mediation-specific failure modes and opens paths to developing LLMs that better support cross-cultural understanding and conflict resolution.

title: Shadow Queries for Private Retrieval in Vector Databases
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) increasingly rely on information retrieval (IR) systems, such as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), to incorporate domain-specific knowledge without costly re-training. These systems often store pre-computed document embeddings in cloud-based vector databases. However, such embeddings are vulnerable to embedding inversion attacks (EIAs), which can reconstruct their underlying text. Existing defenses, such as adding noise or scaling embeddings, often provide limited privacy or significantly reduce retrieval utility.
  We propose SHAQ (shadow query generation), a semantic-decomposition and embedding-decoupling defense against EIAs. SHAQ is based on the insight that EIAs rely on the strong coupling between an embedding and its original text. Instead of storing document embeddings directly, SHAQ uses a generative language model to create diverse shadow queries that capture different semantic aspects of each document. These queries are then encoded and stored in place of the original document embeddings, thereby decomposing document semantics and decoupling stored embeddings from the source text.
  Experiments across diverse IR datasets show that SHAQ substantially improves privacy while preserving retrieval utility, achieving a recovery rate as low as 0.2104, defending up to 19.50% more tokens than baseline defenses, and reaching up to 0.7967 MAP@10 with up to 5.53% utility improvement. These results demonstrate that semantic decomposition and embedding decoupling provide an effective alternative to directly modifying embeddings for defending against EIAs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SHAQ, a defense mechanism for retrieval systems using vector embeddings that mitigates embedding inversion attacks by replacing document embeddings with generated “shadow queries.” This preserves retrieval performance while significantly improving privacy.
AI.motivation: Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems store document embeddings in vector databases, which are vulnerable to embedding inversion attacks that can reconstruct private source texts. Existing defenses either provide weak privacy or harm retrieval utility, creating a need for a method that protects document content without degrading IR performance.
AI.method: SHAQ generates multiple diverse shadow queries for each document using a generative language model. These queries each capture different semantic facets of the document. Instead of storing the original document embeddings, the system stores embeddings of these shadow queries, effectively decomposing the document’s semantics and decoupling stored vectors from any single underlying text. Retrieval is then performed over these shadow-query embeddings rather than document embeddings.
AI.result: On several IR datasets, SHAQ achieves a low reconstruction (recovery) rate of 0.2104 under embedding inversion attacks, protects up to 19.50% more tokens than baseline defenses, and attains up to 0.7967 MAP@10 with as much as 5.53% improvement in retrieval utility compared to existing methods that modify embeddings directly.
AI.conclusion: Semantic decomposition through shadow query generation and embedding decoupling is an effective defense against embedding inversion attacks. It improves privacy without sacrificing, and sometimes even improving, retrieval effectiveness, offering a promising alternative to noisy or scaled embedding defenses in RAG-style IR systems.

title: Cache-Aware Joint Router Adaptation for Memory-Efficient MoE Inference
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models activate only a small subset of experts per token, but the full expert set often exceeds GPU memory, causing repeated weight transfers during decoding. We formulate expert-cache management as a model-side algorithmic problem and propose a cache-aware post-training framework that jointly adapts the MoE backbone and lightweight auxiliary cache routers while preserving the native Top-K expert-selection rule at inference. Its update-only mode, Temporal Router, predicts same-layer reuse and retains experts for future tokens without proactive loading. The full Spatio-Temporal Router adds a Spatio Router that uses the causal predecessor's hidden state to refine the temporal cache before target-layer access. We evaluate both modes on Qwen3 and GPT-OSS across GSM8K, MATH, and CommonsenseQA. Temporal Router consistently improves cache hit rate and reduces expert-weight traffic over matched LM-only baselines. On Qwen3, Spatio-Temporal Router achieves the best load-adjusted efficiency across three tasks, improving adjusted hit rate by 1.15--18.03 points and reducing traffic by 4.6--53.3% relative to the strongest evaluated prefetching baseline; results on GPT-OSS are competitive but task-dependent. An auxiliary-only ablation preserves baseline accuracy but yields modest cache gains, whereas joint post-training produces larger improvements. Sensitivity analyses show that cache capacity controls transfer demand, while the refinement budget governs the trade-off between pre-access coverage and proactive traffic.

AI.tldr: They propose cache-aware routing mechanisms for Mixture-of-Experts LMs that reduce expert weight transfers during decoding without changing the standard Top-K routing rule, leading to higher cache hit rates and lower traffic.
AI.motivation: MoE language models only activate a few experts per token, but storing all experts on GPU is infeasible, so weights must be repeatedly transferred from CPU or other devices during decoding, which becomes a major efficiency bottleneck. Existing solutions focus on system-level prefetching, not on adapting the model itself to be cache-friendly.
AI.method: They frame expert-cache management as a model-side algorithmic problem and introduce a post-training framework that jointly tunes the MoE backbone and small auxiliary cache routers. Two modes are proposed: (1) Temporal Router, which only updates the cache by predicting which experts will be reused in the near future and retains them without proactive loading, keeping the original Top-K routing; (2) Spatio-Temporal Router, which adds a Spatio Router that uses the causal predecessor’s hidden state to refine the temporal cache just before a target layer is accessed. They evaluate these methods on Qwen3 and GPT-OSS across several reasoning and commonsense benchmarks and run ablations (auxiliary-only vs joint post-training) plus sensitivity analyses on cache size and refinement budget.
AI.result: Temporal Router alone consistently improves cache hit rate and reduces expert-weight transfer traffic over LM-only baselines. Spatio-Temporal Router on Qwen3 yields the highest load-adjusted efficiency on GSM8K, MATH, and CommonsenseQA, increasing adjusted hit rate by 1.15–18.03 points and cutting traffic by 4.6–53.3% compared to the strongest prefetching baseline. On GPT-OSS, gains are competitive but vary with the task. Auxiliary-only training keeps accuracy but offers smaller cache benefits, whereas joint post-training yields larger efficiency improvements. Sensitivity experiments show that cache capacity mainly affects total transfer demand, while the refinement budget tunes the balance between better pre-access coverage and added proactive traffic.
AI.conclusion: Cache-aware, model-side routing adaptations can substantially reduce expert-weight transfers in MoE LMs while preserving standard Top-K expert selection and baseline accuracy. The proposed Temporal and Spatio-Temporal Routers restructure expert reuse over time and layers, improving cache hit rates and traffic efficiency beyond system-only prefetching. Jointly adapting the backbone with auxiliary routers is key for larger gains, and efficiency can be controlled via cache size and refinement budget.

title: Diffusion Language Models for Mobile Edge Agentic AI: Foundations, Applications, and Challenges
summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer a non-autoregressive alternative for mobile edge agentic artificial intelligence (AI) by refining tokens through iterative denoising rather than left-to-right decoding. Compared with autoregressive Transformer-based large language models (LLMs), DLMs can update multiple uncertain tokens in parallel and exploit bidirectional context throughout the generation process, enabling more flexible quality-latency trade-offs beyond fixed sequential decoding. These properties are particularly attractive for edge agents, where partial refinement, early exit, and constraint-guided correction can reduce response delay and communication overhead while improving robustness under noisy, incomplete, or dynamic contexts. This survey reviews DLM foundations and analyzes their suitability for edge settings under latency, memory, energy, bandwidth, privacy, and reliability constraints. We cover resource-efficient architectures, training and inference acceleration, compression, edge/cloud deployment, communication-aware serving, Internet of Things (IoT)/wireless applications, and evaluation of DLM-based agents. We further discuss open issues in long-context state management, split inference, trustworthy execution, multimodal grounding, and reproducible benchmarking. The goal is to connect DLM modeling properties, including bidirectionality, parallel refinement, controllability, and quality-latency elasticity, with system-level requirements of future mobile edge intelligence.

AI.tldr: Survey of diffusion language models (DLMs) as non-autoregressive alternatives to Transformers for mobile edge AI agents, focusing on how their modeling properties align with edge device constraints and applications.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive Transformer LLMs are resource-intensive and introduce latency due to strictly sequential decoding, which is problematic for mobile and edge deployments with tight constraints on latency, memory, energy, bandwidth, privacy, and reliability. There is a need to understand whether and how diffusion-based language models, which generate via iterative denoising and parallel token refinement, can better satisfy these system-level constraints for edge agents.
AI.method: Conceptual and system-oriented survey: (1) explain foundations of diffusion language models and contrast them with autoregressive LLMs; (2) analyze DLM properties such as bidirectionality, parallel refinement, controllability, and elastic quality-latency trade-offs; (3) review architectures and techniques for resource-efficient training, inference acceleration, and model compression; (4) examine deployment patterns including edge-only, cloud-only, and split edge/cloud inference, along with communication-aware serving strategies; (5) survey IoT and wireless applications and evaluation methodologies for DLM-based agents; (6) identify open research challenges for long-context management, trustworthy execution, multimodal grounding, and benchmarking.
AI.result: The survey synthesizes existing work to show where DLMs can offer advantages for edge intelligence—such as reduced latency via parallel refinement, improved robustness in noisy or incomplete contexts, and flexible stopping/early-exit strategies—while also highlighting areas where current methods remain immature, e.g., long-context handling, efficient split inference, and standardized evaluation in edge scenarios. It organizes the literature on resource-efficient DLM architectures, compression, and communication-aware deployment, mapping them to different edge constraints and application requirements.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion language models, with their bidirectional context use and parallel, controllable refinement process, are promising building blocks for future mobile edge AI agents, especially when quality-latency elasticity and robustness are critical. However, realizing their full potential on constrained devices requires further research on scalable architectures, long-context state handling, trustworthy and privacy-preserving edge execution, multimodal integration, and rigorous, reproducible benchmarks that jointly consider model quality and system-level metrics.

title: RefactorPlatform: An Open-Source Harness for Controlled Evaluation of Repository-Scale Refactoring Agents
summary: Repository-scale refactoring requires coding agents to propagate a single change across many interdependent files without altering program behavior, yet to our knowledge no existing harness isolates the design choices that determine agent success on this task. We present RefactorPlatform, an open-source evaluation harness that holds the environment fixed and varies each design axis explicitly: model backbone (via OpenRouter and GitHub Copilot CLI), execution regime (baseline, retrieval-augmented, and multi-agent), and prompt specificity. Each run executes in an isolated workspace with live terminal streaming, per-task logging of tokens, diffs, and transcripts, AST-based verification, and exportable telemetry for audit and reproduction. Demonstrating the platform on 100 multi-file RefactorBench tasks across four model families, we illustrate the analyses it supports: AST-aware chunking outperforms naive token-window chunking by 25-30% across prompt modes, whereas naive retrieval falls below the retrieval-free baseline; a lean retrieval-augmented single agent (86%) beats the sub-agent configuration we evaluated (66%) on matched tasks with no task passing under delegation that fails under retrieval; and retrieval's accuracy gains absorb its token overhead, leaving cost per successful refactoring unchanged. RefactorPlatform is open-sourced to make refactoring-agent evaluation reproducible and auditable.

AI.tldr: They introduce RefactorPlatform, a benchmark and harness to systematically evaluate and compare coding agents on large-scale repository refactoring tasks, holding the environment fixed while varying model and orchestration choices.
AI.motivation: Repository-wide refactoring requires agents to correctly propagate coordinated code changes across many interdependent files without breaking behavior. Existing benchmarks and harnesses do not cleanly isolate the design choices—like model backbone, retrieval strategy, multi-agent orchestration, and prompt specificity—that drive success or failure on this task, making it hard to understand what really helps. The authors want a reproducible, auditable way to study and compare these factors at scale.
AI.method: They build RefactorPlatform, an open-source evaluation harness that: (1) runs each refactoring task in an isolated workspace; (2) supports multiple model backbones via OpenRouter and GitHub Copilot CLI; (3) compares execution regimes (plain single-agent, retrieval-augmented, and multi-agent/delegation); (4) varies prompt specificity; and (5) logs rich telemetry, including token usage, code diffs, transcripts, and AST-based verification of correctness. They then run 100 multi-file refactoring tasks from RefactorBench across four model families to showcase the kinds of analyses the platform enables, such as chunking and retrieval strategies and agent orchestration setups.
AI.result: Across their experiments on 100 RefactorBench tasks and four model families, they find: (1) AST-aware code chunking substantially outperforms naive token-window-based chunking by about 25–30% across different prompting regimes; (2) simple retrieval-augmented single-agent setups achieve higher accuracy (86%) than the tested multi-agent (sub-agent) configuration (66%), with no tasks solved by delegation that retrieval alone could not solve; (3) naive retrieval strategies can actually underperform a no-retrieval baseline; and (4) retrieval’s gains in accuracy effectively offset its additional token cost, keeping the cost per successful refactoring roughly constant.
AI.conclusion: RefactorPlatform provides a controlled, instrumented, and open-source harness for systematically evaluating large-scale refactoring agents. Their initial experiments suggest that careful code-aware chunking and lean retrieval-augmented single-agent designs are more effective and cost-neutral per success than naive retrieval or more complex multi-agent delegation schemes. The platform is meant to make future refactoring-agent work more reproducible, comparable, and auditable.

title: DODR: Deterministic Operator-Driven Reasoning in Latent Space
summary: Autoregressive (AR) large language models formulate reasoning as token-level probabilistic sampling, which induces three fundamental defects in complex logical reasoning: error accumulation, probability substituting necessity, and the linear-chain information bottleneck. This paper proposes the Deterministic Operator-Driven Reasoning in Latent Space architecture (DODR), which reconstructs reasoning as reasoning-graph computation in a high-dimensional linear-algebraic space. Reasoning states are represented as snapshot vectors whose primitives are semantic units (phrases or sentences) rather than tokens, and each inference step is a deterministic matrix operation with no token sampling. Peirce's three inference types are formalized as three trainable matrix operators: a rank-deficient deduction operator (information collapse), a full-rank induction operator (information expansion), and an abduction operator defined as the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse of deduction (information hypothesizing). We prove that the operator set is minimal and complete given Peirce's trichotomy, that no single "super-operator" can realize all three types (a rank obstruction), and that reasoning graphs are Turing-complete with contractive backflow converging by Banach's fixed-point theorem. Experiments on 503 sample records (420 deduplicated samples) across dedicated and end-to-end settings show: deduction loss converges to 1.40e-05; induction achieves 0.9996 generalization coverage with 20/20 hard vetoes on counterexamples; abduction solutions exceed the random baseline by 28x with judgment accuracies of 72.5% (58/80, Wilson 95% CI [61.9%, 81.1%]) and 81.7% (49/60, CI [70.1%, 89.4%]); frozen operators attain 100% (60/60) on unseen cross-domain deduction. The architecture provides a structural zero-hallucination guarantee and a three-layer continual-learning mechanism. All data and code are released.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DODR, a deterministic, operator-based reasoning architecture in latent space that replaces token-by-token sampling with matrix-operator reasoning over sentence-level representations, achieving provably sound, complete, and highly accurate logical inference with zero-hallucination guarantees.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive large language models perform reasoning via probabilistic token sampling, which leads to three core issues for complex logic: (1) errors compound over long chains of reasoning; (2) high token probability is mistaken for logical necessity; and (3) the linear, left-to-right token chain limits information flow and global structure. The authors want a reasoning system that is logically grounded, less stochastic, and not forced into token-level sequential generation.
AI.method: They design a new architecture, Deterministic Operator-Driven Reasoning (DODR), where reasoning is modeled as computations over a reasoning graph in a high-dimensional latent vector space. Each reasoning state is a vector summarizing semantic units (phrases/sentences), not tokens. Inference steps are deterministic matrix multiplications, not sampling. They formalize Peirce’s three forms of inference—deduction, induction, abduction—as three distinct trainable linear operators: a rank-deficient deduction operator (compresses information), a full-rank induction operator (expands information), and an abduction operator defined as the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of the deduction operator (hypothesizes missing premises). They analyze the operator set theoretically (minimality, completeness, rank constraints, Turing-completeness of reasoning graphs, and convergence via Banach’s fixed-point theorem) and then empirically evaluate the learned operators on synthetic or curated reasoning tasks.
AI.result: On 503 records (420 unique samples) across dedicated and end-to-end tasks, the model achieves: extremely low deduction loss (1.40e-05), induction with 0.9996 coverage of generalization and correctly vetoing all 20/20 constructed counterexamples, and abduction that is 28x better than random with human-judged accuracies of 72.5% and 81.7% in two settings (with Wilson confidence intervals). When operators are frozen and applied to unseen domains, they still get 100% accuracy (60/60) on cross-domain deduction tasks.
AI.conclusion: The DODR architecture demonstrates that logical reasoning can be recast as deterministic operator application in latent space rather than token sampling. The three Peircean operators form a minimal, complete, and theoretically well-grounded basis for deduction, induction, and abduction, with proofs of computational expressiveness and convergence. Empirically, DODR yields highly accurate, generalizable reasoning with a claimed structural guarantee of zero hallucinations and supports continual learning through a three-layer mechanism. The authors release all data and code to support reproducibility and further exploration.

title: Discourse Dependency: A Continuous Criterion for Translation Difficulty
summary: Recent calls for harder machine translation benchmarks have not clarified what difficulty should mean. We argue that one meaningful and currently unmeasured axis is referential reach, the distance a segment must look back into its document to resolve the entities and pronouns it contains. We formalize this as discourse dependency (DDP), a metric-free, source-side measure computed from named entity re-mentions and pronominal coreference. Validated against gold coreference, DDP errs one-sidedly in 99.2% of segments, so a high-DDP segment is certified to require long-range context. Applying DDP to WMT24++ and WMT25 shows that both are heavily skewed toward low-DDP segments, which domain labels do not distinguish. Building on DDP, we compare five context injection strategies in an English-Korean post-editing setup, varying context size and selection. As DDP grows, no strategy keeps pace with human post-editing. On segments with DDP >= 15 raters prefer human translations, while automatic metrics register no difference. As frontier systems saturate aggregate scores, DDP shifts evaluation from how well models score to how far they can reach.

AI.tldr: Defines and applies a new document-level difficulty axis for MT, called discourse dependency (DDP), to show that current benchmarks under-test long-range context and that models lag far behind humans on high-DDP segments.
AI.motivation: Existing MT benchmarks are said to be too easy, but there is no clear, operational notion of what makes a test set hard. In particular, current evaluations largely ignore how far back into a document a system must look to correctly interpret entities and pronouns. The authors aim to define and measure this kind of long-range, discourse-level difficulty and to see whether current datasets and systems adequately cover and handle it.
AI.method: 1) Propose discourse dependency (DDP), a metric-free, source-side signal of how much prior context a segment needs, based on distances to previous mentions of named entities and their pronominal coreferences. 2) Validate DDP against gold-standard coreference annotations, showing it overestimates but almost never underestimates needed context. 3) Compute DDP for WMT24++ and WMT25 to inspect their difficulty distribution and relation to domain labels. 4) In an English→Korean post-editing setup, design five strategies for injecting document context into MT (varying how much and which context). 5) Evaluate how these strategies and human translators perform as DDP increases, using human raters and automatic metrics.
AI.result: 1) DDP can be computed reliably from automatic coreference and named entity signals and has a strong one-sided agreement with gold coreference: it almost never mislabels low-context segments as high but may underestimate the full distance. 2) WMT24++ and WMT25 are dominated by low-DDP segments, and domain labels fail to separate segments by discourse difficulty. 3) Across five context injection strategies, MT systems increasingly underperform humans as DDP grows; no strategy closes the gap on high-DDP segments. 4) For segments with DDP ≥ 15, human raters significantly prefer human translations, yet standard automatic MT metrics do not capture this quality difference.
AI.conclusion: DDP offers a principled document-level difficulty axis for MT that is not reflected in current WMT test sets or in common domain labels. Current MT systems, even with various context injection methods, struggle to match human performance on segments requiring long-range discourse reasoning, and standard automatic metrics fail to reveal this gap. As MT systems approach saturation on traditional aggregate scores, incorporating DDP-based analysis can reorient evaluation toward the limits of systems’ contextual reach rather than small score differences on mostly easy segments.

title: ProtLingo: Efficient Protein Language Modeling via Conditional Memory and Expert Routing
summary: Proteins perform diverse cellular functions, and even single amino-acid substitutions can alter stability, activity, or molecular interactions. Protein language models (PLMs) provide a scalable approach for modeling such sequence--function relationships from unlabeled sequences, but increasing the size of dense Transformer backbones often brings substantial computational cost without consistently improving mutation-sensitive prediction. We introduce ProtLingo, an efficient PLM framework that augments a pretrained single-sequence backbone with conditional local memory and sparse expert routing. ProtLingo maps contextual residue representations into route-specific discrete codes, composes centered local windows into latent $N$-gram addresses, and retrieves reusable residual signals associated with recurring local sequence contexts. In parallel, selected feed-forward blocks are upcycled into sparse Mixture-of-Experts layers with shared and routed experts, enabling residue-dependent computation while activating only a subset of parameters. Experiments on protein fitness prediction, FLIP benchmarks, and supervised contact prediction show that ProtLingo achieves competitive performance with a 150M-scale backbone, including strong parameter efficiency on mutation-effect prediction and preserved long-range structural representations.

AI.tldr: ProtLingo is an efficient protein language model framework that improves mutation-effect and structural predictions by adding conditional local memory and sparse Mixture-of-Experts to an existing backbone, achieving strong performance with relatively few parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing protein language models use large dense Transformers that are computationally costly and do not consistently improve sensitivity to the effects of single amino-acid mutations. There is a need for models that better capture local sequence–function relationships and mutation effects while remaining parameter- and compute-efficient, and that preserve long-range structural information.
AI.method: ProtLingo takes a pretrained single-sequence protein language model backbone and augments it with two key components: (1) a conditional local memory mechanism, where contextual residue embeddings are discretized into route-specific codes, local windows are composed into latent N-gram addresses, and stored residual signals are retrieved for recurring local contexts; and (2) sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers formed by converting selected feed-forward blocks into MoE with shared and routed experts, so that only a subset of parameters is activated per residue, enabling residue-dependent computation with sparse routing.
AI.result: On protein fitness prediction tasks, FLIP benchmarks, and supervised contact prediction, ProtLingo matches or exceeds the performance of competing models using a relatively small (~150M parameter) backbone. It shows strong parameter efficiency for mutation-effect prediction while maintaining accurate long-range structural representations, demonstrating that the added memory and sparse experts improve performance without requiring very large dense backbones.
AI.conclusion: Augmenting a moderate-scale pretrained protein language model with conditional local memory and sparse expert routing yields an efficient, mutation-sensitive model that maintains long-range structural modeling capabilities. ProtLingo suggests that structured sparsity and reusable local context representations are a promising direction for scalable, parameter-efficient protein sequence–function modeling, reducing the need for ever-larger dense Transformer architectures.

title: BIT.UA at BioASQ 14B: Modular Retrieval with pg_textsearch and Qdrant, and Agent-Based Answer Generation
summary: This paper describes the participation of the BIT.UA team from the University of Aveiro in the 14th edition of the BioASQ Task B challenge on biomedical question answering. Building on our previous submissions, we introduced a substantially refactored and modular codebase, and made significant changes to both the retrieval and generation components of the pipeline. For Phase~A document retrieval, we replaced the PyTerrier PISA index with PostgreSQL-based pg\_textsearch for BM25 retrieval and adopted Qdrant for dense embedding indexing, enabling more efficient storage and GPU-accelerated similarity search. We explored HyDE-based query expansion alongside a Context-1 retrieval strategy. A new reranker training pipeline was developed, incorporating dense retrieval for negative sampling. For Phases A+ and B answer generation, we introduced an LLM-as-a-judge framework and a novel agent quorum mechanism, where multiple agents with diverse prompts debate and iteratively converge on a consensus answer using adaptive document retention. We also participated in the snippets generation subtask for the first time. Our systems achieved competitive results across all batches, with Phase~A systems achieving MAP ranks of 5 (Batch~1,3). We discuss the impact of these architectural changes, lessons learned, and outline directions for future work including SPLADE and ColBERT integration. All code is openly available: https://github.com/bioinformatics-ua/BioASQ14b.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the BIT.UA team’s system for the BioASQ 14b biomedical QA challenge, focusing on a refactored modular pipeline with upgraded retrieval (BM25 + dense + reranking) and novel multi-agent LLM answer-generation mechanisms that achieved competitive rankings.
AI.motivation: Biomedical question answering benchmarks like BioASQ drive progress in information retrieval and generation for clinical and biomedical use. The authors aim to improve over their prior systems by modernizing the architecture, increasing retrieval efficiency and effectiveness, and enhancing answer quality using LLM-based techniques, while making the system more maintainable and extensible for future research.
AI.method: They redesigned the system pipeline for BioASQ Task B. For Phase A (document retrieval), they replaced a PyTerrier/PISA index with PostgreSQL pg_textsearch for BM25 and used Qdrant for dense embeddings to support efficient and GPU-accelerated similarity search. They experimented with HyDE-based query expansion and a Context-1 retrieval strategy. A new reranker was trained using dense-retrieval-based negative sampling. For Phases A+ and B (answer and snippet generation), they implemented an LLM-as-a-judge framework and a new agent quorum mechanism in which multiple LLM agents, each with different prompts, debate and iteratively converge to a consensus answer with adaptive document retention. They also added a new component for snippet generation.
AI.result: Their systems performed competitively across all BioASQ 14b batches. In Phase A document retrieval, they achieved Mean Average Precision (MAP) ranks of 5 in Batches 1 and 3. They successfully deployed the new multi-agent LLM mechanisms and snippet generation, demonstrating that the architectural changes can match or rival state-of-the-art systems in the benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The refactored, modular system and new retrieval and generation strategies proved effective in the BioASQ 14b challenge, yielding strong retrieval performance and competitive end-to-end QA. The authors conclude that their architectural and algorithmic choices—especially dense+BM25 retrieval, trained reranking, and multi-agent LLM-as-a-judge answering—are promising directions. They plan to further enhance the system by integrating SPLADE and ColBERT and encourage community reuse through their open-source codebase.

title: Whose record is this? Diagnosing and authorizing record use in personalized multimodal models
summary: Contextualized visual personalization can retrieve a true record yet apply it to the wrong visual subject. We formalize when a record may condition an answer as \emph{record authorization}: subject presence ($P$), record-edge validity ($E$), and answer support ($S$) must all hold. We call violations visual memory misbinding (VMM). We construct RecordAuth-Diag, a 3,690-case matched diagnostic suite that changes one image--record edge while holding the query, question, record text, and image multiset fixed. Card removal and nonce relabeling attribute these failures to supplied records. Raw-bank failures span Qwen-, Phi-, and Gemma-family interfaces: Gemma-3-4B-IT reaches 63.69\% local unauthorized use at 25.75\% clean recall. CoViP remains at 26.02\%, versus 22.49\% for its Qwen backbone at similar clean recall. Typed pre-generation authorization reduces Qwen card exposure on RecordAuth-Diag from 43.63\% to 3.06\%, while positive recall changes from 86.26\% to 60.90\%. Full $P\wedge E\wedge S$ validation uses 560 localized DAVIS cases: top-1 relevance and typed authorization have comparable release (28.93\% and 28.39\%) but 6.79\% and 0.89\% unsafe release, respectively. Of the 33 additional unsafe cases removed, 27 are support, 4 edge, 2 clean, and 0 boundary cases. Thus the observed increment is an $E\wedge S$ decision dominated by support, not an edge check alone. Appearance supplies $E$ evidence only conditional on $P$; authenticated subject tokens instantiate the missing presence witness as a sufficiency control. The claims concern the evaluated contracts, not natural prevalence, consent, or visual identity

AI.tldr: The paper studies when visual personalization systems incorrectly apply private records to the wrong person in an image, formalizes conditions under which a record is allowed to influence an answer, and proposes tests and mitigation methods to reduce such unsafe misbindings.
AI.motivation: Modern multimodal models can use personal records ("visual personalization") but may attach those records to the wrong face or subject in an image, causing privacy and safety issues. Existing evaluations focus on whether systems retrieve the correct record at all, not whether they bind it to the correct visual subject. The authors want a principled notion of when a record is authorized to affect an answer, and a way to measure and reduce such visual memory misbinding.
AI.method: They define "record authorization" as a conjunction of three conditions: subject presence (P), valid link between the record and the depicted subject (E), and that the record is actually needed to support the answer (S). Violations are called Visual Memory Misbinding (VMM). They build RecordAuth-Diag, a diagnostic dataset with 3,690 controlled cases where only the link between a record and an image changes, with everything else (query, question, record text, and image multiset) held constant. They use card removal and nonce relabeling to show failures are driven by supplied records. They empirically test several model families (Qwen, Phi, Gemma, and CoViP) and then design and evaluate a "typed pre-generation authorization" mechanism and a full P∧E∧S validation using 560 localized DAVIS cases, comparing top-1 relevance selection versus typed authorization.
AI.result: Across multiple models, there is a high rate of unauthorized use of records (visual memory misbinding) even when overall clean recall is modest; e.g., Gemma-3-4B-IT shows 63.69% local unauthorized use at only 25.75% clean recall. The CoViP system slightly improves over its Qwen backbone but still exhibits substantial misbinding. Typed pre-generation authorization greatly reduces unauthorized card exposure on RecordAuth-Diag from 43.63% to 3.06%, though positive recall drops from 86.26% to 60.90%. In the DAVIS setting, top-1 relevance and typed authorization release similar amounts of information (~29%), but typed authorization slashes unsafe release from 6.79% to 0.89%. Among newly filtered unsafe cases, most correspond to failures of support (S), some to edge (E), and none to pure boundary issues, indicating that the main gains come from better checking that the record actually supports the answer, not only that the record is superficially linked to the subject.
AI.conclusion: Visual personalization systems systematically misbind personal records to the wrong visual subjects, and naive relevance-based retrieval is not sufficient to prevent these errors. A formal record-authorization framework based on presence, edge validity, and support reveals the structure of these failures. Typed pre-generation authorization and full P∧E∧S validation can dramatically reduce unsafe disclosures with limited loss in utility, especially by ensuring that records are actually needed to answer the query. Visual appearance alone cannot serve as full evidence of authorization; authenticated subject tokens are required to witness subject presence. The findings are limited to the specific contractual setups evaluated, without making claims about real-world prevalence, consent, or identity at large.

title: MoirfEolas and CríochScore: Developing Resources for and the Evaluation of Tokenization Alignment with Irish Morphology
comment: Accepted as a non-archival poster at the Second Tokenization Workshop (TokShop) at COLM 2026
summary: This paper presents new tokenization resources for Irish and evaluation measures of alignment with the morphological boundaries of the language. We present MoirfEolas, a dataset of over 35,000 Irish words mapped to their respective eclipses, prefixes and suffixes as well as an evaluation metric CríochScore, that evaluates the alignment of tokenizations with the morphological boundaries present in MoirfEolas. We evaluate common tokenization algorithms using CríochScore as well as intrinsic metrics present in the tokenization literature. We find that the Unigram Language Model aligns with Irish morphology more often than the other algorithms evaluated. We also find trade-offs between morphological-alignment of tokenization with both compression as well as vocabulary efficiency, providing practical insights for Irish natural language processing development. This dataset contributes towards combating the Irish language's low-resource status; moreover, the construction process reported in this paper can be emulated by other languages to create specialised morphological resources.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces new Irish tokenization resources and an evaluation metric to measure how well tokenizers align with Irish morphological boundaries, showing Unigram LM performs best and outlining trade-offs with compression and vocabulary efficiency.
AI.motivation: Irish is a low-resource language, and existing tokenization tools are not optimized for its rich morphology. This hinders performance in downstream NLP tasks. The authors aim to create specialized resources and evaluation methods to better align tokenization with Irish morphological structure and to provide a replicable process for other languages.
AI.method: The authors construct MoirfEolas, a dataset of 35,000+ Irish word forms annotated with morphological elements such as eclipses, prefixes, and suffixes. They then define CríochScore, a metric that evaluates how well a tokenizer’s segments align with these annotated morphological boundaries. Several common tokenization algorithms (including Unigram LM and others like BPE/WordPiece) are trained/evaluated on Irish data and compared using CríochScore and standard intrinsic tokenization metrics (e.g., compression ratio, vocabulary efficiency).
AI.result: Experiments show that the Unigram Language Model tokenizer aligns most closely with Irish morphological boundaries compared with other evaluated algorithms. The results also reveal clear trade-offs: tokenizers that better respect morphology may be less optimal in terms of compression and vocabulary efficiency, and vice versa.
AI.conclusion: MoirfEolas and CríochScore provide valuable, language-specific tools for evaluating and improving tokenization for Irish, helping address its low-resource status. The work demonstrates that morphology-aware evaluation can change which tokenizer is considered ‘best’ and that there are practical trade-offs between morphological alignment and efficiency. The dataset design and methodology can be adapted to other languages to create similar morphological resources and evaluation pipelines.

title: Hierarchical Possession-Aware Graph Pointer Network for Pass Receiver Selection
comment: This paper has been accepted by the 27th International Conference on Web Information Systems Engineering (WISE 2026)
summary: Pass receiver selection is a fundamental task in football analytics, aiming to predict the intended receiver under a given game state. This task is challenging with event-centered freeze-frame observations, a broadcast-like setting that provides only partial and variable player visibility without complete trajectories or stable player identities. The model must therefore reason over anonymous visible candidates, opponent pressure, and recent context under partial observation. To address this setting, we propose a Hierarchical Possession-aware Graph Pointer Network (HPGPN), which formulates pass receiver selection as variable-size candidate prediction over visible teammates. HPGPN jointly models current player interactions, local event context, and possession-level temporal dynamics. It represents the current pass situation with a graph, incorporates fixed event context, and uses dynamic possession history to capture how the attacking sequence evolves. Candidate representations are refined hierarchically by integrating spatial, contextual, and historical evidence, and a glimpse pointer head scores the receiver candidates. Experiments on public football event and freeze-frame data show that HPGPN improves pass receiver selection performance. Ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of graph-based interaction modeling, fixed event context, and dual-branch dynamic possession-history modeling.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a model to predict the intended pass receiver in football from partial, freeze-frame event data using a hierarchical graph pointer network.
AI.motivation: In football analytics, identifying the intended pass receiver is important for understanding decision-making and tactics, but most data is limited to event-centric, broadcast-like freeze-frames with partial visibility, no full trajectories, and no stable player IDs. Existing methods struggle to handle variable numbers of visible teammates, anonymity, and the need to reason about context and possession dynamics under partial observation. The authors aim to build a model that can robustly infer the intended receiver in this realistic data setting.
AI.method: The authors introduce a Hierarchical Possession-aware Graph Pointer Network (HPGPN). They model the current pass situation as a graph over currently visible players, capturing player–player interactions. Fixed event context (e.g., static information about the event and situation) is incorporated as additional features. They further model temporal dynamics at the possession level with a dual-branch mechanism that encodes how the attacking sequence has evolved over recent events. Candidate (teammate) representations are refined hierarchically by fusing spatial features, contextual features, and historical possession information. Finally, a glimpse-based pointer head operates over these refined candidate embeddings to output a probability distribution over the visible teammates, effectively selecting the intended receiver among a variable-size candidate set.
AI.result: On public football event and freeze-frame datasets, HPGPN achieves better performance on pass receiver selection than baselines. Ablation experiments show that removing key components—graph-based interaction modeling, fixed event context, or dual-branch possession-history modeling—leads to performance drops, indicating that each contributes meaningfully to the overall accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The proposed HPGPN effectively addresses the pass receiver selection problem under realistic, partially observed, event-centered football data. By combining graph-based interaction modeling, contextual features, and possession-level temporal dynamics in a hierarchical pointer framework, it improves prediction of the intended receiver. The analysis suggests that explicitly modeling interactions and possession history is crucial for understanding passing decisions from limited observational data.

title: Leveraging Low-Level Symbolic Competences for Unsupervised Grounding in Hallucination Detection
summary:
Hallucination-where a language model generates outputs that are factually incorrect or unsupported by the source-is a major challenge for both prompted and fine-tuned language models. Detecting hallucinations is difficult due to the opaque reasoning processes of LLMs, which often provide little insight into why a model's output may be inaccurate.
  In this work, we investigate whether an LLM can use an alternative, low level, symbolic competence such as SQL for unsupervised hallucination detection in some high level task. For this, we make an LLM build an SQL database from reference documents. This SQL database is then used for reasoning over the reference and the sampled response in a hallucination detection pipeline that is grounded in the database, thereby providing a neurosymbolic checkup.
  On RAGTruth and DiaHalu hallucination detection datasets, we find that our approach improves on direct prediction and competes with state-of-the-art hallucination detection methods, while not requiring domain-specific fine-tuning. Instead it relies on a low-level general competence already present in LLMs. This warrants further investigation of low-level LLM competences in neurosymbolic approaches.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using an LLM’s ability to write and query SQL as a neurosymbolic way to detect hallucinations in its own outputs, by grounding checks in a database built from reference documents.
AI.motivation: Hallucinations—factually incorrect or unsupported outputs—are a core limitation of large language models, and current detectors struggle because LLM reasoning is opaque and often not grounded in explicit evidence. The authors want a domain-agnostic, unsupervised method that leverages existing abilities of LLMs rather than task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.method: They first have an LLM construct an SQL database from the given reference documents. Then, for a candidate answer, they use the same database to perform structured reasoning—via SQL queries—over both the references and the answer, forming a hallucination detection pipeline whose decisions are grounded in the database content, i.e., a neurosymbolic check. They compare this to direct hallucination prediction baselines and to existing detectors on standard benchmarks.
AI.result: On the RAGTruth and DiaHalu hallucination detection benchmarks, their SQL-based neurosymbolic pipeline outperforms direct hallucination prediction from the LLM and achieves performance competitive with state-of-the-art hallucination detection methods, without needing domain-specific fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: The results suggest that exploiting low-level symbolic competences already present in LLMs—like building and querying SQL databases—can be an effective, domain-agnostic strategy for hallucination detection. This encourages further work on neurosymbolic methods that harness such low-level abilities for more reliable and interpretable LLM behavior.

title: MedFlow: Class-Aware Multi-Scale Generation for Medical Time-Series Synthesis
summary: Synthetic medical time-series generation can alleviate data scarcity and support the development of reliable clinical prediction models. However, existing methods mainly focus on matching the overall distribution and temporal dynamics of real data, which does not necessarily ensure strong downstream utility on imbalanced medical datasets. Clinically informative patterns often occur at heterogeneous temporal scales, while rare minority-class characteristics can be obscured by dominant population patterns. To address these challenges, we propose MedFlow, a class-aware multi-scale flow matching framework for medical time-series synthesis. MedFlow employs a vector-quantized multi-scale tokenizer to represent medical sequences at complementary temporal resolutions, capturing both coarse clinical trends and fine-grained dynamics. We further introduce Token Marginal Guidance, which incorporates class-conditional token statistics directly into the flow matching process to steer generation toward class-specific regions of the learned tokens. This mechanism strengthens minority-class patterns, while preserving the global and tail distributions of real data. Experiments on four public datasets covering electronic health records, EEG, and ECG signals demonstrate that MedFlow consistently outperforms recent state-of-the-art diffusion-based baselines across downstream prediction tasks. On average, it improves AUPRC by 5.8%, reduces Context-FID by 88.6%, and achieves 3.8$\times$ higher sampling throughput.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MedFlow, a class-aware multi-scale flow matching framework that generates synthetic medical time series with better downstream utility, especially for minority classes, outperforming state-of-the-art diffusion baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing synthetic medical time-series generators mainly match global distributions and temporal dynamics but often fail on imbalanced datasets, where rare but clinically critical patterns are overshadowed by majority-class trends. There is a need for generative models that explicitly preserve and enhance class-specific, especially minority-class, information across multiple temporal scales to improve downstream prediction tasks.
AI.method: The authors propose MedFlow, which combines (1) a vector-quantized multi-scale tokenizer that encodes medical sequences at multiple temporal resolutions to capture both coarse trends and fine-grained dynamics, and (2) Token Marginal Guidance, a mechanism that injects class-conditional token statistics into the flow matching process to bias generation toward class-specific token regions, thereby strengthening minority-class patterns while preserving overall data distributions.
AI.result: On four public datasets involving EHR, EEG, and ECG time series, MedFlow surpasses recent diffusion-based generative baselines on various downstream prediction tasks, yielding on average a 5.8% improvement in AUPRC, an 88.6% reduction in Context-FID (a fidelity/utility metric), and 3.8× faster sampling throughput.
AI.conclusion: Class-aware, multi-scale flow matching with token-level guidance leads to synthetic medical time series that better preserve clinically relevant, especially minority-class, patterns and provide superior downstream predictive performance and efficiency compared with state-of-the-art diffusion-based methods.

title: How do LLMs Evaluate Perceived Moral Agency? Investigating Moral Decision-Making in Human-Artificial Agents Interactions
comment: 43 pages, 14 figures, 29 tables. Preprint under review
summary: As LLMs take on roles requiring moral advice, understanding how they attribute moral agency becomes critical. Humans possess moral agency, the capacity to make ethically guided decisions and bear responsibility for their consequences, a well-established construct in moral psychology. Yet as artificial agents (AAs) such as robots, drones, and disembodied AI systems become increasingly embedded in smart city environments, the question of whether and how moral agency is attributed to them takes on new urgency. This paper presents, to the best of our knowledge, the first empirical study comparing how humans and LLMs evaluate perceived moral agency (PMA) across human and autonomous artificial agents varying in embodiment, situated in plausible smart city scenarios. Using an adaptation of a validated PMA scale, we applied a protocol to 190 human participants as well as various LLMs. Our evaluation reveals higher perceptions of moral agency in humans than in AAs. However, when facing moral dilemmas in concrete scenarios, LLMs reason outward from the situation, prioritizing harm severity and contextual urgency over any stable assessment of the agent itself, amplifying a context-sensitivity also present in human raters. These findings are particularly relevant as LLMs become increasingly involved in everyday moral decisions.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically compares how humans and large language models (LLMs) attribute moral agency to humans vs. artificial agents in smart city scenarios, finding humans are seen as more morally responsible, while LLMs show strong context-sensitivity driven by harm severity and urgency rather than stable agent properties.
AI.motivation: As LLMs begin to provide moral advice and artificial agents become embedded in smart cities, it is crucial to understand whether and how moral agency is attributed to these systems, since this shapes expectations of responsibility, blame, and trust in their decisions. Existing moral psychology has robust constructs for human moral agency, but empirical data on attributions to artificial agents, especially from both humans and LLMs, is lacking.
AI.method: The authors adapt a validated Perceived Moral Agency (PMA) scale to evaluate both human and autonomous artificial agents that vary in embodiment (e.g., robots, drones, disembodied AI) within realistic smart city moral-dilemma scenarios. They administer this protocol to 190 human participants and to several LLMs, eliciting judgments of moral agency as well as scenario-based moral reasoning, and then compare patterns of responses across humans and models.
AI.result: Both humans and LLMs attribute higher moral agency to human agents than to artificial agents overall. However, LLMs do not rely on a stable, agent-focused concept of moral agency when evaluating concrete dilemmas; instead, their judgments are heavily driven by situational features such as severity of potential harm and urgency of the context, which magnifies a context-sensitivity that is also observable—but weaker—in human ratings.
AI.conclusion: LLMs, despite being positioned as moral advisors, exhibit a highly context-driven pattern of moral evaluation that prioritizes situational harm and urgency over consistent attributions of moral agency to different kinds of agents. This divergence from more agent-centered human attributions raises concerns about relying on LLMs in everyday moral decision-making and underscores the need for careful design, governance, and calibration of expectations around AI moral competence and responsibility.

title: When Financial Fine-tuning Fails: A Three-Level Detectability Analysis of Numerical Hallucination in Domain-Adapted Language Models
summary: Financial large language models are increasingly deployed for summarization of reports and disclosures, where numerical hallucination poses significant practical risks. While prior work often attributes such hallucination to insufficient numerical reasoning, this assumption has not been systematically tested under controlled fine-tuning settings. In this paper, we conduct a cost-effective, controlled study of numerical hallucination in financial summarization across three model variants: a base instruction-tuned model, a domain language-adapted model (FT-A), and a numeracy-enhanced domain model (FT-A+B+C). We introduce a three-level detectability taxonomy distinguishing between overt hallucination (currency-denominated fabrication), covert-explicit hallucination (professional-convention numbers), and covert-implicit hallucination (ungrounded quantitative claims). Our results reveal that domain fine-tuning substantially degrades numerical restraint at all detectability levels. While the Base model maintains near-zero hallucination rates (5.4\%), FT-A exhibits 82.5\% overt hallucination and FT-A+B+C reaches 98\%. Contrary to intuition, numeracy supervision amplifies rather than mitigates hallucination across all levels. We identify template injection---the insertion of memorized canonical values regardless of input content---as a primary hallucination mechanism in fine-tuned models. These findings demonstrate that numerical hallucination in financial summarization is driven by the degradation of numerical restraint through domain adaptation, not by insufficient numerical reasoning. We recommend that evaluation protocols assess hallucination across all detectability levels and that deployment practices include explicit mechanisms for grounding-aware generation or abstention.

AI.tldr: Study on why financial LLMs hallucinate numbers more after domain and numeracy fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Financial LLMs are used to summarize reports where incorrect numbers can cause real harm. Prior work assumes hallucinations come from weak numerical reasoning, but this has not been tested in tightly controlled fine-tuning setups. The authors want to separate the effect of domain adaptation and numeracy training from core reasoning ability and to understand how and why hallucinations emerge.
AI.method: They perform a controlled, cost-efficient fine-tuning study on financial summarization using three variants of an LLM: (1) a generic instruction-tuned Base model, (2) a domain language-adapted model (FT-A), and (3) a domain plus numeracy-enhanced model (FT-A+B+C). They define a three-level taxonomy of hallucination detectability (overt, covert-explicit, covert-implicit), and systematically measure hallucination rates across models and levels.
