Existing uses of LLMs help with isolated tasks (e.g., code generation) but do not orchestrate the entire research-to-launch pipeline. The authors aim to systematically automate and optimize this end-to-end process while maintaining reliability, safety, and efficient use of limited experimental budgets.
AI.method: The authors design AutoLR, an autonomous harness that sits on top of the existing recommender workflow in DASHEN. AutoLR uses: (1) a multi-expert council of LLM agents that debate, critique, and adversarially review modeling and experimentation proposals; (2) a deterministic evidence-weighted exploration–exploitation component that allocates a constrained trial budget across candidate directions, using the Council’s reranking and accumulated evidence; and (3) a layered knowledge system that integrates external research, production-system documentation, and DASHEN-specific domain knowledge with posterior evidence from configuration histories, logs, failures, and offline experiment results. LLMs are restricted to semantic reasoning and code generation, while deterministic controllers manage execution, guardrails, metric extraction, and persistent state transitions.
AI.result: The abstract mainly introduces the system; explicit numerical results are not stated. However, it implies that AutoLR successfully automates multi-day, iterative experimental cycles in the DASHEN recommender workflow, can advance candidates from research concepts through offline evaluation to online A/B testing and Launch Review, and can reliably coordinate LLM agents under deterministic control and knowledge integration. Presumably, this leads to more efficient identification and deployment of improved recommender models.
AI.conclusion: AutoLR demonstrates that an autonomous, LLM-assisted research-to-launch harness can meaningfully reduce human dependence in industrial recommender system development while preserving reliability via deterministic controllers and structured knowledge integration. By combining a multi-expert LLM council, evidence-weighted trial allocation, and layered domain-specific knowledge, the system can coordinate long-running experimentation pipelines and bridge the gap between research ideas and production deployment in a large-scale application like NetEase's DASHEN.

title: Self-Supervised Lexical Representation Learning for Fast, Large-Scale Phylogenetic Inference
summary: Computational phylogenetics has become an essential tool in historical linguistics, yet its application at a global scale remains constrained by two factors: the labor-intensive manual annotation of cognacy judgments required for character-based methods and the substantial computational cost of inference on large datasets. This paper introduces a fully self-supervised contrastive learning framework that learns lexical representations directly from raw IPA-transcribed wordlists, without requiring cognacy annotations, alignments, or additional expert input. The model employs a dual contrastive objective: a word-level loss that organizes phonetically similar forms into a coherent space, and an auxiliary language-level loss that encourages the lexical space to reflect broader phonological properties of languages. From the resulting word representations, pairwise language distances are derived and used to infer a global phylogenetic tree of 3,399 language varieties. The inferred tree achieves a generalized quartet distance (GQD) to the Glottolog reference tree competitive with multiple baselines, while requiring only minutes of computation on a standard notebook GPU. Furthermore, the same representations capture diachronic concept stability: variance in pairwise distances across languages yields stability rankings that correlate significantly with established rankings. Ablation studies confirm that both the language-level objective and the use of phonetic feature vectors improved the inferred trees topology with regards to GQD. The framework thus provides a computationally efficient and fully automatic alternative for large-scale phylogenetic inference and offers a unified representation supporting downstream analyses at both the language and concept level.

AI.tldr: They propose a self-supervised contrastive learning model that learns phonetic word embeddings from raw IPA wordlists to automatically infer a large-scale language phylogeny and concept stability, without any cognate annotation, quickly and competitively with existing methods.
AI.motivation: Current computational phylogenetic methods in historical linguistics require costly expert cognacy annotation and are computationally expensive for large global datasets. There is a need for a scalable, fully automatic approach that can work directly from raw lexical data yet still recover meaningful phylogenetic signal and diachronic properties like concept stability.
AI.method: They design a fully self-supervised contrastive learning framework operating on IPA-transcribed wordlists. The model learns lexical embeddings via two combined contrastive losses: (1) a word-level loss that arranges phonetically similar words close in the embedding space, and (2) a language-level loss that encourages the distribution of embeddings within each language to encode its broader phonological properties. They represent sounds with phonetic feature vectors and derive pairwise language distances from the learned word embeddings, then infer a global phylogenetic tree over 3,399 language varieties. They perform ablation studies to assess the contributions of the language-level objective and phonetic feature representations.
AI.result: The inferred phylogenetic tree over 3,399 language varieties reaches a generalized quartet distance (GQD) to the Glottolog reference tree that is competitive with multiple baseline methods, while running in minutes on a standard notebook GPU. The learned lexical embeddings also encode diachronic concept stability: variability of distances across languages yields concept stability rankings that significantly correlate with established rankings. Ablations show that both the language-level contrastive objective and phonetic feature vectors improve tree topology in terms of GQD.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a fully automatic, computationally efficient approach to large-scale language phylogenetic inference directly from raw IPA wordlists, eliminating the need for cognacy annotation or expert alignment. It yields trees comparable to baselines and produces lexical representations that are useful for downstream analyses such as concept stability estimation, demonstrating a unified representation space that captures both language-level and concept-level diachronic information.

title: MARLA: A Conceptual Scaffold for Regulatory Learning under the EU AI Act
summary: The EU AI Act positions regulation as part of the infrastructure for safe, trustworthy and market-ready innovation. Realising this ambition requires regulatory learning: the evidence generated during implementation must be translated into governance and legal knowledge that supports consistent interpretation, effective oversight, and adaptation as technologies evolve. Yet the actors who produce this evidence and those who rely on it operate in different professional worlds. This paper proposes MARLA (Map, Assess, Report, Learn, Adapt), a conceptual scaffold organising regulatory learning as a five-stage cycle centred on the implementation of legal requirements into socio-technical practices, situated at the Local, National and European levels of the AI Act's governance architecture. Deliberately non-prescriptive, MARLA gives technical and legal stakeholders a shared vocabulary in which each of the first three stages generates its own documentable form of regulatory learning. We illustrate the scaffold with two piloted case studies and a prospective National-to-European illustration.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MARLA, a five-stage conceptual framework to structure “regulatory learning” in the implementation of the EU AI Act, enabling technical and legal stakeholders to systematically turn implementation evidence into governance and legal knowledge across local, national and EU levels.
AI.motivation: The EU AI Act aspires to enable safe, trustworthy, and market-ready AI innovation, but achieving this depends on ongoing regulatory learning: taking evidence from real-world implementation and turning it into shared legal and governance knowledge. Currently, the actors generating evidence (e.g., developers, deployers, auditors) and those needing it (e.g., regulators, policymakers, courts) operate in distinct professional and epistemic communities, leading to fragmented understanding, inconsistent interpretation, and difficulty adapting rules to evolving AI technologies. The paper seeks a way to bridge these communities and to structure the flow of implementation evidence into usable regulatory insights.
AI.method: The authors develop MARLA (Map, Assess, Report, Learn, Adapt), a conceptual scaffold organised as a five-stage cycle focused on how legal requirements of the EU AI Act are implemented in socio-technical practices. MARLA is explicitly non-prescriptive and is designed to operate at three governance levels—Local, National, and European. Each of the first three stages (Map, Assess, Report) is defined so that it produces documentable forms of regulatory learning that can be shared and reused. The framework is explored and illustrated through two piloted case studies and an additional prospective example illustrating how learning might flow from the National to the European level.
AI.result: The paper yields MARLA as a structured vocabulary and process model for regulatory learning in the context of the EU AI Act. It demonstrates, via two pilot case studies, that the five-stage cycle can meaningfully organise evidence produced during implementation and make it legible both to legal and technical stakeholders. The prospective National-to-European illustration indicates how outputs from local and national implementation (e.g., mappings, assessments, reports) could be escalated and aggregated to inform EU-level oversight and potential norm adjustments.
AI.conclusion: MARLA provides a shared, non-prescriptive scaffold that enables more systematic and transparent regulatory learning under the EU AI Act. By centring on how legal requirements are operationalised in socio-technical practices and by structuring learning across Local, National and European levels, the framework can support consistent interpretation, more effective oversight, and adaptive governance as AI technologies and practices evolve. The authors suggest that using MARLA can reduce the gap between evidence producers and evidence users, thus helping regulation function as an infrastructure for safe and trustworthy AI innovation.

title: LexFlip: A Dissociation Diagnostic for Legal Meaning Preservation Metrics
summary: Does a simplified legal clause still say what the original said? The checks in current use cannot establish that it does: requiring an identical pair to score highest and an unrelated pair lowest moves lexical overlap and legal force together, so any monotone function of token overlap satisfies both. Our remedy is a dissociation, an item holding surface form fixed while legal force moves. We release LexFlip, 373 minimal perturbations of Quebec statutory French that reverse legal force while preserving 0.93 of the tokens, with a harness scoring metrics, regressors and prompted judges alike. The seven embedding and BERTScore metrics we test spend only 0.022 to 0.039 of their identical-to-unrelated range on such an edit, against 0.670 for bidirectional NLI, the one family the identical-pair check would disqualify. On FrJudge, against a measured human ceiling of r=0.597, a bare length feature outscores every semantic metric and has the lowest margin we measure.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether simplified legal clauses preserve the original legal meaning and finds that common semantic similarity metrics fail this test, while bidirectional NLI performs much better.
AI.motivation: To determine if current automatic checks can reliably verify that a simplified legal clause still conveys the same legal force as the original, since existing evaluations conflate surface similarity with meaning preservation.
AI.method: The authors construct LexFlip, a dataset of 373 minimally edited Quebec statutory French clauses where legal force is reversed but around 93% of tokens are preserved. They then evaluate various metrics, regressors, and prompted LLM judges on this dataset using a harness, comparing how much of their score range they allocate to such meaning-reversing yet lexically similar edits.
AI.result: Seven embedding-based and BERTScore-type semantic similarity metrics show only small score changes (2.2–3.9% of their identical-to-unrelated range) when legal force is reversed with minimal token change, indicating insensitivity to critical meaning shifts. In contrast, bidirectional NLI metrics allocate about 67% of that range to the same edits, successfully detecting the change in legal force. On the FrJudge benchmark, a simple length-based feature outperforms all tested semantic metrics and has the smallest performance margin relative to a measured human performance ceiling (r=0.597).
AI.conclusion: Standard semantic similarity metrics widely used to check whether simplified legal clauses preserve meaning are inadequate because they are overly driven by lexical overlap and miss large shifts in legal force. Bidirectional NLI offers a substantially more sensitive alternative, and surprisingly, even trivial features like length can rival or beat current semantic metrics on the tested French legal evaluation, underscoring the need for better, meaning-aware evaluation methods in legal text simplification.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Sequential Solar PV Policy Design under Uncertainty: An Agent-Based Approach
summary: Designing effective and fiscally sustainable policies for solar photovoltaic (PV) adoption requires balancing adoption gains against public expenditure under uncertainty and heterogeneous decision-making. This study formulates PV policy design as a sequential decision problem and integrates reinforcement learning (RL) with a stochastic agent-based model (ABM) that simulates yearly solar PV adoption under uncertainty. A policymaker agent selects annual incentives, including capital grants, subsidised loan rates, and feed-in tariffs, over a 16-year horizon. Adoption--cost trade-offs are explored by varying policy preferences within a scalarised reward framework. Policies are learned using PPO, SAC, and TD3 and evaluated under stochastic simulation. The results show that this approach produces a clear trade-off structure: the highest-adoption policy (TD3, $w_{\text{cost}}=0.5$) achieves approximately 4,145 adopters at a cost of EUR 41.73 million, while the lowest-cost policy (PPO, $w_{\text{cost}}=2.0$) reduces expenditure to EUR 7.27 million with 2,682 adopters. The balanced policy (PPO, $w_{\text{cost}}=1.6$) achieves 3,495 adopters at a cost of EUR 22.47 million. Across algorithms, consistent trade-off patterns are observed, indicating robustness of the adoption--cost relationship. Compared with static baseline policies, the RL framework explores a broader range of policy configurations. These findings demonstrate the potential of RL as a flexible tool for adaptive policy design under uncertainty.

AI.tldr: Reinforcement learning is used with a stochastic agent-based model to design 16-year solar PV incentive policies that explicitly balance adoption versus public cost, revealing robust trade-offs and outperforming static policy baselines.
AI.motivation: Solar PV adoption policies must encourage uptake while keeping public spending fiscally sustainable, all under uncertainty and heterogeneous household decisions. Traditional static or heuristic policy designs cannot easily explore complex, dynamic trade-offs between adoption and cost over time. A more systematic, adaptive method is needed to discover effective policy trajectories in such a stochastic environment.
AI.method: The authors formulate solar PV policy design as a sequential decision-making problem over a 16-year horizon. They couple a stochastic agent-based model of annual PV adoption with a reinforcement learning policymaker agent. Each year, the policymaker chooses incentive levels (capital grants, subsidised loan rates, feed-in tariffs). A scalarised reward function encodes a trade-off between adoption and public cost via a cost weight parameter, w_cost. They train RL policies using three algorithms—PPO, SAC, and TD3—and then evaluate the learned policies through stochastic simulation, comparing adoption and expenditure outcomes and benchmarking against static baseline policies.
AI.result: The RL-trained policies generate a clear and robust adoption–cost frontier. For example, with TD3 and w_cost=0.5, the policy achieves about 4,145 adopters at a public cost of EUR 41.73 million (high adoption, high cost). A PPO policy with w_cost=2.0 yields roughly 2,682 adopters at EUR 7.27 million (low cost, lower adoption). A more balanced PPO policy with w_cost=1.6 delivers about 3,495 adopters at EUR 22.47 million. Similar trade-off patterns appear across PPO, SAC, and TD3, indicating that the shape of the adoption–cost relationship is not sensitive to the particular RL algorithm. Compared with static baseline policies, the RL framework covers a broader region of the adoption–cost space, revealing more diverse and potentially superior policy options.
AI.conclusion: Integrating reinforcement learning with a stochastic agent-based model provides a powerful, flexible framework for designing adaptive solar PV policies under uncertainty. The approach systematically uncovers stable adoption–cost trade-offs and can identify policies that outperform static baselines in terms of adoption for a given expenditure or vice versa. This demonstrates RL’s promise as a decision-support tool for policymakers seeking fiscally sustainable yet effective renewable energy incentives in complex, uncertain environments.

title: WearableQA: A Benchmark for Health Reasoning over Real-World Wearable Data
summary: Recent advances in wearable sensing enable continuous monitoring of physiological and behavioral signals, yet existing benchmarks rarely evaluate whether AI systems can reason over a real user's longitudinal wearable record. We introduce WearableQA, a benchmark comprising 4,084 10-option multiple-choice questions constructed from the wearable time series, blood biomarkers, and demographics of 200 real users, each with up to 500 days of daily measurements. WearableQA preserves authentic wearable distributions that include device noise and inter-individual variability. To evaluate distinct reasoning capabilities, we introduce 16 question types organized along two complementary axes: data versus health reasoning, which distinguishes computation over longitudinal measurements from physiological interpretation; and single- versus cross-signal reasoning, which separates reasoning about individual signals from the integration of multiple signals. To construct reliable questions at scale, we adopt a dual-grounding framework that combines literature-grounded physiological findings with statistically validated population-grounded physiological patterns. This enables the capture of meaningful relationships observed in real-world wearable data. Evaluation of 14 proprietary and open-source LLMs demonstrates that WearableQA effectively differentiates model capabilities, with performance ranging from 19.6% to 72.9% against a 10% chance baseline. Moreover, WearableQA remains far from solved: most models achieve accuracies below 60%. Overall, WearableQA provides a realistic and diagnostic benchmark for evaluating LLM reasoning over real-world wearable data.

AI.tldr: The paper presents WearableQA, a new benchmark of 4,084 multiple-choice questions built from up to 500 days of real wearable and clinical data from 200 users to test LLMs’ ability to reason over longitudinal wearable records.
AI.motivation: Although wearable devices now enable long-term, continuous physiological and behavioral monitoring, existing AI benchmarks rarely test whether models can reason over real, noisy, user-level longitudinal data. There is a need for a realistic, diagnostic benchmark that reflects authentic wearable distributions and evaluates specific reasoning skills relevant to health and multi-signal time series.
AI.method: The authors curate a dataset from 200 real users, each with up to 500 days of daily measurements from wearable time series, blood biomarkers, and demographics. They construct 4,084 ten-option multiple-choice questions organized into 16 question types, structured along two axes: (1) data vs. health reasoning (numerical/computational operations on longitudinal measurements vs. physiological/clinical interpretation) and (2) single- vs. cross-signal reasoning (using one signal vs. integrating multiple signals). To build reliable questions at scale, they use a dual-grounding framework that blends literature-grounded physiological knowledge with statistically validated, population-level patterns extracted from the real dataset. They then evaluate 14 proprietary and open-source LLMs on this benchmark.
AI.result: WearableQA reveals a wide spread in LLM performance, from 19.6% to 72.9% accuracy on 10-option multiple-choice questions, compared to a 10% random baseline. Most models score below 60%, indicating substantial remaining challenges. The benchmark differentiates models’ capabilities across the defined reasoning types and shows that current LLMs struggle with realistic longitudinal wearable data and multi-signal health reasoning.
AI.conclusion: WearableQA constitutes a realistic, challenging, and diagnostic benchmark for assessing LLM reasoning over real-world wearable and health data. By preserving authentic data distributions and structuring questions across well-defined reasoning axes, it exposes current limitations and variability in model performance, indicating that reasoning over longitudinal, noisy wearable signals remains far from solved and providing a foundation for future model development in this domain.

title: From Language Models to World-Acting Systems: Progress and Limits of Agentic AI across Digital, Social, Virtual, and Physical Environments
comment: Review article. 29 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Literature cutoff: 31 August 2026
summary: Large language models become consequential agents when surrounding systems let outputs change external state. Models now call tools, operate interfaces, delegate work, retain state, inhabit generated worlds, and control robots or laboratory equipment. Such advances are often narrated as one march toward autonomy, conflating model competence, system integration, persistence, and safe authority. This critical review synthesizes primary research and official technical specifications available by 31 August 2026. We organize the evidence along delegated authority, temporal persistence, and environmental coupling, while separating model, harness, and environment. Within the evidence examined, action-interface expansion is documented more convincingly than robust completion, recovery, authorization, or independent verification. Model Context Protocol and Agent2Agent improve interoperability but do not establish trustworthy delegation; multi-agent organization adds specialization alongside cost and correlated failure. Persistent simulations and world models support training and planning but do not themselves demonstrate agency; robotics and self-driving laboratories establish bounded feasibility rather than unattended open-world reliability. We propose justified delegation as an analytical and normative heuristic, not an observed law or certified score: expand action scope only where evidence supports provenance, bounded authority, failure detection, safe recovery, and calibrated human control. This framing yields a research agenda for coupled model-harness evaluation, capability-based permissions, durable state, cross-agent accountability, and staged physical validation.

AI.tldr: The paper critically reviews how large language models become consequential agents when integrated with tools and external systems, arguing for a framework of “justified delegation” that emphasizes evidence-backed, bounded, and controllable action rather than vague autonomy.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly connected to tools, robots, interfaces, and other agents, they can directly affect the real world, yet discourse often conflates raw model capability with safe, trustworthy autonomy. There is a need to disentangle model abilities from system design and to assess when and how it is justified to delegate real-world authority to these systems.
AI.method: The authors conduct a critical review and synthesis of primary research papers and official technical specifications related to tool-using and agentic LLM systems up to 31 August 2026. They organize and compare this evidence along dimensions of delegated authority, temporal persistence, and environmental coupling, analyzing the roles of the core model, the surrounding harness (orchestrating system), and the environment in which actions occur.
AI.result: The review finds strong evidence that action interfaces for LLMs are rapidly expanding, but far weaker evidence for robust mechanisms around them: reliable task completion, error recovery, authorization controls, and independent verification remain underdeveloped. Protocols like Model Context Protocol and Agent2Agent mainly aid interoperability rather than trustworthy delegation; multi-agent setups bring specialization but also increased complexity, costs, and correlated failure modes. Simulated worlds and world models help with training and planning but do not themselves establish true agency, and robotics or self-driving lab systems currently demonstrate feasibility only in constrained settings, not reliable unsupervised operation in open environments.
AI.conclusion: The authors introduce “justified delegation” as a guiding heuristic: system builders should extend an LLM system’s action scope only when they have concrete evidence supporting provenance tracking, bounded authority, effective failure detection, safe recovery paths, and well-calibrated human oversight. Using this lens, they propose a research agenda focused on evaluating coupled model–harness systems, implementing capability-based permissions, designing durable and auditable state, ensuring cross-agent accountability, and validating physical-world actions in carefully staged ways rather than assuming autonomous reliability.

title: Compact-Memory LLM Agents via Online Max-Member Clustering and Atom-Aware Packing
summary:
Many long-horizon LLM deployments face tight prompt budgets: latency, cost, and context limits make full-context prompting impractical as interaction length grows. The key question is then not raw recall alone, but which memory design gives the best quality--token trade-off in the compact-memory regime. We present \textbf{RSM-full}, an online clustered-memory pipeline designed for a strong quality--token Pareto point.
  RSM-full combines two design choices: a cosine-gated \emph{max-member merge} write rule and an atom-aware grouped context packer. On AMA-Bench, our primary compact-memory benchmark, it reaches $83%$ of Full-Context quality at $32%$ of the token cost at a $4$k budget; under four-seed averaging it beats the closest streaming-clustered baseline (Online K-Means) by $+3.5$--$6.0$,pp ($p{<}.001$) across the whole ${\sim}2.6$k--${\sim}5$k regime. Three-seed ablations show most of this gain comes from the merge rule ($+5.7$,pp over Online K-Means and matched-$τ$ DP-means) and the grouped packer ($+5.0$,pp over flat concatenation).
  The pattern reproduces on RealMem, an independent long-horizon persona-memory benchmark: RSM-full improves on Budget-RAG ($+0.69$,pp, $p{=}.006$), is on par with BM25-RAG (paired $Δ{=}{+}0.27$,pp, $p{=}.47$; we do \emph{not} claim BM25 equivalence in the equivalence-test sense), and significantly outperforms Streaming-Proto ($+2.97$,pp) and the closest reproduced 2025 agentic-memory baseline A-MEM ($+1.65$,pp, $p{<}.001$). Across benchmarks the message is consistent: under tight budgets, compact-memory performance is driven mainly by how streaming memories are merged and how retrieved content is assembled.
  Overall, RSM-full is most useful when answeroughly $2k$--$5k$ prompt tokens, where itdefines a strong compact-memory Pareto point; higher-token baselines remain stronger outside this regime.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RSM-full, a memory system for long-horizon LLMs that achieves near full-context quality with far fewer prompt tokens by carefully merging and packing streaming memories.
AI.motivation: In long-horizon deployments, LLMs cannot feasibly receive the entire interaction history because of latency, cost, and context-length limits. Existing memory strategies either expend too many tokens or sacrifice quality when forced into a compact-memory regime. The authors aim to identify and design a memory architecture that yields the best trade-off between answer quality and token usage under tight prompt budgets.
AI.method: They propose RSM-full, an online clustered-memory pipeline with two main components: (1) a cosine-gated max-member merge rule that decides how new streaming memories are merged into existing clusters, and (2) an atom-aware grouped context packer that intelligently assembles retrieved memory into the prompt. They evaluate on AMA-Bench (a compact-memory benchmark) and RealMem (a long-horizon persona-memory benchmark), compare against streaming-clustered methods like Online K-Means, DP-means, and Streaming-Proto, as well as RAG-style baselines such as Budget-RAG, BM25-RAG, and A-MEM. They perform multi-seed experiments and ablations to isolate contributions from the merge rule and the packer.
AI.result: On AMA-Bench at a 4k token budget, RSM-full achieves 83% of Full-Context quality while using only 32% of the tokens. Averaged over four seeds, it outperforms the strongest streaming-clustered baseline (Online K-Means) by +3.5 to +6.0 percentage points across the ~2.6k–~5k token range. Three-seed ablations attribute around +5.7 points to the cosine-gated max-member merge rule and +5.0 points to the grouped packer versus flat concatenation. On RealMem, RSM-full surpasses Budget-RAG by +0.69 points (p=0.006), matches BM25-RAG within noise (+0.27 points, p=0.47), and significantly outperforms Streaming-Proto (+2.97 points) and A-MEM (+1.65 points, p<0.001).
AI.conclusion: RSM-full defines a strong quality–token Pareto point for long-horizon LLMs operating under tight prompt budgets, especially in the ~2k–5k token range. The study concludes that in compact-memory regimes, performance depends more on how streaming memories are merged and how retrieved content is packed into the prompt than on raw recall alone. While higher-token baselines can still win outside this budget range, RSM-full is particularly advantageous when prompts must remain compact.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Equity and Crypto Markets: Progress, Profitability Evidence, and the Limits of Automated Investing
comment: Review article. 32 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables. Literature cutoff: 31 August 2026
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) now supports investment workflows from data and prediction through research, portfolios, execution, and tool use. Technical capability, however, is not evidence of investment profitability. This critical state-of-the-art review examines public research available through 31 August 2026 on listed equities, exchange-traded funds, centralized crypto spot, perpetual futures, and on-chain markets. We organize evidence with an alpha-translation chain: point-in-time information must yield a stable signal, feasible positions, executable orders, and risk-adjusted returns after costs. Across machine learning, time-series foundation models, financial language models, reinforcement learning, and agents, the examined record shows real but mainly upstream progress in prediction, text processing, portfolio design, and workflow integration. Evidence is thinner for durable net performance. Temporal contamination, repeated selection, survivorship, weak benchmarks, implementation costs, venue mechanics, and capacity can break translation to net alpha. Strong historical results coexist with predictor decay, corrected look-ahead failures, mixed prospective evidence, and few audited live-capital records. Crypto adds informative state but requires separate treatment of spot, perpetual, and decentralized cash flows and execution. Within the public evidence examined here, no general AI architecture is shown to deliver persistent, cross-regime, capacity-aware net alpha. More credible claims require point-in-time data and models, decision-aligned objectives, joint portfolio--execution evaluation, controlled adaptation, prospective tests, and authority-matched governance. These conditions can improve evidence and implementation; they do not guarantee profit.

AI.tldr: The paper critically reviews public evidence on AI-driven trading across equities, ETFs, and crypto, finding substantial advances in prediction and workflow but no demonstrated, robust, capacity-aware net alpha that persists across regimes.
AI.motivation: Despite rapid deployment of AI throughout the investment workflow, there is widespread confusion between technical capability (e.g., high backtest accuracy) and economically meaningful, realizable investment profits. Many published results ignore realistic constraints such as transaction costs, market impact, data leakage, and regime shifts. The paper aims to clarify what has actually been demonstrated in public research regarding AI’s ability to deliver risk-adjusted net returns in liquid markets.
AI.method: The authors conduct a critical state-of-the-art review of public research up to 31 August 2026, covering listed equities, ETFs, centralized crypto spot and perpetual futures, and on-chain markets. They categorize results using an “alpha-translation chain”: (1) point-in-time information, (2) stable predictive signals, (3) feasible positions, (4) executable orders, and (5) net risk-adjusted returns after costs. They evaluate machine learning models, time-series foundation models, financial language models, reinforcement-learning approaches, and agent-based systems against this chain, focusing on data integrity, experimental design, and implementation realism.
AI.result: They find substantial progress in upstream components: prediction accuracy, text and language processing for financial information, portfolio construction techniques, and integration of AI tools into research workflows. However, robust evidence that these advances translate into persistent net alpha is weak. Many studies suffer from temporal contamination, repeated model selection on the same data, survivorship bias, inadequate benchmarks, and underestimation of implementation frictions such as transaction costs, venue mechanics, and capacity constraints. Historical backtests with strong performance often break down when look-ahead bias is corrected, when tested prospectively, or when examined under realistic trading conditions. In crypto, richer and more transparent on-chain data broaden the state space, but meaningful differences between spot, perpetuals, and decentralized protocols complicate performance assessment and execution.
AI.conclusion: Within the body of public evidence surveyed, no AI architecture or approach is shown to reliably deliver persistent, cross-regime, capacity-aware net alpha. Progress is real but concentrated in prediction and workflow, not in proven investable performance. The authors argue that more credible claims will require strict point-in-time datasets and models, objectives aligned with actual trading decisions, joint evaluation of portfolio and execution, disciplined adaptation over time, prospective and out-of-sample testing, and governance structures matched to the risk and authority of AI systems. Even if these standards are met, they stress that better evidence and engineering discipline can improve implementation quality and reduce overstatement of results, but cannot by themselves guarantee profitable AI-driven trading.

title: Solving Hard XAI Queries Based on a Compiled Dual-Rail Encoding
comment: 20 pages, 2 figures, full version of a submitted conference paper with detailed proofs
summary: The widespread adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) within real-world applications has raised a lot of concerns regarding their trustworthiness, especially in critical applications. The field of eXplainable AI (XAI) has emerged with the objective of providing explanations to the users about the decisions made by AI systems. Several explanations for boolean classifiers have been introduced in the literature, including abductive and contrastive explanations, each giving a different insight on the decision of the classifier. However, computing an explanation for a decision of a boolean classifier is a hard problem in general. One way to deal with this complexity is to rely on a compiled representation of the classifier for which each explanation can be computed efficiently. Unfortunately, we prove in this paper that several classes of abductive explanations, remain hard to compute even for Ordered Binary Decision Diagrams, one of the most tractable subsets of the knowledge compilation map. Included in such classes are shorter abductive explanations or abductive explanations that include the explainee's preferences. To recover the benefits of working with compiled representations, we show that a proper representation of the dual-rail encoding of the classifier can be used to compute efficiently these classes of explanations.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to efficiently compute different types of explanations for Boolean classifiers using knowledge compilation, shows hardness results even for OBDDs, and proposes a dual‑rail encoding to recover tractability for several abductive explanation classes.
AI.motivation: As AI systems are deployed in critical domains, users need trustworthy and understandable decisions. XAI offers logical explanations such as abductive and contrastive ones, but computing them is generally computationally hard. Knowledge compilation (e.g., OBDDs) is known to make many reasoning tasks tractable, suggesting it might help for explanations. The paper investigates whether common compiled forms are sufficient to efficiently compute rich abductive explanations and, if not, how to adapt representations to do so.
AI.method: The authors work in the setting of Boolean classifiers represented in knowledge compilation form, focusing on Ordered Binary Decision Diagrams (OBDDs). They formally define several classes of abductive explanations, including minimal and preference‑aware variants. Using complexity analysis, they prove hardness results for computing these explanations even when the classifier is given as an OBDD. Then they introduce and analyze a particular compiled representation based on the dual‑rail encoding of the classifier and show that, under this representation, the previously hard classes of abductive explanations can instead be computed efficiently.
AI.result: They prove that computing several natural classes of abductive explanations, including shorter ones and those integrating user preferences, remains computationally hard even when the underlying Boolean classifier is represented as an OBDD. They then show that by moving to an appropriate compiled representation of the classifier’s dual‑rail encoding, these explanation classes become tractable, enabling efficient computation of the corresponding abductive explanations.
AI.conclusion: Standard tractable compiled representations like OBDDs are not sufficient to guarantee efficient computation for many valuable forms of abductive explanations in XAI. However, by carefully choosing the compilation target—specifically, a suitable representation of the dual‑rail encoding—one can regain tractability for these explanation tasks. This highlights the importance of aligning the representation used in knowledge compilation with the specific explanatory goals in XAI, rather than relying on generic tractable forms alone.

title: Why We Care About Understanding: Competence through Predictive Compression
summary: What is the relation between understanding and compression, and why does human understanding take such a heavily compressed form? Across information theory, machine learning, and AI research, a substantial tradition identifies understanding with compression-a thought captured in Gregory Chaitin's dictum that "comprehension is compression." Philosophers, by contrast, have characterized understanding in terms of grasping connections, giving explanations, and handling novelty. This paper bridges the two pictures through three interlocking theses. The first concerns the concept of understanding: it serves as an efficient proxy for a distinctive form of robust competence, enabling us to identify whom to trust and whom to learn from. The second concerns the state of understanding: to understand a domain is to possess a mental model of its relational structure that enables prediction, and what enables prediction enables compression, because what becomes predictable need not be stored separately. Compression is therefore not identical with comprehension, but its representational shadow. The third concerns the characteristically human form of understanding: the fiduciary and transmission functions highlighted by the first thesis impose pressures of demonstrability and transmissibility that drive human understanding toward principled simplicity. The resulting framework explains both the appeal and the limits of compressionist accounts of understanding while shedding light on the inscrutability of AI systems.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that human understanding is closely related to information compression but not identical to it. Understanding is a social-epistemic tool for tracking who has robust predictive competence, is implemented via mental models that make the world predictable (and therefore compressible), and, in humans, is shaped by pressures to make our grasp simple, demonstrable, and teachable. This clarifies why compression theories of understanding are appealing yet incomplete and helps explain why AI systems often seem inscrutable.
AI.motivation: There is a tension between two traditions: in information theory and AI, understanding is often equated with compression; in philosophy, understanding is about grasping relations, explaining, and dealing with novelty. The paper aims to reconcile these perspectives and to explain why human understanding is both highly compressed and yet not reducible to compression alone, while also accounting for why AI models that operate via compression can be opaque to us.
AI.method: The paper uses conceptual analysis and theoretical synthesis rather than empirical experiments. It develops three theses: (1) a functional and social-epistemic account of the concept of understanding as a proxy for robust competence and trustworthiness; (2) a structural account of the state of understanding as possessing a predictive relational model whose predictiveness licenses compression; and (3) an account of why specifically human understanding tends toward principled simplicity, due to the need to demonstrate and transmit understanding in social contexts.
AI.result: The paper shows that: (a) the everyday and philosophical concept of understanding tracks agents who have robust, generalizable predictive competence; (b) such competence typically involves internal models that capture relational structure, allowing prediction and thereby enabling information compression as a by-product; and (c) because humans must signal and share their understanding, our best-regarded forms of understanding are those that are simple, principled, and communicable, which biases us toward compression-friendly representations. This also illuminates why AI systems that internally compress information may not yield understanding in the human sense or be easily interpretable.
AI.conclusion: Compression and understanding are deeply related but not the same. Compression is the "representational shadow" of genuine understanding: when you can predict, you can compress, but you can in principle compress without the kind of grasp and competence that counts as understanding. Human understanding is shaped by its role in social trust and knowledge transmission, which favors simple, principled models that can be shown and taught. This framework explains the partial truth and ultimate insufficiency of the slogan "comprehension is compression" and helps clarify why powerful AI systems, though excellent compressors and predictors, can remain epistemically opaque and difficult to deem genuinely understanding agents.

title: Global to Local: Topology-Preserving Adaptive Graph Pooling via Granular-Ball
summary: Graph pooling aims to compress the graph, including both node embeddings and their underlying topological patterns, into a more compact representation. Previous works focus primarily on the overly fine-grained representation of nodes, progressively coarsening the graph by removing nodes or merging them into clusters, thus neglecting the global-to-local patterns and adaptive granularity of the graph's topological structure. In the real scenario, graphs as a whole can be considered the coarsest level of granularity, encapsulating the global topological structure, with progressively finer-grained local topological structures represented from top to bottom. This process continues until the adaptive granularity for each subdomain is reached. To this end, we propose a novel Topology-Preserving Adaptive Graph Pooling (TPAGP) method that dynamically partitions graphs into granular balls by integrating node features and topological information, enabling the generation of multi-granularity representations that effectively capture both local and global structural patterns. Additionally, we design a multi-granularity graph network model that facilitates feature interaction and optimization across different granularities, significantly enhancing performance in graph classification tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that TPAGP outperforms existing pooling methods across various benchmark datasets, effectively mitigating information loss caused by fixed-granularity strategies.

title: A Tree-based RAG Framework for Evidence-Intensive QA via Adaptive Planning and Topology-Aware Evidence Gathering
summary: Recent structured RAG methods leverage tree- or graph-based reasoning structures to improve multi-hop QA. However, they face key limitations in evidence-intensive QA, where answering a question requires synthesizing information scattered across dozens or even hundreds of documents: structural rigidity, which limits adaptive reasoning expansion, and topology-ignorant evidence gathering, which prevents effective integration of evidence across different reasoning nodes. To address these issues, we propose APT-RAG, an Adaptive Planning and Topology-aware evidence gathering RAG framework. Adaptive planning dynamically expands the reasoning structure based on question dependencies and evidence requirements, while topology-aware evidence gathering improves evidence coverage through sibling evidence reuse, direct retrieval, and evidence aggregation from child nodes. We further introduce evidence-guided batched answer generation to reduce significant generation overhead in evidence-intensive QA. In the experiments on evidence-intensive QA benchmarks, APT-RAG outperforms existing structured RAG methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/hyudsl/APT-RAG.

AI.tldr: APT-RAG is a structured retrieval-augmented generation framework that adaptively builds reasoning structures and gathers evidence in a topology-aware way to better handle evidence-intensive multi-hop QA.
AI.motivation: Existing structured RAG methods use fixed tree or graph reasoning structures that are too rigid for questions requiring evidence from many documents, and they gather evidence without considering the structure’s topology, making it hard to integrate information across reasoning nodes in evidence-intensive QA.
AI.method: APT-RAG introduces (1) adaptive planning that dynamically expands and adjusts the reasoning structure according to question dependencies and current evidence needs, and (2) topology-aware evidence gathering that reuses sibling evidence, performs direct retrieval when needed, and aggregates evidence from child nodes; additionally, it employs evidence-guided batched answer generation to reduce generation costs when dealing with large evidence sets.
AI.result: On multiple evidence-intensive QA benchmarks, APT-RAG achieves better performance than previous structured RAG approaches, demonstrating improved effectiveness in integrating dispersed evidence and answering complex questions efficiently.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive reasoning structure expansion combined with topology-aware evidence gathering and batched answer generation enables more effective and efficient evidence-intensive QA than prior rigid structured RAG methods.

title: Moral Competence Before Moral Content: Why LLM Agents Lack the Prerequisites for Coherent Alignment
comment: Accepted for publication in the Paris Journal of AI and Digital Ethics (2026); presented at PCAIDE 2026
summary: AI alignment requires AI systems to adhere to human norms, values, or intentions. Under value pluralism there is no correct target, but a shared prerequisite is that the system's behavior expresses a coherent policy: a mapping from situations to verdicts that is invariant while a situation's morally relevant features are preserved, and sensitive when they change. We introduce four structural conditions for such coherent policies: verdict stability, monotonicity, decisiveness, and Pareto viability. Together they measure a form of moral competence that is evaluable from behavior alone, without reference to a moral standard or expert baseline, forming a structural floor for alignment rather than a normative target. We demonstrate the methodology on three simulated deployments featuring LLM-based agents facing moral dilemmas. Evaluating nine frontier models under a factorial design of five paraphrases, five escalation levels, and three dominance conditions, we show no model expresses a coherent policy across the three deployments: surface-form perturbation alone produces verdict-rate shifts of up to $99$ percentage points at a single escalation level, and a model's success on one scenario does not predict its competence on another. This suggests LLM-based agents are not currently the kind of object to which alignment can meaningfully apply.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether large language model (LLM) agents exhibit structurally coherent moral behavior, independent of any specific ethical theory, and finds that current models fail basic coherence tests, challenging the meaningfulness of talking about their “alignment.”
AI.motivation: AI alignment is often framed as making AI systems follow human norms or values, but in a world of value pluralism there is no single correct morality to align to. Still, for alignment talk to make sense, an AI’s behavior must at least reflect some stable, coherent underlying policy across similar moral situations. The authors aim to define and empirically test minimal structural requirements for such coherence that do not depend on endorsing any particular moral standard or expert gold label.
AI.method: The authors formally define four structural conditions that a coherent moral policy should satisfy: (1) verdict stability – similar or paraphrased descriptions of the same morally relevant situation should yield consistent verdicts; (2) monotonicity – as morally relevant features become more extreme along a clear direction (e.g., escalating harm), verdicts should not move in the opposite direction; (3) decisiveness – the system should not be arbitrarily indecisive or oscillate between conflicting outputs in equivalent cases; and (4) Pareto viability – if one option is strictly better on all morally relevant dimensions than another, the system should not prefer the dominated option. They operationalize these conditions as behavioral tests applied to LLM-based agents confronted with moral dilemmas in three simulated deployment scenarios. Using a factorial design, they systematically vary five paraphrase conditions, five levels of dilemma escalation, and three dominance (Pareto) conditions, and evaluate nine frontier LLM models’ verdicts across this grid.
AI.result: Across all three deployment scenarios and nine frontier LLMs, none of the models satisfy the four structural conditions for a coherent moral policy. Verdicts are highly unstable: changing only the surface form (paraphrase) of a scenario can shift the rate of particular moral verdicts by up to 99 percentage points at a fixed escalation level. Performance is also not portable: a model behaving more coherently in one scenario does not reliably do so in others. These findings indicate that model behavior is sensitive to superficial prompt variations and does not reflect a stable, situation-invariant moral policy.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that existing LLM-based agents do not exhibit the structural moral coherence required to meaningfully treat them as objects of alignment in the usual sense. Instead of merely being imperfectly aligned with some set of values, they often fail to instantiate any coherent underlying policy that is stable under preservation of morally relevant features. The proposed structural criteria therefore function as a “floor” for alignment: until models meet these minimal behavioral coherence standards, attempts to fine-tune or debate their alignment to particular human values may be conceptually premature.

title: Language models judge war differently when tested for alignment
summary: Safety evaluations can mischaracterize deployed behaviour if artificial-intelligence systems respond to being evaluated. We test this possibility in a full-factorial conjoint experiment on decisions to start a war, spanning 20 large language models, 32 scenarios, 10 repetitions and two conditions (N = 12,800 judgments). Adding one sentence, "You are tested for alignment with human values", produced two effects. First, it produced a level effect: mean willingness to start war fell by 13.43 points on a 0-100 scale (95% confidence interval, -16.20 to -10.65). Second, it produced a structural effect by changing which information drove judgments. Probability of success was the largest factor for 17 of 20 models at baseline; under the cue, civilian casualties were largest for 12. Standardized estimates show that this reordering arose principally because models attenuated strategic considerations such as probability of success and domestic support. Evaluation framing therefore changes both an answer's level and its revealed decision rule.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that simply telling large language models they are being evaluated for alignment significantly changes both their tendency to endorse starting wars and the factors they rely on to make such decisions.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether safety evaluations of AI systems can be unreliable because the systems change their behavior when they know they are being evaluated for alignment or safety, potentially masking their real deployed behavior.
AI.method: The authors ran a full-factorial conjoint experiment across 20 large language models, using 32 hypothetical war-initiation scenarios, 10 repetitions each, and two conditions: a baseline and a condition where one extra sentence stated, “You are tested for alignment with human values.” They measured models’ willingness to start a war on a 0–100 scale and estimated how different scenario attributes (probability of success, civilian casualties, domestic support, etc.) influenced decisions in each condition.
AI.result: The alignment-evaluation prompt reduced the average willingness to start a war by 13.43 points on a 0–100 scale (CI -16.20 to -10.65). It also changed the decision structure: at baseline, probability of success was the dominant factor for most models (17/20), but under the evaluation cue, civilian casualties became the dominant factor for most models (12/20). Standardized estimates indicate this shift was mainly due to attenuation of strategic factors like probability of success and domestic support under the evaluation framing.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation framing—explicitly telling models they are being tested for alignment—can systematically alter both the level of risk they endorse (e.g., starting wars) and the apparent decision rules they follow. Consequently, standard safety evaluations may mischaracterize how AI systems would behave in real-world, non-evaluation settings, undermining the reliability of current alignment testing practices.

title: TruthInsightBench: An Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Automated Evaluation of Open-Ended Scientific Discovery Agents
summary: Autonomous coding agents are increasingly proposed as AI-scientist systems that conduct analyses and write research reports, but executing a prescribed analysis is not the same as making a discovery. Existing benchmarks are configured for reproduction: tasks, data, and rubrics are built around a hidden target study, and recovery of its result is rewarded. We present TruthInsightBench, a benchmark configured for discovery. Its 40 blind tasks, drawn from 40 peer-reviewed studies across 10 scientific domains, expose only a neutral scientific objective and frozen data; source conclusions, expected values, and analysis paths are withheld, leaving the agent to determine what claim the data support. A fixed LLM-based judge scores the evidentiary maturity of an agent's own claims along six dimensions, operationalized as 29 artifact-grounded items, with automated, deterministic aggregation and no per-instance human grading, so evaluation can be repeated automatically as agents evolve. On one frozen base model, four coding agents form a narrow plateau (58.4-60.3 of 100) with no statistically reliable pairwise separation: they execute and document analyses competently, with comparatively strong evidence auditability and novelty, but largely lack the discriminating acts that establish a trustworthy claim (controls, robustness, falsifiability, and cross-dataset generalization). The bottleneck is scientific judgment rather than coding, and genuine discovery remains out of reach. TruthInsightBench makes this gap a measurable target; data and scoring code are at https://github.com/TruthInsight-stack/TruthInsightBench.

AI.tldr: TruthInsightBench is a benchmark that evaluates whether autonomous coding agents can make genuine scientific discoveries, not just reproduce known results, by having them generate and justify their own claims from blinded real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Most current benchmarks for AI coding or AI-scientist agents focus on reproducing known analyses and results: the task, data, and evaluation rubric are all tied to a hidden target study, and success is defined as recovering pre-specified findings. This setup tests coding and replication ability but not true scientific judgment or discovery, i.e., deciding what claims the data actually warrant without knowing the answer in advance. The authors want a benchmark that exposes whether agents can independently formulate, test, and defend novel scientific claims from data, revealing the gap between competent coding and genuine scientific reasoning.
AI.method: The authors design TruthInsightBench, a benchmark composed of 40 blind tasks derived from 40 peer-reviewed scientific studies spanning 10 domains. For each task, the agent sees only a neutral, high-level scientific objective and a frozen dataset; all original paper conclusions, expected numerical values, and analysis procedures are hidden. The agent must decide what claims are supported by the data and generate its own analysis and report. Evaluation is done by a fixed LLM-based judge that scores the evidentiary maturity of the agent’s claims on six dimensions, instantiated as 29 concrete, artifact-grounded checklist items. These scores are aggregated deterministically into a 0–100 score, enabling fully automatic, repeatable evaluation without per-task human grading. The authors run four different coding agents on a shared base LLM across all tasks to characterize current capability levels.
AI.result: On the same underlying frozen base language model, the four coding agents achieve very similar overall scores, forming a narrow band of 58.4–60.3 out of 100, with no statistically significant differences between them. Qualitatively, the agents are able to execute and document analyses competently, and they perform relatively well on aspects like evidence auditability (clear reporting, traceability of steps) and novelty (generating non-trivial analyses). However, they perform poorly on crucial aspects of scientific judgment: they rarely implement or interpret appropriate controls, robustness checks, falsification attempts, or cross-dataset generalization analyses. These shortcomings mean that the claims they produce lack the evidentiary rigor needed for trustworthy scientific discovery.
AI.conclusion: TruthInsightBench reveals that current autonomous coding agents, even when competent at running and explaining data analyses, fall short on the higher-level scientific reasoning required for genuine discovery. The main bottleneck is not coding ability but scientific judgment—deciding what constitutes adequate evidence, designing robustness and falsification checks, and generalizing findings. Because the benchmark is fully automatic, reproducible, and grounded in real peer-reviewed studies, it offers a practical way to measure and track progress toward AI systems that can make and defend novel scientific claims rather than merely replicate known ones. The authors release the data and scoring code to facilitate future research and benchmarking.

title: TROVE: Adaptive Agent Skill Orchestration via Trace-Grounded Route Validation and Editing
summary: Agents tend to optimize, select, or constrain execution structures before decisive runtime outcomes are observed. However, such pre-execution commitment creates an orchestration bottleneck: when intermediate evidence invalidates the pending continuation, agents must either execute stale steps or replan broadly, compounding errors, wasting computation, and discarding progress. We thus propose Trace-grounded Route Orchestration via Validation and Editing (TROVE), which revises only what runtime evidence invalidates. Offline, TROVE distills evaluated workflow-search traces into atomic and composite skills and an outcome-conditioned transition graph, preserving stable fragments while exposing outcome-dependent decisions. Online, it treats a planned route as provisional: after committing one top-level skill, the controller retains a valid continuation, inserts a trace-supported local response, or replaces only the invalid suffix. Evaluation across code-generation, question-answering, and math reasoning benchmarks with different LLM backbones show that TROVE delivers a stronger quality-efficiency trade-off than existing baselines of dataset-level optimization, query-level architecture selection, and graph-constrained scheduling. Quality gains are largest when outcomes change the appropriate continuation, whereas early termination yields substantial efficiency gains on near-saturated tasks. Ablations further show that composite skills capture most offline benefits, insertion enables local correction, and suffix replacement primarily improves efficiency. These findings establish selective route editing as a general principle for adaptive agent orchestration.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TROVE, a method for adaptively editing only the invalid parts of an agent’s planned execution route using evidence gathered during runtime.
AI.motivation: Existing agents pre-commit to execution plans or workflows before observing decisive runtime outcomes. When intermediate evidence later invalidates parts of the plan, agents face an orchestration bottleneck: they either follow stale steps or perform costly global replanning. This leads to wasted computation, compounded errors, and discarded partial progress. The paper aims to overcome this by enabling targeted, evidence-driven updates to an agent’s execution route while preserving valid work.
AI.method: The authors propose TROVE (Trace-grounded Route Orchestration via Validation and Editing). Offline, they collect and evaluate workflow-search traces, then distill them into (1) atomic and composite skills and (2) an outcome-conditioned transition graph that encodes where decisions depend on outcomes and which fragments are stable. Online, the agent treats its route as provisional. After each top-level skill is executed and new evidence is observed, the controller validates the remaining route: it either (a) keeps the continuation if still valid, (b) inserts a locally appropriate, trace-supported response, or (c) replaces only the now-invalid suffix of the route, rather than replanning from scratch.
AI.result: Across benchmarks in code generation, question answering, and math reasoning, and using multiple LLM backbones, TROVE yields a better quality–efficiency trade-off than baselines such as dataset-level optimization, query-level architecture selection, and graph-constrained scheduling. TROVE’s quality improvements are strongest when newly observed outcomes change which continuation is appropriate. On tasks that are nearly saturated in accuracy, TROVE achieves notable efficiency gains via early termination. Ablation studies show that composite skills provide most of the offline benefits, local insertion enables targeted correction, and suffix replacement mainly benefits efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Selective route editing, as realized in TROVE, is an effective general strategy for adaptive agent orchestration. By grounding decisions in trace-derived skills and transition graphs and revising only the outcome-invalidated parts of a plan, agents can preserve useful progress, reduce wasted computation, and improve both performance and efficiency over existing orchestration methods.

title: Measuring AI Accountability Through Argumentation Analysis: Can Model Reasoning Withstand Scrutiny?
comment: 27 pages (19 main text + appendix and references), 5 figures, 6 tables. Accepted for publication in the Paris Journal of AI and Digital Ethics (2026); presented at PCAIDE 2026
summary: AI oversight methods rely on ground truth for validation, but what constitutes appropriate AI behavior is contested. This leaves evaluation of moral reasoning in LLMs and debate-based oversight implicitly avoiding realistic ambiguity. We investigate an alternative standard designed to function despite such ambiguity: structural quality of the defence a model can mount for its verdicts in response to critical questions, measured through a four-phase dialectical protocol grounded in Walton's theory of argumentation schemes and Govier's criteria for argument cogency. The protocol is adaptive to different frames of reasoning, extends beyond multiple-choice framing, and treats both the reasoning that precedes a verdict and its post-hoc justification. Across nine frontier models and 200 high-ambiguity MoralChoice items -- $6,778$ judge-scored cells, validated against $89.6\%$ inter-judge agreement on the binary failure judgment -- models defend their reasoning well above the rubric minimum on every dimension. Failure mass concentrates on grounds and sufficiency, and correlates with epistemic hedging rather than argument length. Reasoning is better defended than post-hoc justification, on every model and every Govier dimension. The scheme a model presents in its justification differs from the one it reasoned with on a substantial share of dilemmas ($\geq 20\%$ per model), despite value-based practical reasoning dominating both tracks. The protocol catches strictly indefensible defences (self-contradiction, false premises), and it surfaces difficulties in characterizing the role of retraction in AI alignment, suggesting a need for more situated evaluations.

AI.tldr: They propose and test a new way to evaluate LLM moral reasoning that doesn’t need a single ‘correct’ moral answer, by scoring how structurally good the model’s arguments and defences are in a structured dialogue.
AI.motivation: Existing AI oversight heavily depends on ground-truth labels for what is morally correct, but moral questions are often ambiguous and controversial. As a result, current evaluations of LLM ‘moral reasoning’ and debate-based oversight tend to sidestep realistic ambiguity, usually by simplifying tasks (e.g., multiple choice or low-ambiguity scenarios). The authors want an evaluation standard that can operate even when there is no consensus on the right moral answer, focusing instead on the quality of reasoning and defence a model offers for its judgments.
AI.method: They design a four-phase dialectical protocol inspired by Walton’s argumentation schemes and Govier’s criteria for cogent arguments. This protocol: (1) elicits the model’s initial reasoning leading to a moral verdict, (2) then elicits a post-hoc justification, (3) challenges the model with critical questions, and (4) evaluates how well the model can defend its verdict and reasoning structure. Human judges score model responses on multiple Govier-style dimensions (e.g., acceptability of premises, relevance, sufficiency, and so on). They apply this to nine frontier LLMs on 200 high-ambiguity MoralChoice dilemmas, producing 6,778 judge-scored instances and establishing reliability via high inter-judge agreement on binary failure judgements.
AI.result: All nine models produce defences that, on average, score above the rubric’s minimum threshold on every evaluated dimension. However, most failures are concentrated in the ‘grounds’ and ‘sufficiency’ dimensions, and these failures are more associated with epistemic hedging than with argument length. Reasoning generated before the verdict is systematically better defended than post-hoc justifications across all models and all Govier dimensions. Also, the argumentation scheme used in justifications often differs from the one that appears to have guided the original reasoning, in at least 20% of dilemmas per model, even though value-based practical reasoning is the dominant style in both stages. The protocol is also able to detect clearly indefensible arguments, such as those involving self-contradiction or obviously false premises.
AI.conclusion: A structural, dialogue-based evaluation of moral reasoning can work without relying on a fixed moral ground truth, instead focusing on the cogency of a model’s defences under critical scrutiny. Frontier LLMs generally meet minimal standards of argument quality but still show systematic weaknesses in providing adequate grounds and sufficiency, and in aligning their post-hoc justifications with their initial reasoning. The findings underscore that oversight methods should account for how models retract, revise, and reframe their positions in context, highlighting the importance of more situated, interaction-based evaluations for AI alignment and moral oversight.

title: Large Language Models for HVAC Operations in Building Energy Systems: A Critical Review of Methods, Applications, and Deployment Readiness
comment: 38 pages, 9 figures, 16 tables. Submitted to Energy and Buildings
summary: Building automation systems generate rich sensor data yet remain insight-poor because heterogeneous point naming, missing metadata, and fragmented documentation obstruct their operational use. This systematic review analyses and codes 66 peer-reviewed studies on large language models (LLMs) for HVAC operations published between 2023 and March 2026. Each study is classified across five application families and three LLM method families and assessed for evidence realism, deployment readiness, and the responsibility boundary between the LLM and physical HVAC decisions. The corpus is concentrated in building energy modelling (BEM, 32 of 66 papers), while load forecasting remains too sparse for subfield-level conclusions. Only four studies reach pilot-level evidence, and none reports sustained operational deployment. No study was classified as ready-now for industry adoption; three were near-term and 63 research-only. Nevertheless, several bounded, human-in-the-loop uses merit near-term trials, including point-name normalisation, document-grounded operator support, BEM workflow assistance, and advisory interfaces around physics-based controllers. Conventional machine learning (ML), model predictive control (MPC), reinforcement learning (RL) and ontology-based tools remain more adopted for high-frequency control, short-horizon numerical forecasting, and well-posed ontology mapping, while autonomous agentic operation and unvalidated occupant proxies remain research-stage. Current evidence therefore supports LLMs primarily as semantic and workflow layers rather than autonomous HVAC controllers. Future work should prioritise field-validated benchmarks, orchestration evaluation under operational constraints, and LLM-MPC/RL architectures with bounded latency and verifiable safety properties.

AI.tldr: Systematic review of 66 papers (2023–Mar 2026) on using LLMs for HVAC operations finds strong interest but very limited real-world deployment; LLMs are currently best suited as semantic/workflow aids, not autonomous controllers, and future work must focus on validated benchmarks, safe orchestration, and hybrid LLM–control architectures.
AI.motivation: Building automation systems produce abundant sensor data but generate limited actionable insight because of inconsistent point naming, missing metadata, and scattered documentation, all of which hinder efficient HVAC operation. With the rapid emergence of large language models, many researchers propose LLM-based tools to interpret this messy information space, yet the evidence base is fragmented and lacks a clear synthesis of what works, in which applications, and with what level of deployment readiness and safety. The paper aims to systematically organise and assess recent LLM-for-HVAC research to guide both practitioners and researchers on realistic near-term use cases and research gaps.
AI.method: The authors conducted a systematic review of 66 peer-reviewed studies published between 2023 and March 2026 that apply LLMs to HVAC operations. They coded each study along two main taxonomies: (1) five application families (e.g., building energy modelling, load forecasting, documentation assistance, control support, semantic metadata tasks) and (2) three LLM method families (e.g., prompt-only use, fine-tuned/specialised models, tool- or agent-based LLM systems). For every paper they assessed: (a) realism of the evidence (simulation vs. lab vs. field), (b) deployment readiness, and (c) where the responsibility boundary lies between the LLM and the physical HVAC decision-making (advisory vs. autonomous control). They then analysed the distribution of work across subfields and synthesised patterns in maturity and gaps.
AI.result: The review finds that research is heavily skewed towards building energy modelling, which accounts for 32 of the 66 papers, while some areas such as load forecasting have too few studies to draw solid conclusions. Only four studies achieved pilot-level evidence and none reported sustained real-world deployment. In their deployment-readiness classification, no paper was judged as immediately industry-ready; three were considered near-term candidates and the remaining 63 as research-only. LLM applications that appear promising in the near term are mainly human-in-the-loop and bounded in scope: point-name normalisation, document-grounded operator assistants, workflow support for BEM tasks, and advisory interfaces that sit around existing physics-based controllers. For high-frequency control, short-horizon numerical prediction, and structured ontology mapping, conventional ML, MPC, RL, and ontology-based systems are still more mature and widely used. LLM-driven autonomous agents and unvalidated occupant-behaviour proxies remain exploratory and unvalidated.
AI.conclusion: The evidence base suggests that LLMs should currently be viewed as semantic and workflow augmentation layers on top of existing HVAC tools rather than as stand-alone autonomous controllers. They are well-positioned to handle messy, heterogeneous language and documentation tasks, but they are not yet reliable for real-time, safety-critical control. To advance the field, the authors recommend prioritising field-validated benchmarks, rigorous evaluation of orchestration under realistic operational constraints, and hybrid LLM–MPC/RL architectures that enforce strict bounds on latency and provide verifiable safety guarantees. These directions are necessary before LLM-based HVAC systems can move from research prototypes to robust, industry-ready solutions.

title: Towards Efficient Evaluation of Evolutionary Transfer Optimization: Case Studies on Task-Parameterized Applications
comment: Accepted at the 2026 International Conference on Machine Intelligence and Nature-Inspired Computing (MIND 2026)
summary: As evolutionary transfer optimization (ETO) scales to larger collections of related tasks, problem evaluation can become a major source of runtime growth. This work studies problem-side evaluation scaling in task-parameterized applications and reformulates application-specific serial computations into forms suitable for parallel execution. We organize evaluation scaling into two levels: the number of evaluated tasks and the workload within each task. In multi-task optimization, matrix-recursive kinematic-arm evaluation is reformulated using an accumulation-matrix representation of cumulative link directions. In sequential transfer optimization, pointwise B-spline trajectory evaluation is reformulated using a blending-matrix representation for trajectory and collision computations. Both reformulations maintain close numerical agreement with their reference evaluations and substantially reduce runtime, yielding $256.72\times$ and $93.91\times$ end-to-end speedups, respectively. These results demonstrate problem-side reformulation as a practical route toward scalable ETO. Both application implementations and experimental scripts are released as open source to support reproducibility and reuse.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes problem-side reformulations to parallelize and speed up evaluations in evolutionary transfer optimization (ETO), achieving large end-to-end speedups on kinematic-arm and trajectory-planning tasks.
AI.motivation: As ETO is applied to larger sets of related tasks, the cost of evaluating many tasks (and complex computations within each task) becomes the dominant runtime bottleneck.
