The authors aim to make ETO scalable by reducing evaluation time without sacrificing numerical accuracy, focusing specifically on applications where tasks are parameterized and evaluations are originally serial.
AI.method: They decompose evaluation scaling into two aspects: (1) scaling with the number of tasks and (2) the workload per task. For multi-task kinematic-arm optimization, they reformulate matrix-recursive forward-kinematics evaluations into an accumulation-matrix representation that is more amenable to parallelism. For sequential transfer optimization of trajectories, they reformulate pointwise B-spline evaluation and collision checking into a blending-matrix representation. Both representations allow batched, matrix-based parallel computations (e.g., on modern hardware) while preserving the semantics of the original serial evaluations.
AI.result: The new formulations match the numerical outputs of the reference, serial implementations closely while drastically reducing runtime. Specifically, they report end-to-end speedups of approximately 256.72× for the multi-task kinematic-arm evaluation and 93.91× for the sequential B-spline trajectory evaluation and collision checking, demonstrating strong practical performance gains.
AI.conclusion: Problem-side reformulation of evaluation routines—expressing serial, task-specific computations in matrix forms suitable for parallel execution—is an effective and practical strategy for scaling evolutionary transfer optimization to large collections of related tasks. The released open-source implementations and scripts further support reproducibility and potential reuse in other ETO applications.

title: Technical Manual for a Toolkit for Measuring Contextual Individuation in Transformer Language Models
comment: 29 pages, 2 figures (one with 2 subfigures), 1 table. Toolkit, source code, and corpora archived separately on Zenodo (see Section 9)
summary: A transformer language model assigns a single, context-independent vector to a word type at its embedding layer, yet is widely believed to individuate that word's occurrences by context in its later layers. Testing this belief cleanly requires a construct that holds the word form fixed while its context and intended sense vary in a controlled, labeled way. This manual documents an open toolkit built around such a construct, which we call a bridge form: a single written word that recurs, unchanged, across two or more subject domains with a different sense in each. We describe, and justify, every stage of the pipeline: the declarative specification of bridge forms and their source domains, corpus acquisition from Wikipedia, occurrence localization, layer-wise representation extraction, a domain-pairwise silhouette measurement of separation in the model's representation space, and a paired visualization protocol. Each design choice is presented together with the methodological failure mode it is meant to avoid (sense contamination from overly broad category labels, the multi-group bias of the silhouette coefficient, subword-tokenization misalignment, and axis-comparability artifacts in dimensionality-reduced plots, among others). This manuscript is a methodological and implementation reference: it does not report or interpret empirical outcomes of running the toolkit on any particular model or bridge-form set. The toolkit, its full source, and the corpora used to exercise it are archived separately (Section 9) under a persistent identifier, and are intended to be cited as an instrument by studies that use it to produce and interpret empirical results.

AI.tldr: Toolkit for rigorously testing how transformer language models represent word senses across different contexts using 'bridge forms'.
AI.motivation: Transformer LMs use fixed embeddings but context-sensitive internal representations. To test sense differentiation properly, we need controlled cases where the same word form has clearly different meanings in different domains, with careful methodology to avoid confounds and artifacts.
AI.method: Define 'bridge forms'—identical written words occurring with different senses in distinct subject domains. Provide a full pipeline: formally specify bridge forms and domains; extract domain-specific corpora from Wikipedia; find word occurrences; extract layer-wise model representations; compute a domain-pairwise silhouette measure to quantify separation of senses in representation space; and visualize the representations with a protocol that controls for axis comparability and other artifacts. Each step is designed with specific failure modes in mind (e.g., sense contamination from broad categories, multi-group bias in silhouette scores, subword-tokenization issues).
AI.result: A fully specified, open-source toolkit and pipeline for constructing bridge-form datasets, extracting model representations, scoring domain/sense separation, and visualizing results, together with documented design rationales and known pitfalls. The paper itself provides methodology and implementation details but no empirical performance results on particular models.
AI.conclusion: The work contributes an instrument, not findings: a standardized, carefully justified toolkit for studying how transformer models individuate word senses through context using bridge forms. Future empirical studies can cite and reuse this toolkit to generate reproducible, interpretable results on sense differentiation in language models.

title: MePo++: Unifying Representation Refinement and Reconciliation for General Continual Learning
summary: General continual learning (GCL) aims to learn from evolving data streams without task identities, explicit boundaries, or repeated access to previous data, making it a realistic yet challenging setting for continual intelligence. Although pretrained models (PTMs) provide rich prior knowledge for addressing the limited supervision and non-stationary nature of GCL, existing PTM-based methods often directly adapt pretrained representations and overlook two critical gaps: the misalignment between upstream pretraining and downstream continual adaptation, and the unreliability of conventional output alignment under blurry streams. Here we propose MePo++, a unified post-training framework that bridges pretrained knowledge and downstream GCL through representation refinement and reconciliation. MePo++ introduces two complementary components: MetaPrep, which improves representation plasticity for continual adaptation through unsupervised meta-refinement over pseudo continual sequences; and StreamAlign, which reinforces representation stability by reconciling evolving online features with a stable pretrained geometry. By improving representation learnability before adaptation and preserving alignment during continual learning, MePo++ enables PTMs to remain both plastic for new concepts and stable over evolving streams. Experiments across diverse PTMs, datasets, and continual learning baselines demonstrate the consistent effectiveness and generality of MePo++ for PTM-based GCL. Our code is available at https://github.com/SunGL001/MePo_Plus.

AI.tldr: MePo++ is a post-training framework that adapts pretrained models to realistic general continual learning without task labels or clear boundaries by refining and aligning representations for both plasticity and stability.
AI.motivation: General continual learning operates on evolving, unlabeled, non-repetitive data streams, which is closer to real-world scenarios but very challenging due to non-stationarity, lack of task IDs, and limited supervision. While pretrained models contain rich prior knowledge that should help, naïvely fine-tuning them in this setting causes two key problems: (1) a mismatch between how models are pretrained and how they are adapted continually, and (2) unreliable output alignment when task boundaries are blurry and data distribution drifts gradually. The paper aims to systematically bridge this gap so that pretrained models can be effectively and robustly used in general continual learning.
AI.method: The authors propose MePo++, a unified post-training framework with two main components: (1) MetaPrep: an unsupervised meta-refinement phase that constructs pseudo continual sequences and updates the pretrained model to improve its representation plasticity and suitability for later continual adaptation; (2) StreamAlign: an alignment mechanism during online continual learning that constrains or reconciles evolving online features with the original stable pretrained feature geometry, thereby encouraging stability. Together, these steps refine the representation space before continual learning begins and then maintain consistent alignment as the data stream evolves.
AI.result: Empirical studies across multiple pretrained models, datasets, and continual learning baselines show that MePo++ consistently improves performance in general continual learning scenarios. The method demonstrates that its combination of pre-adaptation refinement (MetaPrep) and online alignment (StreamAlign) works robustly across varied settings, validating both its effectiveness and generality for PTM-based continual learning.
AI.conclusion: By explicitly addressing the pretraining–adaptation mismatch and unreliable alignment under blurred task boundaries, MePo++ makes pretrained models better suited for realistic general continual learning. Its two components jointly ensure that representations remain plastic enough to incorporate new concepts while retaining stability over non-stationary data streams, leading to consistent gains over existing PTM-based GCL approaches.

title: Does Your Agent's Memory Survive a Model Upgrade? A Controlled Study of Memory Portability
summary:
Model upgrades are routine; memory migrations are not. An agent can keep the same memory store and still forget: a new model may interpret old notes differently, mixed embedding versions may break retrieval, and repair may fail without the original evidence. We compare memory as the same history is preserved verbatim for long-context reading (LC-RAW), divided into chunks for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), compressed by a model into natural-language notes (NOTES), or normalized into a fixed-schema knowledge graph (KG-fixed). The study uses 48 synthetic histories with randomized answer codes, exact scoring, and two open-weight models with sub 10 billion parameters.
  Our measurements show that fixed-schema structures transfer reliably, with KG-fixed accuracy changing by only $+0.0004 \pm 0.0020$ following a writer swap. Conversely, compressed NOTES exhibit high model coupling, with accuracy shifting asymmetrically by $+9.91$ or $-13.28$ percentage points depending on the specific migration direction. In RAG systems, partial embedding migrations using a 50/50 mixed index capture only a 4.96-point accuracy improvement, forfeiting the majority of the 11.90-point gain achieved through full re-embedding. Diagnostic decomposition attributes 80% ($0.467 \pm 0.014$) of the NOTES accuracy deficit to information lost during initial construction, whereas retrieval failures drive 81% ($0.364 \pm 0.012$) of the RAG deficit. Finally, store-only repair of NOTES fails to reach a 90% performance recovery target in all 48 test cases, whereas retaining the raw source history enables successful recovery in 34 of 48 cases for one tested direction. These findings highlight the necessity of direction-specific migration testing, strict embedding space isolation, and the retention of source histories for memory repair.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how different memory representations survive model upgrades and migrations, showing that fixed-schema knowledge graphs transfer reliably, while compressed natural-language notes and partially migrated RAG embeddings can degrade or unpredictably change performance.
AI.motivation: As language models are upgraded, agents often keep their old memories. However, newer models may interpret old notes differently, old and new embeddings may not mix well, and attempts to repair memory without original data may fail. There is little quantitative understanding of how robust different memory formats are to such migrations, which is critical for long-lived AI agents and systems that rely on persistent memory.
AI.method: The authors construct 48 synthetic agent histories with randomized answer codes that allow exact automatic scoring. They compare four memory formats: (1) LC-RAW: entire history preserved verbatim for long-context reading; (2) RAG: the history divided into chunks and stored in an embedding index; (3) NOTES: compressed natural-language summaries produced by a model; and (4) KG-fixed: information normalized into a fixed-schema knowledge graph. They test two open-weight models (<10B parameters) as memory writers and readers, simulate writer–reader swaps and partial embedding migrations (e.g., 50/50 mixed indices), and perform diagnostic decompositions to separate information-loss vs retrieval-failure contributions to accuracy deficits. They also test whether memory can be repaired using only the store versus using the original history.
AI.result: Fixed-schema KG-fixed memories are highly robust to model swaps, with accuracy changes of only about +0.0004 ± 0.0020. NOTES memories are strongly coupled to the specific model that wrote them, with asymmetric accuracy shifts of roughly +9.91 or −13.28 percentage points depending on migration direction. For RAG, partial embedding migrations with a 50/50 mixed index yield only a 4.96-point improvement, much less than the 11.90-point gain from full re-embedding. Decomposition shows that around 80% (0.467 ± 0.014) of the NOTES accuracy deficit is due to information lost during note construction, while about 81% (0.364 ± 0.012) of the RAG deficit is due to retrieval failures. Store-only repair of NOTES never reaches the 90% performance recovery target in any of the 48 cases, whereas keeping the raw history allows successful repair in 34 of 48 cases for one migration direction.
AI.conclusion: Structured, fixed-schema memory representations are far more robust to model upgrades than compressed natural-language notes or partially migrated RAG stores. Natural-language notes tend to lose information and are tightly coupled to the writing model, while RAG systems primarily suffer from retrieval issues during migration, especially when mixing embedding versions. For long-lived systems, it is important to: (1) test migrations direction-specifically rather than assuming symmetry; (2) strictly isolate embedding spaces and prefer full re-embedding over mixed indices; and (3) retain raw source histories so that memory can be reconstructed or repaired after upgrades.

title: Multi-Step Tool-Calling over Korean Open Public APIs: A Benchmark and a Data-Synthesis Recipe
comment: 30 pages, 7 figures, 26 tables. Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Industry Track
summary: Data-sovereignty regulations increasingly require public institutions to deploy open-source, on-premise LLM agents that chain multiple tool-calls across live government APIs. However, open-source models consistently underperform in this multi-step setting, and no existing benchmark measures the gap. We introduce the Korean Open Public API Benchmark (KOPA-Bench), comprising 145 real-world tasks. To close this gap, we present EDGE, an Execution-grounded Dynamic Graph for tool-calling data synthEsis driven by live execution. EDGE builds a graph of how each tool's output can feed another's input, keeps only the links that succeed when actually called against the live APIs, and traverses these verified links to synthesize executable multi-step trajectories. Fine-tuned via GRPO on the resulting dataset, our 9B model nearly matches the untuned 27B model from the same family, improving substantially not only on KOPA-Bench but also on the BFCL benchmark.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces KOPA-Bench to evaluate open-source LLM agents on real Korean government APIs and proposes EDGE, a live-execution-grounded graph method for synthesizing multi-step tool-calling trajectories, enabling a 9B fine-tuned model to nearly match a 27B untuned model on the new benchmark and BFCL.
AI.motivation: Public institutions constrained by data-sovereignty rules must run open-source, on-premise LLM agents that can orchestrate multiple tool calls over live government APIs, but existing open-source models underperform in such multi-step settings and there is no benchmark to quantify or study this gap, especially in the Korean public sector context.
AI.method: They build KOPA-Bench, a benchmark of 145 real-world tasks over Korean public APIs, then propose EDGE, which constructs an execution-grounded dynamic graph that captures how outputs from one tool can serve as inputs to others; edges are retained only if verified via successful live API calls, and the graph is traversed to synthesize valid multi-step tool-use trajectories. They then fine-tune a 9B open-source model using GRPO on the synthesized dataset.
AI.result: The EDGE-generated dataset enables a 9B-parameter model fine-tuned with GRPO to achieve performance close to an untuned 27B model from the same family. The fine-tuned 9B model shows substantial performance improvements on both the newly introduced KOPA-Bench and the existing BFCL benchmark, demonstrating better multi-step tool-calling capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Execution-grounded graph-based synthesis of tool-use trajectories is effective for training compact open-source LLM agents to perform multi-step tool calling over live APIs. KOPA-Bench fills an evaluation gap for public-sector, regulation-constrained deployments, and the EDGE approach significantly narrows the performance gap between smaller fine-tuned models and much larger untuned ones on real-world, API-centric tasks.

title: Constructing and Evaluating Clinical Reasoning Trajectories for Medical Agent
summary: Evaluation of medical artificial intelligence agents remains predominantly answer-centric, assessing only the correctness of final outputs while overlooking the quality of intermediate reasoning. In clinical settings, however, a correct answer reached through fabricated evidence or incoherent logic is as dangerous as an incorrect one. We propose MedTraj, a framework that treats reasoning trajectories as critical objects for construction, evaluation, and optimization. The pipeline generates structured multi-step reasoning chains from medical reasoning sources. Each trajectory is then parsed into clinical observations, evidence, numbered reasoning steps, and a final conclusion, and scored across five quality dimensions: coherence, evidence support, hallucination, completeness, and traceability. Controlled error injection introduces targeted faults into otherwise correct trajectories to establish causal links between specific reasoning failures and measurable quality degradation. Building on this, step-level filtering based on marginal contribution identifies which individual reasoning steps drive or undermine trajectory quality. Finally, quality-weighted context learning feeds trajectory evaluations back into the model at inference time, allowing it to learn from both strong and weak reasoning demonstrations. Experiments across CareQA, PubMedQA, and CECMed demonstrate that trajectory context consistently improves reasoning coherence, with gains of +0.029 to +0.041 over a zero-shot baseline. On CECMed, quality-weighted context nearly doubles the correctness over the zero-shot baseline while cutting the hallucination ratio by 87%. Marginal-contribution analysis further shows that a small minority of reasoning steps carry most of the quality signal, and that extending chains beyond four steps yields diminishing returns.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MedTraj, a framework that evaluates and improves medical AI by analyzing and optimizing full reasoning trajectories, not just final answers.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of medical AI largely focus on whether the final answer is correct, ignoring whether the reasoning path is coherent, evidence-based, and clinically safe. In medicine, a correct answer reached via faulty logic or hallucinated evidence can still be unsafe and untrustworthy. There is a need for a systematic way to construct, evaluate, and leverage multi-step clinical reasoning trajectories to improve both safety and performance of medical AI systems.
AI.method: The authors design MedTraj, a framework that: (1) generates structured multi-step reasoning chains from medical reasoning sources; (2) parses each trajectory into clinical observations, evidence, numbered reasoning steps, and a final conclusion; (3) scores trajectories across five quality dimensions: coherence, evidence support, hallucination, completeness, and traceability; (4) uses controlled error injection to introduce targeted reasoning faults and study their causal impact on quality metrics; (5) applies step-level analysis based on marginal contribution to identify which specific steps most affect trajectory quality; and (6) incorporates quality-weighted trajectory evaluations during inference via context learning, so the model can learn from both strong and weak reasoning examples.
AI.result: On three medical benchmarks (CareQA, PubMedQA, and CECMed), providing trajectory context improves reasoning coherence by 0.029–0.041 over a zero-shot baseline. On CECMed, using quality-weighted context nearly doubles answer correctness and reduces hallucination by 87%. Marginal contribution analysis reveals that a small subset of reasoning steps carries most of the quality signal, and that making reasoning chains longer than about four steps gives limited additional benefit.
AI.conclusion: Focusing on reasoning trajectories rather than only final answers enables more fine-grained evaluation and optimization of medical AI systems. MedTraj demonstrates that quality-aware trajectory construction, scoring, and context learning can significantly improve coherence, correctness, and safety (via reduced hallucination). The analysis also suggests that short, carefully curated reasoning chains and attention to high-impact steps are key for effective reasoning supervision in clinical AI.

title: LLM-Guided Program Evolution for Circle Packing: Breaking 10 Packomania Records for $28
summary: We present Discovery Loop, a lightweight system that uses a large language model (LLM) to iteratively evolve optimization algorithms. Starting from a simple seed solver, the LLM proposes algorithmic improvements guided by a scoreboard of results and a history of prior ideas. Each candidate is evaluated against an independent verifier; improvements are kept and failures discarded. Applied to the Packomania circle-packing benchmark (csqv: maximize the sum of radii of N variable-radius circles in the unit square), the system improved the best known solutions for 10 values of N in the range 101-114, with gains of 2.4%-5.4% over prior records, all within 15 iterations and at a total LLM cost of $27.72. These results have been independently accepted by Packomania. We describe the method, analyze cost-efficiency dynamics including an adaptive plateau-detection mechanism, and discuss implications for democratizing automated scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: Discovery Loop is an LLM-driven loop that automatically proposes and tests new variants of optimization algorithms, achieving state-of-the-art circle packings cheaply and quickly.
AI.motivation: Designing strong optimization algorithms typically requires expert intuition and significant manual effort. Recent progress in LLMs suggests they can reason about algorithms and code, but it is unclear how to systematically harness them to produce genuinely better solvers in a cost-effective, automated way. The authors are motivated to build a lightweight, inexpensive framework where an LLM can repeatedly propose algorithmic modifications, guided by empirical feedback, to push the frontiers of specific hard benchmarks such as circle packing. They also aim to understand the efficiency and dynamics of such an automated discovery process and its potential to make scientific optimization advances more accessible.
AI.method: The authors introduce Discovery Loop, an iterative optimization-algorithm search system powered by an LLM. They start from a simple seed solver and maintain (1) a scoreboard of performance on the target benchmark and (2) a history of past ideas. In each iteration, the LLM reads the history and scoreboard and then proposes a new solver variant—e.g., code-level or algorithmic modifications. Each candidate solver is run and evaluated by an independent verifier on the benchmark instance, which checks its validity and measures objective performance. If the new solver outperforms the prior best, it is kept; otherwise it is discarded. The loop continues for a fixed budget or until a plateau is detected via an adaptive mechanism that monitors gains per iteration and halts when marginal improvement falls below a threshold. The system is applied to the Packomania circle-packing problem (csqv variant) to test whether it can beat long-standing records. Cost-efficiency is tracked by associating each iteration with its LLM usage cost and measuring improvement per dollar spent.
AI.result: On the Packomania csqv circle-packing benchmark—maximizing the sum of radii of N variable-radius circles in the unit square—the Discovery Loop system improved the best-known solutions for 10 different N values between 101 and 114. The improvements over existing records were substantial, ranging from 2.4% to 5.4%. These gains were obtained in at most 15 iterations of the loop and with a total LLM usage cost of $27.72. The Packomania project independently verified and accepted the new records, providing external validation of the correctness and significance of the discovered solutions. The authors also report analyses of how improvements progressed over iterations, how the plateau-detection mechanism curtailed unproductive iterations, and the resulting improvement-per-dollar metrics, though detailed numbers are not in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that a simple, lightweight LLM-in-the-loop framework can nontrivially advance the state of the art on a challenging optimization benchmark at very low financial cost. This suggests that LLMs can effectively participate in the automated discovery of better algorithms, especially when integrated in a structured propose-evaluate-retain loop with independent verification. The adaptive stopping/plateau-detection mechanism helps keep the process cost-efficient. More broadly, the authors argue that such systems can contribute to the democratization of scientific discovery by lowering the expertise and resource barriers for improving complex algorithms, and they point to future opportunities for applying similar loops to other domains and benchmarks.

title: ProCA: Progressive Contrastive Alignment for Robust EEG Visual Decoding
summary: Electroencephalogram (EEG) visual decoding aims to recover visual semantics from non-invasive neural time-series signals, for which robust alignment between noisy neural responses and stable semantic representations is key to achieving high-performance decoding. Despite recent advances in contrastive learning, robust EEG decoding remains challenging because existing methods rely on fixed visual or textual anchors whose semantic relations may become misaligned with EEG representations that vary across trials, subjects, and learning stages. Our empirical evidence shows that this instability appears across both standard EEG decoding protocols and more challenging robustness settings, including strict cross-subject transfer and realistic personalized continual adaptation. We provide a formal analysis showing that fixed semantic supervision can bias optimization when EEG-specific relations evolve, and that structure-agnostic perturbations may distort semantically important EEG components. To address these issues, we propose Progressive Contrastive Alignment (ProCA), a unified and model-agnostic framework for adaptive neural-semantic alignment. ProCA progressively refines class-level contrastive supervision from frozen vision-language priors to EEG-aware semantic relations, and introduces structure-consistent interpolation to constrain feature mixing according to channel-wise and temporal importance. Across subject-dependent, subject-independent, strict cross-subject transfer, and continual adaptation settings, ProCA achieves average relative Top-1/Top-5 gains of 7.4%/3.9%, 10.0%/4.6%, 28.1%/17.8%, and 16.8%/11.6%, respectively.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Progressive Contrastive Alignment (ProCA), a framework that adaptively aligns EEG signals with visual semantic representations to improve EEG-based visual decoding robustness and accuracy across diverse settings.
AI.motivation: EEG-based visual decoding requires robust alignment between noisy, variable neural signals and stable visual or textual semantic representations. Existing contrastive learning approaches use fixed semantic anchors (vision or language features), which can become misaligned because EEG representations shift across trials, subjects, and over training. This instability is especially problematic in harder settings such as cross-subject transfer and continual adaptation, motivating a method that can adapt semantic supervision to EEG-specific structure and dynamics.
AI.method: The authors introduce Progressive Contrastive Alignment (ProCA), a model-agnostic framework. ProCA begins with frozen vision-language priors as initial class-level semantic anchors and progressively refines these into EEG-aware semantic relations as training proceeds. It adjusts the contrastive supervision so that semantic relations are updated to reflect evolving EEG feature structure rather than remaining fixed. Additionally, ProCA incorporates structure-consistent interpolation, which mixes EEG features while respecting estimated channel-wise and temporal importance, so that perturbations do not distort semantically critical EEG components. This yields adaptive, structure-aware contrastive objectives for EEG-visual decoding.
AI.result: ProCA is evaluated under multiple EEG visual decoding protocols: subject-dependent, subject-independent, strict cross-subject transfer, and personalized continual adaptation. Across these settings, it yields substantial average relative performance improvements in Top-1/Top-5 accuracy: 7.4%/3.9% in subject-dependent, 10.0%/4.6% in subject-independent, 28.1%/17.8% in strict cross-subject transfer, and 16.8%/11.6% in continual adaptation, demonstrating both accuracy and robustness gains over baselines.
AI.conclusion: By progressively adapting semantic supervision from fixed vision-language priors to EEG-aware relations and enforcing structure-consistent feature interpolation, ProCA addresses optimization bias and harmful perturbations arising from fixed anchors and structure-agnostic augmentations. This leads to more robust, generalizable EEG visual decoding across subjects and over time, suggesting that adaptive neural-semantic alignment is crucial for scalable, real-world EEG-based semantic decoding systems.

title: Compact Bellman-Grounded Cognitive Maps for Cost-Aware Navigation
summary: Biological agents navigate familiar environments not by re-solving routes for each new goal, but by reusing a learned map built once and read off as goals change. Existing artificial cognitive-map models mimic this reuse, yet their guidance is not explicitly grounded in additive heterogeneous route costs. Furthermore, they often struggle with memory efficiency: representative state-indexed and high-rank spectral constructions incur substantial storage growth as the environment scales. We present BCM, which grounds a reusable cognitive map in local edge costs through a self-supervised Bellman-grounded objective and a compact coordinate encoding, supporting changing goal queries without per-goal retraining. On weighted grids of up to $N=1600$ nodes, BCM maintains full success and only a 5\% mean Gap relative to exact Dijkstra search, compared with about $45\%$ for a connectivity-based spectral baseline. Notably, as the graph size increases from $N=400$ to $N=3600$, its memory footprint grows sublinearly while maintaining competitive performance, making our method scalable to complex environments. Together, these results show that additive route costs can be written into a compact, reusable cognitive-map representation, bridging the gap between biological flexibility and optimal path planning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces BCM, a compact cognitive-map model that encodes additive route costs and supports flexible goal-directed navigation with low memory footprint while remaining near-optimal in path quality.
AI.motivation: Biological agents reuse an internal map to navigate to new goals without recomputing paths from scratch. Many artificial cognitive-map models imitate this behavior but (1) do not explicitly encode additive, heterogeneous route costs, and (2) are memory-inefficient, with state-indexed or high-rank spectral representations scaling poorly as environments grow. There is a need for a cognitive-map representation that is both cost-aware and scalable in memory while remaining reusable across changing goals.
AI.method: The authors propose BCM, a Bellman-grounded cognitive map. It learns a compact coordinate representation of states whose geometry encodes local edge costs, trained with a self-supervised objective derived from the Bellman equation. This representation allows approximate value or distance readout for arbitrary goals without retraining per goal. They evaluate BCM on weighted grid graphs of up to N=3600 nodes, comparing against a connectivity-based spectral baseline and exact Dijkstra search as the optimal reference.
AI.result: On weighted grids with up to N=1600 nodes, BCM achieves 100% success rate and only about 5% mean suboptimality gap relative to exact Dijkstra solutions, while a connectivity-based spectral baseline exhibits about 45% gap. As graph size grows from N=400 to N=3600, BCM’s memory usage increases sublinearly yet preserves competitive performance, demonstrating both accuracy and scalability.
AI.conclusion: BCM shows that additive route costs can be embedded into a compact, reusable cognitive-map representation that supports flexible goal queries without per-goal retraining. This bridges a key gap between biologically inspired cognitive maps, which emphasize flexibility and reuse, and classical optimal path-planning methods, which emphasize cost accuracy but are not typically cast as compact, reusable map encodings.

title: Unifying ICL, SFT, KL-Regularized RL Through a Bayesian Lens
summary: Large language models are now trained and evaluated under a diverse set of paradigms: supervised fine-tuning (SFT), few-shot in-context learning (ICL), KL-regularized RLHF/RLVR, on-policy distillation (OPD), and test-time reasoning with search and chain-of-thought. These methods are often discussed as fundamentally different, and recent empirical results--such as the mixed impact of few-shot prompting on RL-tuned reasoning models--can appear puzzling. This note develops a Bayesian perspective that puts these procedures on the same footing. At the core is a two-step template: (i) construct a (generalized) Bayes or Gibbs posterior q* over outputs or actions given a context, using a prior/reference model and a utility signal (log-likelihood, reward, or advantage); and (ii) approximate q* by a forward-KL projection onto a parametric family, either in-weights (SFT/RL) or in-context (ICL). Part I formalizes few-shot ICL and SFT as amortized and-weights projections onto the Bayes posterior predictive. Parts II-IV show that KL-regularized RLHF/RLVR, reward-weighted SFT, reward-weighted ICL (RW-ICL), and advantage-weighted SFT (AWSFT) are all instances of forward-KL projection onto posteriors induced by rewards or advantages. We disentangle where these equivalences hold (objectives and first-order updates) and where they do not (source and granularity of the learning signal). Part V sketches implications for modern reasoning pipelines: RLHF/RLVR recipes as "posterior design + projection", why cold-start or supervised warm-up is practically unavoidable for importance-weighted KL projections, and DeepSeek-R1 and o1-style reasoning models as combining test-time Bayesian search with training-time KL amortization.

AI.tldr: Unifies SFT, ICL, RLHF/RLVR, and related methods under a single Bayesian/posterior-projection view.
AI.motivation: Current LLM training and inference methods (SFT, ICL, RLHF, RLVR, OPD, CoT search) are often treated as fundamentally different, leading to confusion about their relationships and about empirical phenomena like the inconsistent effect of few-shot prompting on RL-tuned reasoning models. The authors aim to provide a common theoretical framework that explains how these methods relate and why they may behave similarly or differently.
AI.method: Develop a Bayesian/Gibbs posterior framework where each paradigm constructs a target distribution q* over outputs/actions using a prior/reference model plus a utility signal (likelihood, reward, or advantage). Then they view practical methods as forward-KL projections onto q*, either via parameter updates (SFT/RL variants) or in-context adaptation (ICL). They formalize how SFT and ICL are amortized projections onto the Bayes posterior predictive, and show equivalence classes: KL-regularized RLHF/RLVR, reward-weighted SFT/ICL, and advantage-weighted SFT as specific forward-KL projections with different utilities. They analyze where equivalence holds (objectives, first-order updates) and where it breaks (source and granularity of signals). Finally, they sketch implications for reasoning pipelines that combine test-time search with training-time amortization.
AI.result: They demonstrate that many seemingly distinct LLM training and inference paradigms can be expressed as instances of the same two-step procedure: (i) define a (generalized) posterior over actions conditioned on context using a prior model and a utility; (ii) approximate this posterior via forward-KL minimization either in-weights or in-context. This unifies SFT, ICL, KL-regularized RLHF/RLVR, reward- and advantage-weighted variants, and reasoning models with search. They clarify which aspects match exactly (losses, first-order dynamics) and which differ, especially regarding where the learning signal comes from and how fine-grained it is.
AI.conclusion: The paper argues that modern LLM training and reasoning methods are best viewed as “posterior design + forward-KL projection.” This Bayesian lens clarifies relationships among SFT, ICL, RLHF/RLVR, and search-based reasoning, explains practical recipes like requiring supervised warm-up for importance-weighted KL projections, and interprets recent reasoning models (e.g., DeepSeek-R1/o1-style) as combining test-time Bayesian search with training-time KL amortization. This unified view can guide the design and analysis of future LLM training and reasoning pipelines.

title: SciDocBench: A Workflow-Centered Benchmark and Data Pipeline for Scientific Document Understanding
comment: 52 pages, 21 figures, and 20 tables. Project page: https://github.com/InternLM/SciDocBench
summary: Scientific papers require models to reason jointly over text, equations, figures, tables, code, and datasets while preserving the provenance of supporting evidence. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate these capabilities in isolation, leaving unclear whether multimodal models can support realistic scientific-reading workflows. We introduce SciDocBench, a workflow-centered benchmark for scientific document understanding. It contains 124 expert-authored and difficulty-screened questions organized into seven research-assistant capability groups and 19 subtasks across five scientific domains. Each question is instantiated under four matched conditions combining English or Chinese questions with all-images-first or interleaved document representations, yielding 496 evaluation instances for controlled analysis. The strongest evaluated system achieves only 62.6/100, with pronounced weaknesses in document perception, evidence grounding, verification, and cross-document reasoning. To translate these diagnostics into scalable training signals, we introduce SciDocIR, a typed evidence-graph representation that preserves scientific document objects, layout and cross-reference relations, and provenance. Building on SciDocIR, we construct SciDocDataset, comprising approximately 15K supervised fine-tuning samples and 8K reinforcement-learning samples across 14 verifiable subtasks. Together, SciDocBench, SciDocIR, and SciDocDataset form an evaluation-to-training framework for diagnosing and improving scientific-document assistants. The project page is available at https://github.com/InternLM/SciDocBench.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SciDocBench, a workflow-centered benchmark plus an accompanying representation (SciDocIR) and datasets (SciDocDataset) to evaluate and train multimodal scientific document understanding systems across realistic research-assistant tasks.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal models must understand complex scientific documents that mix text, equations, figures, tables, code, and datasets, while also tracking where evidence comes from. Existing benchmarks usually test each modality or skill in isolation, so they do not reveal whether models can actually support end-to-end scientific reading and assistance workflows. The authors aim to create a benchmark and data resources that reflect real research-assistant tasks and provide actionable diagnostics for improving such systems.
AI.method: The authors design SciDocBench, a benchmark of 124 expert-authored, difficulty-screened questions grouped into seven capability categories and 19 subtasks spanning five scientific domains. Each question appears in four controlled variants: English vs. Chinese, and all-images-first vs. interleaved document layouts, yielding 496 instances. They then propose SciDocIR, a typed evidence-graph representation that encodes scientific document objects, layout, cross-references, and provenance. Using SciDocIR, they build SciDocDataset, with about 15K supervised fine-tuning examples and 8K reinforcement-learning examples across 14 verifiable subtasks, integrating evaluation and training signals.
AI.result: Benchmarking shows that the strongest evaluated model achieves only 62.6/100 on SciDocBench, revealing substantial weaknesses in document perception, evidence grounding, verification, and cross-document reasoning. The authors also successfully construct SciDocIR and SciDocDataset, demonstrating that realistic, verifiable scientific-assistant tasks can be encoded into structured evidence graphs and scalable training data.
AI.conclusion: SciDocBench, SciDocIR, and SciDocDataset together provide a comprehensive framework that connects fine-grained evaluation of scientific document understanding with structured training signals. This framework exposes significant current limitations of multimodal models on realistic research workflows and offers practical resources to develop better scientific-document assistants.

title: A Hybrid Predictive Ensemble of Machine Learning and Deep Neural Networks for Early Cardiovascular Disease Risk Assessment
summary: This study introduces an intelligent framework that integrates machine learning and deep neural network ensemble techniques for early detection and prognosis of cardiovascular diseases. The system utilizes real-time physiological data collected from Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) devices, including ECG sensors, heart rate monitors, and blood pressure trackers. To ensure the accuracy and reliability of input data, preprocessing steps such as noise reduction, normalization, and missing value imputation are employed. The most significant health indicators are identified through effective feature selection methods and then processed using optimized classifiers such as Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random Forests, and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), which are combined in an ensemble architecture to improve diagnostic precision. The framework demonstrates remarkable performance in predicting cardiovascular disease risk, achieving higher accuracy, reduced false positives, and enhanced consistency compared to conventional methods. It is designed on a cloud-based infrastructure that ensures scalability and real-time processing for continuous patient monitoring. Experimental evaluation on real-world cardiovascular datasets confirms the framework's efficiency in early-stage risk assessment and clinical decision support. The results highlight the potential of combining traditional machine learning and deep learning paradigms to achieve proactive healthcare management and improve patient outcomes.

AI.tldr: An AI-driven ensemble framework using IoMT data for early detection and prognosis of cardiovascular diseases, showing higher accuracy and reliability than conventional methods.
AI.motivation: Cardiovascular diseases require early detection and continuous monitoring, but traditional diagnostic methods often lack real-time capability, scalability, and high predictive accuracy when handling large, heterogeneous physiological data from connected devices.
AI.method: Collect real-time physiological signals from IoMT devices (ECG, heart rate, blood pressure), apply preprocessing (noise reduction, normalization, missing value imputation), perform feature selection to identify key health indicators, and feed them into an ensemble of optimized machine learning classifiers (SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost) and deep neural networks, deployed on a cloud-based, scalable architecture for real-time processing and monitoring.
AI.result: The proposed framework achieves improved predictive performance for cardiovascular risk, including higher accuracy, fewer false positives, and more consistent predictions than conventional standalone methods, validated on real-world cardiovascular datasets.
AI.conclusion: Integrating traditional machine learning with deep learning in a cloud-based ensemble that leverages IoMT data enables effective early-stage cardiovascular risk assessment and supports clinical decision-making, highlighting the promise of proactive, data-driven healthcare management to improve patient outcomes.

title: The Mirror Agent Model: a Bayesian Architecture for Interpretable Agent Behavior
comment: Accepted at the International Workshop on Explainable, Transparent Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems, 2022
summary: In this paper we illustrate a novel architecture generating interpretable behavior and explanations. We refer to this architecture as the Mirror Agent Model because it defines the observer model, that is the target of explicit and implicit communications, as a mirror of the agent's. With the goal of providing a general understanding of this work, we firstly show prior relevant results addressing the informative communication of agents intentions and the production of legible behavior. In the second part of the paper we furnish the architecture with novel capabilities for explanations through off-the-shelf saliency methods, followed by preliminary qualitative results.

AI.tldr: A paper proposes the Mirror Agent Model, an AI architecture that generates interpretable behavior and explanations by explicitly modeling the observer as a mirror of the agent.
AI.motivation: To create agents whose intentions and actions are easily understandable to humans, improving interpretability, communicative behavior, and the ability to explain decisions.
AI.method: Introduce the Mirror Agent Model, which models the observer as a mirrored copy of the agent, building on prior work on informative intention communication and legible behavior. The architecture is then extended with explanation capabilities using existing saliency methods.
AI.result: Preliminary qualitative results suggesting that the architecture can produce interpretable behavior and explanations, demonstrating feasibility but without extensive quantitative evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The Mirror Agent Model is a promising direction for building agents that are both behaviorally legible and capable of generating explanations via saliency-based methods, although further work is needed for thorough validation and refinement.

title: What Matters in On-Policy Distillation? A Perspective on Data Efficiency and Data Selection
summary: On-Policy Distillation (OPD) has emerged as a widely adopted post-training paradigm for enhancing large language models in reasoning domains. However, the data-centric mechanisms in OPD remain relatively underexplored. This paper presents a empirical study of data efficiency and data selection in OPD. We begin by investigating an extreme setting: training OPD on only one example, namely 1-shot OPD. Surprisingly, we find that 1-shot OPD is consistently effective across all sampled training examples and harder examples often yield superior performance gain. We next investigate what actually drives the student model's improvement in the training data. Our analysis reveals that the improvement is not driven by high token entropy, but the longer CoT paths which hard problems naturally generate. Training on longer CoT can help maintain closer alignment with the teacher over a long reasoning horizon, and learn critical thinking patterns usually missing in short CoTs, such as reflection (e.g., ``Alternatively''). Based on these insights, we propose a simple data selection method that selects only hard examples for training, where even ``unsolvable'' examples that completely exceed the teacher's capability can be successfully used. Our experiments conducted on four models ranging from 1.5B to 7B show that training the student model on only 8 selected hard examples matches the performance of the 17K dataset baseline.

AI.tldr: This paper empirically studies how to make On-Policy Distillation (OPD) for reasoning LLMs far more data-efficient, finding that training on just a few carefully chosen hard examples can match training on a large dataset.
AI.motivation: While OPD is popular for improving reasoning in large language models, little is known about how much data is truly needed or which training examples matter most. Understanding the data efficiency and the characteristics of high-impact training samples could greatly reduce training cost and guide better dataset construction.
AI.method: The authors run systematic experiments on OPD under an extreme regime they call 1-shot OPD, where the student is distilled from the teacher using only a single example. They vary which example is used, analyze performance gains, and examine properties of those examples such as token entropy and chain-of-thought (CoT) length. They then design a data selection method that chooses only hard, long-CoT examples—including ones beyond the teacher’s ability—and train student models of different sizes with this curated subset, comparing against a 17K-example OPD baseline.
AI.result: They find that 1-shot OPD reliably improves the student across many sampled examples, with harder examples typically producing larger gains. Their analysis shows that the improvement is not explained by token-level entropy but correlates strongly with longer CoT trajectories. These longer CoTs help the student maintain alignment with the teacher over extended reasoning and learn nuanced reasoning behaviors like reflection. Using this insight, they show that training on only 8 selected hard examples can match the performance of a baseline trained on 17K examples, across models from 1.5B to 7B parameters, and that even examples unsolved by the teacher can still be beneficial.
AI.conclusion: OPD for reasoning LLMs can be made highly data-efficient by focusing on a small set of hard problems that elicit long, rich chains of thought from the teacher. Model gains are driven less by token uncertainty and more by exposure to extended reasoning patterns, suggesting that future OPD pipelines should prioritize hard, long-CoT examples—even ones beyond the teacher’s competence—rather than large quantities of generic data.

title: CABAL: Multi-Agent Simulacra for Tracing the Effects of Collusive Bidding in Peer Review
summary: Recent reports during the AAAI-27 review cycle highlight the risk of reviewers coordinating bids for reciprocal assignment advantage. Prior work treats bidding, reviewer assignment, and review manipulation as separate stages, leaving the lifecycle effects of collusive bidding unclear. Real-world analysis is further constrained by typically unobservable collusive intent and the lack of counterfactuals for the same conference. Motivated by this gap, we introduce \alg, an end-to-end multi-agent simulacra framework for studying reviewer assignment integrity by holding the conference environment fixed and configuring LLM-driven reviewer agents with honest or collusive policies. We further develop an affinity-guided collusive bidding strategy that uses mutual reviewer-paper affinities to construct collusion rings and select target papers, producing expertise-consistent rather than arbitrarily targeted attacks. Controlled experiments show that collusive bidding more than doubles target-paper capture and that assigned colluders score target papers about two points higher than honest co-reviewers, while conference-wide effects remain comparatively modest. Evaluated bid-phase detectors provide only limited evidence of collusion: in a fixed-triplet detector stress test, native positive-bid graphs are confounded by benign affinity, while a Very-High-only diagnostic view enables precise but low-coverage local recovery.
