title: ACE: Adaptive Calibration-Free Expert Skipping for MoE-based LLMs
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures provide an efficient paradigm for scaling large language models (LLMs), yet fixed top-k routing activates the same number of expert slots for every token, causing substantial redundant computation. Existing expert-skipping methods often rely on router confidence, calibration data, or additional training, and therefore cannot reliably estimate the actual contribution of routed experts. To this end, we propose ACE, a training-free, calibration-free, and checkpoint-preserving framework for token-adaptive expert skipping in MoE-based LLMs. ACE contains two complementary components: 1) Global Spectral Proxy (GSP), which estimates global transformation capacity from the coupled gate, up, and down projections together with RMSNorm scaling; and 2) Router-Conditioned Refinement (RCR), which constructs expert-specific direction prototypes from centered router weights and evaluates expert responses along routing-preferred directions. During inference, ACE combines both estimates with runtime router gates and skips an expert slot only when both views identify it as low-contribution, while always retaining the top-1 expert. All expert statistics are computed offline, leaving only table lookups and lightweight scalar operations online. Extensive experiments across three MoE-based LLMs and eight benchmarks demonstrate that ACE consistently outperforms existing static and dynamic baselines, with increasingly pronounced advantages under aggressive expert skipping. For instance, at a 50% skipping ratio on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, ACE reduces WikiText-2 perplexity by 7.96% and improves average downstream accuracy by 4.15 percentage points over the strongest competing method.

AI.tldr: ACE is a training‑free, calibration‑free framework to dynamically skip low‑impact experts in MoE LLMs, cutting compute while preserving or improving quality.
AI.motivation: Fixed top‑k routing in MoE LLMs activates the same number of experts for every token, wasting computation because many routed experts contribute little. Existing expert‑skipping methods depend on router confidence, calibration data, or extra training, and still do not directly estimate each expert’s true contribution. A new approach is needed that can be applied to existing checkpoints without retraining or calibration and that more accurately measures expert usefulness per token.
AI.method: ACE introduces a token‑adaptive expert skipping mechanism with two offline‑computed, complementary estimators of expert contribution. (1) Global Spectral Proxy (GSP) analyzes the combined linear transformation defined by the gate, up, and down projections plus RMSNorm scaling to estimate each expert slot’s global transformation capacity. (2) Router‑Conditioned Refinement (RCR) builds expert‑specific direction prototypes from centered router weights and scores expert responses along routing‑preferred directions, refining the contribution estimate for each token. At inference, ACE uses router gates plus both GSP and RCR signals to skip an expert only if both views judge it as low‑contribution, while always retaining the top‑1 expert. All statistics are precomputed offline, so online cost reduces to table lookups and simple scalar operations.
AI.result: On three different MoE‑based LLMs and eight benchmarks, ACE surpasses both static and dynamic expert‑skipping baselines, especially when many experts are skipped. At a 50% skipping ratio on Qwen3.6‑35B‑A3B, ACE lowers WikiText‑2 perplexity by 7.96% and increases average downstream task accuracy by 4.15 percentage points compared to the strongest prior method.
AI.conclusion: Token‑adaptive expert skipping can be done effectively without retraining or calibration by leveraging structural properties of MoE layers. ACE’s dual‑view estimation (GSP + RCR) enables more accurate identification of low‑contribution experts, delivering substantial compute savings while improving or maintaining performance over existing methods, and it can be applied directly to existing MoE LLM checkpoints.

title: Substrate-Aware AI Agents: Execution Context as a First-Class Input
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures. Reproducibility artifacts and source-linked evaluation code: https://github.com/manu2/Context-Aware-Agent-Experiment
summary: Autonomous AI agents increasingly select actions in environments whose memory, execution-time, runtime, compute, and operational constraints determine what counts as a suitable plan. We call the absence of this execution context from an agent's planning state substrate blindness. We test this general proposition through numerical code generation, where selected implementation choices and operational consequences are directly observable. Three frontier model configurations--Anthropic Claude Opus 5, OpenAI GPT-5.6-Sol, and Google Gemini 3.7 Flash--generate code for a high-dimensional pairwise Euclidean-distance task either from the task alone or with a 128 MB RAM and 10.0 s wall-time contract. Contract disclosure reduced measured peak process memory in 13 of 14 executable index-aligned task-only versus contract-disclosed comparisons and reduced mean wall time in all three cohorts, making execution up to 3.1x faster. Across the audited corpus, disclosure produced structural code changes including bounded blocking, float32 retention, upper-triangle traversal, and in-place or memory-mapped buffers. At a tighter 96 MB contract, independently sampled contract-disclosed cohorts achieved correct-and-within-budget outcomes of 4/5 for Claude Opus 5, 5/5 for GPT-5.6-Sol, and 3/5 for Gemini 3.7 Flash, compared with task-only outcomes of 0/5, 1/5, and 0/5; cohort mean MaxRSS and wall time were 49-74% and 35-64% lower than their task-only references. These results establish a controlled proof of concept for substrate-aware agent planning: a minimal execution contract induces proactive structural adaptation in generated programs, shifting computation away from unconstrained allocations and substantially improving observed resource-time profiles before execution.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that giving AI code-generation models an explicit resource contract (RAM and time limits) leads them to generate structurally different, more efficient programs, thereby demonstrating substrate-aware planning.
AI.motivation: Autonomous AI agents usually plan actions without explicit awareness of the computational and operational constraints under which their plans will be executed (memory, time, compute). This "substrate blindness" can cause them to propose solutions that fail or are inefficient in real-world environments. The authors want to test whether exposing such constraints at planning time measurably changes the behavior of advanced code-generation models and improves their resource usage.
AI.method: The authors design a controlled experiment using a numerical code-generation task: computing pairwise Euclidean distances in a high-dimensional setting. They prompt three state-of-the-art code models (Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6-Sol, Gemini 3.7 Flash) either with only the task description (task-only) or with an added execution contract specifying RAM limits and wall-clock time (e.g., 128 MB, 10 s; also a stricter 96 MB). They then execute the generated programs, measuring peak memory (MaxRSS), wall-clock time, and correctness. They compare structurally how the generated code differs between task-only and contract-disclosed conditions (e.g., blocking, data types, traversal patterns, memory handling) and aggregate results across multiple sampled cohorts of generations.
AI.result: With a 128 MB RAM and 10 s time contract, contract disclosure reduced peak memory in 13 of 14 index-aligned task-only vs. contract-disclosed pairs and reduced mean wall time in all three model cohorts, improving execution speed by up to 3.1x. Code from contract-aware prompts showed systematic structural optimizations such as bounded blocking, staying in float32, using upper-triangle traversal, and employing in-place or memory-mapped buffers. Under a tighter 96 MB contract, contract-disclosed generations achieved correct-and-within-budget rates of 4/5 (Claude Opus 5), 5/5 (GPT-5.6-Sol), and 3/5 (Gemini 3.7 Flash), compared with 0/5, 1/5, and 0/5 for task-only. Mean MaxRSS and wall time for contract-aware cohorts were 49-74% and 35-64% lower than their task-only baselines.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly informing advanced code-generation models about execution constraints (memory and time) leads them to proactively restructure their programs, reducing memory usage and runtime while preserving or improving correctness. This offers a proof of concept for "substrate-aware" planning, where agents consider the properties and limits of their execution environment when choosing actions. Even simple execution contracts can significantly mitigate substrate blindness and improve real-world performance of autonomous AI agents.

title: Uncensored Open-weight Models: Redistribution as the Persistence Layer
summary: A rapidly expanding ecosystem of actors is removing built-in safety guardrails from open-weight AI models. We profile this ecosystem by identifying key producers, downstream reproductions, and emerging applications. Between January 2024 and March 2026, we identified 3,471 original uncensored models on HuggingFace, each repackaged an average of 2.4 times; three actors account for 52% of all 8,164 compressed redistributions. Once quantized and mirrored across separate accounts, formats, and registries such as Ollama, these models persist regardless of upstream removal and become easier to deploy downstream. Of the 1,643 identified GitHub applications integrating uncensored large language models (ULLMs), 25% were classified as explicitly malicious.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the fast-growing ecosystem that strips safety guardrails from open AI models, quantifies its scale, and highlights the spread and persistence of these uncensored models and their applications.
AI.motivation: As open-weight AI models become more powerful, actors have begun deliberately removing their safety guardrails, creating uncensored large language models (ULLMs). These models can be redistributed and embedded into downstream applications, including harmful ones, and may persist even if the original repositories are taken down. However, there is limited systematic understanding of who produces these uncensored models, how widely they are repackaged, and what kinds of applications they enable. The paper aims to fill this gap to inform risk assessment and governance efforts.
AI.method: The authors empirically map the ULLM ecosystem using large-scale measurements across public platforms. They systematically scan HuggingFace for models whose safety guardrails have been removed, identify original uncensored model releases, and then track their repackaging, compression, and mirroring across different accounts and formats, including registries like Ollama. In parallel, they mine GitHub for software projects that integrate uncensored LLMs, label these applications, and classify a subset as explicitly malicious based on predefined criteria.
AI.result: From January 2024 to March 2026, the authors find 3,471 distinct original uncensored models on HuggingFace, which are on average repackaged 2.4 times each. This results in 8,164 compressed or otherwise redistributed versions, with only three key actors responsible for 52% of these redistributions. They show that once models are quantized and mirrored across separate accounts, formats, and registries, they continue to exist and be deployable even after upstream removals. On GitHub, they identify 1,643 applications that integrate ULLMs and determine that around 25% of them have explicitly malicious purposes.
AI.conclusion: The ecosystem that strips safety guardrails from open-weight models is large, highly concentrated among a few prolific actors, and resilient to takedown efforts. Compression, mirroring, and redistribution practices make uncensored models persist and easier to deploy downstream. A substantial fraction of applications built on top of these models are explicitly malicious, underscoring the need for improved monitoring, coordination between platforms, and targeted governance interventions to address ULLM proliferation and misuse.

title: Do LLMs Exhibit Coherent Knowledge Structures in Mathematical Reasoning? A Perspective from Knowledge Space Theory
summary: Human knowledge is inherently structured and interdependent: mastery of a concept requires prior mastery of its prerequisites, a principle formalized by Knowledge Space Theory (KST). While LLMs achieve strong performance on complex reasoning tasks, it remains unclear whether they exhibit coherent, human-like knowledge structure. We introduce a KST-grounded framework for evaluating LLM knowledge structure in mathematical reasoning, using it as a normative framework to analyze whether LLM behavior adheres to principled knowledge dependencies. Evaluating eight open- and closed-source LLMs against real human learners, we find that (1) LLMs do not adhere to human knowledge structure -- they frequently violate knowledge dependencies and fail to leverage related knowledge provided in context to improve performance on dependent questions; (2) LLMs do not share a consistent knowledge structure among themselves, as reflected by low overlap in their knowledge distributions. Furthermore, these structural deficiencies remain largely invisible to accuracy-based and LLM-as-judge evaluations. Together, our results provide behavioral evidence that current LLMs knowledge does not follow a human-like structure.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether LLMs’ mathematical knowledge is organized in coherent, human-like prerequisite structures, and finds that it is not.
AI.motivation: Humans learn concepts in structured ways: understanding advanced ideas depends on mastering prerequisites, captured formally by Knowledge Space Theory (KST). Although LLMs perform well on complex reasoning benchmarks, we do not know if their internal “knowledge” follows similar prerequisite relations or is instead fragmented and unstructured. The authors want a principled, theory-driven way to probe LLM knowledge structure, beyond simple accuracy metrics.
AI.method: They build an evaluation framework based on Knowledge Space Theory for mathematical reasoning tasks. Using KST as a normative model of how prerequisite relationships should look, they design questions with explicit dependency relations and compare: (a) how often different LLMs respect these dependencies (i.e., only succeed on advanced items when they also succeed on prerequisites), (b) whether LLMs can use explicitly provided related knowledge in context to perform better on dependent questions, and (c) how similar the induced “knowledge spaces” are across eight different open- and closed-source LLMs, benchmarked against data from real human learners.
AI.result: They find that LLMs frequently violate prerequisite structures that humans typically respect: models can answer harder, dependent questions while failing their prerequisites, and they often do not improve on dependent questions even when prerequisite information is placed in context. Different LLMs also do not agree with each other on which concepts they “know,” showing low overlap in their inferred knowledge distributions. Standard evaluation methods based purely on accuracy or LLM-as-judge scores largely fail to reveal these structural problems.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs, despite high task accuracy, do not exhibit human-like, coherent knowledge structures as characterized by Knowledge Space Theory. Their “knowledge” appears structurally inconsistent, idiosyncratic across models, and weakly sensitive to explicit prerequisite information. This suggests that future model development and evaluation should account for knowledge structure, not just overall performance, if we want systems that more closely mirror human conceptual mastery and reasoning.

title: A Unified Physics-Aware Quantum Machine Learning Framework across Power GaN HEMTs and Logic Nanowire FETs: Predicting Unseen Process Splits and Held-Out Geometry Combinations with Lower Error and Tighter Split-to-Split Variability
summary: We present a unified reinforcement-learning (RL) framework that discovers compact parametrized quantum circuits (PQCs) for data-scarce device modeling. A graph neural network (GNN) policy optimized by proximal policy optimization (PPO) searches circuit architectures using leave-one-group-out cross-validation (LOGOCV) error on held-out process or geometry groups as the reward. The framework achieves the lowest mean absolute error (MAE) on all 11 targets versus six classical baselines, with 59% lower error (Ioff) and 81% tighter fold variability (VTH) for HEMTs and 84% lower error (VTH, SS, Ioff) and 82% tighter fold variability (Ioff) for NWFETs. These results demonstrate the potential of RL-selected, classically simulated PQCs as compact surrogates with low OOD error and improved physical consistency, despite imposing no explicit physical constraints, penalty terms, or device-specific equations, on the two evaluated device datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an RL-based framework using GNN policies and PPO to automatically design compact parametrized quantum circuits that accurately model semiconductor devices, outperforming classical methods in accuracy and robustness on scarce data.
AI.motivation: Accurate and compact device models are needed for semiconductor technologies, but data is often scarce and classical surrogate models can have high out-of-distribution (OOD) error and poor physical consistency. There is interest in exploiting parametrized quantum circuits as flexible function approximators, yet systematically discovering good PQC architectures for specific device-modeling tasks remains difficult. The work aims to create an automated way to design PQCs that generalize well across different device processes and geometries under data scarcity.
AI.method: The authors build a reinforcement-learning framework where a graph neural network (GNN) acts as the policy network that sequentially constructs parametrized quantum circuit architectures. The policy is trained using proximal policy optimization (PPO). To enforce generalization, the reward signal is defined as the leave-one-group-out cross-validation (LOGOCV) error on held-out groups corresponding to different process or geometry conditions. The RL agent explores the space of PQC architectures and is guided toward those that minimize LOGOCV error, effectively selecting architectures with good OOD performance. The PQCs are classically simulated during training and evaluation.
AI.result: On two device datasets (HEMTs and NWFETs) and 11 prediction targets, the RL-designed PQCs achieve the lowest mean absolute error among all tested models, beating six classical baselines. For HEMTs, the method reduces Ioff error by 59% and VTH fold variability by 81%. For NWFETs, it reduces errors for VTH, SS, and Ioff by 84% and Ioff fold variability by 82%. This indicates improved accuracy and significantly tighter variability across cross-validation folds, suggesting better robustness and generalization.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that reinforcement learning can effectively discover compact PQC architectures that serve as accurate, robust surrogate models for semiconductor devices under data scarcity. The RL-selected PQCs, even when only classically simulated and without embedding explicit physical constraints or device equations, still exhibit low out-of-distribution error and improved physical consistency. This highlights the promise of automated RL-driven architecture search for quantum-inspired modeling in scientific and engineering applications.

title: Commonsense Reasoning in Computer Vision: Foundations, Recent Advancements, and Future Directions
summary: Commonsense reasoning in computer vision encompasses integrating visual data and contextual knowledge, crucial for enhancing AI's understanding of everyday scenarios. This understanding not only improves machine learning models but also enhances their ability to interact meaningfully with humans and the environment. Unlike CNN-based conventional vision models, which are designed to identify objects within a specific image, incorporating commonsense knowledge enables models to interpret scenes in a more holistic manner, thereby improving their spatial ability to reason about relationships among objects and actions. This integration not only enhances object recognition but also facilitates a deeper understanding of the contextual factors, ultimately leading to more precise predictions and interactions in real-world applications. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of recent developments that integrate commonsense knowledge into computer vision tasks. We systematically review approaches based on knowledge graphs, scene graphs, neuro-symbolic models, and commonsense-augmented transformers. We also outline current limitations related to dataset bias, knowledge incompleteness, and integration challenges. Finally, we highlight prospective research trajectories in cross-modal reasoning, scalable commonsense knowledge injection, and neuro-symbolic hybrid architectures to develop truly intelligent visual systems.

AI.tldr: Survey of methods that inject commonsense knowledge into computer vision to enable holistic scene understanding and better reasoning about object relationships and actions.
AI.motivation: Traditional CNN-based vision models focus on recognizing objects in isolated images and struggle with holistic scene understanding and contextual reasoning. Real-world AI systems need commonsense to understand everyday scenarios, reason about object relationships and actions, and interact meaningfully with humans and their environment. There is rapid, fragmented progress in integrating commonsense into vision, creating a need for a systematic overview of approaches, limitations, and future directions.
AI.method: Conduct a comprehensive survey of recent computer vision methods that explicitly integrate commonsense knowledge. Categorize and analyze works into four main approach families: knowledge-graph-based methods, scene-graph-based methods, neuro-symbolic models, and commonsense-augmented transformers. For each, summarize how commonsense is represented, how it is injected into visual pipelines, what tasks it supports, and how it is evaluated. Additionally, examine cross-cutting issues such as dataset bias, knowledge incompleteness, and technical integration challenges.
AI.result: Provide a structured taxonomy and critical review of commonsense-enhanced computer vision approaches, clarifying the design space across knowledge representation choices and integration strategies. Identify common strengths (e.g., improved relational reasoning, better contextual predictions) and recurring weaknesses (e.g., sensitivity to biased datasets, limited coverage of commonsense knowledge bases, and engineering complexity when coupling symbolic and neural components).
AI.conclusion: Integrating commonsense knowledge is key to advancing from object-centric recognition toward truly intelligent visual systems capable of robust, context-aware reasoning. Existing methods demonstrate clear benefits but are constrained by biased data, incomplete knowledge, and difficult integration pipelines. Future research should focus on cross-modal reasoning across vision and language, scalable and flexible mechanisms for injecting commonsense into large models, and principled neuro-symbolic hybrid architectures that combine the strengths of neural perception with symbolic reasoning for real-world deployment.

title: Trace2Tower: Transition-Aware EigenTrace Induction of Multi-Level Skills for LLM Agents
summary: Large language model agents increasingly rely on execution traces to master complex interactive tasks. However, current paradigms are bottlenecked by shallow trajectory retrieval and flat skill summarization, fundamentally ignoring the temporal dependencies and outcome-conditioned topology of agent behavior. We introduce Trace2Tower, a transition-aware EigenTrace framework that distills raw trajectories into a robust skill hierarchy. Trace2Tower abstracts step-level interactions into canonical events, constructing a unified graph governed by semantic compatibility, transition dynamics, and outcome evidence. Through a novel contrastive spectral decomposition, it isolates stable, success-aligned behavioral modes while rigorously suppressing failure-prone shortcuts. These modes organically populate a dynamic skill tower of action templates, procedural routines, and overarching task strategies, continuously refined via verifier-guided feedback. On ALFWorld, Trace2Tower achieves 87.31% success requiring only 10.35 steps and 0.26 invalid actions; on WebShop, it reaches 50.67% exact success. Across both benchmarks, Trace2Tower significantly outperforms existing baselines in task mastery and context-efficient experience reuse.

AI.tldr: Trace2Tower is a framework that converts raw execution traces of LLM agents into a hierarchical skill tower using a transition-aware graph and spectral analysis, leading to better performance and sample-efficient experience reuse on interactive benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent methods depend on execution traces but treat them with shallow retrieval and flat summarization, failing to leverage temporal dependencies, outcome-conditioned structure, and transition dynamics in trajectories. This limits their ability to derive robust, reusable skills and to separate success patterns from failure-prone behaviors. The paper aims to build a more principled way to distill structured, hierarchical skills from raw interaction data.
AI.method: The paper proposes Trace2Tower, which first abstracts low-level action sequences into canonical events and builds a unified graph over these events, where edges encode semantic compatibility, transition structure, and task outcome signals. It then applies a novel contrastive spectral decomposition (EigenTrace) over this graph to identify latent behavioral modes that are stable and success-aligned while suppressing behaviors associated with failures. These modes are organized into a dynamic, multi-level skill tower including atomic action templates, mid-level routines, and high-level strategies. The hierarchy is iteratively refined with verifier-guided feedback based on task outcomes.
AI.result: On the ALFWorld benchmark, Trace2Tower achieves 87.31% success with an average of 10.35 steps and only 0.26 invalid actions per episode; on WebShop, it reaches 50.67% exact success. Across both benchmarks, it notably surpasses existing baselines both in final task success and in efficiency, demonstrating improved task mastery and more effective reuse of prior experience in new contexts.
AI.conclusion: Trace2Tower demonstrates that modeling trajectories as a transition-aware event graph and applying contrastive spectral decomposition can effectively distill robust, outcome-aligned behavioral modes from raw traces. Organizing these modes into a hierarchical skill tower yields more sample-efficient, reliable LLM agents that outperform baselines on interactive tasks, highlighting the value of explicit temporal and outcome-aware structure in experience reuse and skill abstraction.

title: AI for Computational Design Science: A Responsible Human-AI Framework and Case Study on Short-Form Video Safety Surveillance
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming not only what information systems researchers design, but also how design research is conducted. Yet existing literature offers limited guidance for computational design science (CDS) when AI actively participates in problem formulation, resource construction, design search, evaluation, and knowledge abstraction. We develop AI for Computational Design Science (AI4CDS), a five-phase methodological framework in which AI expands problem and design search while researchers retain responsibility for domain grounding, admissibility, verification, and scientific judgment. Collaboration is governed by graduated trust, reversibility, auditability, and differentiated reproducibility. We instantiate AI4CDS through ChildRiskGuard, an interpretable artifact for detecting short-form videos inappropriate for children, while documenting AI interactions, rejected alternatives, corrections, and audit trails. The case translates audience-dependent safety and explanation faithfulness into three technical challenges and develops an artifact that separates generic from child-specific risk, represents distinct developmental-risk mechanisms, and makes concept-level explanations part of the predictive computation. ChildRiskGuard achieves an F1 score of 0.769, substantially outperforming direct application of a general-purpose content-safety model while remaining competitive with strong benchmarks. The primary contribution is AI4CDS as a responsible framework for AI-enabled CDS; ChildRiskGuard provides process and artifact evidence of how AI-expanded, researcher-governed design can generate and evaluate novel computational design knowledge.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes AI4CDS, a framework for integrating AI into all stages of computational design science while keeping researchers in control, and demonstrates it via ChildRiskGuard, a system for detecting inappropriate short-form videos for children.
AI.motivation: AI is increasingly used not only in the artifacts that information systems researchers design but also in the design process itself. However, there is little methodological guidance for how to conduct computational design science when AI participates actively in core research activities such as problem formulation, design search, evaluation, and knowledge abstraction. This gap creates risks around responsibility, transparency, and scientific rigor when leveraging powerful AI tools in design research.
AI.method: The authors develop AI4CDS, a five-phase methodological framework for computational design science in which AI assists in expanding problem and design spaces, while human researchers maintain control over domain grounding, admissibility criteria, verification, and scientific judgment. The framework introduces collaboration principles including graduated trust, reversibility, auditability, and differentiated reproducibility. They instantiate and illustrate the framework through the design of ChildRiskGuard, an interpretable AI artifact for detecting child-inappropriate short-form videos, systematically documenting AI interactions, rejected alternatives, corrections, and audit trails throughout the project.
AI.result: Using AI4CDS, the authors build ChildRiskGuard, which operationalizes audience-dependent safety and explanation faithfulness into three technical challenges: distinguishing generic from child-specific risk, modeling distinct developmental-risk mechanisms, and embedding concept-level explanations directly into predictive computation. Empirically, ChildRiskGuard achieves an F1 score of 0.769, significantly outperforming a directly applied general-purpose content-safety model and remaining competitive with strong baseline models.
AI.conclusion: AI4CDS is presented as a responsible, methodologically grounded framework for AI-enabled computational design science that balances AI-augmented exploration with human governance over scientific decisions. The ChildRiskGuard case offers both a concrete artifact and a process demonstration, showing how AI-extended but researcher-governed design can produce novel computational design knowledge with improved performance and interpretable, audience-aware safety mechanisms.

title: Don't Drop Dropout: Optimizing Layer Sparsity for Efficient LLM Training and Inference
comment: This is a slightly extended version of the paper published at ICML 2026
summary: Layer dropout (a.k.a. stochastic depth) has been shown to enable faster training, higher accuracy, and robustness to zero-shot layer pruning in both language and vision transformers. However, as models and datasets have scaled, dropout - particularly layer dropout - has largely disappeared from large language models (LLMs) pre-training recipes. While some prior work has reported that dropout can degrade accuracy, no comprehensive study has quantified, let alone mitigated, this effect. In this study, we show that layer dropout should be used in state-of-the-art LLM training, establishing best practices and scaling analysis for both training and post-training benefits. Concretely, with optimal layer distribution, time schedule, and optimizer hyperparameters, we observe that at the same training FLOPs layer dropout leads to lower loss. For a given number of training steps, LLMs can achieve lower or similar validation loss while saving upto 25% of training FLOPs. Moreover, layer dropout enables significant post-training optimizations, such as early exit, intermediate-layer skipping, and self-speculative decoding, yielding up to 1.5x inference speedup with negligible accuracy loss. Across more than 2400 training experiments, spanning models from 271M to 8.2B parameters and datasets up to 160B tokens, we demonstrate that these findings extend reliably to large-scale training regimes. All pre-training experiments were run on Cerebras CS-3 systems.

AI.tldr: The paper revisits layer dropout (stochastic depth) for modern LLMs and shows that, when carefully configured, it improves training efficiency and enables faster inference without hurting accuracy.
AI.motivation: Although layer dropout previously showed benefits in transformers, it has mostly disappeared from large-scale LLM pre-training because some reports suggested it hurts accuracy; there has been no large, systematic study on when and how to use it effectively at scale.
AI.method: The authors perform over 2400 training experiments on LLMs ranging from 271M to 8.2B parameters and datasets up to 160B tokens, systematically varying layer dropout distributions across depth, time schedules, and optimizer hyperparameters. They compare models under equal FLOPs and equal-step budgets, and evaluate both training loss and downstream inference-time techniques enabled by layer dropout, such as early exit, layer skipping, and self-speculative decoding. All pre-training is done on Cerebras CS-3 systems.
AI.result: With well-chosen layer dropout configurations, models achieve lower loss at equal training FLOPs and can save up to 25% training FLOPs at the same step count while maintaining similar or better validation loss. Layer dropout also enables post-training optimizations—including early exit, intermediate-layer skipping, and self-speculative decoding—that yield up to 1.5× inference speedup with negligible accuracy loss. These effects are consistent across model sizes and dataset scales in their experiments.
AI.conclusion: Layer dropout should be reintroduced as a standard component in state-of-the-art LLM pre-training pipelines. When properly tuned in terms of depth distribution, scheduling, and optimizer settings, it improves training efficiency and unlocks substantial inference-time speedups with minimal impact on accuracy, and these benefits hold across a wide range of model sizes and data regimes.

title: Testing Interchangeability in LLM Agent Teams
summary: Production multi-agent systems replace agents constantly, on the assumption that an agent filling a role is interchangeable with any other agent that can do the job. We test that assumption. Eight teams per setting are formed independently from one base model on the same tasks, each agent keeping a private notebook across ten formation episodes; we then trade role-matched agents between teams and measure what changes on held-out tasks. Against a placebo that reproduces the disruption of a roster change without changing who occupies the seat, a swap costs little in task score but raises the communication a team spends per unit of progress by 16 to 63 percent, and in Hanabi a swapped agent is more expensive than an inexperienced one, consistent with interference from conventions learned with its former partner. In Collab-Overcooked, when the agent that sets the agenda is replaced, most of the extra communication comes from the agent that stayed. Three ablations, over base models, decoding temperature and formation length, move the swap penalty alongside one other quantity: how far independently formed teams drift apart. Greedy decoding lowers both; doubling a team's history raises both. In these settings, agents are more fungible in task outcome than in coordination efficiency, with larger swap effects after longer formation histories.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether agents in multi-agent systems are truly interchangeable by measuring the impact of swapping agents between independently formed teams.
AI.motivation: In many practical multi-agent systems, we assume that any agent that can technically perform a role can be seamlessly substituted for another in that role. This assumption underlies design choices like dynamic replacement, scaling, and robustness, yet is rarely stress-tested, especially for agents that have built up partner-specific coordination conventions over time. The authors want to understand to what extent agents are actually fungible once they have history and conventions with specific partners.
AI.method: The authors create multiple teams from the same base model, each trained/formed independently on the same collaborative tasks. Each agent maintains a private notebook across ten formation episodes, allowing it to build history and conventions with its teammate(s). After formation, they swap role-matched agents between teams, so that each agent now works with a different partner, and evaluate performance on held-out tasks. They compare this with a placebo manipulation that preserves team composition while reproducing the disruption of a roster change. They measure both task performance and communication efficiency (communication per unit of progress). They run experiments in environments such as Hanabi and Collab-Overcooked, and conduct ablations over base models, decoding temperature, and formation length to see how these factors affect the swap penalty and inter-team drift.
AI.result: Swapping agents between teams has little effect on final task scores but significantly increases the communication required per unit of progress, by 16–63% compared to the placebo. In Hanabi, a swapped agent harms efficiency more than an inexperienced one, suggesting that conventions learned with former partners interfere with coordination with new partners. In Collab-Overcooked, when the agenda-setting agent is replaced, most of the extra communication burden falls on the agent that stayed. Across ablations, the magnitude of the swap penalty tracks how far independently formed teams’ conventions drift from one another: greedy decoding reduces both drift and swap penalty, while doubling a team's history increases both.
AI.conclusion: Agents in these multi-agent systems are more interchangeable with respect to final task performance than with respect to coordination efficiency. Partner-specific coordination conventions and team histories create path dependence: longer shared histories increase the cost of swapping agents, primarily as extra communication rather than outright task failure. Design choices that reduce convention drift (e.g., greedy decoding, shorter histories) make agents more fungible, while those that encourage distinct team conventions make agent replacement more costly in efficiency terms.

title: GUT: Quantifying and Optimizing the Reasoning Uncertainty of LLMs via Graph Complexity
summary: Recent years have witnessed great advances in the reasoning ability of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, the reasoning processes of LLMs often exhibit uncertainty, where LLMs often produce a proliferation of divergent branches at each reasoning step even when fed the same prompting inputs, and certain branches exhibit evidently incredible, even nonsensical, reasoning chains and results. In this paper, we propose the Graph-complexity-based UncerTainty (GUT) method for investigating the reasoning uncertainty of LLMs. The key idea of GUT is to characterize the potential branches of each reasoning chain with a directed acyclic graph, thereby ensuring that all potential branches are comprehensively covered within the graph space. Building upon this recognition, we further build two modules of GUT, that is, a Quantification (GUT-Q) module and an Optimization (GUT-O) module, for quantifying and reducing the reasoning uncertainty of LLMs, respectively. GUT-Q measures LLM reasoning uncertainty by approximating the reasoning space complexity with graph complexity. GUT-O implements uncertainty optimization by treating negative uncertainty as the reward function in reinforcement learning. Experimental results conducted on four LLMs and five datasets validate the effectiveness of GUT.

AI.tldr: They analyze and reduce reasoning uncertainty in LLMs using a graph-based representation of reasoning paths, with modules for quantifying and optimizing this uncertainty via RL.
AI.motivation: LLMs, while strong at reasoning, produce many divergent and sometimes nonsensical reasoning branches even under the same prompt. There is a lack of systematic ways to characterize and reduce this "reasoning uncertainty." This paper aims to formally represent and measure this uncertainty and then improve LLM reasoning reliability.
AI.method: They introduce GUT (Graph-complexity-based UncerTainty), which represents all potential reasoning branches as a directed acyclic graph, capturing the full reasoning space. On top of this, GUT-Q approximates reasoning uncertainty by measuring graph complexity, and GUT-O reduces uncertainty by using negative uncertainty as a reward signal in a reinforcement learning framework to guide the LLM toward more stable reasoning paths.
AI.result: Experiments on four LLMs and five datasets show that their graph-based uncertainty metric correlates with reasoning instability and that optimizing against this uncertainty improves reasoning performance and consistency compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Modeling reasoning as a DAG enables a principled definition of reasoning uncertainty in LLMs. By quantifying this via graph complexity and optimizing it via RL, the GUT framework both diagnoses and reduces unstable, divergent reasoning, leading to more reliable LLM reasoning across models and tasks.

title: Beyond Aggregate Scores: Behavioral Correctness Assumptions for Assessing Reference-Based Automatic Evaluation Methods
summary: Automated reference-based evaluation methods play a critical role in assessing natural language generation systems. Existing meta-evaluation primarily measures agreement with human judgments or benchmark labels, providing limited insight into evaluator behavior under controlled conditions. We introduce behavioral correctness assumptions, a complementary framework for evaluating reference-based automatic evaluation methods. We define a taxonomy of correctness-preserving and correctness-altering assumptions and operationalize them through controlled response transformations that specify expected scoring behaviors. We evaluate diverse lexical, character-level, semantic, LLM-based, and hybrid evaluators and analyze their assumption-level behavior, stability, sensitivity, repeat-run variability, configuration sensitivity, and reproducibility. Our experiments reveal distinct behavioral trade-offs across evaluation paradigms: no evaluator satisfies all proposed correctness assumptions, and evaluators with similar aggregate performance can exhibit substantially different behavioral profiles. These findings demonstrate that behavioral correctness assumptions provide diagnostic information obscured by conventional aggregate meta-evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new way to evaluate automatic evaluation metrics for text generation by testing their behavior under controlled transformations, showing that different metrics have distinct behavioral trade-offs that standard meta-evaluation hides.
AI.motivation: Current meta-evaluation of NLG metrics mostly checks their correlation with human judgments or benchmark labels, which does not reveal how these metrics behave under specific, controlled changes to system outputs. This limits our understanding of their reliability, robustness, and the kinds of errors they make. A more behavior-focused evaluation is needed to diagnose strengths and weaknesses of different evaluators beyond aggregate scores.
AI.method: The authors introduce a framework based on "behavioral correctness assumptions" for reference-based evaluators. They define a taxonomy distinguishing correctness-preserving vs. correctness-altering assumptions and instantiate them as controlled response transformations (e.g., edits to model outputs) where the expected change in metric scores is known. They then test a wide variety of evaluators—lexical, character-level, semantic, LLM-based, and hybrids—by applying these transformations to responses and measuring whether the evaluators’ scores follow the expected behavior. They additionally analyze stability, sensitivity, variability across runs, configuration sensitivity, and reproducibility of evaluator behavior.
AI.result: Empirical analysis shows that no existing evaluator satisfies all the defined behavioral correctness assumptions. Evaluators that achieve similar aggregate meta-evaluation performance can nevertheless differ markedly in which assumptions they satisfy and how they respond to controlled transformations. The study also exposes important trade-offs across evaluator types in terms of stability, sensitivity to changes, and robustness to configuration and run-to-run differences.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral correctness assumptions offer a complementary, diagnostic perspective on evaluation metrics for NLG that is not captured by standard aggregate meta-evaluation. By revealing systematic behavioral differences and trade-offs among evaluators, this framework can guide the selection, design, and improvement of automatic evaluation methods and underscores that high aggregate correlation with human judgments does not guarantee desirable behavior under controlled conditions.

title: RISE: Recursive Improvement via Self-Extrapolating Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense, per-token supervision for language model post-training, but its effectiveness is bottlenecked by teacher quality: external teachers suffer from distribution mismatch, while self-distillation with privileged conditioning is limited by in-context learning capacity. We propose \textbf{RISE} (\textbf{R}ecursive \textbf{I}mprovement via \textbf{S}elf-\textbf{E}xtrapolating Policy Distillation), which constructs a synthetic teacher directly from the model's own RLVR training trajectory. By extrapolating the displacement between the current checkpoint and a trailing anchor---in parameter space or output logit space---RISE converts a sparse outcome-induced parameter update into a dense token-level target, without any external model or privileged conditioning. RISE combines RLVR and OPD in a complementary loop: outcome rewards ground the extrapolation toward correct reasoning, while the extrapolated teacher refines token-level decisions. Moreover, since the teacher is refreshed every iteration as the student improves, distillation becomes a recursive improvement mechanism rather than a one-shot compression step. Experiments spanning mathematical reasoning, multi-domain STEM, code generation, and multi-turn agentic tasks show that RISE outperforms RLVR-only training and on-policy self-distillation across all settings.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RISE, a method that turns sparse RL updates into dense token-level supervision for language models by extrapolating along the model’s own training trajectory, enabling recursive self-improvement without external teachers.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation is powerful but constrained by the quality and form of the teacher: external teachers don’t match the on-policy distribution, and self-distillation with privileged prompts is limited by in-context learning and requires extra conditioning. The authors want a way to get dense, high-quality token-level supervision directly from the model’s own learning process, avoiding external models and privileged inputs, and to make distillation a continual improvement mechanism rather than a one-off compression step.
AI.method: They introduce RISE (Recursive Improvement via Self-Extrapolating Policy Distillation). RISE builds a synthetic teacher from the model’s RLVR training trajectory by taking a trailing anchor checkpoint and extrapolating the displacement between that anchor and the current model, either in parameter space or in logit (output) space. This extrapolation produces token-level targets that convert sparse, trajectory-level RL outcome rewards into dense per-token supervision. The method is integrated in a loop where RLVR provides outcome-level feedback and RISE’s extrapolated teacher supplies per-token distillation signals, and the teacher is refreshed every iteration as the model improves.
AI.result: Across a range of tasks—mathematical reasoning, multi-domain STEM benchmarks, code generation, and multi-turn agentic tasks—RISE achieves better performance than using RLVR alone and also outperforms standard on-policy self-distillation baselines in all evaluated settings.
AI.conclusion: RISE effectively fuses RLVR with on-policy distillation by using self-extrapolation along the training trajectory to create a continually improving teacher, eliminating the need for external teachers or privileged conditioning while turning sparse rewards into dense supervision. This recursive distillation loop leads to consistently stronger models across diverse reasoning and generation tasks.

title: LLM-Driven Algorithm Design for Quantum Circuit Synthesis based on Binary Decision Diagrams
summary: Quantum circuits are central to implementing quantum algorithms on quantum devices, where quantum gates must be reversible. Many quantum algorithms rely on Boolean functions, which must therefore be implemented reversibly within quantum circuits. Reversible circuit synthesis provides a way to translate such Boolean functions into reversible circuits. Binary decision diagrams (BDDs) offer a scalable approach to this task, but the resulting BDDs and circuits depend heavily on variable ordering. Existing ordering heuristics commonly minimize BDD size because it is closely tied to the circuit size. However, BDD size is an imperfect proxy for the quantum cost of the synthesized circuit (QCC). We propose \texttt{QuantumEvo}, an evolutionary framework that uses an LLM as a heuristic generator for QCC-aware BDD variable ordering. Instead of predicting orderings directly, \texttt{QuantumEvo} searches over ordering heuristics initialized from multiple heuristic families. Candidate heuristics directly manipulate variable orderings using standard BDD operations and are selected by downstream QCC. The discovered heuristic, HGA-QE, modifies the sifting step inside a genetic algorithm so that the procedure is better aligned with QCC. Across the benchmark set, HGA-QE achieves a 70.9\% tie-or-win rate against the per-function best baseline and is strictly best on 13.5\% of the functions. The results demonstrate broadly competitive QCC performance, with HGA-QE showing a clearer relative advantage in strict wins on the two benchmark suites drawn from sources different from the data used for heuristic discovery.

AI.tldr: An evolutionary framework, QuantumEvo, uses an LLM to generate BDD variable-ordering heuristics optimized for quantum circuit cost rather than just BDD size, yielding a new heuristic (HGA-QE) that improves or matches state-of-the-art performance on many benchmarks.
AI.motivation: In quantum computing, Boolean functions need to be implemented as reversible quantum circuits. Binary decision diagrams (BDDs) are a scalable tool for reversible circuit synthesis, but the efficiency of the resulting quantum circuit depends critically on the ordering of variables in the BDD. Existing heuristics target minimizing BDD size, assuming it correlates with the quantum cost of the final circuit (QCC), but this correlation is imperfect. There is a need for variable-ordering strategies that explicitly optimize the actual quantum cost of synthesized circuits rather than relying on BDD size as an indirect proxy.
AI.method: The paper introduces QuantumEvo, an evolutionary search framework that leverages a large language model (LLM) to generate and refine heuristics for BDD variable ordering. Instead of directly predicting specific orderings for each function, QuantumEvo searches over heuristic families, initializing them from diverse heuristic seeds. Candidate heuristics operate by manipulating variable orders with standard BDD operations and are evaluated based on the quantum cost of the circuits synthesized from the resulting BDDs. Through this process, the framework discovers HGA-QE, a heuristic that modifies the sifting procedure within a genetic algorithm to better align ordering decisions with quantum cost metrics.
AI.result: The discovered heuristic HGA-QE demonstrates strong empirical performance on benchmark suites. It achieves a 70.9% tie-or-win rate compared to the best existing baseline heuristic per function, and it is strictly best (i.e., strictly lower QCC) on 13.5% of the benchmark functions. Its relative advantage in strict wins is more pronounced on two benchmark suites originating from sources different from those used for heuristic discovery, suggesting good generalization and reduced overfitting to the training data.
AI.conclusion: QuantumEvo shows that LLM-guided evolutionary search over variable-ordering heuristics can yield BDD-based reversible circuit synthesis methods that are better aligned with quantum cost than traditional BDD-size-focused heuristics. The resulting heuristic, HGA-QE, is broadly competitive and often superior to existing baselines, particularly on out-of-distribution benchmark sets, indicating that directly optimizing for QCC is a promising direction for designing practical synthesis heuristics for quantum circuits.

title: Who Should Grade My Work? Student Perspectives on Transparent AI-Assisted Writing Assessment in Higher Education
summary: The integration of GenAI tools into higher education assessment raises important questions about how students understand, interpret, and respond to AI-mediated evaluation. As instructors increasingly explore AI tools for providing feedback, prior research has examined whether GenAI-generated feedback improves writing performance and how students perceive its usefulness; comparatively little is known, however, about how students interpret such evaluation when they are explicitly informed that an AI system, rather than a human instructor, produced the feedback and the score. This study reports findings from a qualitative pedagogical inquiry conducted in an undergraduate technical communication course for computing students at a Saudi public university. Thirteen male undergraduate computing students completed an in-class handwritten writing task; the scanned submissions were evaluated by ChatGPT using a rubric-based prompt aligned with the task objectives. Students were then explicitly informed that ChatGPT had generated the score and feedback and were invited to reflect on the evaluation in writing. Inductive thematic analysis of these reflections identified four themes: perceived usefulness of feedback; awareness of AI's contextual and pedagogical limitations; conditional trust, distinguishing feedback utility from evaluative authority; and reflection on the institutional and pedagogical role of the human instructor. Participants accepted GenAI feedback as useful for surface-level revision but consistently positioned the human instructor as the appropriate authority over grading decisions. The study identifies this as a distinction between feedback utility and evaluative authority, two judgments that students treat as analytically separate rather than as opposite ends of a single approval scale...

AI.tldr: Explores how students perceive and interpret AI‑generated assessment when clearly told it comes from ChatGPT.
AI.motivation: GenAI tools are increasingly used for giving feedback and even grading in higher education, but most work focuses on whether such feedback improves performance or is seen as useful. Much less is known about how students interpret and position AI feedback and scores when they explicitly know that an AI, not a human, is the evaluator. Understanding this is important for responsible assessment design and role allocation between humans and AI.
AI.method: Qualitative pedagogical inquiry in an undergraduate technical communication course for computing students at a Saudi public university. Thirteen male computing students completed an in‑class handwritten writing task; their scanned work was scored by ChatGPT via a rubric-based prompt aligned with course objectives. Students were then told that ChatGPT produced the score and feedback and asked to write reflections on this evaluation. The researchers conducted inductive thematic analysis of these written reflections.
AI.result: Thematic analysis revealed four main themes: (1) students saw GenAI feedback as useful, mainly for surface-level revision; (2) they were aware of AI’s contextual and pedagogical limitations; (3) they expressed conditional trust—separating the practical utility of feedback from trusting AI as a grading authority; and (4) they reflected on and reaffirmed the institutional and pedagogical role of the human instructor in assessment. Overall, students accepted AI feedback but were reluctant to grant it full evaluative authority.
AI.conclusion: Students distinguish between the usefulness of AI feedback and the legitimacy of AI as a grading authority, treating these as two separate judgments rather than points on a single approval continuum. While they welcome GenAI for low‑level feedback and revision support, they still see human instructors as the appropriate final arbiters of grades and high‑stakes evaluation. This has implications for designing AI‑mediated assessment that leverages feedback utility without displacing human evaluative authority.

title: CUA-Universe: A Scalable and Dynamic Environment for Hybrid GUI+CLI Agents
summary: Computer-use agents have advanced on benchmarks like OSWorld and AndroidWorld, but still act mostly through the GUI, often producing inefficient trajectories. Real-world computer work is hybrid, combining visual-state inspection with precise, high-throughput command-line operations, so capable agents must coordinate both modalities over shared application state. Yet scalable hybrid environments remain scarce because supporting both GUI and CLI over real applications typically requires substantial manual engineering for each application. Existing agents also struggle to use the two interfaces complementarily: CLI-native agents lack visual perception for tasks involving interface state or layout, while GUI-native agents are inefficient for operations better executed through commands. We introduce CUA-Universe, a scalable environment-to-data pipeline that turns real desktop software into hybrid GUI+CLI environments. App-Forge adapts applications into reproducible VMs and command-line surfaces it discovers, wraps, or generates, scaling to 16 applications; Task-Weave synthesizes diverse hybrid tasks of controllable difficulty from reusable operations over seed files; and Path-Steer steers rollouts along efficient hybrid paths and harvests verified trajectories for post-training. Training on this data shifts behavior from inefficient GUI interaction and brittle CLI scripting toward effective GUI+CLI orchestration. Our 9B model improves both success and efficiency on CUA-Verse (Score +39.3 pts; -37% steps, -60% tokens), OSWorld (SR +16.8 pts; -57% steps, -44% tokens), and OSWorld-MCP (Score +7.84 pts; -27% steps, -30% tokens). CUA-Universe provides a scalable path toward more capable and efficient computer-use agents.

AI.tldr: The paper presents CUA-Universe, a scalable framework that turns real desktop software into hybrid GUI+CLI environments and uses them to train computer-use agents that efficiently coordinate graphical and command-line interactions, yielding large gains in success and efficiency on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current computer-use agents mostly operate through GUIs even though real-world computer work is hybrid, combining graphical state inspection with fast, precise command-line operations. There is a lack of scalable environments that expose both GUI and CLI over real applications without heavy per-app engineering. Existing GUI-centric agents are inefficient for tasks better suited to CLI, while CLI-centric agents lack visual perception and struggle with tasks involving layout and interface state. The authors want to enable and study agents that can orchestrate GUI and CLI complementarily over shared application state.
AI.method: They build CUA-Universe, an environment-to-data pipeline that converts real desktop software into hybrid GUI+CLI environments. It has three components: (1) App-Forge, which adapts applications into reproducible VMs and automatically discovers, wraps, or generates command-line interfaces, scaling to 16 apps; (2) Task-Weave, which programmatically synthesizes diverse hybrid tasks of controllable difficulty using reusable operations on seed files; and (3) Path-Steer, which guides agent rollouts along efficient hybrid trajectories and collects verified trajectories for post-training. They then train a 9B-parameter model on this hybrid data and evaluate it on CUA-Verse, OSWorld, and OSWorld-MCP.
AI.result: Training on CUA-Universe data changes agent behavior away from inefficient, purely GUI-based interaction and brittle, purely CLI-based scripting, toward coordinated GUI+CLI use. The 9B model achieves substantial gains in both task success and interaction efficiency: on CUA-Verse, the score increases by 39.3 points with 37% fewer steps and 60% fewer tokens; on OSWorld, success rate improves by 16.8 points with 57% fewer steps and 44% fewer tokens; and on OSWorld-MCP, the score rises by 7.84 points with 27% fewer steps and 30% fewer tokens.
AI.conclusion: CUA-Universe offers a scalable way to turn real desktop software into hybrid GUI+CLI environments and to generate data that teaches agents to orchestrate both modalities effectively. The resulting agents are more capable and efficient across several benchmarks, suggesting that hybrid GUI+CLI training is a promising direction for advancing general-purpose computer-use agents.

title: Molecular Déjà Vu: Digit-Level Retrieval of Published Values in Frontier Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated on molecular property benchmarks, but accuracy cannot distinguish a model that predicts a property from one that retrieves a published number. We audit 22 frontier models on 12 regression benchmarks for verbatim retrieval and find that it is widespread but relatively benchmark-specific: on five datasets more than $50\%$ of the LLMs show verbatim retrieval, while on the remaining datasets it appears only in isolated cells. We run our experiments at two reasoning levels and find that reasoning changes retrieval. The same experiments, on the same molecules and with the same prompt, are flagged $89\%$ more often at the higher reasoning level than at the lowest one. Finally, we test a way to interrupt retrieval in our most contaminated cases, and find that the strongest models in some cases still recognise a combination of transformed SMILES strings and original labels. Furthermore, suppressing retrieval moves the prediction errors of the different models closer together in relative terms, while their differing use of verbatim retrieval spreads them apart. This indicates that the general predictive capability of an LLM is not determined solely by the amount of memorised values. This work provides an overview of the amount and depth of verbatim retrieval in molecular regression benchmarks using LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper audits large language models on molecular property prediction benchmarks to measure how often they retrieve memorized values instead of truly predicting, and analyzes how reasoning level and retrieval suppression affect performance.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used and evaluated for molecular property prediction, simple accuracy scores cannot distinguish genuine predictive reasoning from mere memorization and verbatim retrieval of known property values from training data or literature. This undermines fair model comparison and trust in their scientific utility, especially if some benchmarks are heavily contaminated by memorized entries.
AI.method: The authors systematically audit 22 state-of-the-art LLMs across 12 molecular regression benchmarks for signs of verbatim retrieval. They look for exact matches between model outputs and published property values, study how this varies per dataset, and run experiments at two levels of chain-of-thought reasoning to see how reasoning affects retrieval frequency. They also design and test a retrieval-interruption strategy by transforming SMILES representations and labels to disrupt direct lookup and then measure how models behave under these transformations, including error distributions across models.
AI.result: Verbatim retrieval is common but uneven across benchmarks: on five datasets, more than half of the models show substantial verbatim retrieval, whereas on the remaining datasets retrieval appears only sporadically. Increasing the reasoning level leads to substantially more retrieval, with the same molecules and prompts being flagged 89% more often at higher reasoning levels. Even with retrieval-interruption techniques (e.g., transformed SMILES and modified labels), strong models can still recognize and use underlying associations. When retrieval is suppressed, performance differences between models shrink in relative error, suggesting that differences previously observed were partly driven by unequal reliance on memorized values rather than genuine predictive ability.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that many LLMs rely significantly on verbatim retrieval for molecular regression benchmarks, and that this dependence is dataset- and reasoning-level-specific. However, because model performance converges when retrieval is disrupted, the authors conclude that general predictive capability is not simply a function of memorized property values. Their work highlights the need to explicitly audit and control for retrieval when evaluating LLMs on scientific prediction tasks, and provides a first systematic picture of retrieval depth in molecular property benchmarks.

title: Necessary or Sufficient? Evaluating LLM Explanations With Behavioural Evidence
summary: LLM decision components that can operate within agent workflows often produce action-relevant recommendations or judgements together with explanations. Operators may use the named factors to monitor a system, diagnose errors, or decide when to escalate an output. Such use assumes that the explanations agree with the component's observable decision behaviour. We test two interpretations of the named factors: necessity, meaning that changing a factor would change the output, and sufficiency, meaning that retaining it while removing other changeable information would preserve the output. We evaluate these interpretations in two synthetic use cases: recommending advisors to clients and judging prompts for harmfulness or risk. Models return an output and the top three factors that most influenced it. Controlled black-box interventions estimate a necessity score for each factor by measuring how often changing it changes the output, and a sufficiency score by measuring how often retaining it preserves the output. Across eight models from the Claude, GPT, and Gemini families, the mean Spearman correlations between the cited ranking and the necessity and sufficiency scores are 0.349 and 0.354 for advisor recommendation, and 0.431 and 0.580 for prompt monitoring. Furthermore, an uncited factor scores above the lowest-scoring cited factor in 57.6% of advisor responses under necessity and 58.1% under sufficiency; the corresponding prompt-monitoring rates are 25.8% and 8.9%. The cited top three contain useful information but do not reliably identify the three factors with the strongest measured influence under necessity or sufficiency. The framework provides a black-box reliability check for explanations used in agent oversight while remaining scoped to individual LLM decisions.

AI.tldr: They test whether the factors LLMs cite as influencing a decision actually line up with what truly drives the model’s outputs, and find only moderate alignment.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents often produce decisions plus a short list of ‘key factors’ or explanations, which operators may rely on for monitoring, debugging, and escalation. This practice presumes that the named factors faithfully reflect the model’s internal decision process, but this assumption is largely untested and may be false. The authors aim to rigorously evaluate how well such cited factors correspond to actual decision influence at the level of individual model outputs.
AI.method: The authors conceptualize two influence notions for cited factors: (1) necessity—changing the factor changes the decision; (2) sufficiency—keeping the factor while perturbing other information preserves the decision. In two synthetic tasks (advisor recommendation and harmfulness/risk judgement of prompts), multiple LLMs (Claude, GPT, Gemini families) output both a decision and the ‘top three’ influential factors. Using controlled black-box interventions on inputs, they empirically estimate necessity and sufficiency scores for each potential factor by measuring how often interventions alter or preserve the decision. They then compute correlations (Spearman) between the model-cited importance ranking and these empirical influence scores, and examine how often uncited factors outrank the cited ones under the measured influence metrics.
AI.result: Across eight models, in the advisor recommendation task the mean Spearman correlations between the cited factor ranking and necessity/sufficiency scores are modest (~0.35). For the prompt monitoring task, correlations are higher but still imperfect (~0.43 for necessity and ~0.58 for sufficiency). Additionally, many uncited factors empirically have more influence than at least one of the cited ‘top three’ factors: in advisor recommendation, an uncited factor beats the lowest-ranked cited factor in 57.6% of cases for necessity and 58.1% for sufficiency; in prompt monitoring, the corresponding rates are 25.8% and 8.9%. Thus the cited factors are informative but far from a perfect ranking of true influence.
AI.conclusion: The explanations that LLM components provide—specifically, the ‘top factors’ said to drive a decision—partly but unreliably track true decision influence as measured via necessity and sufficiency. While these factors contain useful information, they should not be trusted as faithful attributions of what most influenced the decision. The authors propose their intervention-based, per-decision framework as a practical, black-box reliability check for explanation quality in agent oversight pipelines, helping to assess whether explanations are dependable enough for monitoring and escalation decisions.

title: A Deep Generative Model for Synthesizing Labeled Wireless Signals
summary: Wireless signals with position-related labels are pivotal for both performance evaluation and model training in the realm of wireless sensing. However, acquiring real-world datasets is often challenged by significant measurement and labeling costs. Traditional methods for synthesizing labeled wireless signals typically rely on environmental models, leading to extensive hyper-parameter tuning and inadequate realism for comprehensive model training purposes. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel deep learning (DL)-based method, namely Inter-Instance Generative Adversarial Networks (IIns-GAN), to generate realistic labeled wireless signals. The generated signals are particularly adaptive to different environment scenarios and well-suited for various model training tasks, including distance estimation and environment identification. We have conducted extensive experiments on public Ultra-Wideband (UWB) datasets to evaluate the realism and utility of the generated signals. The results demonstrate that the signals generated by IIns-GAN mirror the physical characteristics of real-world measurements, and significantly contribute to the improvement of model training in diverse wireless sensing tasks.

AI.tldr: Proposes IIns-GAN, a GAN-based method to generate realistic, labeled wireless signals for training and evaluating wireless sensing models, reducing data collection and labeling costs while improving performance.
AI.motivation: Wireless sensing models need large amounts of labeled, position-related wireless signal data (e.g., for distance estimation and environment identification). Collecting such real-world datasets is expensive and time-consuming due to measurement and labeling costs. Existing synthetic data approaches depend on hand-crafted environmental models and heavy hyper-parameter tuning, often failing to capture the full realism and diversity of real wireless environments, which limits their effectiveness for training robust models.
AI.method: Introduce Inter-Instance Generative Adversarial Networks (IIns-GAN), a deep learning-based generative model designed to produce realistic wireless signals paired with position-related labels. Instead of relying on explicit physical or environmental models, IIns-GAN learns directly from real datasets, capturing complex dependencies between signals, positions, and environment types. The framework is evaluated on public Ultra-Wideband (UWB) datasets, and the generated signals are then used to train downstream models for tasks such as distance estimation and environment identification. Performance and realism are assessed by comparing models trained on synthetic versus real data and by examining signal characteristics against physical expectations.
AI.result: Experiments on public UWB datasets show that IIns-GAN can generate signals whose statistical and physical characteristics closely resemble those of real-world measurements. When these generated signals are used for training, downstream models for distance estimation and environment identification achieve improved performance compared to using traditional synthetic data, and can approach or enhance performance obtained from real data alone.
AI.conclusion: IIns-GAN effectively addresses the limitations of traditional simulation-based approaches for labeled wireless signal generation by learning realistic signal–label relationships from data. The method produces high-fidelity, labeled synthetic signals that are adaptable to various environments and beneficial for multiple wireless sensing tasks, reducing dependence on costly real-world data collection and labeling while improving model training quality.
